column2: E.G.H.]] (1945 – 10 June 2012) was a Kenyan politician, businessman and American- and British-trained [[economist]], mathematician and development policy thinker.

column1: As a [[mathematician]], Saitoti served as head of the Mathematics Department at the [[University of Nairobi]], pioneered the founding of the [[African Mathematical Union]] and served as its vice-president from 1976 to 1979.
As an economist, Saitoti served as the Executive Chairman of the [[World Bank]] and the [[International Monetary Fund
column2: International Monetary Fund (IMF)]] in 1990–91, and as President of the [[African, Caribbean and Pacific Group of States
column3: African Caribbean and Pacific (ACP)]] Group of States in 1999–2000, at the crucial phase of re-negotiating the new development partnership agreement to replace the expired [[Lomé Convention]] between the ACP bloc and the [[European Union]] (EU). His book ''The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa''<ref>{{Cite book
column5: title=The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa
column11: language=en}}</ref> influenced practical policy directions on an array of areas during the turbulent 1980s and 1990s.

column1: Saitoti joined politics as a nominated Member of Parliament and Minister for Finance in 1983, rising to become Kenya's [[Vice-President of Kenya
column2: longest-serving Vice-President]], a proficient Minister for education, Internal Security and Provincial Administration and Foreign Affairs. Few recognise him as a ""reformist"",[[Category:All articles with unsourced statements]][[Category:Articles with unsourced statements from September 2012]]<sup class=""noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact"" style=""white-space:nowrap;"">[<i>[[Wikipedia:Citation needed
column3: citation needed]]] but his recommendations as the Chair of the KANU Review Committee, popularly known as the ""Saitoti Committee"" in 1990–91, opened KANU to internal changes and set the stage for the repeal of [[Constitutional Reforms in Kenya
column4: Section 2A]] and Kenya's return to pluralist democracy. Saitoti left KANU and joined the opposition, becoming a kingpin figure in the negotiations that led to the ""[[National Rainbow Coalition
column5: NARC Revolution]]"" in 2002. As Minister for Internal Security and Provincial Administration, Acting Minister for Foreign Affairs and key member of the National Security Advisory Committee (NSAC), he later worked closely with the national Ministry of Defense to see through the [[Operation Linda Nchi]] against the [[Al-Shabaab insurgent group]]. In addition, rival factions had for decades invoked the infamous [[Goldenberg scandal
column6: Goldenberg]] fraud to knock Saitoti out of politics, but the legal courts cleared him of the scandal in July 2006.<ref>{{Cite news
column11: language=en-GB}}</ref> Saitoti's dual heritage as a Maasai with Kikuyu family members predisposed him to a pan-Kenyan vision, but also denied him a strong ethnic base unlike his competitors. Saitoti was running as a candidate to succeed President [[Mwai Kibaki]] when he died in a helicopter crash in 2012.

column1: George Saitoti attended Ololua Primary School, [[Kajiado]] where he acquired his basic education in the 1950s. Between 1960 and 1963, he secured a place at [[Mang'u High School]] in [[Thika]] where he attained his high school education. He joined the ranks of Mang'u High School's highly decorated alumni including Kenya's third President, Mwai Kibaki, former Vice-President [[Moody Awori]], Catholic Archbishop Ndingi Mwana-a-Nzeki, the late Environment Minister [[John Michuki]], the late Trade Unionist and former Minister for Justice and Constitutional Affairs, [[Tom Mboya]], and late Cardinal [[Maurice Michael Otunga]].

Saitoti was one of the recipients of [[the Kennedy Airlift]] scholarships in 1963 at the age of 18.<ref name=""ReferenceA"">Airlift to America. How Barack Obama Sr., John F. Kennedy, Tom Mboya, and 800 East African Students Changed Their World and Ours. By Tom Shachtman. St. Martin's Press. 2009</ref> This was a scholarship program started by [[Tom Mboya]] and William X. Scheinmann and supported by the [[John F. Kennedy]] foundation and the African American Students Association to address the educational needs of newly independent Kenya. Through this program, hundreds of East Africans studied in the [[United States of America]] and [[Canada]].<ref name=""ReferenceA""/> Saitoti studied at [[Brandeis University]] between 1963 and 1967 where he was a mathematician. During his time there, he was on the [[Wien Scholarship]], specialising in Mathematics and Economics.<ref name=""Wien_profile"">{{cite web
column7: archive-date=28 May 2010}}</ref> His colleagues at the time remember that he enjoyed spending time in Cholmondeleys (the coffeehouse in the Castle) and excelled at high jump, ranking as one of the best in [[New England]].<ref name=""Wien_profile""/> In 1988, Saitoti received the first Brandeis Alumni Achievement Award, the highest honour the university bestows upon its graduates.<ref name=""Wien_profile""/><ref>[http://alumni.brandeis.edu/web/aassociation/awards/alumni_achievement_award.html Alumni Association Awards] {{webarchive

column1: Saitoti later moved to the [[United Kingdom]] where he acquired a Master of Science (MSc) degree in mathematics from the [[University of Sussex]], Brighton. He enrolled for his doctoral studies at the [[University of Warwick]] where he acquired his PhD in mathematics in 1972; writing his dissertation under the supervision of professor Luke Hodgkin in the area of algebraic topology under the topic: ''Mod-2 K-Theory of the Second Iterated Loop Space on a Sphere.''<ref name=""math.buffalo"">[http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/Africa-today/%20AllAfricanDoctorates.html Africa Mathematics Union], Africa Doctorates in Mathematics (1995).</ref>

Upon his graduation, Saitoti returned to [[Kenya]] in 1972, commencing a career as a Mathematics lecturer at the [[University of Nairobi]]. One of his contributions was the institutionalisation of Mathematics as a discipline in Africa. During the first Pan-African Conference of Mathematicians held in [[Rabat]], Morocco, in 1976, Saitoti was involved in the creation of the African Mathematical Union (AMU).<ref>{{Cite web
column5: access-date=2017-11-16}}</ref> He was elected the AMU's vice-president, a post which he held on up to 1979.<ref name=""math.buffalo"" /> By 1983, Saitoti's academic career was on the rise as associate professor and Head of the Mathematics Department.

column1: Outside the academy, Saitoti received several public appointments. On 3 November 1972, the [[List of ministers of Kenya#Ministry of Labour and Human Resource Development
column2: Minister of Labour]] appointed him as the chairman of the Agricultural Wages Council (AWC).<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=AJ2pr0bxaZcC& ''Kenya Gazette'' (Republic of Kenya)], 17 November 1972.</ref> On 4 September 1979, the [[List of ministers of Kenya#Ministry of Tourism
column3: Minister for Tourism and Wildlife]], John Ogutu, also appointed him as a committee member of the Natural Sciences Advisory Research Committee (TNSARC) chaired by professor S. O. Wandiga.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=MwTc8E3OkR8C&pg=PA1167&dq=Kenya+Gazette+4+Sep+1979+saitoti ''Kenya Gazette'' (Republic of Kenya)], 14 September 1979.</ref> In September 1983, he was appointed chairperson of the board of directors for the [[Rift Valley Institute of Science and Technology]].<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=E3jJJ5zdFx8C&pg=PA1296&dq=saitoti ''Kenya Gazette'' (Republic of Kenya)], 23 September 1983.</ref> He also served in other public capacities as chairman of [[Mumias Sugar Company]] and the [[Kenya Commercial Bank]].

column1: Top decision-makers in government had recognised Saitoti as a policy thinker and technocrat, of whom the [[Kenya African National Union
column2: KANU]] desperately needed to fix its institutions, politics and the economy. His seminal book, ''The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa'' was widely praised by leading officials as providing practical policy proposals to deal with the various challenges facing Kenya and Africa.<ref name=""bare_url"">[https://books.google.com/books?id=A-C1AAAAIAAJ ''The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa'']</ref>

column1: The book drew from Saitoti's experience as a seasoned scholar, consultant and experienced policy-maker/thinker, presenting a rigorous and multidisciplinary analysis of strategies for poverty alleviation, sustainable development, poverty reduction, combating HIV/AIDS and [[Diplomacy
column2: peace diplomacy]]. Saitoti also emphasised the importance of institutional reforms and sound public policies to sustainable economic growth in Africa.<ref>Saitoti, G. (2002). ''The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa''. Ashgate Publishers Limited.</ref>

column1: Long before joining mainstream politics, Saitoti had a stint in the legislative duties. From 1974 to 1977, he represented Kenya in the defunct (since-revived) [[East African Community]] as a member of the [[East African Legislative Assembly]].<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Saitoti, the man Kenyans never got to understand
President Daniel arap Moi]] nominated Saitoti as a member of parliament and subsequently appointed him to the Cabinet as Minister for Finance. He held the position until 1989.<ref>{{usurped
column3: 1=[https://archive.today/20120907105134/http://www.marsgroupkenya.org/multimedia/cache/cache_c21f969b5f03d33d43e04f8f136e7682_c012b78a927d02a4ff1a3bc41f75eb15 ""Ruto now takes over Home Affairs docket""]}}, ''The People Daily'' (October 2002).</ref> During the [[1988 Kenyan general election
column4: 1988 general elections]], Saitoti entered competitive politics and won the [[Kajiado North Constituency
column5: Kajiado North]] parliamentary seat that was previously held by [[Kajiado North Constituency
column6: Philip Odupoy]]. Prior to the tenure of Adupoy and Saitoti, the Kajiado North multi-ethnic constituency was held by the popular politician, [[Kajiado North Constituency
column7: John Keen]], another half-Maasai who champion a nationalist vision and worked over the years to ensure the advancement of his mother's people.<ref>[[Kajiado North Constituency

column1: For more than 25 years, professor George Saitoti has represented Kajiado North since 1988, recapturing the seat in consecutive elections in 1992, 1997, 2002 and 2007. Building on John Keen's legacy of a cosmopolitan constituency, Saitoti transformed Kajiado North into Kenya's most ethnically integrated multi-ethnic legislative area that also provided a safe haven to Kenyans, forcibly displaced by the 1991–2008 cycles of ethnic violence in neighbouring areas.<ref name=Wachira>Wachira, Charles, [http://allafrica.com/stories/201202132318.html ""Kenya: Saitoti—the Dark Horse""], ''The Star'' (Nairobi), 11 February 2012. AllAfrica.</ref>

The area is also ranked among the top ten wealthiest, economically dynamic and fastest growing regions in Kenya. According to figures released by the Government of Kenya in 2009, Kajiado North has had an average poverty index of 10.66 per cent for the last three years, making it one of the richest constituencies in Kenya (see table 1).<ref>Opiyo, P., {{usurped
column2: 1=[https://archive.today/20120903145615/http://www.marsgroupkenya.org/multimedia/?StoryID=308484 ""Now We Know Whose Constituency Is Poorest""]}} (2010).</ref>
1988 General Election]], [[President Moi]] appointed Saitoti as Kenya's sixth vice-president. Saitoti became Kenya's longest sitting vice-president serving for 13 years under [[President Moi
column3: President Daniel arap Moi]] between May 1989 and January 1998 and again between April 1999 and August 2002 (see table 2).<ref>Rashid, I., [http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/commentaries/InsidePage.php?id=2000034729&cid=15& ""Will Kibaki be the only President not to Sack VP?""] {{webarchive
column5: date=23 May 2011 }} (2011).</ref> At the same time, he served as Minister for Finance.

column1: In 1990–1991, Saitoti was the Executive Chairman of the [[World Bank]] and the [[International Monetary Fund]] (IMF).[[Category:All articles with unsourced statements]][[Category:Articles with unsourced statements from May 2020]]<sup class=""noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact"" style=""white-space:nowrap;"">[<i>[[Wikipedia:Citation needed
column2: citation needed]]] In 1999–2000, Saitoti also served as president of the [[African, Caribbean and Pacific Group of States]], becoming instrumental in helping negotiate a new development partnership agreement to succeed the previous Lomè Convention that expired in February 2000 between the ACP and the [[European Union]].[http://intelligencebriefs.com/?p=1713 ""ICC Kenya Cases Latest Development And The George Saitoti Presidency Factor""], Intelligence News, 22 February 2012.

column1: The hallmarks of Saitoti tenure as vice-president were efficiency, sobriety and loyalty as President Moi's most trusted lieutenant. Even when President Moi dithered in naming a new deputy after the 1997 elections, Saitoti was still his favoured choice 14 months down the line.<ref name=Chronicle>[http://nairobichronicle.wordpress.com/2009/03/01/saitotis-elusive-presidency/ ""Saitoti's Elusive Presidency""], ''Nairobi Chronicle'' (2009).</ref> The same traits of efficiency, patience and loyalty would make him one of President [[Mwai Kibaki
When Saitoti was appointed vice-president on 1 May 1989, [[Kenya African National Union
column2: KANU]] was back-pedaling on re-democratizing the country. At the same time, the party was fragmented over the succession divide between a sit-tight ""KANU-A"" and a more pro-change ""KANU-B"" led by Saitoti. The new vice-president was, therefore, compelled to walk the tightrope between being the face of change in the ruling party and remaining loyal to his principal who, after re-election as president in 1988, had amended the constitution to increase his power to dismiss judges and widened police powers.

column1: On New Year's Day 1990, the vocal cleric Rev. Timothy Njoya called on all Africans to demand a multiparty system of government. Following the [[Saba Saba Day
column2: Saba Saba riots]] on 7 July 1990, [[President Moi]] announced the formation of the KANU Review Committee under the chairmanship of Prof George Saitoti, popularly known as ''the Saitoti Committee''.<ref name=""The Rise of a Party-State in Kenya"">{{Cite web
column4: title=The Rise of a Party-State in Kenya

column1: The Saitoti Review Committee was mandated to investigate the party's internal electoral and disciplinary conduct.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Democratization and Law Reform in Kenya (Wanjala Smokin) – African information centre
column6: access-date=2018-06-12}}</ref> The committee traversed the country collecting people's opinions on the party, astounding foe, friend and critics alike and offering a rare forum for direct criticism and outbursts.<ref>The Report of the KANU Review Committee Presented to the President by George Saitoti, October 1990. Nairobi, Government Printer.</ref>

column1: In January 1991, KANU's executive committee adopted the recommendation by George Saitoti, that critics of the party cease being expelled but suspended for one or two years.<ref>{{Cite book
The recommendations of the report were open for debate during the [[Kenya African National Union
column2: National Delegates Conference]] at Karasani in [[Nairobi]]. President Moi backed the adoption and implementation of the report in ''toto'', against what many speakers at the conference had expected. This opened the reforms gates, eventually setting the stage for the [[Constitutional Reforms in Kenya
column3: repeal of Section 2A]] in 1991 that returned Kenya to back to a multiparty system of government.<ref>Steeves, J., ""Re-Democratization in Kenya: 'Unbounded Politics' and the Political Trajectory Towards National Elections"", in D. Pal S. Ahuluwalia, Paul F. Lursey – Bray, ''The Post Colonial Condition: Contemporary Politics in Africa''.</ref> The Saitoti Review Committee thrust the party on the reform path, but also widened internal ideological schisms between ""KANU-A"" conservatives and ""KANU-B"" pro-reformers over the Moi succession question.<ref>Throup, D., and Hornsby C., ''Multi-Party Politics in Kenya''. Nairobi: East African Education Publishers, 1998.</ref>

column1: Saitoti was in the eye of a nasty succession storm that rocked [[Kenya African National Union
column2: KANU]] before and after the [[1997 Kenyan general election
column3: 1997 elections]]. Maasai purists led by Minister [[William Ole Ntimama]] and senior [[Maasai people
column4: Maasai elders]] 're-Kikuyunized' Saitoti's dual ancestry, amplifying his [[Gikuyu language
column5: Kikuyu]] family linkages as a scheme to weaken his political base and to challenge his status as a Maasai elder.

column1: Despite his steadfast loyalty to KANU and President Moi, Saitoti was frequently ignored, humiliated and frustrated by the party and its top echelons. Around the same time [[Robert Ouko (politician)
column2: Foreign Affairs Minister Robert Ouko]] was murdered in February 1990, Saitoti claims that attempts were made on his life.<ref>Ndegwa, A., [http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/archives/InsidePage.php?id=2000025251&cid=4 ""Saitoti: When Ouko was killed, Someone wanted me dead""]{{dead link
column5: fix-attempted=yes }}, ''Standard'', 22 October 2012.</ref> After the [[1997 Kenyan general election
column6: 1997 general elections]], he was dropped as vice-president, although no replacement was appointed. Even as President Moi reappointed him in April 1999, on the roadside in Limuru, Kiambu he made a scathing remark to the effect that: ""I've given back Prof Saitoti the seat of Vice-President, hopefully now your sufurias (pots) will be full of food.""<ref name=Wachira /> Months before the [[2002 Kenya general election
column7: general elections of 2002]], Saitoti's name was deleted from the list of KANU delegates and his ascendancy to the presidency blocked by 'unknown' party members.<ref>Ilado P., and G. Peterson, [http://www.the-star.co.ke/national/national/47122-prof-saitoti-speaks-out ""Prof Saitoti Speaks Out""] {{webarchive

column1: On 18 March 2002, when KANU held its national delegates conference at the [[Moi International Sports Centre
column2: Kasarani sports complex]], the move to block Saitoti from the succession game was manifest.<ref>Throup D., and Hornsby C., Multi-Party Politics in Kenya. Nairobi: East African Education Publishers 1998.</ref> The meeting amended the party constitution to allow for the merger between [[Kenya African National Union
column5: National Development Party (NDP)]] to create the [[Constitutional Reforms in Kenya
column6: New KANU""]]. But it also introduced four new positions of party vice-chairmen primarily to water down Saitoti's position as vice-president and Moi's most likely successor as president.<ref>Karega, M., 2003, [http://web.peacelink.it/wajibu/18_issue/p3.html ""Polarisation of politics in Kenya along Ethnic Lines""], ''Wajibu'', vol.18, no.1- 2, pp. 3–16.</ref>

column1: It was clear that Moi did not even want him as one of the four vice-chairmen posts reserved for [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], [[Kalonzo Musyoka]], [[Ganze Constituency
column2: Katana Ngala]] and [[Musalia Mudavadi]]. Moi told Saitoti to his face that he was not ""presidential material"".<ref name=Chronicle /> As a ""Maasai-Kikuyu,"" Saitoti lacked the ethnic numbers he needed in the political horse-trading in Moi's power game. Instead, Moi finger-pointed as his heir [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], perceived to have a large ethnic base as a pure-bred Kikuyu with the [[Jomo Kenyatta

column1: Saitoti gracefully bowed out of the race, living to fight another day, but not without his famous line: ''There comes a time when the nation is much more important than an individual''.<ref>Khamisi, J., ''The Politics of Betrayal: Diary of a Kenyan Legislator'', Trafford Publishing, 2011.</ref><ref>[http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/archives/InsidePage.php?id=2000003044&cid=4 “There comes a time when the nation is much more important than an individual”]{{dead link

But the KANU-NDP marriage came to a tragic end when Moi named Uhuru rather than Raila Odinga as his successor.<ref>[http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/InsidePage.php?id=2000050046&cid=4& KANU-NDP marriage] {{webarchive
column3: date=10 March 2012 }}</ref> In August 2002, Odinga left KANU to defeat Moi's ""use and dump game,""<ref name=""Badejo"">{{cite book
column6: title=Raila Odinga: an Enigma in Kenyan Politics
column8: publisher=Yintab Books}}</ref> and joined a group of KANU rebels"" coalesced around the ""Rainbow Alliance"" lobby that later transformed itself into the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Saitoti also walking out of KANU and became a key LDP figure. In October 2002, LDP joined the National Alliance of Kenya (NAK) of Mwai Kibaki, Charity Ngilu and Wamalwa Kijana to form the National Rainbow Coalition (NARC).<ref name=""Badejo""/> Saitoti became a member of the NARC Summit, the highest organ of the coalition.

column1: When the NARC flag-bearer, [[Mwai Kibaki]], decisively defeated [[Kenya African National Union
column2: KANU]] and [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], Saitoti was appointed to the Ministry of Education. He was the man in charge of implementing NARC's flagship and globally acclaimed free primary education in Kenya.<ref>{{Cite news
column4: title=Kenya: Free primary education brings over 1 million into school

column1: After 2004, as the NARC consensus crumbled, Saitoti left the agitating LDP camp and threw his lot behind President Kibaki.<ref>[https://fpc.state.gov/documents/organization/101803.pdf NARC consensus]</ref> He canvassed for the government-sponsored draft Constitution, which lost to a combined KANU-LDP campaign during the [[2005 Kenyan constitutional referendum
column4: title=VOA Standard English – Polls Show Majority of Kenyans Do Not Favor Draft Constitution
column6: access-date=2018-06-12}}</ref> During the 2007 elections, Saitoti defended his [[Kajiado North Constituency
column7: Kajiado North parliamentary]] seat on the [[Party of National Unity (Kenya)
column8: Party of National Unity (PNU)]] ticket, Kibaki's re-election vehicle, launched three months to the election on 16 September 2007.

column1: The courts ordered a vote recount in [[Kajiado North Constituency
column2: Kajiado North]], but Saitoti beat his closest competitor, Moses Ole Sakuda with close to 20,000 votes.<ref>IREC, 2008. Report of the Independent Review Commission on the General Elections held in Kenya on 27 December 2007.</ref> Saitoti blamed his re-election glitch on intrigues of power by KANU forces within the PNU campaign which underwrote his rivals to knock him out of politics and potentially out of the [[2013 Kenyan presidential election
column3: 2012 Presidential elections]]. But he had remained reticent about it.

column1: [[File:Kenya Minister of State for Provincial Administration & Internal Security (6375911923).jpg
column5: British]] Foreign Office Minister [[Henry Bellingham (Norfolk MP)
column6: Henry Bellingham]] meeting George Saitoti, the Kenyan Minister of State for Provincial Administration & Internal Security in [[London]], 21 November 2011]]

column1: Saitoti's traits of patience, efficiency and loyalty to Kibaki paid off. On 8 January 2008, he was appointed Minister of State for Internal Security and Provincial Administration in the Office of the President, a position previously occupied by a Kibaki confidant, [[John Michuki]].<ref>[http://allafrica.com/stories/200801080673.html ""Kibaki Names Cabinet""], ''The Standard'', 8 January 2008.</ref> Saitoti retained the Internal Security docket even after President Kibaki and Prime Minister [[Raila Odinga]] established the power-sharing government that ended the [[2007-2008 Kenyan crisis
column2: 2008 post-election crisis]]. Between October 2010 and August 2011, Saitoti was appointed Minister for Foreign Affairs on an acting capacity after the incumbent, [[Moses Wetangula]], stepped aside to allow investigations on alleged corruption.<ref>Momanyi, B., [http://69.4.236.48/news/Kenyanews/Saitoti-takes-up-Foreign-Affairs-docket.html ""Saitoti Takes up Foreign Affairs Docket""] {{webarchive

column1: In July 2009, Saitoti was appointed to head a special cabinet sub-committee formed to oversee the affairs of the [[International Criminal Court
column2: International Criminal Court (ICC)]] in Kenya.<ref>Leftie, P., and B. Namunane, [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/-/1056/627744/-/ul1499/-/index.html ""Cabinet Team to Weigh Options""], ''Daily Nation'', 21 July 2009.</ref> Members of this bi-partisan committee include; George Saitoti, [[Mutula Kilonzo]] and [[Moses Wetangula]] (PNU) and [[James Orengo]], [[Otieno Kajwang]] and [[Amason Kingi Jeffah
column3: Amason Kingi]] (ODM). (Following a cabinet reshuffle in April 2012, [[Eugene Wamalwa]] and [[Sam Ongeri
column4: Prof. Sam Ongeri]] have replaced Kilonzo and Wetangula). The role of the sub-Committee as a liaison and co-ordination body between the ICC and the Kenyan government took a center-stage from December 2010 when the [[Luis Moreno Ocampo
column5: ICC Chief Prosecutor, Luis Moreno Ocampo]], indicted six prominent Kenyans for alleged crimes against humanity relating to the [[2007-2008 Kenyan crisis

column1: As the Minister of Internal Security and the chairman of the [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iVfO05CJl4o Cabinet Sub-committee on ICC] on [[YouTube video (identifier)
column2: YouTube]] and security matters, Saitoti is the guarantor of the government's commitment to the ICC process. Arising from this, several analysts have claimed the suspects' fate lie with the sub-committee.<ref>Mahamad Fazul, [http://www.the-star.co.ke/opinions/others/67198-uhuru-ruto-future-is-in-saitotis-hands ""Uhuru, Ruto Future is in Saitoti Hands""] {{webarchive
column4: date=12 September 2012 }}, 16 March 2012.</ref> Saitoti came out strongly criticising the invocation of [[Mwai Kibaki
column5: President Kibaki]] in the ICC debate, calling for sobriety from politicians.<ref>Mwilu Aisha, [https://web.archive.org/web/20120209233344/http://ktnkenya.tv/?id=2000051619 ""Saitoti Defends Kibaki over ICC""]. 7 February 2012.</ref> Saitoti has maintained a legal interpretation on whether the suspects can vie for presidency in the coming elections, stressing that only the constitution can bar or let them free to enter the race.<ref>Ongiri Isaac, [http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/m/news.php?id=2000050443 ""PNU: Cabinet has no power to decide fate of presidential aspirants""], ''The Standard'', 20 January 2012.</ref>

column2: Vice-President]] and Finance Minister at the height of the 1991–1993 [[Goldenberg scandal]]. Even though his own culpability in the fraud has never been established, for decades the [[Goldenberg scandal
column3: Goldenberg]] has become the proverbial [[Sword of Damocles]] used against Saitoti in intra-elite power wars. In early 1999, [[Raila Odinga]] as a presidential contender to succeed Moi as president, sued Saitoti and others over alleged role in the [[Goldenberg scandal]].<ref name=""Badejo""/> Three months after his re-appointment as vice-president on 3 April 1999, [[Otieno Kajwang]]', a Raila ally, moved a private member's motion of no confidence in the vice-president for his alleged role in the [[Goldenberg scandal
column4: Goldenberg fraud]]. Saitoti survived the onslaught.<ref name=""Badejo""/>

column1: The Goldenberg spectre returned to haunt Saitoti in the wake of the fierce political infighting between the LDP/KANU faction and Kibaki supporters in NARC that followed the [[2005 Kenyan constitutional referendum
column2: 2005 referendum]]. On 3 February 2006 a report by the Goldenberg Commission of Inquiry, chaired by Justice [[Samuel Bosire]], recommended that George Saitoti should face criminal charges for his involvement in the Goldenberg scandal.<ref>[https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/4676690.stm ""Moi 'Knew about' Kenya Gold Scam""], BBC News, 3 February 2006.</ref><ref>[http://www.assetrecovery.org/kc/node/c800a8aa-dc00-11dd-8d28-f13739c882dc.0;jsessionid=0613A4AE3F34437A9DD1F3BB1063DB41 Goldenberg Commission of Inquiry] {{webarchive
column4: date=23 September 2015 }}</ref> On 13 February 2006, Saitoti voluntarily stepped aside from his ministerial docket to pave way for investigations into the allegations.<ref>{{Cite web

column1: However, on 31 July 2006, a three-judge bench headed by Justice Joseph Nyamu issued a certiorari order clearing Prof Saitoti of any wrongdoing, expunging his name from the Bosire Commission Report and issuing an order on permanent stay of prosecution against Saitoti.<ref name=""sudanvisiondaily"">[http://www.sudanvisiondaily.com/modules.php?name=News&file=article&sid=14359 ""Saitoti wins 16-year Fight to be Cleared""] {{webarchive
In dismissing the 23 paragraphs of the report, the [[High Court (Kenya)]] bench cited three inter-related errors of commission and omission by the Bosire Commission:

* The inquiry into the Goldenberg fraud had created a pyramid of noticeable bias, discriminatory treatment of evidence, submissions and factual errors that undermined the pursuit of justice and fairness.<ref name=""sudanvisiondaily""/>

* The factual flaws, biased and unprofessional handling of evidence by Inquiry led to wrong findings. The Inquiry's claim that Prof Saitoti illegally approved the 15 per cent ex-gratia payments as additional payment over and above the 20 per cent export compensation allowed at the time under the law were factually wrong. Indeed, the customs refunds, which Saitoti was accused of approving, were actually passed by Parliament.
* Long delay and wrong findings by the Goldenberg inquiry denied Prof. Saitoti any conceivable chance fair trial and justice.

E.G.H.]] (1945 – 10 June 2012) was a Kenyan politician, businessman and American- and British-trained [[economist]], mathematician and development policy thinker.

As a [[mathematician]], Saitoti served as head of the Mathematics Department at the [[University of Nairobi]], pioneered the founding of the [[African Mathematical Union]] and served as its vice-president from 1976 to 1979.

As an economist, Saitoti served as the Executive Chairman of the [[World Bank]] and the [[International Monetary Fund
column116: International Monetary Fund (IMF)]] in 1990–91, and as President of the [[African, Caribbean and Pacific Group of States
column117: African Caribbean and Pacific (ACP)]] Group of States in 1999–2000, at the crucial phase of re-negotiating the new development partnership agreement to replace the expired [[Lomé Convention]] between the ACP bloc and the [[European Union]] (EU). His book \'\'The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa\'\'<ref>{{Cite book
column119: title=The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa
column125: language=en}}</ref> influenced practical policy directions on an array of areas during the turbulent 1980s and 1990s.\n\nSaitoti joined politics as a nominated Member of Parliament and Minister for Finance in 1983, rising to become Kenya\'s [[Vice-President of Kenya
column126: longest-serving Vice-President]], a proficient Minister for education, Internal Security and Provincial Administration and Foreign Affairs. Few recognise him as a ""reformist"",{{citation needed
column127: date=September 2012}} but his recommendations as the Chair of the KANU Review Committee, popularly known as the ""Saitoti Committee"" in 1990–91, opened KANU to internal changes and set the stage for the repeal of [[Constitutional Reforms in Kenya
column128: Section 2A]] and Kenya\'s return to pluralist democracy. Saitoti left KANU and joined the opposition, becoming a kingpin figure in the negotiations that led to the ""[[National Rainbow Coalition
column129: NARC Revolution]]"" in 2002. As Minister for Internal Security and Provincial Administration, Acting Minister for Foreign Affairs and key member of the National Security Advisory Committee (NSAC), he later worked closely with the national Ministry of Defense to see through the [[Operation Linda Nchi]] against the [[Al-Shabaab insurgent group]]. In addition, rival factions had for decades invoked the infamous [[Goldenberg scandal
column130: Goldenberg]] fraud to knock Saitoti out of politics, but the legal courts cleared him of the scandal in July 2006.<ref>{{Cite news
column135:
language=en-GB}}</ref> Saitoti's dual heritage as a Maasai with Kikuyu family members predisposed him to a pan-Kenyan vision, but also denied him a strong ethnic base unlike his competitors. Saitoti was running as a candidate to succeed President [[Mwai Kibaki]] when he died in a helicopter crash in 2012.

', sections=[Section(title='==Early life and education==', content='
George Saitoti attended Ololua Primary School, [[Kajiado]] where he acquired his basic education in the 1950s. Between 1960 and 1963, he secured a place at [[Mang'u High School]] in [[Thika]] where he attained his high school education. He joined the ranks of Mang'u High School's highly decorated alumni including Kenya's third President, Mwai Kibaki, former Vice-President [[Moody Awori]], Catholic Archbishop Ndingi Mwana-a-Nzeki, the late Environment Minister [[John Michuki]], the late Trade Unionist and former Minister for Justice and Constitutional Affairs, [[Tom Mboya]], and late Cardinal [[Maurice Michael Otunga]].

Saitoti was one of the recipients of [[the Kennedy Airlift]] scholarships in 1963 at the age of 18.<ref name=""ReferenceA"">Airlift to America. How Barack Obama Sr., John F. Kennedy, Tom Mboya, and 800 East African Students Changed Their World and Ours. By Tom Shachtman. St. Martin's Press. 2009</ref> This was a scholarship program started by [[Tom Mboya]] and William X. Scheinmann and supported by the [[John F. Kennedy]] foundation and the African American Students Association to address the educational needs of newly independent Kenya. Through this program, hundreds of East Africans studied in the [[United States of America]] and [[Canada]].<ref name=""ReferenceA""/> Saitoti studied at [[Brandeis University]] between 1963 and 1967 where he was a mathematician. During his time there, he was on the [[Wien Scholarship]], specialising in Mathematics and Economics.<ref name=""Wien_profile"">{{cite web
column141: archive-date=28 May 2010}}</ref> His colleagues at the time remember that he enjoyed spending time in Cholmondeleys (the coffeehouse in the Castle) and excelled at high jump, ranking as one of the best in [[New England]].<ref name=""Wien_profile""/> In 1988, Saitoti received the first Brandeis Alumni Achievement Award, the highest honour the university bestows upon its graduates.<ref name=""Wien_profile""/><ref>[http://alumni.brandeis.edu/web/aassociation/awards/alumni_achievement_award.html Alumni Association Awards] {{webarchive
column143:
date=9 March 2012 }}</ref>

Saitoti later moved to the [[United Kingdom]] where he acquired a Master of Science (MSc) degree in mathematics from the [[University of Sussex]], Brighton. He enrolled for his doctoral studies at the [[University of Warwick]] where he acquired his PhD in mathematics in 1972; writing his dissertation under the supervision of professor Luke Hodgkin in the area of algebraic topology under the topic: ''Mod-2 K-Theory of the Second Iterated Loop Space on a Sphere.''<ref name=""math.buffalo"">[http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/Africa-today/%20AllAfricanDoctorates.html Africa Mathematics Union], Africa Doctorates in Mathematics (1995).</ref>

'), Section(title='==Academic career==', content='
Upon his graduation, Saitoti returned to [[Kenya]] in 1972, commencing a career as a Mathematics lecturer at the [[University of Nairobi]]. One of his contributions was the institutionalisation of Mathematics as a discipline in Africa. During the first Pan-African Conference of Mathematicians held in [[Rabat]], Morocco, in 1976, Saitoti was involved in the creation of the African Mathematical Union (AMU).<ref>{{Cite web
column147: access-date=2017-11-16}}</ref> He was elected the AMU\'s vice-president, a post which he held on up to 1979.<ref name=""math.buffalo"" /> By 1983, Saitoti\'s academic career was on the rise as associate professor and Head of the Mathematics Department.\nOutside the academy, Saitoti received several public appointments. On 3 November 1972, the [[List of ministers of Kenya#Ministry of Labour and Human Resource Development
column148: Minister of Labour]] appointed him as the chairman of the Agricultural Wages Council (AWC).<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=AJ2pr0bxaZcC& \'\'Kenya Gazette\'\' (Republic of Kenya)], 17 November 1972.</ref> On 4 September 1979, the [[List of ministers of Kenya#Ministry of Tourism
column149:
Minister for Tourism and Wildlife]], John Ogutu, also appointed him as a committee member of the Natural Sciences Advisory Research Committee (TNSARC) chaired by professor S. O. Wandiga.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=MwTc8E3OkR8C&pg=PA1167&dq=Kenya+Gazette+4+Sep+1979+saitoti ''Kenya Gazette'' (Republic of Kenya)], 14 September 1979.</ref> In September 1983, he was appointed chairperson of the board of directors for the [[Rift Valley Institute of Science and Technology]].<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=E3jJJ5zdFx8C&pg=PA1296&dq=saitoti ''Kenya Gazette'' (Republic of Kenya)], 23 September 1983.</ref> He also served in other public capacities as chairman of [[Mumias Sugar Company]] and the [[Kenya Commercial Bank]].

'), Section(title='===Development thinker===', content='
Top decision-makers in government had recognised Saitoti as a policy thinker and technocrat, of whom the [[Kenya African National Union
column150: KANU]] desperately needed to fix its institutions, politics and the economy. His seminal book, \'\'The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa\'\' was widely praised by leading officials as providing practical policy proposals to deal with the various challenges facing Kenya and Africa.<ref name=""bare_url"">[https://books.google.com/books?id=A-C1AAAAIAAJ \'\'The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa\'\']</ref>\nThe book drew from Saitoti\'s experience as a seasoned scholar, consultant and experienced policy-maker/thinker, presenting a rigorous and multidisciplinary analysis of strategies for poverty alleviation, sustainable development, poverty reduction, combating HIV/AIDS and [[Diplomacy
column151:
peace diplomacy]]. Saitoti also emphasised the importance of institutional reforms and sound public policies to sustainable economic growth in Africa.<ref>Saitoti, G. (2002). ''The Challenges of Economic and Institutional Reforms in Africa''. Ashgate Publishers Limited.</ref>

column158: Kenya Poverty Index by Constituency 2009]]\nIn October 1983, [[Daniel arap Moi
column159: President Daniel arap Moi]] nominated Saitoti as a member of parliament and subsequently appointed him to the Cabinet as Minister for Finance. He held the position until 1989.<ref>{{usurped
column160: 1=[https://archive.today/20120907105134/http://www.marsgroupkenya.org/multimedia/cache/cache_c21f969b5f03d33d43e04f8f136e7682_c012b78a927d02a4ff1a3bc41f75eb15 ""Ruto now takes over Home Affairs docket""]}}, \'\'The People Daily\'\' (October 2002).</ref> During the [[1988 Kenyan general election
column161: 1988 general elections]], Saitoti entered competitive politics and won the [[Kajiado North Constituency
column162: Kajiado North]] parliamentary seat that was previously held by [[Kajiado North Constituency
column163: Philip Odupoy]]. Prior to the tenure of Adupoy and Saitoti, the Kajiado North multi-ethnic constituency was held by the popular politician, [[Kajiado North Constituency
column164: John Keen]], another half-Maasai who champion a nationalist vision and worked over the years to ensure the advancement of his mother\'s people.<ref>[[Kajiado North Constituency
column165:
Wikipedia, Kajiado North Constituency]] (2010).</ref>
For more than 25 years, professor George Saitoti has represented Kajiado North since 1988, recapturing the seat in consecutive elections in 1992, 1997, 2002 and 2007. Building on John Keen's legacy of a cosmopolitan constituency, Saitoti transformed Kajiado North into Kenya's most ethnically integrated multi-ethnic legislative area that also provided a safe haven to Kenyans, forcibly displaced by the 1991–2008 cycles of ethnic violence in neighbouring areas.<ref name=Wachira>Wachira, Charles, [http://allafrica.com/stories/201202132318.html ""Kenya: Saitoti—the Dark Horse""], ''The Star'' (Nairobi), 11 February 2012. AllAfrica.</ref>

The area is also ranked among the top ten wealthiest, economically dynamic and fastest growing regions in Kenya. According to figures released by the Government of Kenya in 2009, Kajiado North has had an average poverty index of 10.66 per cent for the last three years, making it one of the richest constituencies in Kenya (see table 1).<ref>Opiyo, P., {{usurped
column166:
1=[https://archive.today/20120903145615/http://www.marsgroupkenya.org/multimedia/?StoryID=308484 ""Now We Know Whose Constituency Is Poorest""]}} (2010).</ref>

'), Section(title=""===Kenya's sixth Vice-President ==="", content='
After the [[1988 Kenyan general election
column167: 1988 General Election]], [[President Moi]] appointed Saitoti as Kenya\'s sixth vice-president. Saitoti became Kenya\'s longest sitting vice-president serving for 13 years under [[President Moi
column168: President Daniel arap Moi]] between May 1989 and January 1998 and again between April 1999 and August 2002 (see table 2).<ref>Rashid, I., [http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/commentaries/InsidePage.php?id=2000034729&cid=15& ""Will Kibaki be the only President not to Sack VP?""] {{webarchive
column170: date=23 May 2011 }} (2011).</ref> At the same time, he served as Minister for Finance.\nIn 1990–1991, Saitoti was the Executive Chairman of the [[World Bank]] and the [[International Monetary Fund]] (IMF).{{Citation needed
column171: date=May 2020}} In 1999–2000, Saitoti also served as president of the [[African, Caribbean and Pacific Group of States]], becoming instrumental in helping negotiate a new development partnership agreement to succeed the previous Lomè Convention that expired in February 2000 between the ACP and the [[European Union]].<ref>[http://intelligencebriefs.com/?p=1713 ""ICC Kenya Cases Latest Development And The George Saitoti Presidency Factor""], Intelligence News, 22 February 2012.</ref>\nThe hallmarks of Saitoti tenure as vice-president were efficiency, sobriety and loyalty as President Moi\'s most trusted lieutenant. Even when President Moi dithered in naming a new deputy after the 1997 elections, Saitoti was still his favoured choice 14 months down the line.<ref name=Chronicle>[http://nairobichronicle.wordpress.com/2009/03/01/saitotis-elusive-presidency/ ""Saitoti\'s Elusive Presidency""], \'\'Nairobi Chronicle\'\' (2009).</ref> The same traits of efficiency, patience and loyalty would make him one of President [[Mwai Kibaki
column172:
Mwai Kibaki's]] trusted Ministers.

'), Section(title=""===Reforming KANU'S one-party system==="", content='
When Saitoti was appointed vice-president on 1 May 1989, [[Kenya African National Union
column173: KANU]] was back-pedaling on re-democratizing the country. At the same time, the party was fragmented over the succession divide between a sit-tight ""KANU-A"" and a more pro-change ""KANU-B"" led by Saitoti. The new vice-president was, therefore, compelled to walk the tightrope between being the face of change in the ruling party and remaining loyal to his principal who, after re-election as president in 1988, had amended the constitution to increase his power to dismiss judges and widened police powers.\nOn New Year\'s Day 1990, the vocal cleric Rev. Timothy Njoya called on all Africans to demand a multiparty system of government. Following the [[Saba Saba Day
column174: Saba Saba riots]] on 7 July 1990, [[President Moi]] announced the formation of the KANU Review Committee under the chairmanship of Prof George Saitoti, popularly known as \'\'the Saitoti Committee\'\'.<ref name=""The Rise of a Party-State in Kenya"">{{Cite web
column176: title=The Rise of a Party-State in Kenya
column179:
access-date=2018-06-12}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===The Saitoti Review Committee===', content='
The Saitoti Review Committee was mandated to investigate the party's internal electoral and disciplinary conduct.<ref>{{Cite web
column181: title=Democratization and Law Reform in Kenya (Wanjala Smokin) – African information centre
column184: access-date=2018-06-12}}</ref> The committee traversed the country collecting people\'s opinions on the party, astounding foe, friend and critics alike and offering a rare forum for direct criticism and outbursts.<ref>The Report of the KANU Review Committee Presented to the President by George Saitoti, October 1990. Nairobi, Government Printer.</ref>\nIn January 1991, KANU\'s executive committee adopted the recommendation by George Saitoti, that critics of the party cease being expelled but suspended for one or two years.<ref>{{Cite book
column192: language=en}}</ref>\n\nThe recommendations of the report were open for debate during the [[Kenya African National Union
column193: National Delegates Conference]] at Karasani in [[Nairobi]]. President Moi backed the adoption and implementation of the report in \'\'toto\'\', against what many speakers at the conference had expected. This opened the reforms gates, eventually setting the stage for the [[Constitutional Reforms in Kenya
column194:
repeal of Section 2A]] in 1991 that returned Kenya to back to a multiparty system of government.<ref>Steeves, J., ""Re-Democratization in Kenya: 'Unbounded Politics' and the Political Trajectory Towards National Elections"", in D. Pal S. Ahuluwalia, Paul F. Lursey – Bray, ''The Post Colonial Condition: Contemporary Politics in Africa''.</ref> The Saitoti Review Committee thrust the party on the reform path, but also widened internal ideological schisms between ""KANU-A"" conservatives and ""KANU-B"" pro-reformers over the Moi succession question.<ref>Throup, D., and Hornsby C., ''Multi-Party Politics in Kenya''. Nairobi: East African Education Publishers, 1998.</ref>

'), Section(title=""===KANU'S war on Saitoti==="", content='
Saitoti was in the eye of a nasty succession storm that rocked [[Kenya African National Union
column195: KANU]] before and after the [[1997 Kenyan general election
column196: 1997 elections]]. Maasai purists led by Minister [[William Ole Ntimama]] and senior [[Maasai people
column197: Maasai elders]] \'re-Kikuyunized\' Saitoti\'s dual ancestry, amplifying his [[Gikuyu language
column198: Kikuyu]] family linkages as a scheme to weaken his political base and to challenge his status as a Maasai elder.\nDespite his steadfast loyalty to KANU and President Moi, Saitoti was frequently ignored, humiliated and frustrated by the party and its top echelons. Around the same time [[Robert Ouko (politician)
column199: Foreign Affairs Minister Robert Ouko]] was murdered in February 1990, Saitoti claims that attempts were made on his life.<ref>Ndegwa, A., [http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/archives/InsidePage.php?id=2000025251&cid=4 ""Saitoti: When Ouko was killed, Someone wanted me dead""]{{dead link
column202: fix-attempted=yes }}, \'\'Standard\'\', 22 October 2012.</ref> After the [[1997 Kenyan general election
column203: 1997 general elections]], he was dropped as vice-president, although no replacement was appointed. Even as President Moi reappointed him in April 1999, on the roadside in Limuru, Kiambu he made a scathing remark to the effect that: ""I\'ve given back Prof Saitoti the seat of Vice-President, hopefully now your sufurias (pots) will be full of food.""<ref name=Wachira /> Months before the [[2002 Kenya general election
column204: general elections of 2002]], Saitoti\'s name was deleted from the list of KANU delegates and his ascendancy to the presidency blocked by \'unknown\' party members.<ref>Ilado P., and G. Peterson, [http://www.the-star.co.ke/national/national/47122-prof-saitoti-speaks-out ""Prof Saitoti Speaks Out""] {{webarchive
column206: date=11 September 2012 }}. \'\'Nairobi Star\'\', 1 November 2011.</ref>\nOn 18 March 2002, when KANU held its national delegates conference at the [[Moi International Sports Centre
column207: Kasarani sports complex]], the move to block Saitoti from the succession game was manifest.<ref>Throup D., and Hornsby C., Multi-Party Politics in Kenya. Nairobi: East African Education Publishers 1998.</ref> The meeting amended the party constitution to allow for the merger between [[Kenya African National Union
column210: National Development Party (NDP)]] to create the [[Constitutional Reforms in Kenya
column211:
New KANU""]]. But it also introduced four new positions of party vice-chairmen primarily to water down Saitoti's position as vice-president and Moi's most likely successor as president.<ref>Karega, M., 2003, [http://web.peacelink.it/wajibu/18_issue/p3.html ""Polarisation of politics in Kenya along Ethnic Lines""], ''Wajibu'', vol.18, no.1- 2, pp. 3–16.</ref>

'), Section(title='===The National Rainbow Coalition (NARC)===', content='
It was clear that Moi did not even want him as one of the four vice-chairmen posts reserved for [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], [[Kalonzo Musyoka]], [[Ganze Constituency
column212: Katana Ngala]] and [[Musalia Mudavadi]]. Moi told Saitoti to his face that he was not ""presidential material"".<ref name=Chronicle /> As a ""Maasai-Kikuyu,"" Saitoti lacked the ethnic numbers he needed in the political horse-trading in Moi\'s power game. Instead, Moi finger-pointed as his heir [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], perceived to have a large ethnic base as a pure-bred Kikuyu with the [[Jomo Kenyatta
column213: Kenyatta"" mystique]].\nSaitoti gracefully bowed out of the race, living to fight another day, but not without his famous line: \'\'There comes a time when the nation is much more important than an individual\'\'.<ref>Khamisi, J., \'\'The Politics of Betrayal: Diary of a Kenyan Legislator\'\', Trafford Publishing, 2011.</ref><ref>[http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/archives/InsidePage.php?id=2000003044&cid=4 “There comes a time when the nation is much more important than an individual”]{{dead link
column216: fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>\nBut the KANU-NDP marriage came to a tragic end when Moi named Uhuru rather than Raila Odinga as his successor.<ref>[http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/InsidePage.php?id=2000050046&cid=4& KANU-NDP marriage] {{webarchive
column218: date=10 March 2012 }}</ref> In August 2002, Odinga left KANU to defeat Moi\'s ""use and dump game,""<ref name=""Badejo"">{{cite book
column221: title=Raila Odinga: an Enigma in Kenyan Politics
column223:
publisher=Yintab Books}}</ref> and joined a group of KANU rebels"" coalesced around the ""Rainbow Alliance"" lobby that later transformed itself into the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Saitoti also walking out of KANU and became a key LDP figure. In October 2002, LDP joined the National Alliance of Kenya (NAK) of Mwai Kibaki, Charity Ngilu and Wamalwa Kijana to form the National Rainbow Coalition (NARC).<ref name=""Badejo""/> Saitoti became a member of the NARC Summit, the highest organ of the coalition.

'), Section(title='==The ""NARC revolution""==', content=""
When the NARC flag-bearer, [[Mwai Kibaki]], decisively defeated [[Kenya African National Union
column224: KANU]] and [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], Saitoti was appointed to the Ministry of Education. He was the man in charge of implementing NARC's flagship and globally acclaimed free primary education in Kenya.<ref>{{Cite news
column226: title=Kenya: Free primary education brings over 1 million into school
column229:
language=en}}</ref>

""), Section(title='===The Kibaki stalwart===', content='
After 2004, as the NARC consensus crumbled, Saitoti left the agitating LDP camp and threw his lot behind President Kibaki.<ref>[https://fpc.state.gov/documents/organization/101803.pdf NARC consensus]</ref> He canvassed for the government-sponsored draft Constitution, which lost to a combined KANU-LDP campaign during the [[2005 Kenyan constitutional referendum
column232: title=VOA Standard English – Polls Show Majority of Kenyans Do Not Favor Draft Constitution
column234: access-date=2018-06-12}}</ref> During the 2007 elections, Saitoti defended his [[Kajiado North Constituency
column235: Kajiado North parliamentary]] seat on the [[Party of National Unity (Kenya)
column236: Party of National Unity (PNU)]] ticket, Kibaki\'s re-election vehicle, launched three months to the election on 16 September 2007.\nThe courts ordered a vote recount in [[Kajiado North Constituency
column237: Kajiado North]], but Saitoti beat his closest competitor, Moses Ole Sakuda with close to 20,000 votes.<ref>IREC, 2008. Report of the Independent Review Commission on the General Elections held in Kenya on 27 December 2007.</ref> Saitoti blamed his re-election glitch on intrigues of power by KANU forces within the PNU campaign which underwrote his rivals to knock him out of politics and potentially out of the [[2013 Kenyan presidential election
column238: 2012 Presidential elections]]. But he had remained reticent about it.\n\n[[File:Kenya Minister of State for Provincial Administration & Internal Security (6375911923).jpg
column242: British]] Foreign Office Minister [[Henry Bellingham (Norfolk MP)
column243: Henry Bellingham]] meeting George Saitoti, the Kenyan Minister of State for Provincial Administration & Internal Security in [[London]], 21 November 2011]]\n\nSaitoti\'s traits of patience, efficiency and loyalty to Kibaki paid off. On 8 January 2008, he was appointed Minister of State for Internal Security and Provincial Administration in the Office of the President, a position previously occupied by a Kibaki confidant, [[John Michuki]].<ref>[http://allafrica.com/stories/200801080673.html ""Kibaki Names Cabinet""], \'\'The Standard\'\', 8 January 2008.</ref> Saitoti retained the Internal Security docket even after President Kibaki and Prime Minister [[Raila Odinga]] established the power-sharing government that ended the [[2007-2008 Kenyan crisis
column244: 2008 post-election crisis]]. Between October 2010 and August 2011, Saitoti was appointed Minister for Foreign Affairs on an acting capacity after the incumbent, [[Moses Wetangula]], stepped aside to allow investigations on alleged corruption.<ref>Momanyi, B., [http://69.4.236.48/news/Kenyanews/Saitoti-takes-up-Foreign-Affairs-docket.html ""Saitoti Takes up Foreign Affairs Docket""] {{webarchive
column246:
date=8 July 2012 }}. 28 October 2010.</ref>

'), Section(title='===Cabinet sub-committee on ICC===', content='
In July 2009, Saitoti was appointed to head a special cabinet sub-committee formed to oversee the affairs of the [[International Criminal Court
column247: International Criminal Court (ICC)]] in Kenya.<ref>Leftie, P., and B. Namunane, [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/-/1056/627744/-/ul1499/-/index.html ""Cabinet Team to Weigh Options""], \'\'Daily Nation\'\', 21 July 2009.</ref> Members of this bi-partisan committee include; George Saitoti, [[Mutula Kilonzo]] and [[Moses Wetangula]] (PNU) and [[James Orengo]], [[Otieno Kajwang]] and [[Amason Kingi Jeffah
column248: Amason Kingi]] (ODM). (Following a cabinet reshuffle in April 2012, [[Eugene Wamalwa]] and [[Sam Ongeri
column249: Prof. Sam Ongeri]] have replaced Kilonzo and Wetangula). The role of the sub-Committee as a liaison and co-ordination body between the ICC and the Kenyan government took a center-stage from December 2010 when the [[Luis Moreno Ocampo
column250: ICC Chief Prosecutor, Luis Moreno Ocampo]], indicted six prominent Kenyans for alleged crimes against humanity relating to the [[2007-2008 Kenyan crisis
column251: 2008 post-election violence]].\n\nAs the Minister of Internal Security and the chairman of the {{YouTube
column253: Cabinet Sub-committee on ICC}} and security matters, Saitoti is the guarantor of the government\'s commitment to the ICC process. Arising from this, several analysts have claimed the suspects\' fate lie with the sub-committee.<ref>Mahamad Fazul, [http://www.the-star.co.ke/opinions/others/67198-uhuru-ruto-future-is-in-saitotis-hands ""Uhuru, Ruto Future is in Saitoti Hands""] {{webarchive
column255: date=12 September 2012 }}, 16 March 2012.</ref> Saitoti came out strongly criticising the invocation of [[Mwai Kibaki
column256:
President Kibaki]] in the ICC debate, calling for sobriety from politicians.<ref>Mwilu Aisha, [https://web.archive.org/web/20120209233344/http://ktnkenya.tv/?id=2000051619 ""Saitoti Defends Kibaki over ICC""]. 7 February 2012.</ref> Saitoti has maintained a legal interpretation on whether the suspects can vie for presidency in the coming elections, stressing that only the constitution can bar or let them free to enter the race.<ref>Ongiri Isaac, [http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/m/news.php?id=2000050443 ""PNU: Cabinet has no power to decide fate of presidential aspirants""], ''The Standard'', 20 January 2012.</ref>

'), Section(title='===PNU party politics===', content='
On 19 December 2008, [[Mwai Kibaki
column257: President Mwai Kibaki]] who was unanimously endorsed as Party Leader at the PNU National Delegates Conference (NDC) held at [[Moi International Sports Centre
column258: Kasarani sports complex]] in Nairobi.<ref>[http://www.the-star.co.ke/national/national/72319-saitoti-wants-pnu-alliance-banned PNU National Delegates Conference (NDC)] {{webarchive
column260: date=26 April 2012 }}</ref><ref>Munyori, G., and K. Keya, [http://www.capitalfm.co.ke/search/index.php?q=Internal%20Security%20Minister ""The Time has come for Saitoti""], Capital FM, 19 December 2008.</ref> In accordance with the Political Parties Act (2008), Saitoti was elected PNU chairman, becoming the second-in-command in the party hierarchy since he lost as KANU Vice-President in the battle for the Moi succession in March 2002.<ref>{{Cite book
column262: title=The Moi Succession: The 2002 Elections in Kenya
column272: language=en}}</ref> His elevation, however, complicated coalition politics and raised the stakes for the Kibaki succession in PNU.<ref>[http://africanpress.me/2008/04/28/5440/ Kibaki succession] {{webarchive
column274: date=9 June 2013 }}</ref> Other presidential hopefuls, [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] and [[Kalonzo Musyoka]], shunned the party and embarked on consolidating their respective parties.\nIn November 2010, Musyoka, Kenyatta and Saitoti signed a protocol to form and transform the PNU Alliance into a common political vehicle for the [[2013 Kenyan presidential election
column278: fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> But the imperative to comply with the Political Parties Act (2011) forced them to abandon the Alliance and shift attention to their respective parties.<ref>[http://cickenya.org/bills/political-parties-act-2011 Political Parties Act (2011)] {{webarchive
column280:
date=22 September 2012 }}</ref>

'), Section(title='==Goldenberg scandal==', content='
Saitoti was both [[Vice-President of Kenya
column281: Vice-President]] and Finance Minister at the height of the 1991–1993 [[Goldenberg scandal]]. Even though his own culpability in the fraud has never been established, for decades the [[Goldenberg scandal
column282: Goldenberg]] has become the proverbial [[Sword of Damocles]] used against Saitoti in intra-elite power wars. In early 1999, [[Raila Odinga]] as a presidential contender to succeed Moi as president, sued Saitoti and others over alleged role in the [[Goldenberg scandal]].<ref name=""Badejo""/> Three months after his re-appointment as vice-president on 3 April 1999, [[Otieno Kajwang]]\', a Raila ally, moved a private member\'s motion of no confidence in the vice-president for his alleged role in the [[Goldenberg scandal
column283: Goldenberg fraud]]. Saitoti survived the onslaught.<ref name=""Badejo""/>\n\nThe Goldenberg spectre returned to haunt Saitoti in the wake of the fierce political infighting between the LDP/KANU faction and Kibaki supporters in NARC that followed the [[2005 Kenyan constitutional referendum
column284: 2005 referendum]]. On 3 February 2006 a report by the Goldenberg Commission of Inquiry, chaired by Justice [[Samuel Bosire]], recommended that George Saitoti should face criminal charges for his involvement in the Goldenberg scandal.<ref>[https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/4676690.stm ""Moi \'Knew about\' Kenya Gold Scam""], BBC News, 3 February 2006.</ref><ref>[http://www.assetrecovery.org/kc/node/c800a8aa-dc00-11dd-8d28-f13739c882dc.0;jsessionid=0613A4AE3F34437A9DD1F3BB1063DB41 Goldenberg Commission of Inquiry] {{webarchive
column286: date=23 September 2015 }}</ref> On 13 February 2006, Saitoti voluntarily stepped aside from his ministerial docket to pave way for investigations into the allegations.<ref>{{Cite web
column293: access-date=2018-06-12}}</ref>\nHowever, on 31 July 2006, a three-judge bench headed by Justice Joseph Nyamu issued a certiorari order clearing Prof Saitoti of any wrongdoing, expunging his name from the Bosire Commission Report and issuing an order on permanent stay of prosecution against Saitoti.<ref name=""sudanvisiondaily"">[http://www.sudanvisiondaily.com/modules.php?name=News&file=article&sid=14359 ""Saitoti wins 16-year Fight to be Cleared""] {{webarchive
column295:
date=30 June 2007 }}, ''Sudan Vision'', 5 August 2006.</ref>

In dismissing the 23 paragraphs of the report, the [[High Court (Kenya)]] bench cited three inter-related errors of commission and omission by the Bosire Commission:
* The inquiry into the Goldenberg fraud had created a pyramid of noticeable bias, discriminatory treatment of evidence, submissions and factual errors that undermined the pursuit of justice and fairness.<ref name=""sudanvisiondaily""/>
* The factual flaws, biased and unprofessional handling of evidence by Inquiry led to wrong findings. The Inquiry's claim that Prof Saitoti illegally approved the 15 per cent ex-gratia payments as additional payment over and above the 20 per cent export compensation allowed at the time under the law were factually wrong. Indeed, the customs refunds, which Saitoti was accused of approving, were actually passed by Parliament.
* Long delay and wrong findings by the Goldenberg inquiry denied Prof. Saitoti any conceivable chance fair trial and justice.

On 15 November 2006, [[Mwai Kibaki
column296: President Kibaki]] reappointed Saitoti back to Cabinet.<ref>HBB, [https://web.archive.org/web/20150409195431/http://business.highbeam.com/3548/article-1G1-154528611/saitoti-and-kiraitu-back-cabinet-after-shuffle ""Saitoti and Kiraitu Back in Cabinet after Shuffle""], 15 November 2006.</ref>\nIn April 2012, the [[Kenya Judges and Magistrates Vetting Board
column297: vetting board]] found Justice [[Samuel Bosire]] unfit to serve in the judiciary citing fails as the Chairman of the [[Goldenberg scandal
column298: Goldenberg Commission of Inquiry]]. He ignored a High Court Order to summon retired President [[Daniel arap Moi]], [[Musalia Mudavadi]] and [[Nicholas Biwott]] as witnesses. The vetting board also accused Justice Nyamu of undermining public confidence in the courts for issuing a [[Stay of proceedings
column299:
permanent stay of prosecution]] against Saitoti.

'), Section(title='==Linda Nchi==', content='
Starting October 2011, Saitoti worked closely with national Minister of Defence [[Mohamed Yusuf Haji]] to see through [[Operation Linda Nchi
column301: title=Kenya: Defense Minister appointed as acting Internal Security Minister
column308: archive-date=30 November 2012 }}</ref> a coordinated operation in southern [[Somalia]] between the [[Military of Somalia
column309: Somali military]] and the [[Kenya Defence Forces
column311: Al-Shabaab]] group of insurgents.<ref name=""Tssgskfm"">{{cite web
column313: title=Somalia government supports Kenyan forces\' mission
column317: archive-date=14 March 2012 }}</ref><ref name=""Jointc"">[http://www.mfa.go.ke/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=399:joint-communique&catid=35:news Joint Communique – Operation Linda Nchi]</ref> The mission was officially led by the Somali army, with the Kenyan forces providing a support role.<ref name=""Jointc""/> In early June 2012, Haji signed another agreement re-hatting Kenya\'s deployed military forces in Somalia under the [[AMISOM]] general command.<ref name=""Gkdmaaaism""/>\n\n[[File:Foreign Office Minister Henry Bellingham meeting Acting Kenyan Foreign Minister Hon Prof George Saitoti in London, 10 February 2011. (5433279579).jpg
column321: British]] Foreign Office Minister [[Henry Bellingham (Norfolk MP)
column322:
Henry Bellingham]] meeting the Acting Kenyan Foreign Minister Hon Prof George Saitoti in [[London]], 10 February 2011]]

'), Section(title='==The Kibaki succession race==', content='
In November 2011, Saitoti confirmed that he was in the race to succeed President Kibaki, who is set to retire after the next general election. Saitoti reiterated his candidature in January 2012,<ref>Odalo, B., [https://archive.today/20120714052525/http://mobile.nation.co.ke/I+am+firmly+in++the+State+House+race+says+Saitoti+/-/1292/1315796/-/format/xhtml/-/p4mem4/-/index.html ""I am Firmly in the State House Race""], ''Daily Nation'', 28 January 2012.</ref> continuing to tour Kenya, with meet-the-people excursions to the Rift Valley, Eastern and Central provinces.

It appeared to be history repeating itself in the battle for the soul of the Kikuyu between, Saitoti, a [[Maasai people
column324:
Kikuyu]] kith and kin, and [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], a thorough-bred Kikuyu. Uhuru is widely thought as the presumptive successor to President Kibaki, but Saitoti was emerging also, as a likely candidate. In the event that Uhuru's run for the presidency is thwarted by the confirmed charges by the ICC, it remains a too-up as to whether Saitoti would have benefited from the spin-off.<ref name=Wachira />

'), Section(title='==Private life==', content='
Saitoti was a businessman who had interests in agriculture, horticulture, real estates, hospitality and pastoralism.

Saitoti's family life received little publicity. His wife, Margaret Saitoti, was with him when the High Court dropped charges in the 16-year Goldenberg case.<ref name=""sudanvisiondaily"" /> His brother, [[Ronald Musengi]], has been a banking executive with the [[Kenya Commercial Bank]]. In February 2012, Ronald Musengi applied to be a member of the National Police Service Commission.<ref>[http://allafrica.com/stories/201202260146.html ""Saitoti's brother on Shortlist for Police Job""], ''The Star'', 25 February 2012.</ref>

'), Section(title='==Death==', content='
{{main
column325: 2012 Nairobi Eurocopter AS350 crash}}\nSaitoti died on Sunday 10 June 2012 at around 9:00 am when a [[Eurocopter AS350]] helicopter belonging to the [[Kenya Police]] Air Wing registration 5Y-CDT,<ref>[http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/?articleID=2000059628&story_title=Helicopter-bought-last-year-after-old-fleet-was-grounded Helicopter bought last year after old fleet was grounded], \'\'The Standard\'\', 10 June 2012.</ref> carrying him and the Assistant Minister for Internal Security, [[Joshua Orwa Ojode]], crashed in the Kibiku area of [[Ngong Hills
column326: Ngong]] forest, killing them and four others.<ref>Patrick Mayoyo and Lucas Barasa, [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/Saitoti+Ojode+killed+in+Police+chopper+crash/-/1056/1424382/-/4kdoyi/-/index.html ""Ministers Saitoti, Ojode killed in chopper crash""], \'\'The Daily Nation\'\', 10 June 2012.</ref><!--<ref name=""saitoti"">{{cite web
column327: title=Saitoti, Ojode feared dead in Police chopper crash
column331: date=10 June 2012}}</ref>--> He was buried on 16 June in Kajiado North constituency. After the Maasai elders agreed to abandon the traditional burial rites and embrace the Catholic way, fifty bulls were slaughtered at the funeral in accordance with Maasai tradition.<ref>{{cite web
column332: title=Fifty bulls to be slaughtered during Saitoti\'s burial
column339: fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Al Shabaab militias and drug traffickers are the main suspects for the disaster. Investigations have not yet found anyone guilty.[https://correctiv.org/en/latest-stories/mafia-en/2015/04/16/kenyas-drug-barons/]  Saitoti was to table a ministerial statement in Parliament.<ref>{{YouTube
column340:
tsAoiyQ-xDY}}</ref>

He was a one-time [[Mayor of Nairobi]]<ref name=""jvl"" /><ref name=""sousa"" /><ref name=""nicholls"" /> and later [[Israel]]'s Honorary Consul to [[Kenya]].<ref name=""goldstein"" />

column1: Somen's family emigrated to Kenya in the early part of the twentieth century and was among those that established successful businesses in the country. The Somens owned the leading furniture store Hutchings Biemer as well as coffee and other interests. Somen, who was also a one time president of the Board of [[History of the Jews in Kenya
column2: Kenya Jews]], lived in Kenya for over 40 years. His wife Sophie Biemer was born in Kenya. He was elected mayor of Nairobi in 1955<ref>{{Cite news
column8: language=en-US}}</ref> together with deputy mayor Dobbs Johnson.

column1: Somen played a leading role in establishing amicable [[Israel–Kenya relations
column2: relations between Kenya and Israel]] both pre and post independence. He left Kenya in the late 1960s moving first to Switzerland and then to London where he died. His nephew Michael and a number of his family and relations still live in Kenya.

column1: His great nephews, David and [[Jonathan Somen]], founded an [[Internet service provider
column2: ISP]] in Kenya called AccessKenya Group. His other great nephew, Mark Somen, is a successful hospitality professional and started The Conduit- a community focused on positive social change.

column1: Somen died in London, England in October 1984.<ref>[https://allafrica.com/stories/200707190048.html Kenya: Israel Gets Reprieve in Dispute]</ref>

column1: Mboya was educated at various Catholic mission schools. In 1942, he joined [[St. Mary's School Yala]] – a Catholic secondary school in Yala, located in [[Nyanza Province
column2: Nyanza province]] where Mboya began his education in English and History. In 1946, he attended the Holy Ghost College (later [[Mang'u High School]]), where he passed well enough to proceed to do his Cambridge School Certificate. In 1948, Mboya joined the Royal Sanitary Institute's Medical Training School for Sanitary Inspectors at Nairobi, qualifying as an inspector in 1950. He also enrolled in a certificate course in economics at Efficiency Correspondence College of South Africa. In 1955, he received a scholarship from the [[Trades Union Congress]] to attend [[Ruskin College]], where he studied industrial management.<ref name=""biography"" /> After his graduation in 1956, he returned to Kenya and joined politics at a time when the British colonial authorities were gradually suppressing the [[Mau Mau rebellion]] spearheaded by the [[Kenya Land and Freedom Army]].{{citation needed

column1: Mboya's political life started immediately after he was employed at [[Nairobi]] City Council as a sanitary inspector in 1950. During his stint at Nairobi City Council, Mboya was elected as African Staff Association's president and immediately embarked on moulding the association into a trade union named the Kenya Local Government Workers' Union.<ref name=""evening"" /> This made his employer suspicious, but he resigned from his position before he could be laid off.  He was, however, able to continue working for the Kenya Labour Workers Union as secretary-general before embarking on his studies in Britain.{{citation needed

In 1953, during the [[Mau Mau War]] for Independence, [[Jomo Kenyatta]] and other leaders of the independence party, [[Kenya African Union]] (KAU), were arrested. They asked Mboya to lead the KAU and continue the struggle. However, the government banned the KAU. Mboya then turned to use the trade unions as a platform to fight for independence. He was elected as Secretary General of the Kenya Federation of Labour (KFL), the umbrella body for trade unions in Kenya. In that role, Mboya gave speeches in [[London]] and [[Washington, D.C.]] opposing British colonial rule in Kenya. He also organized several strikes seeking better working conditions for African workers. At that point, the colonial government nearly closed down the labour movement in the effort to suppress his activities.<ref name=""evening"" /> Mboya reached out to other labour leaders across the world, more so in the [[ICFTU]], including American [[A. Philip Randolph]], with whom he was close. Mboya raised funds to build a headquarters for the KFL.{{citation needed

In 1956, after Mboya had returned from the United Kingdom, the colonial government allowed black Africans to run for office and serve in the Legislative Assembly. Tom Mboya was elected from Nairobi.<ref>Ogot and Ochieng (1995), ''Decolonization and Independence in Kenya: 1940 – 1963'', p. 58.</ref> He was elected secretary of the African Caucus (called African Elected Members Organization – AEMO) and continued a campaign for independence, as well as seeking freedom for [[Jomo Kenyatta]] and other political prisoners.<ref name=""evening"" /> He used his incredible diplomacy skills to get support for the independence movement from foreign countries. column1: When Kenya became a republic on 12 December 1964, the new President Kenyatta appointed Tom Mboya to the Economic Planning and Development Ministry and transferred all functions of his former Justice ministry to the office of Attorney General under Charles Mugane Njonjo. Together with his deputy then [[Mwai Kibaki]], he issued ''Sessional Paper 10,'' which defined Kenya's form of economic policies, when it was debated and passed by parliament in 1965. Mboya presented the Sessional Paper No. 10 for debate in parliament in April 1965 covering the period of 1964 – 1970 under the title African Socialism and its Application to Planning in Kenya. Kenyatta and Mboya were known advocates of a non-aligned international policy, not wanting blanket application of capitalism while completely abhorring scientific socialism. In 1966, Tom Mboya was removed from the economic planning ministry and Kibaki was appointed for the first time as full Minister for Commerce and Industry. Mboya's development plans at the Economic Planning Ministry were credited for Kenya's development rate of 7%, which was sustained during his tenure as the Planning Minister.<ref name=""evening"" />
He retained the portfolio as Minister for Economic Planning and Development until his death at the age of 38 when he was gunned down on 5 July 1969 at Government Road (now [[Moi Avenue (Nairobi)
column2: Moi Avenue]]), Nairobi CBD, after visiting Chaani's Pharmacy.<ref name=""widow"">{{cite news
column6: title=Mboya widow dies in SA after illness
column11: url=http://www.nation.co.ke/News/-/1056/520412/-/u1sfu8/-/index.html}}</ref> Nahashon Isaac Njenga Njoroge was convicted for the murder and later [[hanging
column12: hanged]]. After his arrest, Njoroge asked: ""Why don't you go after the [[big man (political science)
column25: quote=Four months after the murder of Kenya's brilliant young Economic Planning Minister Tom Mboya, prison officials in Nairobi announced tersely last week that Nahashon Isaac Njenga Njoroge, the Kikuyu tribesman convicted of the shooting, had been hanged secretly ""in accordance with the law."" The officials refused to disclose the date or details of the execution, but it was reported in Nairobi that Njoroge had died at 3 a.m. on November 8. According to these reports, he went to his death without explaining what he had meant when he asked police after his arrest: 'Why don't you go after the big man?'}}</ref> Due to such statements, suspicions arose that Mboya's shooting was a political assassination.

column1: Outrage over his assassination led to riots in the major cities of Kenya. President [[Jomo Kenyatta]] gave a eulogy at Mboya's requiem mass, saying of his colleague: ""Kenya's independence would have been seriously compromised were it not for the courage and steadfastness of Tom Mboya.""<ref name=""evening"" /> A [[Tom Mboya Monument
column2: statue]] of Mboya was installed on Moi Avenue, where he was killed, and the nearby busy Victoria Street was renamed [[Tom Mboya Street]] in his honour.

column1: Mboya left a wife and five children. He is buried in a [[mausoleum]] on [[Rusinga Island]], which was built in 1970.<ref>{{cite web

Mboya's role in Kenya's politics and transformation is the subject of increasing interest, especially with the prominence of American politician [[Barack Obama]]. Obama's father, [[Barack Obama Sr.]], was a US-educated Kenyan who benefited from Mboya's scholarship program in the 1960s, going on to get married during his stay there, fathering the future [[Illinois]] Senator and President. Obama Sr. had seen Mboya shortly before the assassination and testified at the ensuing trial. Obama Sr. believed he was later targeted in a hit-and-run incident as a result of this testimony.<ref>{{cite news
In a 1976 interview, [[James Jesus Angleton]], a retired senior [[Central Intelligence Agency
column2: CIA]] official, expressed his opinion that Mboya was killed by the KGB as part of a Cold War campaign against pro-Western politicians in Africa.<ref>{{cite web

column1: In 2023, [[Robert F. Kennedy Jr.]], who had known Mboya in his boyhood, publicly accused [[Daniel arap Moi]] of orchestrating Mboya's assassination.<ref>{{Cite news

Tom Mboya married Pamela Odede on Saturday, 20 January 1962 at St. Peter Claver’s Catholic Church on Racecourse Road, in Nairobi. Pamela, a graduate of the [[Makerere University]], was the daughter of politician Walter Odede. The couple had five children. Their daughters are Maureen Odero, a high court judge in [[Mombasa]] and Susan Mboya, a [[Coca-Cola]] [[Business executive
column2: executive]], who continues the education airlift program initiated by Tom Mboya, and is married to former [[Nairobi County
column3: Nairobi]] governor [[Evans Kidero]]. Their sons included Lucas Mboya, and twin brothers Peter (died in a 2004 motorcycle accident) and Patrick (died aged four).

column1: After Mboya's death, Pamela had one child, Tom Mboya Jr, with Alphonse Okuku, the brother of Tom Mboya.<ref>{{cite news
column5: title=Final journey of an icon, tribute to Pamela Mboya
column13: archive-date=20 February 2009 }}</ref> Pamela died of an illness in January 2009 while seeking treatment in [[South Africa]].<ref name=""widow""/>
