column1: On 12 July 2007, with Kibaki's reelection bid drawing close, Odinga alleged that the government was withholding [[Identity document
column2: identity cards]] from voters in opposition strongholds with the intention to skew the election in favour of Kibaki. He also claimed that the intended creation of 30 new constituencies was a means by the government to fraudulently engineer victory in the [[2007 Kenyan parliamentary election
column3: December 2007 parliamentary election]].<ref>David Schlesinger and Barry Moody, [http://www.int.iol.co.za/index.php?set_id=1&click_id=87&art_id=nw20070713104933431C315734 ""Presidential hopeful doubts free, fair polls""] {{webarchive
column5: date=15 June 2006 }}, Reuters (''IOL''), 13 July 2007.</ref> In August 2007, Odinga's own Orange Democratic Movement-Kenya suffered a setback when it split into two, with Odinga becoming head of the [[Orange Democratic Movement]] (ODM) while the other faction, the ODM-K, was headed by [[Kalonzo Musyoka]] who parted ways with Odinga.<ref>Peter Clottey, [http://www.voanews.com/english/Africa/2007-08-16-voa1.cfm ""Kenya's Opposition Split Brightens Kibaki's Second Term Bid""] {{webarchive

column1: On 1 September 2007, the ODM elected Odinga as its presidential candidate in a National Delegates Conference held at the [[Moi International Sports Centre]] in Nairobi. Odinga received 2,656 votes; the only other candidates who received significant numbers of votes were [[Musalia Mudavadi]] with 391 and [[William Ruto]] with 368. Earlier, [[Najib Balala]] had withdrawn his candidature and endorsed Odinga.<ref>[http://allafrica.com/stories/200709010028.html ""Kenya: It's Raila for President""] {{webarchive
column3: date=26 September 2007 }}, ''The Standard'', 1 September 2007.</ref> The defeated candidates expressed their support for Odinga afterwards, and Mudavadi was named as his [[running mate]].<ref>Maina Muiruri, {{usurped
column4: 1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20230407161112/http://www.eastandard.net/InsidePage.php?id=1143973907 ""ODM ‘pentagon’ promises to keep the team intact""]}}, ''The Standard'' (Kenya), 2 September 2007.</ref>

column1: Odinga's bid for the presidency however failed when after the 27 December [[2007 Kenyan presidential election
column2: presidential election]], the Electoral Commission declared Kibaki the winner on 30 December 2007, placing him ahead of Odinga by about 232,000 votes. [[Jeffrey Sachs]] (Professor of Economics and Director of [[the Earth Institute]] at [[Columbia University]], and Special Advisor to former [[Secretary-General of the United Nations
column3: UN Secretary-General]]) faulted the United States' approach to the post-election crisis and recommended an independent recount of the vote.<ref>{{cite web

column1: Odinga and ODM leaders rallied against the decision, with [[James Orengo]] and [[Anyang' Nyong'o]] calling for mass action.  [[2007–2008 Kenyan crisis
column2: Violence broke out]] in the country.<ref>{{Cite web
column4: title=Kibaki re-elected Kenyan president: official results
column11: url-status=live}}</ref> The government responded by deploying police and paramilitary units to counter public protests.<ref>{{Cite web
column17: url= http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/africa/7239554.stm}}</ref> Following two months of unrest, which led to the death of about 1,000 people and the displacement of about 250,000, a deal between Odinga and Kibaki, which provided for power-sharing and the creation of the post of prime minister, was signed in February 2008; it was brokered by former [[UN Secretary-General]] [[Kofi Annan]]. Odinga was sworn in as prime minister, along with the power-sharing Cabinet, on 17 April 2008. The post of prime minister was last held by [[Jomo Kenyatta]] between 1963 and 1964 following independence. Odinga was thus the second person in Kenya's history to hold the position.<ref>Eric Ombok, [https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601087&sid=abAJ_3lpr8WA&refer=home ""Kenya's Raila Odinga Sworn in as Prime Minister, Ending Crisis""] {{webarchive

column1: Main articles: [[:2013 Kenyan general election]] and [[:2013 Kenyan presidential election petition]]
[[File:Raila Odinga speaking at visit to Peace Corps.jpg
column3: Odinga speaking at a visit to Peace Corps]]

column1: The next presidential election in which Odinga was to run was the 2013 March poll, involving Kibaki's handover of power. Uncertainty loomed over Odinga's main rivals, Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto, who had both been indicted by the [[International Criminal Court
column2: ICC]] of [[the Hague]] for their alleged role in the 2007 election violence. Despite their pending case, the duo had been nominated by the [[Jubilee Party
column3: Jubilee party]] with Uhuru as presidential candidate and Ruto as running mate.<ref>{{Cite web
column4: title=Kenyan election alliance between bitter enemies united by ICC charges
column9: url= https://www.theguardian.com/world/2012/dec/04/kenya-election-alliance-rival}}</ref> A Synovate survey released in October 2012 found Odinga to enjoy a leading 45 percent approval rate against Uhuru and Ruto.<ref>{{cite web
column11: title=allAfrica.com: Kenya: Raila's Ratings Fall But Still Ahead of the Pack

column1: To contest the election, Odinga's ODM joined Kalonzo Musyoka's Wiper Party and [[Moses Wetangula]]'s Ford Kenya in a coalition known as CORD (Coalition for Reforms and Democracy).<ref name=""NgiluDecamp"">{{Cite web
column2: title=Ngilu cuts cord with Kalonzo, Raila
column8: url= https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2012/12/ngilu-cuts-cord-with-kalonzo-raila/}}</ref> Odinga was named as the coalition's presidential candidate, with Kalonzo as his running mate.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia
column14: url= https://www.britannica.com/biography/Raila-Odinga/2013-elections}}</ref> Their opponents were a coalition known as [[The National Alliance]], consisting of Kenyatta's [[Jubilee Party]], Ruto's [[United Republican Party (Kenya)
column16: title=Letter from Africa: Party time in Kenya
column21: url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-37339114}}</ref> NARC (now headed by [[Charity Ngilu]]),<ref name=""NgiluDecamp""/> and [[Najib Balala]]'s (Republican Congress – RC)).<ref>{{Cite web
column22: title=Kenya: TNA, URP to Battle in 40 Constituencies

column1: A number of western countries were not in favour of the Uhuru and Ruto candidacy in view of their pending ICC cases and association with ""[[crimes against humanity]]"". Former UN Secretary-General [[Kofi Annan]] voiced his reservations,<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Kenya: to the elections, and beyond. Part Two. {{!}} Democracy in Africa
column5: work=Democracy in Africa {{!}} A Resource for the Study of Democracy in Africa
column8: url= https://democracyinafrica.org/kenya-to-the-elections-and-beyond-part-two/}}</ref> as did former [[U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs]] [[Johnnie Carson]] who cautioned against the election of Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto. He was notably quoted as saying that ""Choices have consequences"", referring to the fate of U.S.-Kenyan relations, with a Uhuru administration.<ref>{{Cite web
column9: title=US Official Says Kenya's Elections Have 'Consequences'

column1: Odinga ran for president in the elections held on 4 March 2013 and garnered 5,340,546 votes (43.70%) out of the 12,221,053 valid votes cast. The winner, Uhuru Kenyatta garnered 6,173,433 votes (50.51%). As this was above the 50% plus 1 vote threshold, the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission
column2: IEBC]] declared Uhuru the president-elect in the first round without requiring a run-off between the top two candidates.<ref>{{cite web
column4: title=Summary of 2013 Presidential Results Declared on 9/3/2013

column1: However, in a press conference shortly after the results were announced, Odinga said that the election had been marred by the manual tallying process and that he would appeal the result to [[The Kenya Presidential Election Petition 2013
column2: contest the result]] in Kenya's highest court, The Supreme Court.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=High Court to rule on vote – DW – 03/29/2013
column9: url= https://www.dw.com/en/crucial-court-ruling-in-kenya/a-16704934}}</ref> In anticipation of the legal challenge, Odinga and his lawyers George Oraro, Mutula Kilonzo, and James Orengo, secretly instructed Raj Pal Senna,<ref>[http://rajpalsenna.com/index/ Landing Page] {{webarchive
column11: date=2 November 2014 }}. Raj Pal Senna (25 April 2014). Retrieved on 21 April 2015.</ref> a Management Consultant from Barcelona to carry out a forensic investigation of the technology used in the Kenyan General Election 2013, during which the IEBC made claims on TV and media that there were ""technological challenges"", that servers overloaded and that the database crashed.<ref>[http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/print/2000083919/the-raila-supreme-court-evidence Standard Digital News – Kenya : Breaking News, Latest, Business, Jobs, Football, Travel, Tourism, Elections, National, Nairobi, County, East Africa, Media] {{webarchive
column13: date=2 November 2014 }}. Standardmedia.co.ke (15 April 2015). Retrieved on 21 April 2015.</ref><ref>[https://www.ktnkenya.tv/?articleID=2000083919&story_title=what-raila-failed-to-tell-in-petition-against-uhuru&pageNo=2 Standard Digital News – Kenya : What Raila failed to tell in petition against Uhuru] {{webarchive

column1: During the Petition hearing, Chief Justice [[Willy Mutunga]] made a finding rejecting the second [[affidavit]] of Odinga which comprised 900 pages, on the basis that it amounted to ""new evidence"", which is not permitted under the Constitution. Subsequently, the Supreme Court issued a ruling dismissing the petition on 30 March 2013. The Supreme Court while declaring Uhuru the next president also declared that the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission
column2: IEBC]] should not have included the invalid/spoilt votes in the calculation of the final figures and percentages.

column1: Chief Justice Willy Mutunga also directed that the EACC (Ethics and Anti Corruption Commission) and the DPP (Director of Public Prosecutions) carry out a criminal investigation of the IEBC in relation to the BVR, EVID, RTS and RPS.<ref name=""businessdailyafrica.com"">{{Cite web
column2: title=Poll officials, IT vendors face probe over glitches

column1: Odinga and his team did not attend Kenyatta's April 2013 inauguration, which marked the end of his tenure as prime minister, travelling instead to South Africa.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Odinga team in South Africa as Uhuru is sworn in
column7: url= https://www.monitor.co.ug/uganda/news/national/odinga-team-in-south-africa-as-uhuru-is-sworn-in-1539850}}</ref> The full findings of the supreme court investigation were later published as the OpCo Report,<ref>{{Cite web
column14: access-date=27 July 2020}}</ref> and inspired a documentary by documentary by KTN journalists John Namu and Mohammed Ali titled ""50+1 – The Inside Story"".<ref>[http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/ktn/video/watch/2000077350/-part-one-the-inside-story-50-1-what-really-happened-during-the-2013-elections Standard Digital News – KTN : KTN Video {{!}} Part One: The Inside Story 50+1 (What really happened during the 2013 elections)] {{Webarchive

column1: Main articles: [[:2017 Kenyan general election]] and [[:2017 Kenyan presidential election petition]]

Odinga, through his lawyers James Orengo, Otiende Amollo and Clifford Ochieng claimed that forces associated with his main competitor Uhuru Kenyatta had hacked into the IEBC (Kenya's electoral body) server and tampered with its database.<ref>{{cite book
column9: country=in}}}}</ref> He stated that the results that were being transmitted by IEBC were false because they had been manipulated via a computer algorithm designed to maintain an 11% gap between him and Uhuru's votes. As such, he proved the votes were not real votes cast by human voters but the outcome of a computer generated formula producing artificial values. This intrusion into IEBC's system, he further said, affected not just the presidential results but the entire election, including the votes cast for MPs, senators, governors and women representatives. He called the alleged intrusion ""the biggest vote theft in Kenya's history"". Later while vote tallying was still in progress and the country was awaiting the announcement of the final results, Odinga revealed that his team had received information from a confidential source in IEBC indicating that results from its server showed him leading with an unassailable 8.04 million votes over Uhuru's 7.75 million votes. Based on this, he demanded he be declared the fifth [[president of Kenya]]. The IEBC however rejected Odinga's contention, saying the winner could not be announced before the tallying was complete and also being an independent body it could not be compelled by one of the candidates to announce the results. The IEBC finally announced the results declaring Uhuru the winner with 8.1 million votes against Odinga's 6.7 million. The results showed massive losses for NASA, with Jubilee invading traditional NASA strongholds. NASA refused to recognize the results.<ref>{{Cite web
column10: title=Kenya election chief: Hacking attempt did not succeed
column15: url= https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2017/8/11/election-chief-says-hacking-attempt-did-not-succeed}}</ref> Shortly after Uhuru's declared victory, violence was reported in some parts of the country which are opposition strongholds. However the violence was not of the scale witnessed in the 2007 election aftermath and broke out only sporadically.<ref>{{Cite web
column16: title=Relative calm in Kisumu after Kenya election clashes

column1: After initially declining to take his case to court on the grounds that the court had previously made an unfavourable judgment against him, Odinga reconsidered and lodged a petition. After 2 days of hearings, the judges in a majority 4–2 decision returned a verdict on 1 September annulling the presidential results and ordered a new election to be held within 60 days. The court decision, read by Chief Justice David Maraga and widely viewed as unprecedented both in Africa and globally, held that the IEBC failed to conduct the election in the manner provided by the Constitution and so could not stand.<ref>{{cite news
column4: title=Kenya Supreme Court Nullifies Presidential Election

column1: Despite the Supreme Court ruling, Odinga announced his withdrawal from the presidential election, scheduled for 26 October,<ref name=""veconomist"">{{cite news
column2: title=Raila Odinga takes a gamble by threatening to boycott Kenya's election
column8: archive-date=12 October 2017}}</ref> on 10 October.<ref name=odingwithd>{{cite web
column9: title=I will not be forced to participate in election re-run, says Raila Odinga
column14: archive-date=10 October 2017}}</ref> The reason for his withdrawal was his belief that the election would again not be free or fair, since no electoral process reforms had been made since the annulment of the last election,<ref name=""veconomist"" /> as well as various defections which occurred from his coalition.<ref name=odingwithd /> The IEBC later stated that Odinga had not officially withdrawn from the race for presidency and his name would still appear on the ballot on 26 October among other candidates who contested the 8 August General Elections.<ref name="":0"">{{Cite news
column16: title=IEBC: Raila has not withdrawn from presidential race – Nairobi News
column23: archive-date=12 October 2017}}</ref> This resulted in violent uproar in various parts of the country some few days before and after the repeat polls especially in the NASA dominated zones. Alleged police brutality was reported as independent medic research organization (IMLU) cited 39 deaths and a high number of assault cases.<ref>{{Cite web
column24: title=The Future of Election Observation after Kenya's Supreme Court Judgement

column1: On 30 January, Odinga staged a swearing-in ceremony in Nairobi where he named himself ""People's President"". During and a while after this ceremony, the government through Communications Authority of Kenya shutdown TV stations and a few radio stations across Kenya to prevent live coverage of the event, a move which was criticised by the media freedom campaigners. Political tension was at its height throughout the country.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=State was right to shut down live broadcast of 2018 Raila 'swearing-in'

column1: Main article: [[:2018 Kenya handshake]]

On 9 March 2018, amidst the heightened political tension and in an unexpected move, Odinga and president Uhuru Kenyatta shook hands at Harambee House, in what is widely known as the ''2018 Handshake''  and made a joint televised appearance, in which they referred to each other as ""brothers"", and agreed to put aside political differences to allow Kenya to move forward. This brought to an end the then acrimony between the two major political divides.<ref>{{cite web
column3: title=Kenyans Name a 'People's President,' and TV Broadcasts Are Cut
column10: title=Kenya TV off air despite court ruling
column17: title=Kenya's Uhuru Kenyatta and Raila Odinga now 'brothers'
column26: title=How we got here: The story of handshake

column1: Main article: [[:2022 Kenyan general election]]

<templatestyles src=""Template:Blockquote/styles.css"" /><blockquote class=""templatequote "" >I Raila Amolo Odinga, having been faithful and committed to building a national, democratic, and progressive Kenya in our lifetime, having worked with many patriotic Kenyans to achieve this goal, I do hereby accept to present myself as a presidential candidate at the presidential election on 9 August 2022, following the request and unanimous decision of this Azimio la Umoja.<ref>{{cite web
column2: title=Kenyan opposition leader Odinga announces fifth bid for president
column10:
url-status=live }}

— Raila Odinga, 10 December 2021

column1: Odinga was cleared to run for the presidency for the fifth time on 5 June 2022 by the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission]] (IEBC).<ref>{{cite web
column6: title=Raila Odinga cleared for fifth stab at the presidency
column13: url-status=live }}</ref> He filed his candidacy papers as a candidate for the [[Azimio La Umoja]]–One Kenya Coalition party with the IEBC.<ref name=""auto1""/> [[Martha Karua]] was Odinga's running mate.<ref>{{cite web
column17: title=Raila names Martha Karua as his running mate
column24: url-status=live }}</ref> On 6 June, Odinga launched his 10-point manifesto at the Nyayo stadium, flanked by his running mate, and hundreds of his supporters detailing his plan for the first 100 days in office if his camp carries the day in the August election.<ref>{{cite web
column28: title=Kenya 2022: Raila promises the moon with Azimio manifesto
column34: url-status=live}}</ref> Odinga outlined a key component of his vision for the country, dubbed ""the People's Programmes"", which he promised as the foundation for his platform.<ref>{{cite web
column38: title=Azimio Manifesto: Raila Odinga promises to grow the economy, fight corruption
column45: url-status=live}}</ref> Social protection, universal healthcare, job development, women's empowerment, investing in youth, education for all, food security, water for everyone, enterprise Kenya, and building on past triumphs were all part of the ten-point plan.<ref>{{cite web
column55: url-status=live}}</ref> He vied for the presidency against [[United Democratic Alliance (Kenya)
column56: United Democratic Alliance]]'s candidate [[William Ruto]] who garnered 50.5% of votes cast. After coming second in the presidential election, he filed a legal case challenging the result, which was dismissed by the Supreme Court.<ref>{{Cite news
column58: title=Kenya's Raila Odinga challenges presidential election result

column1: [[File:Foreign Office Minister Henry Bellingham meeting Kenyan Prime Minister Raila Odinga in London, 7 July 2011. (5911639399).jpg
column3: British Foreign Office Minister [[Henry Bellingham (Norfolk MP)
column4: Henry Bellingham]] meeting Odinga in London, 7 July 2011]]

column1: Odinga's political ideology can be loosely styled as [[social democracy]], more closely aligned with [[American left-wing politics]]. His position was once in favour of a parliamentary system as he initially backed a constitution giving executive powers to a prime minister; he subsequently changed his position to support a presidential system with a devolved power structure, which is reflected in Kenya's Constitution.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Why Raila has changed tune on calls for parliamentary system

column1: Odinga was seen as one of the main forces behind the devolution now enshrined in the constitution as an essential part of Kenya's governance system.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=How Raila Odinga shaped Kenya's path to devolution and democracy
column8: url= https://www.citizen.digital/article/how-raila-odinga-shaped-kenyas-path-to-devolution-and-democracy-n371482}}</ref> He is also noted for his contribution to the evolution of multi-party democracy in Kenya and his desire to see the country have a Western-style democratic system.<ref>{{Cite web
column9: title=Raila Odinga: The man who shaped Kenyan politics
column15: url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c15p3k9kxkeo}}</ref> Due to an economic downturn and extreme [[Drought in Kenya
column16: drought]], Odinga called for the suspension of taxes on fuels and certain foods that disproportionately impact the poor.<ref>Kenya Broadcasting Corporation, 1 June 2011: [http://www.kbc.co.ke/news.asp?nid=70521 Principles Unite in Addressing High Cost of Living] {{webarchive

column1: On social issues, Odinga took a more conservative line. On [[LGBT rights in Kenya
column2: LGBT]] issues, Odinga stated that ""the constitution is very clear on this issue and men or women found engaging in homosexuality will not be spared"", adding, ""If we find a man engaging in homosexuality or a woman in lesbianism, we'll arrest them and put them in jail"". These comments were widely condemned from LGBT activists, who stated that his rhetoric put the lives of LGBT Kenyans in danger.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Gay, lesbian groups criticize Kenyan leader's remarks
column15: url-status=live}}</ref> In response, his office walked back Odinga's statement, claiming he only meant to clarify that same-sex marriage is illegal under the constitution.<ref>{{Cite web
column16: title=The Fight for LGBT Rights in Kenya

column1: Odinga died from a cardiac arrest at the Devamatha Hospital at [[Koothattukulam]] in Kerala, India, on 15 October 2025, at the age of 80. He had collapsed while taking a routine morning walk at the Sreedhareeyam [[Ayurvedic]] Eye Hospital and Research Centre, where he had been seeking medical treatment for diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease.<ref name=NYTobit>{{cite web
column3: title=Raila Odinga, Champion of Kenyan Democracy and Former Prime Minister, Dies at 80
column9: title=Raila Odinga, former Prime Minister of Kenya, dies in Kerala
column15: title=Raila Odinga Dies at 80 – Breaking News: Kenyan Opposition Figure Passes in India
column19: language=en-GB}}</ref> Shortly after his death, Indian prime minister [[Narendra Modi]] published a tweet honouring Odinga's legacy, describing him as a ""towering statesman and a cherished friend of India"". Kenyan President [[William Ruto]] announced a [[state funeral]] and a seven-day period of mourning with flags placed at [[half-mast]], with Friday 17 October also declared as a public holiday.<ref>{{Cite web
column21: title='Father of our democracy': Kenya's Raila Odinga dies in India aged 80
column26: title=Former Kenyan premier Raila Odinga, a key figure in African democracy efforts, dies at 80
column29: website=AP News}}</ref> South African president [[Cyril Ramaphosa]] and Tanzanian president [[Samia Suluhu]] as well as various politicians across the globe paid tribute and expressed their respects.<ref>{{Cite web
column31: title=Tributes pour in for former Kenyan prime minister Raila Odinga, who has died at 80

column1: [[Kenya Airways]], which carried his corpse, renamed its flight KQ203 to RAO001,<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Kenya: Raila Flight Becomes Most Tracked Worldwide Ahead of Arrival
column10: title=KQ flight to Nairobi to adopt special call sign 'RAO001' in honor of Raila
column11: website=The Star}}</ref> a special code assigned in his honour as the aircraft entered Kenyan airspace.<ref>{{Cite web
column13: title=Flight RAO001 carrying Raila's body touches down at JKIA
column17: title=KQ renames flight carrying late Raila Odinga to RAO001
column20: date=16 October 2025}}</ref> On 16 October, thousands of mourners gathered at [[Jomo Kenyatta International Airport]] in Nairobi to receive Odinga's body, briefly halting operations and disrupting a state ceremony attended by President Ruto.<ref>{{Cite web
column21: title=Thousands turn out to receive body of former Kenyan PM Raila Odinga
column25: language=en}}</ref> Waving flags and twigs, some supporters broke through airport barriers as the coffin was unloaded, forcing the [[Kenya Airports Authority]] (KAA) to issue a two-hour suspension of flights and closure of the country's airspace.<ref>{{Cite news
column27: title=Kenya aviation authority temporarily suspends operations at main Nairobi airport

column2: Parliament Buildings]], where Odinga was to be accorded a state public viewing in keeping with a long-standing government protocol. To accommodate the massive, surging crowds that had gathered outside parliament and at the airport, officials were forced to move the ceremony to a much larger venue, redirecting the procession and public viewing of Odinga's body to the [[Moi International Sports Centre]].<ref>{{cite web
column7: title=Mourners briefly storm Kenyan airport to receive Odinga's body
column12: title=Mourners storm Kenyan airport to receive Odinga's body
column18: title=Kenya mourns Raila Odinga, a Pillar of democracy
column22: language=en}}</ref> At least four people were killed after [[Kenya Police
column23: police]] opened fire to [[crowd control]] tens of thousands of people mourning following a gate breach at the stadium.<ref>{{Cite news
column25: title=Four dead after Kenyan forces fire shots, teargas to disperse crowds at Odinga viewing
column32: title=At least three dead after Kenya police open fire to disperse mourners of ex-PM Raila Odinga
column35: date=16 October 2025}}</ref> On 17 October, [[Doctors Without Borders]] reported that two people had died and more than 160 others were injured in a stampede at the state funeral.<ref>{{cite web
column36: title=Dozens of mourners injured at Odinga memorial in Kenya, Red Cross official says
column44: title=Two dead, many injured at stampede at funeral for Kenyan opposition leader Odinga
column47: date=17 October 2025}}</ref> Odinga was buried next to his father on 19 October 2025 at his residence in [[Bondo, Kenya
column51: title=Heavy security after deadly violence in Kenya, as thousands mourn former Prime Minister Raila Odinga
column57: title=Kenya ex-Prime Minister Raila Odinga buried as the country faces political uncertainty

column1: During his premiership, Odinga appointed [[Miguna Miguna]] as his advisor on coalition affairs, whom he later suspended in August 2011,<ref>Daily Nation, 4 August 2011, [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/politics/Raila+kicks+out+key+aide/-/1064/1213684/-/irw5r6z/-/index.html Raila kick out Key aid] {{webarchive
column3: date=18 May 2014 }}.</ref> citing ""gross misconduct"". The ''[[Daily Nation]]'' quoted his reason for suspension as being ""accused of misrepresenting the office of the Prime Minister, possibly a reference to his having aired strong views which may have embarrassed the PM"". Miguna Miguna later published controversial books about his working relationship with Odinga. According to one of Miguna Miguna's books, ''Peeling Back the Mask: A Quest for Justice in Kenya'', instances of [[abuse of office]], corruption, political trickery as well as public deception were planned, coordinated and covered up in Odinga's office in the three years where he worked there as an advisor of Odinga.<ref>{{cite news
column6: title=Raila scoffs at Miguna call, to soldier on
column17: title=Peeling Back the Mask: A Quest for Justice in Kenya

column1: His suspension came at a time when the electoral body, the [[Interim Independent Electoral Commission of Kenya
column2: IIEC]], was in an uproar and unsettled by anonymously authored complaints which the commissioners characterise as a hate campaign but which raise troubling questions on corruption and nepotism. Later Miguna, after suspension, issued a statement that said he ""was instructed to write my article on the IIEC chairman and the position he had taken with respect to the party's decision to kick out rebellious [[Member of Parliament
column3: MP]]s and Councillors"". He later denied this, according to the ''[[Nairobi Star]]''.<ref>''Nairobi Star''. 13 August 2011. In a twist of events however there were rumours that he would stand down and let one of the CORD principals Mr. Wetangula vie for presidency and back the Jubilee Party to be launched in September 2016. Odinga was the leader of the opposition who let hundreds of people get killed for no cause. [http://www.the-star.co.ke/national/national/35896-miguna-slams-raila Miguna Slam Raila] {{webarchive

column1: During Odinga's tenure, the office of the prime minister was implicated in the 'Kazi kwa Vijana scandal' whereby a World Bank funded project was suspended due to embezzlement of funds.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=World Bank cancels funding for Kazi Kwa Vijana over graft
column9: fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Similarly, the 'Maize scandal' whereby aflatoxin contaminated maize was imported into Kenya was also linked to The Office of the Prime Minister leading to the suspension of Odinga's top aides Permanent Secretary Mohammed Isahakia and Chief of Staff Caroli Omondi.<ref>{{Cite web
column10: title=I told Raila about rot but he did not act, says Gachoka
column16: title=Top aides in Raila's office quit over maize scandal

column1: Odinga has been reportedly linked to a 2019 multi-million dollar [[advance-fee scam]] of non-existent and ""fake gold"" in [[Kenya]] by a number of politicians from both sides of the political divide in Kenya.<ref>{{cite news
column4: title=Focus on Africa: Kenya in 'fool's gold' controversy
column13: title=DCI should grill Raila over gold scam role, leaders say » Capital News
column20: url-status=live }}</ref> According to the reports [[United Arab Emirates
column21: UAE]] Prime Minister [[Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum]]'s cousin lost money in disguised transactions for non-existent or otherwise ""fake gold"" in Kenya.<ref name=""bdaily""/><ref name=""star""/><ref>{{cite news
column22: title=Haji defends Uhuru, Raila and Matiang'i after fake gold claims
column30: url-status=live }}</ref> In May 2019, in a leaked video recording, a voice of [[Moses Wetangula]], the then senator of Bungoma, appeared to implicate Odinga in a gold deal gone sour, a deal in which millions of dollars were lost by the [[United Arab Emirates
column31: UAE]] royal family in an advance fee scam of non-existent gold in Kenya.<ref name=""bdaily"">{{Cite web
column32: title=Fake gold scam is a non-issue, says Wetangula
column44: title=Wetang'ula drags Uhuru, Raila names into fake gold scam in leaked audio
column52: url-status=live }}</ref> In the same video as was reported Wetangula claimed Odinga runs [[Orange Democratic Movement
column53: ODM]] like a [[gestapo]] where nothing happens without his concessions, and that Odinga met the president to explain the matter of the gold deal.<ref name=""star""/> In the same month Odinga claimed that he was the one that outed the confidence tricksters to the Dubai-based complainants.<ref>{{cite news
column58: title=Raila: I blew the whistle over the fake gold scam
column67: title=Raila Odinga: This is what I know about the fake gold
column74: url-status=live }}</ref> Later in the same month a number of political leaders in Kenya called for Odinga to be investigated by the [[Criminal Investigation Department (Kenya)
column75: DCI]] for international conmanship. The legislators claimed they had compelling evidence against Odinga. According to them Odinga cannot be part of a criminal transaction and then claim to be a whistleblower at the same time, whilst being a direct individual beneficiary of proceeds of the scam.<ref name=""capital""/><ref>{{cite news
column76: title=I am clean in gold saga, says Raila as MPs call for probe
column85: title=Raila used his AU post to try and con the president of the UAE with fake gold – MP Didimus
column96: title=Raila behaviour shows there are persons of interest in gold scam

column1: In 2018 [[Kipchumba Murkomen]], who was then the senator from Elgeyo Marakwet, linked Odinga to the NYS scandal, in which KES1.6 billion was lost through corruption. He linked Odinga and Suna East MP [[Junet Mohamed]], alleging they had pocketed some of the money. Odinga termed the claims untrue.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Kipchumba Murkomen Links Raila Odinga to Sh1.6 Billion NYS Scandal
column6: language=en }}</ref> Political analyst Mutahi Ngunyi accused Odinga of having killed the development agenda spearheaded by NYS, thus killing the dreams of young people in [[Kibera]].<ref>{{Cite web
column7: title=Mutahi Ngunyi Explains What Raila Took Away from Kibra People in the NYS Scandal

column1: During the August 2022 Kenyan general election, Odinga was the subject of several false claims and fake news stories. One example of misinformation involved a fabricated image of a banknote with Odinga's face on it. This image was circulated on social media, and some people believed that it was a legitimate banknote; however, fact-checkers confirmed that the image was a satire and not a real banknote.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Satire: This image showing a KSh6,000 banknote with Raila Odinga's face is fabricated

column1: Misinformation was spread through old or outdated photos. For example, a photo claiming to show Odinga collapsing at his Karen home was circulated on social media. It was found that the photo was not recent and had been taken out of context.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Misleading: This photo claiming to show Raila Odinga after collapsing at his Karen home is old
column10: url-status=live}}</ref> Video footage can also be manipulated to spread false information. A video claiming to show Odinga partying while William Ruto was at the presidential campaign was shared on social media; however, PesaCheck confirmed that the video was fake and had been doctored.<ref>{{Cite web
column12: title=False: This video claiming to show Raila Odinga partying while William Ruto was at the presidential…
column19: url-status=live }}</ref> Photos were circulated that claimed to show youth disrupting Odinga's rally in Embakasi, Nairobi; however, PesaCheck confirmed that the photos were not related to the rally, and they were taken at a different location.<ref>{{Cite web
column21: title=False: These photos that claim to show youth disrupting Raila Odinga's rally in Embakasi, Nairobi…

column1: It was falsely claimed that Azimio's Narok gubernatorial candidate, Moitalel Ole Kenta, had disowned Odinga. PesaCheck found that the claim was false, and Moitalel Ole Kenta had not made any such statement.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=False: Azimio's Narok gubernatorial candidate Moitalel ole Kenta has not disowned Raila and…
column10: url-status=live}}</ref> A fake tweet attributed to Ruto was circulated on social media, congratulating Odinga for winning the 2022 presidential election. PesaCheck confirmed that the tweet was fake and had not been posted by William Ruto.<ref>{{Cite web
column12: title=Fake: William Ruto did not tweet congratulating Raila Odinga for winning the 2022 presidential…
column19: url-status=live}}</ref> Another fake congratulatory statement allegedly from the US Embassy in Nairobi was circulating on social media where Odinga was being applauded on his ""win"" in the 9 August 2022 Kenyan general elections. This statement was looked into by PesaCheck who found out that the statement was FAKE. To firm this up, Andrew Veveiros who is the embassy spokesperson also shared an email to PesaCheck to dismiss the congratulatory statement by the US Embassy to Odinga.<ref>{{Cite web
column20: title=Fake: This statement from the US Embassy in Nairobi congratulating Raila Odinga on 'his electoral win' is fabricated

column1: Doctored presidential election results were also being shared across different media platforms. Of key interest was a fake statement shared on Facebook claiming that two local media houses, namely Royal Media Services and The Standard Group, had called the elections in favour of Odinga. According to this fake statement, Odinga was leading the 2022 presidential elections with 51.13% while Ruto was at 48.22%. These claims were denounced by the media houses' senior editors and PesaCheck also confirmed that they were fake.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Fake: This statement claiming that two Kenyan media houses called the 2022 general election in favour of Raila Odinga is fabricated

Raila Odinga, a member of the Luo ethnic group,<ref>{{Cite web
column182: url-status=live}}</ref> was born at the Anglican Church Missionary Society Hospital in [[Maseno]], [[Kisumu District]], Nyanza Province, on 7 January 1945. His parents were Mary Juma Odinga and [[Jaramogi Oginga Odinga]], who served as the first [[Vice President of Kenya]] under [[Jomo Kenyatta]].<ref name=usatoday>{{cite news
column185: title=Kibaki, Odinga have a long history
column193: access-date=30 November 2025}}</ref> He went to Kisumu Union Primary, Maranda primary in Bondo and [[Maranda High School]], where he studied until 1962, when he was transferred by his father to Germany.<ref>{{Cite web
column194: title=Raila Amolo Odinga: Who was he?
column200:
url= https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/infographics/2025-10-15-raila-amolo-odinga-who-was-he}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===East Germany===', content='
He spent the next two years at the Herder Institution, which trained foreign students in the German language and was part of the [[Philology
column202: University of Leipzig]] in [[East Germany]].<ref name=""bridge"">Daily Nation, 9 December 2007: [http://politics.nationmedia.com/inner.asp?fs=1&sid=520 Raila Odinga: I’m the bridge] {{webarchive
column204: date=2 October 2008 }}</ref> He received a scholarship that in 1965 sent him to the \'\'[[Technische Hochschule]]\'\' (technical college) of [[Magdeburg]] (now a part of [[Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg]]) in [[East Germany
column205: the GDR]]. In 1970, he graduated with a master\'s degree in [[mechanical engineering]].<ref>{{cite news
column208: title=Raila Odinga: The man who shaped Kenyan politics
column211: date=15 October 2025}}</ref> While studying in East Germany during the [[Cold War]], as a Kenyan he was able to visit [[West Berlin]] through [[Checkpoint Charlie]]. When visiting [[West Berlin]], he used to smuggle goods not available in [[East Berlin]] and bring them to his friends in East Germany.<ref name=""newsweek"">Newsweek Web Exclusive, 22 January 2008: [http://www.newsweek.com/id/97058 The Man Who Would Be President] {{webarchive
column213:
date=29 October 2008 }}</ref>

'), Section(title='===Personal life===', content='
According to his book ''Flames of Freedom'', Odinga showed that he was given a Christian name Rayila upon baptism. Before him being christenend, his father Jaramogi Oginga had refused to give him a Christian name. Jaramogi wrote to a Christian priest informing him of his intention to baptize his three children with purely African names who included Omuoda Agola, [[Oburu Odinga]], and Raila to be baptized. The priest accepted on condition that he first gets them Christian names as those already recognized in the Church.<ref>{{Cite news
column217: title=Tale of Raila\'s Dramatic Church Ordeal During Baptism
column223: url-status=live}}</ref> During the real baptism event, Jaramogi refused the set conditions, which made the priest refuse to baptise the three children including Raila Odinga. Him being a traditional African man, Jaramogi had wanted his children to have names of illustrous ancestors which the bishop strongly declined. He had wanted them to be named Ng\'ong\'a Molo Oburu, Rayila Amolo Odinga and Ngire Omuodo Agola.<ref>{{Cite web
column232: Ida]] at a political rally]]\nBaptised as an Anglican Christian in the [[Church Mission Society
column233: Church Missionary Society]] (CMS) in his childhood,<ref>The Standard, 5 November 2007: [http://allafrica.com/stories/200711050379.html ODM promises smooth transition if it wins] {{webarchive
column235: date=12 October 2012 }}</ref> Odinga later became a [[born-again]] Christian.<ref>{{cite news
column243: archive-date=9 May 2009  }}</ref> Odinga was married to [[Ida Odinga]] (Ida Anyango Oyoo). They lived in [[Karen, Kenya
column244: Karen]], Nairobi, and had a second home at Central Farm in [[Siaya County]]. The couple had four children: Fidel (1973–2015),<ref>{{Cite news
column253: title= Raila family in mourning as eldest son found dead in bed after night partying
column263: Winnie]] (born 1990). Fidel was named after [[Fidel Castro]] and Winnie after [[Winnie Mandela]].<ref name=""price"">Daily Nation, 2 June 2001 {{cite web
column265: title=The Price of being Raila Odinga\'s wife
column269: archive-date=28 January 2008  }}</ref>\n\nIn an interview with [[BBC News]] in January 2008, Odinga asserted that he was the first cousin of US president [[Barack Obama]] through Obama\'s father;<ref name=""Obama"">{{Cite news
column271: title=Odinga says Obama is his cousin
column277: url-status=live}}</ref> however, Barack Obama\'s paternal uncle denied any direct relation to Odinga, stating ""Odinga\'s mother came from this area, so it is normal for us to talk about cousins. But he is not a blood relative.""<ref name=""Said Obama"">[http://africa.reuters.com/wire/news/usnL08727241.html Some Kenyans forget crisis to root for Obama] {{webarchive
column279: date=14 October 2008 }}, [[Reuters]], 1/8/08.</ref> Odinga briefly played association football for Luo Union (now [[Gor Mahia F.C.
column281: midfielder]].<ref name=""bridge"" /> He was a supporter of English [[Premier League]] club [[Arsenal F.C.
column284: title=Top Kenyan Politicians and Teams they follow (EPL)
column285: date=24 December 2022 }}</ref> Odinga was appointed by the [[African Union]] to mediate the [[2010–2011 Ivorian crisis]], which involved [[Alassane Ouattara]] and [[Laurent Gbagbo]].\nOdinga wrote \'\'Flame of Freedom\'\', a 1040-page autobiography which talks about his life from childhood. It was launched on 6 October 2013 in Kenya and subsequently in United States on 15 October 2013.<ref>{{Cite web
column287: title=Raila Odinga, CORD governors head to US
column291:
language=en}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===1982 Kenyan coup attempt===', content=""
{{Main
column330: 1982 Kenyan coup attempt}}\nAt 3 a.m. on Sunday, 1 August 1982, a group of soldiers from the [[Kenya Air Force]] led by [[Private (rank)
column331: Senior Private]] [[Hezekiah Ochuka]] attempted to [[1982 Kenyan coup d'état attempt
column332: overthrow the government]] of President [[Daniel arap Moi
column335: title=President of Kenya announces crushing of attempted coup
column341: url-status=live }}</ref> After the failed attempt to overthrow him, President Moi re-organized Kenya's security architecture, staffing it with his loyalists and then he ensured a law was passed in parliament that gave him emergency powers while placing the provincial administration under the office of the president.<ref>{{cite web
column343: title=Moment of bravado that changed Kenya
column350: url-status=live }}</ref> Odinga was arrested and charged with [[treason]] after being accused of being among the masterminds of the 1982 coup.<ref>{{cite web
column362: title=35 years later, Kenya's Odinga is enigmatic on coup attempt
column369: url-status=live }}</ref> He was released six years later in February 1988 but was detained again that August; he was finally released in June 1989.<ref>{{cite web
column373: title=What Mzee told me after Raila left detention – Ida Odinga
column380:
url-status=live }}</ref>

""), Section(title='===Detention===', content='
In an era of unrelenting [[human rights]] abuse by the Kenyan government, Odinga was placed under [[house arrest]] for seven months after evidence seemed to implicate him along with his late father Oginga Odinga for collaborating with the plotters of a [[1982 Kenyan coup
column381: failed coup attempt]] against President [[Daniel Arap Moi]] in 1982. Hundreds of Kenyan civilians and thousands of rebel soldiers died in the coup. Several foreigners also died. Odinga was later charged with treason and detained without trial for six years.<ref>[[Human Rights Watch]], 1992: [https://www.hrw.org/reports/1992/WR92/AFW-03.htm Kenya: Human Rights Developments] {{webarchive
column383: date=28 November 2016 }}</ref>\n\nA biography released 14 years later in July 2006, apparently with Odinga\'s approval, indicated that Odinga was far more involved in the attempted coup than he had previously admitted. After its publication, some Members of Parliament in Kenya called for Odinga to be arrested and charged,<ref>The Standard, 17 July 2006: [http://allafrica.com/stories/200607171148.html ’82 coup: Arrest Raila, say MPs] {{webarchive
column385: date=16 October 2012 }}</ref> but the [[statute of limitations]] had already passed and the information contained in the biography did not amount to an open confession on his part.<ref>[[The Standard (Kenya)
column386: The Standard]], 21 July 2006: [http://allafrica.com/stories/200607210225.html Why A-G won’t charge Raila] {{webarchive
column388: date=16 October 2012 }}</ref> Among some of his most painful experiences was when his mother died in 1984 but the prison wardens took two months to inform him of her death.<ref>{{Cite web
column389: title=KANU regime made me miss my mother\'s burial, Raila reveals
column396: title=Raila remembers his mother as Kenya joins world to mark big day
column403: url-status=live}}</ref>\n\nHe was released on 6 February 1988 only to be rearrested in September 1988 for his pro-democracy and human rights agitation at a time when the country continued to descend deep into the throes of poor governance<ref>[[University of Pennsylvania]], African Studies Centre, East Africa Living Encyclopedia: [http://www.africa.upenn.edu/Hornet/irin_121397.html Kenya: IRIN Election Briefing, 12/13/97] {{webarchive
column405: date=16 March 2007 }}</ref> and the despotism of single-party rule. Kenya, was then, by law, a [[one-party state]]. His encounters with the authoritarian government generated an aura of intrigue about him and it was probably due to this that his political followers christened him ""Agwambo"", [[Luo dialect
column408: title=Meet woman who gave Raila Odinga the name \'Agwambo\'
column415: title=Baba is fine, Joho and Junet say after visiting Raila in Dubai
column419: url= https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2020/07/baba-is-fine-joho-and-junet-say-after-visiting-raila-in-dubai/}}</ref>\n\nOdinga was released on 12 June 1989, only to be incarcerated again on 5 July 1990, together with [[Kenneth Matiba]], and former Nairobi mayor [[Charles Rubia]], both multiparty system and human rights crusaders.<ref>University of Pennsylvania, African Studies Centre, East Africa Living Encyclopedia: [http://www.africa.upenn.edu/NEH/khistory.htm Kenya – History] {{webarchive
column421: date=27 November 2014 }}</ref> Odinga was finally released on 21 June 1991, and in October he fled the country to Norway amid indications that the increasingly corrupt Kenyan government was attempting to assassinate him without success.<ref>The Standard, 16 July 2006: {{cite web
column423: title=Day Raila fled disguised as a priest
column427:
archive-date=12 January 2008  }}</ref>

'), Section(title='===Multi-party politics===', content='
At the time of Odinga's departure to Norway, the [[Forum for the Restoration of Democracy]] (FORD), a movement formed to agitate for the return of multi-party democracy to Kenya, was newly formed. In February 1992, Odinga returned to join FORD, then led by his father [[Jaramogi Oginga Odinga]]. He was elected Vice Chairman of the General Purposes Committee of the party. In the months running up to the 1992 General Election, FORD split into [[Ford-Kenya political party
column428: FORD-Kenya]], led by Odinga\'s father [[Jaramogi Oginga Odinga]], and [[Forum for the Restoration of Democracy-Asili
column429: FORD-Asili]] led by [[Kenneth Matiba]]. Odinga became Ford-Kenya\'s Deputy Director of Elections. Odinga won the [[Langata Constituency]] parliamentary seat, previously held by [[Philip Leakey]] of KANU. Odinga became the second father of multi-party democracy in Kenya after Kenneth Matiba.<ref name=""multiparty"">Center for Multiparty Democracy: [http://www.cmd.or.ke/images/Politics%20and%20Paliamenterians%20in%20Kenya.pdf Politics and Parliamentarians in Kenya 1944–2007] {{webarchive
column431: date=28 October 2008 }}</ref> When Jaramogi Oginga Odinga died in January 1994 and [[Michael Wamalwa Kijana]] succeeded him as FORD-Kenya chairman, Odinga challenged him for the party leadership. The elections were marred by controversy after which Odinga resigned from FORD-Kenya to join the [[National Development Party (Kenya)
column441: 1997 Kenyan parliamentary election}}\n\nIn his first bid for the presidency in the [[1997 Kenyan general election]], Odinga finished third after [[Daniel arap Moi
column442: President Moi]], the incumbent, and Democratic Party candidate [[Mwai Kibaki]]. He however retained his position as the [[Langata Constituency
column443:
Langata]] MP.<ref name=""multiparty"" />

'), Section(title='===KANU-NDP merger===', content='
Immediately after the 1997 election, Odinga appeared alongside Kibaki to denounce the results, saying that they were rigged. In the subsequent months, however, he forged a deal to support Moi, entering into a cooperation deal between his party, NDP, and Moi's [[Kenya African National Union
column452: isbn=978-0-85255-843-0 }}</ref> He accepted a position in Moi\'s cabinet as Energy Minister, serving from June 2001 to 2002, during Moi\'s final term.<ref>{{Cite web
column453: title=Former Kenyan premier Raila Odinga, a key figure in African politics, dies at 80 {{!}} CNN
column458: url= https://edition.cnn.com/2025/10/15/africa/kenyas-raila-odinga-has-died-intl}}</ref> In 2002, the NDP and KANU formally merged, with the NDP being dissolved and the new party being dubbed the ""New KANU"".<ref>{{Cite web
column459: title=KANU/ NDP merger set to transform national politics
column464: url= https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/report/30707/kenya-kanu-ndp-merger-set-transform-national-politics}}</ref> In the subsequent KANU elections held later that year, he was elected the party\'s Secretary General (replacing [[Joseph Kamotho]]).<ref>[http://allafrica.com/stories/200208060047.html Kenya: Saitoti, Raila And Kamotho Hold Breakfast Meeting] {{webarchive
column468: title=The Politics of Betrayal: Diary of a Kenyan Legislator
column477: url-status=live}}</ref>\n\nIn 2002, much to the chagrin of Odinga and many other hopefuls in the party, Moi endorsed [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] – son of Kenya\'s first president [[Jomo Kenyatta]] but a relative newcomer in politics – to be his successor. Moi publicly asked Odinga and others to support Uhuru as well.<ref>BBC News, 16 September 2002: [http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/2261085.stm Anti-Moi alliance emerging] {{webarchive
column479: date=17 July 2004 }}</ref> This was taken as an affront by many of the party loyalists who felt they were being asked to make way for a newcomer who, unlike them, had done little to build the party. Odinga and other KANU members, including [[Kalonzo Musyoka]], [[George Saitoti]], and [[Joseph Kamotho]], opposed this step arguing that the then 38-year-old Uhuru was politically inexperienced and lacked the leadership qualities needed to govern.<ref>{{Cite web
column480: title=Factional Intrigues and Alliance Politics: The Case of NARC in Kenya\'s 2002 Elections
column482: work=[[Electoral Institute for Sustainable Democracy in Africa]]
column486: page=2}}</ref> Moi stood his ground, maintaining that the country\'s leadership needed to pass to the younger generation as well as someone that Moi could rely on personally.<ref>{{Cite web
column492: title=Kenyan elections give hope for the future
column495: url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-hamilton-spectator/183023135/}}</ref>\n\nDissent ran through the party with some members openly disagreeing with Moi, despite his reputation as an autocrat. It was then that the Rainbow Movement was founded, comprising disgruntled KANU members who exited KANU. The exodus, led by Odinga, saw most big names fleeing the party. Moi was left with his handpicked successor almost alone with a party reduced to an empty shell with poor electoral prospects. The Rainbow Movement went on to join the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Kenya)
column496: Liberal Democratic Party]] (LDP), which later teamed up with opposition Mwai Kibaki\'s [[National Alliance Party of Kenya]] (NAK), a coalition of several other parties, to form the [[National Rainbow Coalition]] (NARC).<ref>{{Cite web
column497: title=Kenyans signal it\'s time for change
column504:
url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-ottawa-citizen/183023215/}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===National Rainbow Coalition===', content='
[[File:Gordon Brown Raila Odinga.JPG
column506: Odinga with [[Gordon Brown]] at [[Kibera]]]]\nAmid fears that this opposition ""super alliance"" would fail to unite and rally behind a common candidate as in previous occasions and thus easily hand victory to the government, Odinga declared \'\'Kibaki tosha\'\', Swahili for ""Kibaki is sufficient"", an endorsement of a Kibaki ticket. This resolved the matter of candidacy and Narc went on to defeat Moi\'s protege, [[Uhuru Kenyatta]].<ref>{{Cite web
column507: title=How Raila\'s declaration of ""Kibaki Tosha"" decided 2002 elections
column513: url= https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2025-10-15-how-railas-kibaki-tosha-decided-2002-elections}}</ref> Kibaki himself had been injured in a road accident prior to the election, leaving Odinga and others to lead the campaign for him.<ref name=""auto"">{{Cite web
column514: title=Raila recalls Kibaki road accident and 2002 election win
column521: url= https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001417265/raila-recalls-kibaki-road-accident-and-2002-election-win}}</ref>\n\nOn assuming office, President Kibaki did not appoint Odinga as prime minister in the new government, contrary to a pre-election Memorandum Of Understanding. (Kenya\'s constitution had no provision for prime minister yet); neither did he give LDP (Odinga\'s faction) half of the cabinet positions as per the MOU. He instead sought to entrench and increase his own NAK\'s side in cabinet, even appointing MPs from the opposition parties (KANU and FORD people) to the cabinet.<ref>BBC News, 30 September 2003: [http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/3356431.stm Uproar over Kenya leader\'s decree] {{webarchive
column523:
date=20 July 2004 }}</ref>

The perceived ""betrayal"" started a simmering disquiet which in time led to an open rebellion and a split within the cabinet. A key point of disagreement was a proposed new constitution for the country, which was a major campaign issue that had united Kibaki's NAK and Odinga's LDP in the campaign. This constitution included provisions to trim presidential powers to rein in what was seen as an autocratic presidency, a feature of both the Moi and first president Jomo Kenyatta's regimes which had led to a lot of power abuse and an unaccountable leadership. This proposed document was called the ""Bomas Draft"", but Kibaki's government opposed it and withdrew from the process in March 2004.<ref name=""auto""/>

'), Section(title='===2005 referendum===', content='
{{Main
column524: 2005 Kenyan constitutional referendum}}\n\nKibaki\'s government went on to write a new proposed Constitution which had a reduced role for parliament and the new prime minister compared with the Bomas Draft, instead retaining more powers for the presidency.<ref>{{Cite web
column525: title=Kenyans say no to new constitution
column530: url= https://www.theguardian.com/world/2005/nov/22/kenya.davidfickling}}</ref> Odinga opposed this and went on to campaign with his LDP cabinet colleagues on the referendum \'No\' side, opposing the president and his lieutenants in a bruising countrywide campaign. When the document was put to a [[2005 Kenyan constitutional referendum
column531: referendum]] on 21 November 2005, the government lost by a 57% to 43% margin.<ref>{{Cite web
column532: title=Of Oranges and Bananas: The 2005 Kenya Referendum on the Constitution
column540: url= https://www.researchgate.net/publication/37166419}}</ref> Embarrassingly for Kibaki, out of 8 provinces, only one (Central Province where his tribe the [[Kikuyu people
column541: Kikuyu]] are dominant) voted ""yes"" for the document, isolating his own tribe from the rest of Kenya and exposing his campaign as ethnic-based.<ref>{{cite journal
column545: title=The Fruits of Perception: \'Ethnic Politics\' and the Case of Kenya\'s Constitutional Referendum
column550: pages=233–270 }}</ref> In the aftermath of the referendum, Kibaki sacked the entire cabinet on 23 November 2005.<ref>{{Cite web
column551: title=Snubbed leader sacks entire Kenyan cabinet
column557: url= https://www.theguardian.com/world/2005/nov/24/kenya.jeevanvasagar}}</ref> When it was reconstituted two weeks later, Odinga and several of his allies were not given a role, while many others from the LDP group and FORD-Kenya refused the posts they were offered.<ref>{{Cite web
column558: title=Political unease as some MPs reject cabinet positions
column563:
url= https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news/2005/12/08/political-unease-some-mps-reject-cabinet-positions}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===Orange Democratic Movement===', content='
Odinga led the formation of a new opposition outfit, the [[Orange Democratic Movement]] (ODM) – an Orange was the symbol for the ""No"" vote in the constitutional referendum.
In January 2006, Odinga was reported to have told police that he believed his life was in danger, having received assassination threats.<ref>BBC News, 10 January 2006: [http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/africa/4599834.stm Kenyan opponent 'fears for life'] {{webarchive
column565:
date=13 January 2006 }}</ref>

'), Section(title=""=== Unconstitutional swearing in as people's president ==="", content='
{{Main
column566: 2017 Kenyan presidential election petition}}\n\nHaving lost the 2017 election to Uhuru Kenyatta,<ref>{{Cite web
column567: title=Kenya\'s 2017 presidential elections: a preliminary results analysis, by county – Africa Research Institute
column574: url-status=live }}</ref> and boycotted the rerun,<ref>{{Cite web
column576: title=Kenya: Raila Odinga withdraws from election rerun
column585: url-status=live }}</ref> Odinga had himself sworn in as ""the people\'s president"".<ref>{{Citation
column586: title=🇰🇪 Kenya\'s Raila Odinga self-sworn in as \'people\'s president\'
column593: url-status=live }}</ref> [[Miguna Miguna]], who administered the oath, was deported, while Odinga faced no consequences.<ref>{{Cite news
column595: title=Kenya deports Miguna Miguna over Odinga \'swearing-in\'
column602:
url-status=live }}</ref>

'), Section(title='=== Handshake with Kenyatta ===', content='
{{Main
column603: 2018 Kenya handshake}}\n\nIn March 2018, Odinga and Kenyatta had a political handshake intended to cool the political temperatures after the [[2017 Kenyan general election]]. The handshake resulted in [[William Ruto]] being sidelined in the Government he formed with Uhuru Kenya, with Raila Odinga being elevated to de facto Deputy President of the Republic of Kenya. The handshake gave birth to the [[2021 Kenyan constitutional referendum attempt
column604: Building Bridges Initiative]] alias BBI.<ref>{{cite web
column613: title=Letter from Africa: The handshake that left millions of Kenyans confused
column619:
url-status=live }}</ref>

'), Section(title='=== Building Bridges Initiative ===', content='
Following the March 2018 truce between Odinga and President Kenyatta, the two commissioned a joint task force that would collect views from Kenyans and report their findings. After touring the country and holding consultative sessions, the team compiled and submitted the report to President Kenyatta at [[State House, Nairobi]] on 26 November 2019<ref>{{Cite web
column628: url-status=live}}</ref> which was followed by a public launch at the [[Bomas of Kenya]] the following day.<ref>{{Citation
column629: title=Kenya unites behind BBI at Bomas – VIDEO
column635: url-status=live}}</ref> The efforts by Kenyatta and Odinga to bring peace and cohesion in the country were applauded by several leaders locally and internationally with the duo being invited to a [[National Prayer Breakfast]] \'\'International Lunch\'\' in [[Washington, D.C.
column636: Washington DC]], US in February 2020.<ref name=""DailyNation_peace_deal_earns"">{{Cite news
column638: title=Peace deal earns Uhuru and Raila US invite
column644: url-status=live}}</ref> In  2022 the [[Supreme Court of Kenya

The election, held in [[Addis Ababa]], Ethiopia, was decided by the [[member states of the African Union]] after seven rounds of voting.<ref>{{Cite web

'), Section(title='===2007 presidential election===', content='
{{Main
column716: 2007 Kenyan presidential election}}\n\n[[File:Raila and the media.jpg
column718: Odinga addressing the Kenyan media during the [[2007–08 Kenyan crisis]]]]\n[[File:Raila Amolo Odinga with Obamas.jpg
column720: President [[Barack Obama]] and First Lady [[Michelle Obama]] of the United States pose for a photo during a reception at the Metropolitan Museum in New York with Odinga and his wife [[Ida Odinga]] (2009).]]\n[[File:Prime Minister of Kenya (7752141076).jpg
column722: [[British Foreign Secretary]] [[William Hague]] meeting Odinga, then Prime Minister of Kenya, in London, 10 August 2012]]\n[[File:Opening Plenary - World Economic Forum on Africa 2008.jpg
column724: Odinga, Prime Minister of Kenya, with, from left, [[Pierre Nkurunziza]], [[President of Burundi]], [[Bingu Wa Mutharika]], [[President of Malawi]], [[Thabo Mbeki]], [[President of South Africa]], [[Klaus Schwab]], Founder and Executive chairman, [[World Economic Forum]], and [[John Agyekum Kufuor]], [[President of Ghana]], during the Opening Plenary of the World Economic Forum on Africa 2008 in [[Cape Town]], South Africa, 4 June 2008]]\n\nOn 12 July 2007, with Kibaki\'s reelection bid drawing close, Odinga alleged that the government was withholding [[Identity document
column725: identity cards]] from voters in opposition strongholds with the intention to skew the election in favour of Kibaki. He also claimed that the intended creation of 30 new constituencies was a means by the government to fraudulently engineer victory in the [[2007 Kenyan parliamentary election
column726: December 2007 parliamentary election]].<ref>David Schlesinger and Barry Moody, [http://www.int.iol.co.za/index.php?set_id=1&click_id=87&art_id=nw20070713104933431C315734 ""Presidential hopeful doubts free, fair polls""] {{webarchive
column728: date=15 June 2006 }}, Reuters (\'\'IOL\'\'), 13 July 2007.</ref> In August 2007, Odinga\'s own Orange Democratic Movement-Kenya suffered a setback when it split into two, with Odinga becoming head of the [[Orange Democratic Movement]] (ODM) while the other faction, the ODM-K, was headed by [[Kalonzo Musyoka]] who parted ways with Odinga.<ref>Peter Clottey, [http://www.voanews.com/english/Africa/2007-08-16-voa1.cfm ""Kenya\'s Opposition Split Brightens Kibaki\'s Second Term Bid""] {{webarchive
column731: VOA News]], 16 August 2007.</ref>\n\nOn 1 September 2007, the ODM elected Odinga as its presidential candidate in a National Delegates Conference held at the [[Moi International Sports Centre]] in Nairobi. Odinga received 2,656 votes; the only other candidates who received significant numbers of votes were [[Musalia Mudavadi]] with 391 and [[William Ruto]] with 368. Earlier, [[Najib Balala]] had withdrawn his candidature and endorsed Odinga.<ref>[http://allafrica.com/stories/200709010028.html ""Kenya: It\'s Raila for President""] {{webarchive
column733: date=26 September 2007 }}, \'\'The Standard\'\', 1 September 2007.</ref> The defeated candidates expressed their support for Odinga afterwards, and Mudavadi was named as his [[running mate]].<ref>Maina Muiruri, {{usurped
column734: 1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20230407161112/http://www.eastandard.net/InsidePage.php?id=1143973907 ""ODM ‘pentagon’ promises to keep the team intact""]}}, \'\'The Standard\'\' (Kenya), 2 September 2007.</ref>\n\nOdinga\'s bid for the presidency however failed when after the 27 December [[2007 Kenyan presidential election
column735: presidential election]], the Electoral Commission declared Kibaki the winner on 30 December 2007, placing him ahead of Odinga by about 232,000 votes. [[Jeffrey Sachs]] (Professor of Economics and Director of [[the Earth Institute]] at [[Columbia University]], and Special Advisor to former [[Secretary-General of the United Nations
column736: UN Secretary-General]]) faulted the United States\' approach to the post-election crisis and recommended an independent recount of the vote.<ref>{{cite web
column744: archive-date=6 June 2011  }}</ref>\n\nOdinga and ODM leaders rallied against the decision, with [[James Orengo]] and [[Anyang\' Nyong\'o]] calling for mass action.  [[2007–2008 Kenyan crisis
column745: Violence broke out]] in the country.<ref>{{Cite web
column747: title=Kibaki re-elected Kenyan president: official results
column754: url-status=live}}</ref> The government responded by deploying police and paramilitary units to counter public protests.<ref>{{Cite web
column760: url= http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/africa/7239554.stm}}</ref> Following two months of unrest, which led to the death of about 1,000 people and the displacement of about 250,000, a deal between Odinga and Kibaki, which provided for power-sharing and the creation of the post of prime minister, was signed in February 2008; it was brokered by former [[UN Secretary-General]] [[Kofi Annan]]. Odinga was sworn in as prime minister, along with the power-sharing Cabinet, on 17 April 2008. The post of prime minister was last held by [[Jomo Kenyatta]] between 1963 and 1964 following independence. Odinga was thus the second person in Kenya\'s history to hold the position.<ref>Eric Ombok, [https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601087&sid=abAJ_3lpr8WA&refer=home ""Kenya\'s Raila Odinga Sworn in as Prime Minister, Ending Crisis""] {{webarchive
column762:
date=13 June 2010 }}, Bloomberg.com, 17 April 2008.</ref>

'), Section(title='===2013 presidential election===', content='
{{Main
column764: 2013 Kenyan presidential election petition}}\n\n[[File:Raila Odinga speaking at visit to Peace Corps.jpg
column766: Odinga speaking at a visit to Peace Corps]]\n\nThe next presidential election in which Odinga was to run was the 2013 March poll, involving Kibaki\'s handover of power. Uncertainty loomed over Odinga\'s main rivals, Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto, who had both been indicted by the [[International Criminal Court
column767: ICC]] of [[the Hague]] for their alleged role in the 2007 election violence. Despite their pending case, the duo had been nominated by the [[Jubilee Party
column768: Jubilee party]] with Uhuru as presidential candidate and Ruto as running mate.<ref>{{Cite web
column769: title=Kenyan election alliance between bitter enemies united by ICC charges
column774: url= https://www.theguardian.com/world/2012/dec/04/kenya-election-alliance-rival}}</ref> A Synovate survey released in October 2012 found Odinga to enjoy a leading 45 percent approval rate against Uhuru and Ruto.<ref>{{cite web
column776: title=allAfrica.com: Kenya: Raila\'s Ratings Fall But Still Ahead of the Pack
column782: url-status=live }}</ref>\n\nTo contest the election, Odinga\'s ODM joined Kalonzo Musyoka\'s Wiper Party and [[Moses Wetangula]]\'s Ford Kenya in a coalition known as CORD (Coalition for Reforms and Democracy).<ref name=""NgiluDecamp"">{{Cite web
column783: title=Ngilu cuts cord with Kalonzo, Raila
column789: url= https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2012/12/ngilu-cuts-cord-with-kalonzo-raila/}}</ref> Odinga was named as the coalition\'s presidential candidate, with Kalonzo as his running mate.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia
column795: url= https://www.britannica.com/biography/Raila-Odinga/2013-elections}}</ref> Their opponents were a coalition known as [[The National Alliance]], consisting of Kenyatta\'s [[Jubilee Party]], Ruto\'s [[United Republican Party (Kenya)
column797: title=Letter from Africa: Party time in Kenya
column802: url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-37339114}}</ref> NARC (now headed by [[Charity Ngilu]]),<ref name=""NgiluDecamp""/> and [[Najib Balala]]\'s (Republican Congress – RC)).<ref>{{Cite web
column803: title=Kenya: TNA, URP to Battle in 40 Constituencies
column809: url= https://allafrica.com/stories/201301251817.html}}</ref>\n\nA number of western countries were not in favour of the Uhuru and Ruto candidacy in view of their pending ICC cases and association with ""[[crimes against humanity]]"". Former UN Secretary-General [[Kofi Annan]] voiced his reservations,<ref>{{Cite web
column810: title=Kenya: to the elections, and beyond. Part Two. {{!}} Democracy in Africa
column813: work=Democracy in Africa {{!}} A Resource for the Study of Democracy in Africa
column816: url= https://democracyinafrica.org/kenya-to-the-elections-and-beyond-part-two/}}</ref> as did former [[U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs]] [[Johnnie Carson]] who cautioned against the election of Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto. He was notably quoted as saying that ""Choices have consequences"", referring to the fate of U.S.-Kenyan relations, with a Uhuru administration.<ref>{{Cite web
column817: title=US Official Says Kenya\'s Elections Have \'Consequences\'
column823: url= https://www.voanews.com/a/us-official-says-kenya-elections-have-consequences/1599063.html}}</ref>\n\nOdinga ran for president in the elections held on 4 March 2013 and garnered 5,340,546 votes (43.70%) out of the 12,221,053 valid votes cast. The winner, Uhuru Kenyatta garnered 6,173,433 votes (50.51%). As this was above the 50% plus 1 vote threshold, the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission
column824: IEBC]] declared Uhuru the president-elect in the first round without requiring a run-off between the top two candidates.<ref>{{cite web
column826: title=Summary of 2013 Presidential Results Declared on 9/3/2013
column832: archive-date=15 March 2013  }}</ref>\n\nHowever, in a press conference shortly after the results were announced, Odinga said that the election had been marred by the manual tallying process and that he would appeal the result to [[The Kenya Presidential Election Petition 2013
column833: contest the result]] in Kenya\'s highest court, The Supreme Court.<ref>{{Cite web
column834: title=High Court to rule on vote – DW – 03/29/2013
column840: url= https://www.dw.com/en/crucial-court-ruling-in-kenya/a-16704934}}</ref> In anticipation of the legal challenge, Odinga and his lawyers George Oraro, Mutula Kilonzo, and James Orengo, secretly instructed Raj Pal Senna,<ref>[http://rajpalsenna.com/index/ Landing Page] {{webarchive
column842: date=2 November 2014 }}. Raj Pal Senna (25 April 2014). Retrieved on 21 April 2015.</ref> a Management Consultant from Barcelona to carry out a forensic investigation of the technology used in the Kenyan General Election 2013, during which the IEBC made claims on TV and media that there were ""technological challenges"", that servers overloaded and that the database crashed.<ref>[http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/print/2000083919/the-raila-supreme-court-evidence Standard Digital News – Kenya : Breaking News, Latest, Business, Jobs, Football, Travel, Tourism, Elections, National, Nairobi, County, East Africa, Media] {{webarchive
column844: date=2 November 2014 }}. Standardmedia.co.ke (15 April 2015). Retrieved on 21 April 2015.</ref><ref>[https://www.ktnkenya.tv/?articleID=2000083919&story_title=what-raila-failed-to-tell-in-petition-against-uhuru&pageNo=2 Standard Digital News – Kenya : What Raila failed to tell in petition against Uhuru] {{webarchive
column846: date=2 November 2014 }}. Ktnkenya.tv. Retrieved 21 April 2015.</ref>\n\nDuring the Petition hearing, Chief Justice [[Willy Mutunga]] made a finding rejecting the second [[affidavit]] of Odinga which comprised 900 pages, on the basis that it amounted to ""new evidence"", which is not permitted under the Constitution. Subsequently, the Supreme Court issued a ruling dismissing the petition on 30 March 2013. The Supreme Court while declaring Uhuru the next president also declared that the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission
column847: IEBC]] should not have included the invalid/spoilt votes in the calculation of the final figures and percentages.\nChief Justice Willy Mutunga also directed that the EACC (Ethics and Anti Corruption Commission) and the DPP (Director of Public Prosecutions) carry out a criminal investigation of the IEBC in relation to the BVR, EVID, RTS and RPS.<ref name=""businessdailyafrica.com"">{{Cite web
column848: title=Poll officials, IT vendors face probe over glitches
column854: url-status=live}}</ref>\n\nOdinga and his team did not attend Kenyatta\'s April 2013 inauguration, which marked the end of his tenure as prime minister, travelling instead to South Africa.<ref>{{Cite web
column855: title=Odinga team in South Africa as Uhuru is sworn in
column860: url= https://www.monitor.co.ug/uganda/news/national/odinga-team-in-south-africa-as-uhuru-is-sworn-in-1539850}}</ref> The full findings of the supreme court investigation were later published as the OpCo Report,<ref>{{Cite web
column867: access-date=27 July 2020}}</ref> and inspired a documentary by documentary by KTN journalists John Namu and Mohammed Ali titled ""50+1 – The Inside Story"".<ref>[http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/ktn/video/watch/2000077350/-part-one-the-inside-story-50-1-what-really-happened-during-the-2013-elections Standard Digital News – KTN : KTN Video {{!}} Part One: The Inside Story 50+1 (What really happened during the 2013 elections)] {{Webarchive
column869:
date=2 November 2014 }}. Standardmedia.co.ke. (25 April 2014).</ref>
