column36: House of Commons]]. Kenyatta told Shiels that he was not affiliated with communist circles and was unaware of the nature of the newspaper which published his articles.{{sfnm
column42: 2pp=22–23}} Shiels advised Kenyatta to return home to promote Kikuyu involvement in the constitutional process and discourage violence and extremism.{{sfn

column1: After eighteen months in Europe, Kenyatta had run out of money. The [[Anti-Slavery International
column2: Anti-Slavery Society]] advanced him funds to pay off his debts and return to Kenya.{{sfn
column5: p=131}} Although Kenyatta enjoyed life in London and feared arrest if he returned home,{{sfn
column8: p=125}} he sailed back to Mombasa in September 1930.{{sfnm
column14: 2p=29}} On his return, his prestige among the Kikuyu was high because of his time spent in Europe.{{sfnm

column1: In his absence, [[female genital mutilation]] (FGM) had become a topic of strong debate in Kikuyu society. The [[Protestantism
column2: Protestant]] churches, backed by European medics and the colonial authorities, [[Campaign against female genital mutilation in colonial Kenya
column3: supported the abolition of this traditional practice]], but the KCA rallied to its defence, claiming that its abolition would damage the structure of Kikuyu society.{{sfnm
column12: 3p=25}} Anger between the two sides had heightened, several churches expelling KCA members from their congregations, and it was widely believed that the January 1930 killing of an American missionary, [[Hulda Stumpf]], had been due to the issue.{{sfn
column15: pp=134, 139}} As Secretary of the KCA, Kenyatta met with church representatives. He expressed the view that although personally opposing FGM, he regarded its legal abolition as counter-productive, and argued that the churches should focus on eradicating the practice through educating people about its harmful effects on women's health.{{sfnm
column22: 2p=25}} The meeting ended without compromise, and [[John Arthur (missionary)
column23: John Arthur]]—the head of the Church of Scotland in Kenya—later expelled Kenyatta from the church, citing what he deemed dishonesty during the debate.{{sfnm
column30: 2p=25}} In 1931, Kenyatta took his son out of the church school at Thogota and enrolled him in a KCA-approved, independent school.{{sfn

column4: quote=""With the support of all revolutionary workers and peasants we must redouble our efforts to break the bonds that bind us. We must refuse to give any support to the British imperialists either by paying taxes or obeying any of their slave laws! We can fight in unity with the workers and toilers of the whole world, and for a Free Africa.""

column1: In May 1931, Kenyatta and [[Parmenas Githendu Mukiri]] sailed for Britain, intent on representing the KCA at a [[Joint committee of the Parliament of the United Kingdom
column2: Joint Committee of Parliament]] on the future of East Africa.{{sfnm
column11: 3p=31}} Kenyatta would not return to Kenya for fifteen years.{{sfnm
column17: 2p=151}} In Britain, he spent the summer attending an [[Independent Labour Party]] [[summer school]] and [[Fabian Society]] gatherings.{{sfn
column20: p=153}} In June, he visited [[Geneva]], Switzerland to attend a [[Save the Children]] conference on African children.{{sfnm
column26: 2p=51}} In November, he met the Indian independence leader [[Mohandas Gandhi]] while in London.{{sfn
column29: p=157}} That month, he enrolled in the [[Woodbrooke Quaker Study Centre
column30: Woodbrooke Quaker College]] in [[Birmingham]], where he remained until the spring of 1932, attaining a certificate in English writing.{{sfnm

column1: In Britain, Kenyatta befriended an Afro-Caribbean Marxist, [[George Padmore]], who was working for the Soviet-run [[Comintern]].{{sfnm
column11: 3p=44}} Over time, he became Padmore's protégé.{{sfn
column14: p=171}} In late 1932, he joined Padmore in Germany.{{sfn
column17: p=166}} Before the end of the year, the duo relocated to Moscow, where Kenyatta studied at the [[Communist University of the Toilers of the East]].{{sfnm
column27: 3pp=69–71}} There he was taught arithmetic, geography, natural science, and political economy, as well as [[Marxism-Leninism
column28: Marxist-Leninist]] doctrine and the history of the Marxist-Leninist movement.{{sfn
column31: p=70}} Many Africans and members of the African diaspora were attracted to the institution because it offered free education and the opportunity to study in an environment where they were treated with dignity, free from the [[institutionalised racism]] present in the U.S. and British Empire.{{sfn
column34: p=71}} Kenyatta complained about the food, accommodation, and poor quality of English instruction.{{sfn
column38: p=27}} There is no evidence that he joined the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]],{{sfn
column41: p=72}} and one of his fellow students later characterised him as ""the biggest reactionary I have ever met.""{{sfn
column44: p=73}} Kenyatta also visited [[Siberia]], probably as part of an official guided tour.{{sfnm

column2: Nazi]] government shifted political allegiances in Europe; the Soviet Union pursued formal alliances with France and Czechoslovakia,{{sfnm
column9: 2p=27}} and thus reduced its support for the movement against British and French colonial rule in Africa.{{sfn
column12: p=6}} As a result, Comintern disbanded the [[International Trade Union Committee of Negro Workers]], with which both Padmore and Kenyatta were affiliated. Padmore resigned from the Soviet Communist Party in protest, and was subsequently vilified in the Soviet press.{{sfnm
column18: 2p=45}} Both Padmore and Kenyatta left the Soviet Union, the latter returning to London in August 1933.{{sfnm
column25: 2p=27}} The British authorities were highly suspicious of Kenyatta's time in the Soviet Union, suspecting that he was a Marxist-Leninist, and following his return the [[MI5]] intelligence service intercepted and read all his mail.{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta continued writing articles, reflecting Padmore's influence.{{sfn
column4: p=176}} Between 1931 and 1937 he wrote several articles for the ''Negro Worker'' and joined the newspaper's editorial board in 1933.{{sfn
column7: pp=66, 68}} He also produced an article for a November 1933 issue of ''[[Labour Monthly]]'',{{sfn
column10: p=177}} and in May 1934 had a letter published in ''[[The Guardian
column14: p=64}} He also wrote the entry on Kenya for ''Negro'', an anthology edited by [[Nancy Cunard]] and published in 1934.{{sfnm
column24: 3p=62}} In these, he took a more radical position than he had in the past, calling for complete self-rule in Kenya.{{sfn
column27: pp=175–176}} In doing so he was virtually alone among political Kenyans; figures like Thuku and Jesse Kariuki were far more moderate in their demands.{{sfn
column30: p=179}} The pro-independence sentiments that he was able to express in Britain would not have been permitted in Kenya itself.{{sfn

column1: ===University College London and the London School of Economics: 1933–1939===
Between 1935 and 1937, Kenyatta worked as a [[Informant (linguistics)
column2: linguistic informant]] for the Phonetics Department at [[University College London]] (UCL); his Kikuyu voice recordings assisted [[Lilias Armstrong]]'s production of ''The Phonetic and Tonal Structure of Kikuyu''.{{sfnm
column8: 2p=46}} The book was published under Armstrong's name, although Kenyatta claimed he should have been listed as co-author.{{sfn
column11: p=180}} He enrolled at UCL as a student, studying an English course between January and July 1935 and then a [[phonetics]] course from October 1935 to June 1936.{{sfnm
column17: 2p=46}} Enabled by a grant from the [[International African Institute]],{{sfnm
column29: 4p=46}} he also took a [[social anthropology]] course under [[Bronisław Malinowski]] at the [[London School of Economics]] (LSE). Kenyatta lacked the qualifications normally required to join the course, but Malinowski was keen to support the participation of indigenous peoples in anthropological research.{{sfnm
column38: 3p=59}} For Kenyatta, acquiring an advanced degree would bolster his status among Kenyans and display his intellectual equality with white Europeans in Kenya.{{sfn

column1: Over the course of his studies, Kenyatta and Malinowski became close friends.{{sfnm
column8: 2p=30}} Fellow course-mates included the anthropologists [[Audrey Richards]], [[Lucy Mair]], and [[Elspeth Huxley]].{{sfn
column11: p=189}} Another of his fellow LSE students was [[Prince Peter of Greece and Denmark]], who invited Kenyatta to stay with him and his mother, [[Princess Marie Bonaparte]], in Paris during the spring of 1936.{{sfnm

column2: image1 = JOMO KENYATTA - 95 Cambridge Street Pimlico London SW1V 4PY.jpg
footer = 95 Cambridge Street, London, where Kenyatta resided for much of his time in London; it is now marked by a [[blue plaque]].

column1: Kenyatta returned to his former dwellings at 95 Cambridge Street,{{sfn
column4: p=181}} but did not pay his landlady for over a year, owing over £100 in rent.{{sfn
column7: p=182}} This angered Ross and contributed to the breakdown of their friendship.{{sfn
column10: pp=181, 182}} He then rented a [[Camden Town]] flat with his friend Dinah Stock, whom he had met at an anti-imperialist rally in [[Trafalgar Square]].{{sfnm
column16: 2p=63}} Kenyatta socialised at the [[Student Movement House]] in [[Russell Square]], which he had joined in the spring of 1934,{{sfn
column19: p=183}} and befriended Africans in the city.{{sfn
column22: p=185}} To earn money, he worked as one of 250 black [[Extra (acting)
column23: extras]] in the film ''[[Sanders of the River]]'', filmed at [[Shepperton Studios]] in Autumn 1934.{{sfn
column26: p=185}} Several other Africans in London criticized him for doing so, arguing that the film degraded black people.{{sfn
column29: p=186}} Appearing in the film also allowed him to meet and befriend its star, the African-American [[Paul Robeson]].{{sfn

column2: Italy invaded Ethiopia (Abyssinia)]], incensing Kenyatta and other Africans in London; he became the honorary secretary of the [[International African Friends of Abyssinia]], a group established by Padmore and [[C. L. R. James]].{{sfnm
column11: 3pp=55–56}} When Ethiopia's monarch [[Haile Selassie]] fled to London in exile, Kenyatta personally welcomed him at [[London Waterloo station
column18: 2p=58}} This group developed into a wider [[pan-Africanism
column19: pan-Africanist]] organisation, the [[International African Service Bureau]] (IASB), of which Kenyatta became one of the vice chairs.{{sfnm
column25: 2pp=47–48}} Kenyatta began giving anti-colonial lectures across Britain for groups like the IASB, the [[Workers' Educational Association]], [[British Committee of the Indian National Congress
column26: Indian National Congress of Great Britain]], and the [[League of Coloured Peoples]].{{sfnm
column32: 2pp=49, 53–55}} In October 1938, he gave a talk to the Manchester Fabian Society in which he described British colonial policy as [[fascism]] and compared the treatment of indigenous people in East Africa to the [[Anti-Jewish legislation in prewar Nazi Germany
column36: p=203}} In response to these activities, the British Colonial Office reopened their file on him, although could not find any evidence that he was engaged in anything sufficiently seditious to warrant prosecution.{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta assembled the essays on Kikuyu society written for Malinowski's class and published them as ''[[Facing Mount Kenya]]'' in 1938.{{sfnm
column11: 3p=59}} Featuring an introduction written by Malinowski,{{sfnm
column18: 2p=32}} the book reflected Kenyatta's desire to use anthropology as a weapon against colonialism.{{sfn
column21: p=189}} In it, Kenyatta challenged the Eurocentric view of history by presenting an image of a golden African past by emphasising the perceived order, virtue, and self-sufficiency of Kikuyu society.{{sfn
column32: 2p=36}} he promoted the idea that traditional Kikuyu society had a cohesion and integrity that was better than anything offered by European colonialism.{{sfn
column35: p=191}} In this book, Kenyatta made clear his belief that the rights of the individual should be downgraded in favour of the interests of the group.{{sfn
column38: p=193}} The book also reflected his changing views on female genital mutilation; where once he opposed it, he now unequivocally supported the practice, downplaying the medical dangers that it posed to women.{{sfnm

column1: The book's jacket cover featured an image of Kenyatta in traditional dress, wearing a skin cloak over one shoulder and carrying a spear.{{sfnm
column11: 3p=31}} The book was published under the name ""Jomo Kenyatta"", the first time that he had done so; the term ''Jomo'' was close to a Kikuyu word describing the removal of a sword from its scabbard.{{sfn
column14: pp=194, 196}} ''Facing Mount Kenya'' was a commercial failure, selling only 517 copies, but was generally well received;{{sfn
column17: p=195}} an exception was among white Kenyans, whose assumptions about the Kikuyu being primitive savages in need of European civilization it challenged.{{sfn
column20: pp=168–169}} Murray-Brown later described it as ""a propaganda ''tour de force''. No other African had made such an uncompromising stand for tribal integrity.""{{sfn
column23: p=192}} Bodil Folke Frederiksen, a scholar of [[development studies]], referred to it as ""probably the most well-known and influential African scholarly work of its time"",{{sfn
column26: p=36}} while for fellow scholar Simon Gikandi, it was ""one of the major texts in what has come to be known as the invention of tradition in colonial Africa"".{{sfn

column4: quote=""In the last war 300,000 of my people fought in the British Army to drive the Germans from East Africa and 60,000 of them lost their lives. In this war large numbers of my people have been fighting to smash fascist power in Africa and have borne some of the hardest fights against the Italians. Surely if we are considered fit enough to take our rifles and fight side by side with white men we have a right to a direct say in the running of our country and to education.""

column1: After the United Kingdom entered [[World War II]] in September 1939, Kenyatta and Stock moved to the [[Sussex]] village of [[Storrington]].{{sfnm
column11: 3p=81}} Kenyatta remained there for the duration of the war, renting a flat and a small plot of land to grow vegetables and raise chickens.{{sfnm
column17: 2p=81}} He settled into rural Sussex life,{{sfnm
column23: 2p=81}} and became a regular at the village pub, where he gained the nickname ""Jumbo"".{{sfnm
column32: 3p=81}} In August 1940, he took a job at a local farm as an agricultural worker—allowing him to evade [[Conscription in the United Kingdom
column33: military conscription]]—before working in the tomato greenhouses at [[Lindfield, West Sussex
column43: 3p=81}} He attempted to join the local [[Home Guard (United Kingdom)
column44: Home Guard]], but was turned down.{{sfn
column47: p=211}} On 11 May 1942 he married an English woman, Edna Grace Clarke, at [[Register office (United Kingdom)
column54: 2p=84}} In August 1943, their son, Peter Magana, was born.{{sfnm

column1: Intelligence services continued monitoring Kenyatta, noting that he was politically inactive between 1939 and 1944.{{sfn
column4: p=85}} In Sussex, he wrote an essay for the United Society for Christian Literature, ''My People of Kikuyu and the Life of Chief Wangombe'', in which he called for his tribe's political independence.{{sfnm
column14: 3p=95}} He also began—although never finished—a novel partly based on his life experiences.{{sfnm
column21: 2p=35}} He continued to give lectures around the country, including to groups of East African soldiers stationed in Britain.{{sfnm
column27: 2pp=83–84}} He became frustrated by the distance between him and Kenya, telling Edna that he felt ""like a general separated by 5000 miles from his troops"".{{sfn
column30: pp=216–217}} While he was absent, Kenya's authorities banned the KCA in 1940.{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta and other senior IASB members began planning the fifth [[Pan-African Congress]], held in Manchester in October 1945.{{sfnm
column10: 3p=85}} They were assisted by [[Kwame Nkrumah]], a [[Gold Coast (British colony)
column11: Gold Coast]] (Ghanaian) who arrived in Britain earlier that year.{{sfnm
column17: 2p=53}} Kenyatta spoke at the conference, although made no particular impact on the proceedings.{{sfn
column20: pp=220–221}} Much of the debate that took place centred on whether indigenous Africans should continue pursuing a gradual campaign for independence or whether they should seek the military overthrow of the European imperialists.{{sfn
column23: p=220}} The conference ended with a statement declaring that while delegates desired a peaceful transition to African self-rule, Africans ""as a last resort, may have to appeal to force in the effort to achieve Freedom"".{{sfn
column26: pp=220–221}} Kenyatta supported this resolution, although was more cautious than other delegates and made no open commitment to violence.{{sfnm
column32: 2pp=54–55}} He subsequently authored an IASB pamphlet, ''Kenya: The Land of Conflict'', in which he blended political calls for independence with romanticised descriptions of an idealised pre-colonial African past.{{sfnm

column1: [[File:Jomo Kenyatta. Nairobi. 1949. Photo by Gopal Singh of Star Studio.jpg
After British victory in World War II, Kenyatta received a request to return to Kenya in September 1946, sailing back that month.{{sfnm
column10: 3p=106}} He decided not to bring Edna—who was pregnant with a second child{{sfnm
column16: 2p=106}}—with him, aware that if they joined him in Kenya their lives would be made very difficult by the colony's racial laws.{{sfn
column19: p=60}} On his arrival in Mombasa, Kenyatta was greeted by his first wife, Grace Wahu and their children.{{sfn
column22: pp=222–228}} He built a bungalow at [[Gatundu]], near to where he was born, and began farming his 32-acre estate.{{sfn
column25: p=230}} Kenyatta met with the new Governor of Kenya, [[Philip Euen Mitchell]], and in March 1947 accepted a post on an African Land Settlement Board, holding the post for two years.{{sfnm
column37: 4p=114}} He also met with [[Mbiyu Koinange]] to discuss the future of the Koinange Independent Teachers' College in Githungui, Koinange appointing Kenyatta as its Vice-Principal.{{sfn
column40: pp=229–230}} In May 1947, Koinange moved to England, leaving Kenyatta to take full control of the college.{{sfnm
column46: 2p=230}} Under Kenyatta's leadership, additional funds were raised for the construction of school buildings and the number of boys in attendance rose from 250 to 900.{{sfn
column49: pp=230–231}} It was also beset with problems, including a decline in standards and teachers' strikes over non-payment of wages. Gradually, the number of enrolled pupils fell.{{sfn
column52: p=231}} Kenyatta built a friendship with Koinange's father, a Senior Chief, who gave Kenyatta one of his daughters to take as his third wife.{{sfn

column1: They had another child, but she died in childbirth.{{sfn
column4: p=243}} In 1951, he married his fourth wife, [[Ngina Kenyatta
column5: Ngina]], who was one of the few female students at his college; she then gave birth to a daughter.{{sfnm

column4: In October 1951 Kenyatta selected colors for the KAU flag: green for the land, black for the skin of the people, and red for the blood of liberty.{{sfn

column1: In August 1944, the [[Kenya African Union]] (KAU) had been founded; at that time it was the only active political outlet for indigenous Africans in the colony.{{sfnm
column7: 2p=113}} At its June 1947 [[annual general meeting]], KAU's President [[James Gichuru]] stepped down and Kenyatta was elected as his replacement.{{sfnm
column19: 4p=117}} Kenyatta began to draw large crowds wherever he travelled in Kikuyuland,{{sfn
column22: p=233}} and Kikuyu press began describing him as the ""Saviour"", ""Great Elder"", and ""Hero of Our Race"".{{sfn
column25: p=234}} He was nevertheless aware that to achieve independence, KAU needed the support of other indigenous tribes and ethnic groups.{{sfn
column28: p=225}} This was made difficult by the fact that many Maasai and [[Luo people of Kenya and Tanzania
column29: Luo]]—tribes traditionally hostile to the Kikuyu—regarded him as an advocate of Kikuyu dominance.{{sfn
column32: p=226}} He insisted on intertribal representation on the KAU executive and ensured that party business was conducted in [[Swahili language
column33: Swahili]], the ''lingua franca'' of indigenous Kenyans.{{sfn

column1: To attract support from Kenya's Indian community, he made contact with [[Jawaharlal Nehru]], the first [[Prime Minister of India
column2: Prime Minister]] of the new Indian republic. Nehru's response was supportive, sending a message to Kenya's Indian minority reminding them that they were the guests of the indigenous African population.{{sfn
column5: p=233}} Relations with the white minority remained strained; for most white Kenyans, Kenyatta was their principal enemy, an agitator with links to the Soviet Union who had the impertinence to marry a white woman.{{sfn
column8: p=227}} They too increasingly called for further Kenyan autonomy from the British government, but wanted continued white-minority rule and closer links to the white-minority governments of South Africa, [[Northern Rhodesia]], and [[Southern Rhodesia]]; they viewed Britain's [[Attlee ministry
column9: newly elected Labour government]] with great suspicion.{{sfn
column12: pp=226–227}} The white Electors' Union put forward a ""Kenya Plan"" which proposed greater white settlement in Kenya, bringing Tanganyika into the British Empire, and incorporating it within their new British East African Dominion.{{sfn
column15: p=237}} In April 1950, Kenyatta was present at a joint meeting of KAU and the [[East African Indian National Congress]] in which they both expressed opposition to the Kenya Plan.{{sfn

column1: By 1952, Kenyatta was widely recognized as a national leader, both by his supporters and by his opponents.{{sfn
column4: p=181}} As KAU leader, he was at pains to oppose all illegal activity, including workers' strikes.{{sfn
column7: p=229}} He called on his supporters to work hard, and to abandon laziness, theft, and crime.{{sfnm
column13: 2p=119}} He also insisted that in an independent Kenya, all racial groups would be safeguarded.{{sfn
column16: p=244}} Kenyatta's gradualist and peaceful approach contrasted with the growth of the [[Mau Mau Uprising]], as armed guerrilla groups began targeting the white minority and members of the Kikuyu community who did not support them. By 1959, the Mau Mau had killed around 1,880 people.{{sfn
column19: p=32}} For many young Mau Mau militants, Kenyatta was regarded as a hero,{{sfn
column22: p=98}} and they included his name in the oaths they gave to the organisation; such oathing was a Kikuyu custom by which individuals pledged allegiance to another.{{sfn
column25: p=123}} Kenyatta publicly distanced himself from the Mau Mau.{{sfn
column28: p=121}} In April 1952, he began a speaking tour in which he denounced the Mau Mau to assembled crowds, insisting that independence must be achieved through peaceful means.{{sfnm
column40: 4p=123}} In August he attended a much-publicised mass meeting in Kiambu where—in front of 30,000 people—he said that ""Mau Mau has spoiled the country. Let Mau Mau perish forever. All people should search for Mau Mau and kill it.""{{sfn
column43: pp=248–249}} Despite Kenyatta's vocal opposition to the Mau Mau, KAU had moved towards a position of greater militancy.{{sfn
column46: p=241}} At its 1951 AGM, more militant African nationalists had taken senior positions and the party officially announced its call for Kenyan independence within three years.{{sfn
column49: p=242}} In January 1952, KAU members formed a secret Central Committee devoted to direct action, formulated along a [[Clandestine cell system
column53: p=242}} Whatever Kenyatta's views on these developments, he had little ability to control them.{{sfn
column56: p=243}} He was increasingly frustrated, and—without the intellectual companionship he experienced in Britain—felt lonely.{{sfn

column4: quote=""We Africans are in the majority [in Kenya], and we should have self-government. That does not mean we should not take account of whites, provided we have the key position. We want to be friendly with whites. We don't want to be dominated by them.""
column5: source= —Kenyatta, quoted by the ''[[Daily Express]]'', September 1952{{sfn

column1: In October 1952, Kenyatta was arrested and driven to Nairobi, where he was taken aboard a plane and flown to [[Lokitaung]], northwest Kenya, one of the most remote locations in the country.{{sfn
column4: pp=253–254, 257}} From there he wrote to his family to let them know of his situation.{{sfn
column7: p=257}} Kenya's authorities believed that detaining Kenyatta would help quell civil unrest.{{sfn
column10: p=258}} Many white settlers wanted him exiled, but the government feared this would turn him into a martyr for the anti-colonialist cause.{{sfnm
column16: 2p=60}} They thought it better that he be convicted and imprisoned, although at the time had nothing to charge him with, and so began searching his personal files for evidence of criminal activity.{{sfn
column19: p=258}} Eventually, they charged him and five senior KAU members with masterminding the Mau Mau, a proscribed group.{{sfn
column22: p=259}} The historian John M. Lonsdale stated that Kenyatta had been made a ""scapegoat"",{{sfn
column25: p=403}} while the historian A. B. Assensoh later suggested that the authorities ""knew very well"" that Kenyatta was not involved in the Mau Mau, but that they were nevertheless committed to silencing his calls for independence.{{sfn

column1: The trial took place in [[Kapenguria]], a remote area near the Ugandan border that the authorities hoped would not attract crowds or attention.{{sfnm
column7: 2p=134}} Together, Kenyatta, [[Bildad Kaggia]], [[Fred Kubai]], [[Paul Ngei]], [[Achieng Oneko]] and [[Kung'u Karumba]]—the ""[[Kapenguria Six]]""—were put on trial.{{sfn
column10: p=258}} The defendants assembled an international and multiracial team of defence lawyers, including [[Chaman Lall]], [[H. O. Davies]], [[Fitz Remedios Santana de Souza
column11: F. R. S. De Souza]], and [[Dudley Thompson]], led by British barrister and Member of Parliament [[Denis Nowell Pritt]].{{sfn
column14: p=259}} Pritt's involvement brought much media attention;{{sfn
column17: p=259}} during the trial he faced government harassment and was sent death threats.{{sfnm
column23: 2p=142}} The judge selected, [[Ransley Thacker]], had recently retired from the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]];{{sfn
column26: p=259}} the government knew he would be sympathetic to their case and gave him £20,000 to oversee it.{{sfn
column29: p=129}} The trial lasted five months: [[Rawson Macharia]], the main prosecution witness, turned out to have perjured himself; the judge had only recently been awarded an unusually large pension and maintained secret contact with the then colonial Governor [[Evelyn Baring, 1st Baron Howick of Glendale
column33: p=65}} The prosecution failed to produce any strong evidence that Kenyatta or the other accused had any involvement in managing the Mau Mau.{{sfn

column1: In April 1953, Judge Thacker found the defendants guilty.{{sfnm
column10: 3p=129}} He sentenced them to seven years' [[hard labour]], to be followed by indefinite restriction preventing them from leaving a given area without permission.{{sfnm
column19: 3p=129}} In addressing the court, Kenyatta stated that he and the others did not recognise the judge's findings; they claimed that the government had used them as scapegoats as a pretext to shut down KAU.{{sfnm
column25: 2p=274}} The historian Wunyabari O. Maloba later characterised it as ""a rigged political trial with a predetermined outcome"".{{sfn
column28: p=129}} The government followed the verdict with a wider crackdown, banning KAU in June 1953,{{sfn
column31: p=255}} and closing down most of the independent schools in the country, including Kenyatta's.{{sfn
column34: p=255}} It appropriated his land at Gatundu and demolished his house.{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta and the others were returned to Lokitaung, where they resided on [[Remand (detention)
column2: remand]] while awaiting the results of the [[appeal]] process.{{sfn
column5: p=278}} Pritt pointed out that Thacker had been appointed magistrate for the wrong district, a technicality voiding the whole trial; the Supreme Court of Kenya concurred and Kenyatta and the others were freed in July 1953, only to be immediately re-arrested.{{sfn
column8: p=278}} The government took the case to the [[East African Court of Appeal]], which reversed the Supreme Court's decision in August.{{sfn
column11: p=278}} The appeals process resumed in October 1953, and in January 1954 the Supreme Court upheld the convictions against all but Oneko.{{sfn
column14: p=279}} Pritt finally took the case to the [[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
column15: Privy Council]] in London, but they refused his petition without providing an explanation. He later noted that this was despite the fact his case was one of the strongest he had ever presented during his career.{{sfnm
column27: 4p=135}} According to Murray-Brown, it is likely that political, rather than legal considerations, informed their decision to reject the case.{{sfn

column4: Tanganyikan children with signs demanding Kenyatta's release]]

column1: During the appeal process, a prison had been built at Lokitaung, where Kenyatta and the four others were then interned.{{sfnm
column7: 2p=135}} The others were made to break rocks in the hot sun but Kenyatta, because of his age, was instead appointed their cook, preparing a daily diet of beans and [[posho]].{{sfnm
column13: 2p=136}} In 1955, P. de Robeck became the District Officer, after which Kenyatta and the other inmates were treated more leniently.{{sfn
column16: pp=283–284}} In April 1954, they had been joined by a captured Mau Mau commander, [[Waruhiu Itote]]; Kenyatta befriended him, and gave him English lessons.{{sfnm
column22: 2p=139}} By 1957, the inmates had formed into two rival cliques, with Kenyatta and Itote on one side and the other KAU members—now calling themselves the ""National Democratic Party""—on the other.{{sfnm
column28: 2p=138}} In one incident, one of his rivals made an unsuccessful attempt to stab Kenyatta at breakfast.{{sfn
column31: pp=294–295}} Kenyatta's health had deteriorated in prison; manacles had caused problems for his feet and he had [[eczema]] across his body.{{sfnm

column1: Kenyatta's imprisonment transformed him into a political martyr for many Kenyans, further enhancing his status.{{sfn
column4: p=181}} A Luo anti-colonial activist, [[Jaramogi Oginga Odinga]], was the first to publicly call for Kenyatta's release, an issue that gained growing support among Kenya's anti-colonialists.{{sfn
column7: pp=93, 199}} In 1955, the British writer [[Montagu Slater]]—a socialist sympathetic to Kenyatta's plight—released ''The Trial of Jomo Kenyatta'', a book which raised the profile of the case.{{sfnm
column13: 2pp=27, 34}} In 1958, Rawson Macharia, the key witness in the state's prosecution of Kenyatta, signed an affidavit swearing that his evidence against Kenyatta had been false; this was widely publicised.{{sfn
column16: p=161}} By the late 1950s, the imprisoned Kenyatta had become a symbol of African nationalism across the continent.{{sfn

column1: His sentence served, in April 1959 Kenyatta was released from Lokitaung.{{sfnm
column7: 2p=140}} The administration then placed a restricting order on Kenyatta, forcing him to reside in the remote area of [[Lodwar]], where he had to report to the district commissioner twice a day.{{sfnm
column13: 2pp=140, 143}} There, he was joined by his wife Ngina.{{sfn
column16: p=296}} In October 1961, they had another son, [[Uhuru Kenyatta
column17: Uhuru]], and later on another daughter, Nyokabi, and a further son, Muhoho.{{sfn
column20: p=320}} Kenyatta spent two years in Lodwar.{{sfn
column23: p=297}} The Governor of Kenya, [[Patrick Muir Renison]], insisted that it was necessary; in a March 1961 speech, he described Kenyatta an ""African leader to darkness and death"" and stated that if he were released, violence would erupt.{{sfn

column2: footer = Among those lobbying for Kenyatta's release from indefinite detention were Tanganyika's Julius Nyerere and Ghana's Kwame Nkrumah.

column1: This indefinite detention was widely interpreted internationally as a reflection of the cruelties of British imperialism.{{sfn
column4: p=144}} Calls for his release came from the Chinese government,{{sfn
column10: pp=155–156}} and Tanganyika's Prime Minister [[Julius Nyerere]].{{sfnm
column16: 2p=152}} Kwame Nkrumah—whom Kenyatta had known since the 1940s and who was now President of a newly independent Ghana—personally raised the issue with British Prime Minister [[Harold Macmillan]] and other UK officials,{{sfn
column19: pp=147–149}} with the Ghanaian government offering Kenyatta asylum in the event of his release.{{sfn
column22: p=147}} Resolutions calling for his release were produced at the [[All-African Peoples' Conference]]s held in [[Tunis]] in 1960 and [[Cairo]] in 1961.{{sfn
column25: p=96}} Internal calls for his release came from Kenyan Asian activists in the [[Kenya Indian Congress]],{{sfn
column28: p=169}} while a colonial government commissioned poll revealed that most of Kenya's indigenous Africans wanted this outcome.{{sfn

column1: By this point, it was widely accepted that Kenyan independence was inevitable, the British Empire having been dismantled throughout much of Asia and Macmillan having made his ""[[Wind of Change (speech)
column5: pp=287–288}} In January 1960, the British government made its intention to free Kenya apparent.{{sfn
column8: p=299}} It invited representatives of Kenya's anti-colonial movement to [[Lancaster House Conferences (Kenya)
column9: discuss the transition]] at London's [[Lancaster House]]. An agreement was reached that an election would be called for a new 65-seat Legislative Council, with 33 seats reserved for black Africans, 20 for other ethnic groups, and 12 as 'national members' elected by a pan-racial electorate.{{sfn
column12: p=62}} It was clear to all concerned that Kenyatta was going to be the key to the future of Kenyan politics.{{sfn

column1: After the Lancaster House negotiations, the anti-colonial movement had split into two parties, the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU), which was dominated by Kikuyu and Luo, and the [[Kenya African Democratic Union]] (KADU), which was led largely by members of smaller ethnic groups like the Kalenjin and Maasai.{{sfnm
column10: 3p=204}} In May 1960, KANU nominated Kenyatta as its president, although the government vetoed it, insisting that he had been an instigator of the Mau Mau.{{sfn
column13: p=300}} KANU then declared that it would refuse to take part in any government unless Kenyatta was freed.{{sfn
column16: p=303}} KANU campaigned on the issue of Kenyatta's detainment in the [[1961 Kenyan general election
column17: February 1961 election]], where it gained a majority of votes.{{sfnm
column23: 2p=49}} KANU nevertheless refused to form a government, which was instead created through a KADU-led coalition of smaller parties.{{sfnm
column35: 4p=59}} Kenyatta had kept abreast of these developments, although he had refused to back either KANU or KADU,{{sfn
column38: p=304}} instead insisting on unity between the two parties.{{sfnm

column1: Renison decided to release Kenyatta before Kenya achieved independence. He thought public exposure to Kenyatta prior to elections would make the populace less likely to vote for a man Renison regarded as a violent extremist.{{sfn
column4: p=182}} In April 1961, the government flew Kenyatta to [[Maralal]], where he maintained his innocence of the charges but told reporters that he bore no grudges.{{sfnm
column13: 3pp=182–183}} He reiterated that he had never supported violence or the illegal oathing system used by the Mau Mau,{{sfn
column16: p=50}} and denied having ever been a Marxist, stating: ""I shall always remain an African Nationalist to the end"".{{sfn
column19: pp=304–305}} In August, he was moved to Gatundu in Kikuyuland, where he was greeted by a crowd of 10,000.{{sfnm
column28: 3p=191}} There, the colonial government had built him a new house to replace that they had demolished.{{sfn
column31: p=186}} Now a free man, he travelled to cities like Nairobi and Mombasa to make public appearances.{{sfn

column1: After his release, Kenyatta set about trying to ensure that he was the only realistic option as Kenya's future leader.{{sfn
column4: p=149}} In August he met with Renison at Kiambu,{{sfnm
column13: 3p=191}} and was interviewed by the [[BBC]]'s ''[[Face to Face (British TV series)
column17: p=307}} In October 1961, Kenyatta formally joined KANU and accepted its presidency.{{sfnm
column26: 3p=209}} In January 1962 he was elected unopposed as KANU's representative for the [[Murang'a
column27: Fort Hall]] constituency in the legislative council after its sitting member, Kariuki Njiiri, resigned.{{sfnm

column4: Kenyatta became close friends with the last British Governor of Kenya, Malcolm MacDonald, who helped speed the process of independence.]]

column1: Kenyatta traveled elsewhere in Africa, visiting Tanganyika in October 1961 and Ethiopia in November at the invitation of their governments.{{sfn
column4: pp=192–193}} A key issue facing Kenya was a border dispute in [[North Eastern Province (Kenya)
column5: North East Province]], alongside Somalia. Ethnic Somalis inhabited this region and claimed it should be part of Somalia, not Kenya.{{sfnm
column11: 2p=52}} Kenyatta disagreed, insisting the land remain Kenyan,{{sfn
column14: pp=174–175}} and stated that Somalis in Kenya should ""pack up [their] camels and go to Somalia"".{{sfn
column17: p=104}} In June 1962, Kenyatta travelled to [[Mogadishu]] to discuss the issue with the Somalian authorities, but the two sides could not reach an agreement.{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta sought to gain the confidence of the white settler community. In 1962, the white minority had produced 80% of the country's exports and were a vital part of its economy, yet between 1962 and 1963 they were emigrating at a rate of 700 a month; Kenyatta feared that this white exodus would cause a [[brain drain]] and [[Labour shortage
column2: skills shortage]] that would be detrimental to the economy.{{sfn
column5: p=66}} He was also aware that the confidence of the white minority would be crucial to securing Western investment in Kenya's economy.{{sfn
column8: p=309}} Kenyatta made it clear that when in power, he would not sack any white civil servants unless there were competent black individuals capable of replacing them.{{sfn
column11: p=187}} He was sufficiently successful that several prominent white Kenyans backed KANU in the subsequent election.{{sfn

column1: In 1962 he returned to London to attend one of the Lancaster House conferences.{{sfnm
column7: 2p=55}} There, KANU and KADU representatives met with British officials to formulate a new constitution.{{sfn
column10: p=152}} KADU desired a federalist state organised on a system they called ''[[Majimbo]]'' with six largely autonomous regional authorities, a two-chamber legislature, and a central Federal Council of Ministers who would select a rotating chair to serve as head of government for a one-year term. Renison's administration and most white settlers favoured this system as it would prevent a strong central government implementing radical reform.{{sfn
column13: pp=209–213}} KANU opposed ''Majimbo'', believing that it served entrenched interests and denied equal opportunities across Kenya; they also insisted on an elected head of government.{{sfn
column16: p=215}} At Kenyatta's prompting, KANU conceded to some of KADU's demands; he was aware that he could amend the constitution when in office.{{sfnm
column22: 2pp=217–218}} The new constitution divided Kenya into six regions, each with a regional assembly, but also featured a strong central government and both an upper and a lower house.{{sfn
column25: p=152}} It was agreed that a temporary coalition government would be established until independence, several KANU politicians being given ministerial posts.{{sfn
column28: p=220}} Kenyatta accepted a minor position, that of the Minister of State for Constitutional Affairs and Economic Planning.{{sfnm

column1: The British government considered Renison too ill at ease with indigenous Africans to oversee the transition to independence and thus replaced him with [[Malcolm MacDonald]] as Governor of Kenya in January 1963.{{sfn
column4: pp=222–223}} MacDonald and Kenyatta developed a strong friendship;{{sfn
column7: p=230}} the Briton referred to the latter as ""the wisest and perhaps strongest as well as most popular potential Prime Minister of the independent nation to be"".{{sfn
column10: p=234}} MacDonald sped up plans for Kenyan independence, believing that the longer the wait, the greater the opportunity for radicalisation among African nationalists.{{sfn
column13: p=239}} An election was scheduled for May, with self-government in June, followed by full independence in December 1964.{{sfn

column2: May 1963 general election]] pitted Kenyatta's KANU against KADU, the Akamba People's Party, and various independent candidates.{{sfnm
column8: 2p=120}} KANU was victorious with 83 seats out of 124 in the [[House of Representatives (Kenya)
column12: p=308}} a KANU majority government replaced the pre-existing coalition.{{sfn
column15: p=244}} On 1 June 1963, Kenyatta was sworn in as prime minister of the autonomous Kenyan government.{{sfnm
column27: 4pp=244, 245}} Kenya remained a monarchy, with Queen [[Elizabeth II]] as its head of state.{{sfn
column30: p=99}} In November 1963, Kenyatta's government introduced a law making it a criminal offence to disrespect the Prime Minister, exile being the punishment.{{sfn
column33: p=315}} Kenyatta's personality became a central aspect of the creation of the new state.{{sfn
column36: p=315}} In December, Nairobi's Delamere Avenue was renamed Kenyatta Avenue,{{sfnm
column42: 2p=155}} and a bronze statue of him was erected beside the country's [[National Assembly (Kenya)
column46: p=315}} Photographs of Kenyatta were widely displayed in shop windows,{{sfn
column49: p=315}} and his face was also printed on the new currency.{{sfn
column52: p=315}} In 1964, [[Oxford University Press]] published a collection of Kenyatta's speeches under the title of ''Harambee!''.{{sfn

column4: Kenyatta initially agreed to merge Kenya with Tanganyika, Uganda and Zanzibar to form an [[East African Federation]].]]

column1: Kenya's first cabinet included not only Kikuyu but also members of the Luo, Kamba, Kisii, and Maragoli tribal groups.{{sfn
column4: p=155}} In June 1963, Kenyatta met with Julius Nyerere and Ugandan President [[Milton Obote]] in Nairobi. The trio discussed the possibility of merging their three nations (plus Zanzibar) into a single [[East African Federation]], agreeing that this would be accomplished by the end of the year.{{sfnm
column13: 3p=58}} Privately, Kenyatta was more reluctant regarding the arrangement and as 1964 came around the federation had not come to pass.{{sfn
column16: p=174}} Many radical voices in Kenya urged him to pursue the project;{{sfn
column19: p=95}} in May 1964, Kenyatta rejected a back-benchers resolution calling for speedier federation.{{sfn
column22: p=174}} He publicly stated that talk of a federation had always been a ruse to hasten the pace of Kenyan independence from Britain, but Nyerere denied that this was true.{{sfn

column1: Continuing to emphasize good relations with the white settlers, in August 1963 Kenyatta met with 300 white farmers at [[Nakuru]]. He reassured them that they would be safe and welcome in an independent Kenya, and more broadly talked of forgiving and forgetting the conflicts of the past.{{sfnm
column10: 3pp=258–259}} Despite his attempts at wooing white support, he did not do the same with the Indian minority.{{sfn
column13: p=153}} Like many indigenous Africans in Kenya, Kenyatta bore a sense of resentment towards this community, despite the role that many Indians had played in securing the country's independence.{{sfn
column16: p=316}} He also encouraged the remaining Mau Mau fighters to leave the forests and settle in society.{{sfn
column19: p=309}} Throughout Kenyatta's rule, many of these individuals remained out of work, unemployment being one of the most persistent problems facing his government.{{sfn

column1: A celebration to mark independence was held in a specially constructed stadium on 12 December 1963. During the ceremony, [[Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh]]—representing the British monarchy—formally handed over control of the country to Kenyatta.{{sfnm
column7: 2p=63}} Also in attendance were leading figures from the Mau Mau.{{sfn
column10: p=60}} In a speech, Kenyatta described it as ""the greatest day in Kenya's history and the happiest day in my life.""{{sfn
column13: p=311}} He had flown Edna and Peter over for the ceremony, and in Kenya they were welcomed into Kenyatta's family by his other wives.{{sfn

column1: Disputes with Somalia over the Northern Frontier District (NFD) continued; for much of Kenyatta's rule, Somalia remained the major threat to his government.{{sfn
column4: pp=153–154}} To deal with sporadic violence in the region by Somali ''[[shifta]]'' guerrillas, Kenyatta sent soldiers into the region in December 1963 and gave them broad powers of arrest and seizure in the NFD in September 1964.{{sfn
column7: p=154}} British troops were assigned to assist the Kenyan Army in the region.{{sfn
column10: p=155}} Kenyatta also faced domestic opposition: in January 1964, sections of the army launched a mutiny in Nairobi, and Kenyatta called on the British Army to put down the rebellion.{{sfnm
column16: 2p=51}} Similar armed uprisings had taken place that month in neighboring Uganda and Tanganyika.{{sfnm
column22: 2p=51}} Kenyatta was outraged and shaken by the mutiny.{{sfn
column25: p=52}} He publicly rebuked the mutineers, emphasising the need for law and order in Kenya.{{sfn
column28: p=157}} To prevent further military unrest, he brought in a review of the salaries of the army, police, and prison staff, leading to pay rises.{{sfn
column31: p=52}} Kenyatta also wanted to contain parliamentary opposition and at Kenyatta's prompting, in November 1964 KADU officially dissolved and its representatives joined KANU.{{sfnm
column40: 3pp=265–266}} Two of the senior members of KADU, [[Ronald Ngala]] and [[Daniel arap Moi]], subsequently became some of Kenyatta's most loyal supporters.{{sfn
column43: p=160}} Kenya therefore became a ''de facto'' one-party state.{{sfnm

column4: The presidential standard of Jomo Kenyatta, adopted in 1970]]

column1: In December 1964, Kenya was officially proclaimed a republic.{{sfn
column4: p=34}} Kenyatta became its executive president,{{sfnm
column10: 2p=60}} combining the roles of [[head of state]] and [[head of government]].{{sfnm
column19: 3p=63}} Over the course of 1965 and 1966, several constitutional amendments enhanced the president's power.{{sfn
column22: p=35}} For instance, a May 1966 amendment gave the president the ability to order the [[preventive detention]] of individuals without trial if he deemed them to be security risks.{{sfnm
column28: 2p=152}} Seeking the support of Kenya's second largest ethnic group, the Luo, Kenyatta appointed the Luo Oginga Odinga as his vice president.{{sfn
column31: p=20}} The Kikuyu—who made up around 20 percent of population—still held most of the country's important government and administrative positions.{{sfnm
column37: 2p=340}} This contributed to a perception among many Kenyans that independence had simply seen the dominance of a British elite replaced by the dominance of a Kikuyu elite.{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta's calls to forgive and forget the past were a keystone of his government.{{sfnm
column7: 2p=63}} He preserved some elements of the old colonial order, particularly in relation to [[Law and order (politics)
column11: p=312}} The police and military structures were left largely intact.{{sfn
column14: p=312}} White Kenyans were left in senior positions within the judiciary, civil service, and parliament,{{sfnm
column20: 2p=63}} with the white Kenyans [[Bruce Mackenzie]] and [[Humphrey Slade]] being among Kenyatta's top officials.{{sfnm
column29: 3p=63}} Kenyatta's government nevertheless rejected the idea that the European and Asian minorities could be permitted [[dual citizenship]], expecting these communities to offer total loyalty to the independent Kenyan state.{{sfn
column32: p=112}} His administration pressured whites-only social clubs to adopt multi-racial entry policies,{{sfn
column35: p=115}} and in 1964 schools formerly reserved for European pupils were opened to Africans and Asians.{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta's government believed it necessary to cultivate a united Kenyan national culture.{{sfn
column4: p=138}} To this end, it made efforts to assert the dignity of indigenous African cultures which missionaries and colonial authorities had belittled as ""primitive"".{{sfn
column7: p=139}} An [[East African Literature Bureau]] was created to publish the work of indigenous writers.{{sfn
column10: p=140}} The Kenya Cultural Centre supported indigenous art and music, and hundreds of traditional music and dance groups were formed; Kenyatta personally insisted that such performances were held at all national celebrations.{{sfn
column13: p=141}} Support was given to the preservation of historic and cultural monuments, while street names referencing colonial figures were renamed and symbols of colonialism—like the statue of British settler [[Hugh Cholmondeley, 3rd Baron Delamere]] in Nairobi city centre—were removed.{{sfn
column16: p=140}} The government encouraged the use of Swahili as a national language, although English remained the main medium for parliamentary debates and the language of instruction in schools and universities.{{sfn
column19: p=139}} The historian Robert M. Maxon nevertheless suggested that ""no national culture emerged during the Kenyatta era"", most artistic and cultural expressions reflecting particular ethnic groups rather than a broader sense of Kenyanness, while Western culture remained heavily influential over the country's elites.{{sfn

column1: Independent Kenya had an economy heavily molded by colonial rule; agriculture dominated while industry was limited, and there was a heavy reliance on exporting primary goods while importing capital and manufactured goods.{{sfn
column4: p=83}} Under Kenyatta, the structure of this economy did not fundamentally change, remaining externally oriented and dominated by [[multinational corporation]]s and foreign capital.{{sfn
column17: 3p=6}} with no serious socialist policies being pursued;{{sfn
column20: p=208}} its focus was on achieving [[economic growth]] as opposed to equitable redistribution.{{sfn
column23: p=85}} The government passed laws to encourage foreign investment, recognising that Kenya needed foreign-trained specialists in scientific and technical fields to aid its economic development.{{sfn
column26: pp=157–158}} Under Kenyatta, Western companies regarded Kenya as a safe and profitable place for investment;{{sfn
column29: p=177}} between 1964 and 1970, large-scale foreign investment and industry in Kenya nearly doubled.{{sfn

column1: [[File:COLLECTIE TROPENMUSEUM President Jomo Kenyatta kijkt toe bij de keuring van stamboekvee tijdens de Eldoret Agricultural Show TMnr 20038663.jpg
column4: Kenyatta at an agricultural show in 1968]]

column1: In contrast to his economic policies, Kenyatta publicly claimed he would create a [[democratic socialism
column2: democratic socialist]] state with an equitable distribution of economic and social development.{{sfn
column5: p=91}} In 1965, when [[Thomas Mboya]] was minister for economic planning and development, the government issued a session paper titled ""African Socialism and its Application to Planning in Kenya"", in which it officially declared its commitment to what it called an ""[[African socialism
column15: 3p=77}} The session proposed a [[mixed economy]] with an important role for private capital,{{sfnm
column21: 2p=84}} with Kenyatta's government specifying that it would only consider [[nationalisation]] in instances where national security was at risk.{{sfnm
column27: 2p=64}} Left-wing critics highlighted that the image of ""African socialism"" portrayed in the document provided for no major shift away from the colonial economy.{{sfn

column1: Kenya's agricultural and industrial sectors were dominated by Europeans and its commerce and trade by Asians; one of Kenyatta's most pressing issues was to bring the economy under indigenous control.{{sfn
column4: p=85}} There was growing black resentment towards the Asian domination of the small business sector,{{sfn
column7: p=171}} with Kenyatta's government putting pressure on Asian-owned businesses, intending to replace them with African-owned counterparts.{{sfn
column10: p=521}} The 1965 session paper promised an ""Africanization"" of the Kenyan economy,{{sfn
column13: pp=64–65}} with the government increasingly pushing for ""black capitalism"".{{sfn
column16: p=521}} The government established the [[Industrial and Commercial Development Corporation]] to provide loans for black-owned businesses,{{sfn
column19: p=521}} and secured a 51% share in the Kenya National Assurance Company.{{sfn
column22: p=522}} In 1965, the government established the Kenya National Trading Corporation to ensure indigenous control over the trade in essential commodities,{{sfn
column25: p=64}} while the Trade Licensing Act of 1967 prohibited non-citizens from involvement in the rice, sugar, and maize trade.{{sfnm
column37: 4p=64}} During the 1970s, this expanded to cover the trade in soap, cement, and textiles.{{sfn
column40: p=64}} Many Asians who had retained British citizenship were affected by these measures.{{sfnm
column46: 2p=170}} Between late 1967 and early 1968, growing numbers of Kenyan Asians migrated to Britain;{{sfn
column49: p=114}} in February 1968 large numbers migrated quickly before [[Immigration Act 1971
column50: a legal change revoked their right to do so]].{{sfn
column53: p=172}} Kenyatta was not sympathetic to those leaving: ""Kenya's identity as an African country is not going to be altered by the whims and malaises of groups of uncommitted individuals.""{{sfn

column1: Under Kenyatta, corruption became widespread throughout the government, civil service, and business community.{{sfn
column4: pp=215–216}} Kenyatta and his family were tied up with this corruption as they enriched themselves through the mass purchase of property after 1963.{{sfn
column7: pp=236–237}} Their acquisitions in the Central, Rift Valley, and Coast Provinces aroused great anger among landless Kenyans.{{sfn
column10: p=241}} His family used his presidential position to circumvent legal or administrative obstacles to acquiring property.{{sfn
column13: p=238}} The Kenyatta family also heavily invested in the coastal hotel business, Kenyatta personally owning the Leonard Beach Hotel.{{sfn
column16: p=242}} Other businesses they were involved with included ruby mining in [[Tsavo East National Park
column17: Tsavo National Park]], the casino business, the charcoal trade—which was causing significant deforestation—and the ivory trade.{{sfn
column20: pp=242–244}} The Kenyan press, which was largely loyal to Kenyatta, did not delve into this issue;{{sfn
column23: p=236}} it was only after his death that publications appeared revealing the scale of his personal enrichment.{{sfn
column26: pp=237–238}} Kenyan corruption and Kenyatta's role in it was better known in Britain, although many of his British friends—including McDonald and Brockway—chose to believe Kenyatta was not personally involved.{{sfn

column1: Despite Kenyatta's shortcomings on economic policy, compared with the economic performance of the vast majority of countries in independent Africa, Kenya's economic success during Kenyatta's tenure was outstanding. During the years following its independence in December, 1963, Kenya attained such a high rate of economic growth that it came to be widely regarded as something of an economic ""miracle."" According to World Bank figures, Kenya's economy attained an average growth rate of 6.4 percent per year from 1965 to 1980.<ref name="":0"">{{Cite journal
column13: url-access=subscription }}</ref> Among the 40 or more independent countries in sub-Saharan Africa, only 3 exceeded that growth rate; Nigeria, Ivory Coast, and Botswana. Kenyatta's success can be attributed to his focus on the agricultural sector, particularly on cash crops such as tea and coffee.<ref name="":0"" />

column1: [[File:Dr Banda of Malawi and Jomo Kenyatta of Kenya.jpg
The question of land ownership had deep emotional resonance in Kenya, having been a major grievance against the British colonialists.{{sfn
column4: p=195}} As part of the Lancaster House negotiations, Britain's government agreed to provide Kenya with £27 million with which to buy out white farmers and redistribute their land among the indigenous population.{{sfn
column7: p=196}} To ease this transition, Kenyatta made [[Bruce McKenzie]], a white farmer, the Minister of Agriculture and Land.{{sfn
column10: p=196}} Kenyatta's government encouraged the establishment of private land-buying companies that were often headed by prominent politicians.{{sfn
column13: p=81}} The government sold or leased lands in the former White Highlands to these companies, which in turn subdivided them among individual shareholders.{{sfn
column16: p=81}} In this way, the land redistribution programs favoured the ruling party's chief constituency.{{sfn
column19: p=82}} Kenyatta himself expanded the land that he owned around Gatundu.{{sfn
column22: p=316}} Kenyans who made claims to land on the basis of ancestral ownership often found the land given to other people, including Kenyans from different parts of the country.{{sfn
column25: p=82}} Voices began to condemn the redistribution; in 1969, the MP [[Jean-Marie Seroney]] censured the sale of historically [[Nandi people
column26: Nandi]] lands in the Rift to non-Nandi, describing the settlement schemes as ""Kenyatta's colonization of the rift"".{{sfnm

column1: In part fuelled by high rural unemployment, Kenya witnessed growing rural-to-urban migration under Kenyatta's government.{{sfn
column4: pp=124–125}} This exacerbated urban unemployment and housing shortages, with squatter settlements and slums growing up and urban crime rates rising.{{sfn
column7: pp=125–126}} Kenyatta was concerned by this, and promoted the reversal of this rural-to-urban migration, but in this was unsuccessful.{{sfn
column10: p=126}} Kenyatta's government was eager to control the country's trade unions, fearing their ability to disrupt the economy.{{sfn
column13: p=522}} To this end it emphasised social welfare schemes over traditional industrial institutions,{{sfn
column16: p=522}} and in 1965 transformed the Kenya Federation of Labour into the Central Organization of Trade (COT), a body which came under strong government influence.{{sfnm
column22: 2p=91}} No strikes could be legally carried out in Kenya without COT's permission.{{sfn
column25: p=523}} There were also measures to Africanise the civil service, which by mid-1967 had become 91% African.{{sfn
column28: p=113}} During the 1960s and 1970s the [[public sector]] grew faster than the private sector.{{sfn
column31: p=118}} The growth in the public sector contributed to the significant expansion of the indigenous [[middle class]] in Kenyatta's Kenya.{{sfn

column4: The University of Nairobi, Kenya's first institution of higher education, was established under Kenyatta's administration.]]

column1: The government oversaw a massive expansion in education facilities.{{sfn
column4: p=110}} In June 1963, Kenyatta ordered the Ominda Commission to determine a framework for meeting Kenya's educational needs.{{sfn
column7: pp=126–127}} Their report set out the long-term goal of universal free primary education in Kenya but argued that the government's emphasis should be on secondary and higher education to facilitate the training of indigenous African personnel to take over the civil service and other jobs requiring such an education.{{sfn
column10: p=127}} Between 1964 and 1966, the number of primary schools grew by 11.6%, and the number of secondary schools by 80%.{{sfn
column13: p=127}} By the time of Kenyatta's death, Kenya's first universities—the [[University of Nairobi]] and [[Kenyatta University]]—had been established.{{sfnm
column19: 2p=147}} Although Kenyatta died without having attained the goal of free, universal primary education in Kenya, the country had made significant advances in that direction, with 85% of Kenyan children in primary education, and within a decade of independence had trained sufficient numbers of indigenous Africans to take over the civil service.{{sfn

column1: Another priority for Kenyatta's government was improving access to healthcare services.{{sfn
column4: p=132}} It stated that its long-term goal was to establish a system of free, universal medical care.{{sfn
column7: p=133}} In the short-term, its emphasis was on increasing the overall number of doctors and registered nurses while decreasing the number of expatriates in those positions.{{sfn
column10: p=132}} In 1965, the government introduced free medical services for out-patients and children.{{sfn
column13: p=133}} By Kenyatta's death, the majority of Kenyans had access to significantly better healthcare than they had had in the colonial period.{{sfn
column16: p=133}} Before independence, the average life expectancy in Kenya was 45, but by the end of the 1970s it was 55, the second-highest in Sub-Saharan Africa.{{sfn
column19: p=134}} This improved medical care had resulted in declining mortality rates while birth rates remained high, resulting in a rapidly growing population; from 1962 to 1979, Kenya's population grew by just under 4% a year, the highest rate in the world at the time.{{sfn
column22: p=122}} This put a severe strain on social services; Kenyatta's government promoted [[family planning]] projects to stem the birth-rate, but these had little success.{{sfn

column1: [[File:Roy Innis, Jomo Kenyatta, Doris Funnye Innis in Kenya Circa 1970.jpg
column4: Kenyatta meets an American delegation from the [[Congress of Racial Equality]], including [[Roy Innis]].]]

column1: In part due to his advanced years (he was already 66–67 years old at the time of independence), Kenyatta rarely traveled outside of Eastern Africa.{{sfn
column4: p=167}} Under Kenyatta, Kenya was largely uninvolved in the affairs of other states, including those in the [[East African Community]].{{sfn
column7: p=320}} Despite his reservations about any immediate East African Federation, in June 1967 Kenyatta signed the Treaty for East African Co-operation.{{sfn
column10: p=175}} In December he attended a meeting with Tanzanian and Ugandan representatives to form the East African Economic Community, reflecting Kenyatta's cautious approach toward regional integration.{{sfn
column13: p=175}} He also took on a mediating role during the [[Congo Crisis]], heading the [[Organisation of African Unity]]'s Conciliation Commission on the Congo.{{sfn

column1: Facing the pressures of the [[Cold War]],{{sfn
column4: p=188}} Kenyatta officially pursued a policy of ""positive non-alignment"".{{sfn
column7: p=515}} In reality, his foreign policy was pro-Western and in particular pro-British.{{sfnm
column13: 2p=96}} Kenya became a member of the [[Commonwealth of Nations]],{{sfn
column16: p=313}} using this as a vehicle to put pressure on the white-minority [[apartheid]] regimes in South Africa and Rhodesia.{{sfn
column19: pp=167–168}} Britain remained one of Kenya's foremost sources of foreign trade; British aid to Kenya was among the highest in Africa.{{sfn
column22: p=515}} In 1964, Kenya and the UK signed a Memorandum of Understanding, one of only two military alliances Kenyatta's government made;{{sfn
column25: p=515}} the British [[Special Air Service]] trained Kenyatta's own bodyguards.{{sfn
column28: p=54}} Commentators argued that Britain's relationship with Kenyatta's Kenya was a [[Neo-colonialism
column29: neo-colonial]] one, with the British having exchanged their position of political power for one of influence.{{sfn
column32: p=514}} The historian Poppy Cullen nevertheless noted that there was no ""dictatorial neo-colonial control"" in Kenyatta's Kenya.{{sfn

column1: [[File:Bundesarchiv B 145 Bild-F021917-0014, Kenia, Staatsbesuch Bundespräsident Lübke.jpg
column4: Jomo Kenyatta and his son meet the [[President of Germany
column5: President of West Germany]] [[Heinrich Lübke]] in 1966.]]

column1: Although many white Kenyans accepted Kenyatta's rule, he remained opposed by white [[far right politics
column2: far-right]] activists; while in London at the [[1964 Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference
column3: July 1964 Commonwealth Conference]], he was assaulted by [[Martin Webster]], a British [[Neo-Nazism
column7: p=296}} Kenyatta's relationship with the United States was also warm; the [[United States Agency for International Development]] played a key role in helping respond to a maize shortage in [[Kamba people
column11: pp=63–65}} Kenyatta also maintained a warm relationship with Israel, including when other East African nations endorsed Arab hostility to the state;{{sfn
column14: pp=79–80}} he for instance permitted Israeli jets to refuel in Kenya on their way back from the [[Entebbe raid]].{{sfnm
column20: 2pp=190–193}} In turn, in 1976 the Israelis warned of a plot by the [[Palestinian Liberation Army]] to assassinate him, a threat he took seriously.{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta and his government were anti-communist,{{sfnm
column7: 2p=147}} and in June 1965 he warned that ""it is naive to think that there is no danger of imperialism from the East. In world power politics the East has as much designs upon us as the West and would like to serve their own interests. That is why we reject Communism.""{{sfnm
column13: 2p=76}} His governance was often criticised by communists and other leftists, some of whom accused him of being a fascist.{{sfn
column16: p=177}} When Chinese Communist official [[Zhou Enlai]] visited Dar es Salaam, his statement that ""Africa is ripe for revolution"" was clearly aimed largely at Kenya.{{sfn
column19: p=177}} In 1964, Kenyatta impounded a secret shipment of Chinese armaments that passed through Kenyan territory on its way to Uganda. Obote personally visited Kenyatta to apologise.{{sfnm
column25: 2pp=59–60}} In June 1967, Kenyatta declared the Chinese Chargé d'Affairs ''persona non grata'' in Kenya and recalled the Kenyan ambassador from [[Peking]].{{sfn
column28: p=177}} Relations with the Soviet Union were also strained; Kenyatta shut down the Lumumba Institute—an educational organisation named after the Congolese independence leader [[Patrice Lumumba]]—on the basis that it was a front for Soviet influence in Kenya.{{sfnm

column1: [[File:COLLECTIE TROPENMUSEUM President Jomo Kenyatta staande in een landrover tijdens de opening van de Eldoret Agricultural Show TMnr 20038660.jpg
column4: Kenyatta at the Eldoret Agricultural Show, 1968]]

column1: Kenyatta made clear his desire for Kenya to become a one-party state, regarding this as a better expression of national unity than a multi-party system.{{sfn
column4: p=314}} In the first five years of independence, he consolidated control of the central government,{{sfn
column7: p=84}} removing the autonomy of Kenya's provinces to prevent the entrenchment of ethnic power bases.{{sfn
column10: p=18}} He argued that centralised control of the government was needed to deal with the growth in demands for local services and to assist quicker economic development.{{sfn
column13: p=18}} In 1966, it launched a commission to examine reforms to local government operations,{{sfn
column16: p=18}} and in 1969 passed the Transfer of Functions Act, which terminated grants to local authorities and transferred major services from provincial to central control.{{sfn

column1: A major focus for Kenyatta during the first three and a half years of Kenya's independence were the divisions within KANU itself.{{sfn
column4: p=32}} Opposition to Kenyatta's government grew, particularly following the assassination of [[Pio Pinto]] in February 1965.{{sfn
column7: p=316}} Kenyatta condemned the assassination of the prominent leftist politician, although UK intelligence agencies believed that his own bodyguard had orchestrated the murder.{{sfn
column10: p=68}} Relations between Kenyatta and Odinga were strained, and at the March 1966 party conference, Odinga's post—that of party vice president—was divided among eight different politicians, greatly limiting his power and ending his position as Kenyatta's automatic successor.{{sfnm
column16: 2p=105–106}} Between 1964 and 1966, Kenyatta and other KANU conservatives had been deliberately trying to push Odinga to resign from the party.{{sfn
column19: pp=70–71}} Under growing pressure, in 1966 Odinga stepped down as state vice president, claiming that Kenya had failed to achieve economic independence and needed to adopt socialist policies. Backed by several other senior KANU figures and trade unionists, he became head of the new [[Kenya Peoples Union]] (KPU).{{sfnm
column37: 6p=108}} In its manifesto, the KPU stated that it would pursue ""truly socialist policies"" like the nationalisation of public utilities; it claimed Kenyatta's government ""want[ed] to build a capitalist system in the image of Western capitalism but are too embarrassed or dishonest to call it that.""{{sfn
column40: pp=99, 100}} The KPU were legally recognised as the [[official opposition]],{{sfn
column43: p=146}} thus restoring the country's [[two party system]].{{sfn

column1: The new party was a direct challenge to Kenyatta's rule,{{sfn
column4: p=144}} and he regarded it as a communist-inspired plot to oust him.{{sfn
column7: p=98}} Soon after the KPU's creation, the Kenyan Parliament amended the constitution to ensure that the defectors—who had originally been elected on the KANU ticket—could not automatically retain their seats and would have to stand for re-election.{{sfnm
column13: 2pp=110–111}} This resulted in the [[1966 Kenyan parliamentary by-elections
column20: 2p=111}} The Luo increasingly rallied around the KPU,{{sfn
column23: p=318}} which experienced localized violence that hindered its ability to campaign, although Kenyatta's government officially disavowed this violence.{{sfn
column26: p=147}} KANU retained the support of all national newspapers and the government-owned radio and television stations.{{sfn
column29: p=119}} Of the 29 defectors, only nine were re-elected on the KPU ticket;{{sfnm
column35: 2p=125}} Odinga was among them, having retained his Central Nyanza seat with a high majority.{{sfn
column38: p=164}} Odinga was replaced as vice president by [[Joseph Murumbi]],{{sfn
column41: p=67}} who in turn would be replaced by Moi.{{sfnm

column5: A British newsreel about Kenyatta's rule, produced in 1973]]

column1: In July 1969, Mboya—a prominent and popular Luo KANU politician—was assassinated by a Kikuyu.{{sfnm
column19: 6p=135}} Kenyatta had reportedly been concerned that Mboya, with U.S. backing, could remove him from the presidency,{{sfn
column22: p=101}} and across Kenya there were suspicions voiced that Kenyatta's government was responsible for Mboya's death.{{sfn
column25: p=67}} The killing sparked tensions between the Kikuyu and other ethnic groups across the country,{{sfnm
column31: 2p=137}} with riots breaking out in Nairobi.{{sfn
column34: p=318}} In October 1969, Kenyatta visited [[Kisumu]], located in Luo territory, to open a hospital. On being greeted by a crowd shouting KPU slogans, he lost his temper. When members of the crowd started throwing stones, Kenyatta's bodyguards opened fire on them, killing and wounding several.{{sfnm
column40: 2pp=140–143}} In response to the rise of KPU, Kenyatta had introduced oathing, a Kikuyu cultural tradition in which individuals came to Gatundu to swear their loyalty to him.{{sfnm
column52: 4p=138}} Journalists were discouraged from reporting on the oathing system, and several were deported when they tried to do so.{{sfn
column55: p=317}} Many Kenyans were pressured or forced to swear oaths, something condemned by the country's Christian establishment.{{sfnm
column61: 2p=139}} In response to the growing condemnation, the oathing was terminated in September 1969,{{sfnm
column67: 2p=139}} and Kenyatta invited leaders from other ethnic groups to a meeting in Gatundu.{{sfnm

column1: Kenyatta's government resorted to un-democratic measures to restrict the opposition.{{sfn
column4: p=21}} It used laws on detention and deportation to perpetuate its political hold.{{sfn
column7: p=23}} In 1966, it passed the Public Security (Detained and Restricted Persons) Regulations, allowing the authorities to arrest and detain anyone ""for the preservation of public security"" [[Indefinite detention without trial
column14: 2p=129}} In October 1969 the government banned the KPU,{{sfnm
column26: 4p=145}} and arrested Odinga before putting him under indefinite detainment.{{sfnm
column35: 3p=145}} With the organised opposition eliminated, from 1969, Kenya was once again a ''de facto'' one-party state.{{sfnm
column45: December 1969 general election]]—in which all candidates were from the ruling KANU—resulted in Kenyatta's government remaining in power, but many members of his government lost their parliamentary seats to rivals from within the party.{{sfnm
column51: 2p=319}} Over coming years, many other political and intellectual figures considered hostile to Kenyatta's rule were detained or imprisoned, including Seroney, Flomena Chelagat, [[George Anyona]], [[Martin Shikuku]], and [[Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o]].{{sfnm
column57: 2p=67}} Other political figures who were critical of Kenyatta's administration, including Ronald Ngala and [[Josiah Mwangi Kariuki]], were killed in incidents that many speculated were government assassinations.{{sfn

column4: Kenyatta in the last year of his life]]

column1: For many years, Kenyatta had suffered health problems. He had a mild stroke in 1966,{{sfnm
column10: p=516}} He suffered from [[gout]] and heart problems, all of which he sought to keep hidden from the public.{{sfn
column13: p=239}} By 1970, he was increasingly feeble and senile,{{sfn
column16: p=103}} and by 1975 Kenyatta had—according to Maloba—""in effect ceased to actively govern"".{{sfn
column19: p=282}} Four Kikuyu politicians—Koinange, James Gichuru, [[Njoroge Mungai]], and [[Charles Njonjo]]—formed his inner circle of associates, and he was rarely seen in public without one of them present.{{sfn
column22: p=102}} This clique faced opposition from KANU back-benchers spearheaded by Josiah Mwangi Kariuki. In March 1975 Kariuki was kidnapped, tortured, and murdered, and his body was dumped in the [[Ngong Hills]].{{sfnm
column28: 2pp=264–265}} After Kariuki's murder, Maloba noted, there was a ""noticeable erosion"" of support for Kenyatta and his government.{{sfn
column31: p=274}} Thenceforth, when the president spoke to crowds, they no longer applauded his statements.{{sfn

column1: In 1977, Kenyatta had several further strokes or heart attacks.{{sfn
column4: p=239}} On 22 August 1978, he died of a heart attack in the State House, Mombasa.{{sfnm
column13: 3p=305}} The Kenyan government had been preparing for Kenyatta's death since at least his 1968 stroke; it had requested British assistance in organising his [[state funeral]] as a result of the UK's longstanding experience in this area.{{sfnm
column19: 2p=311}} McKenzie had been employed as a go-between,{{sfn
column22: p=516}} and the structure of the funeral was orchestrated to deliberately imitate that of deceased British Prime Minister [[Winston Churchill]].{{sfn
column25: p=524}} In doing so, senior Kenyans sought to project an image of their country as a modern nation-state rather than one incumbent on tradition.{{sfn
column28: p=516}} The funeral took place at St. Andrew's Presbyterian Church, six days after Kenyatta's death.{{sfn
column31: p=518}} Britain's heir to the throne, [[Charles, Prince of Wales]], attended the event, a symbol of the value that the British government perceived in its relationship with Kenya.{{sfnm
column37: 2p=314}} African heads of state also attended, including Nyerere, [[Idi Amin]], [[Kenneth Kaunda]], and [[Hastings Banda]], as did India's [[Morarji Desai]] and Pakistan's [[Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq]].{{sfn
column40: p=316}} His body was buried in a [[mausoleum]] in the grounds of the [[Parliament Buildings (Kenya)

column1: Kenyatta's succession had been an issue of debate since independence,{{sfn
column4: p=22}} and Kenyatta had not unreservedly nominated a successor.{{sfn
column7: p=516}} The Kikuyu clique surrounding him had sought to amend the constitution to prevent vice president Moi—who was from the [[Kalenjin people]] rather than the Kikuyu—from automatically becoming acting president, but their attempts failed amid sustained popular and parliamentary opposition.{{sfnm
column13: 2pp=279, 281}} After Kenyatta's death, the transition of power proved smooth,{{sfn
column19: p=29}} As vice president, Moi was sworn in as acting president for a 90-day interim period.{{sfnm
column31: 4pp=308, 309}} In October he was unanimously elected KANU President and subsequently declared President of Kenya itself.{{sfn
column34: pp=30–31}} Moi emphasised his loyalty to Kenyatta—""I followed and was faithful to him until his last day, even when his closest friends forsook him""—and there was much expectation that he would continue the policies inaugurated by Kenyatta.{{sfn
column37: pp=33–34}} He nevertheless criticised the corruption, [[land grabbing]], and capitalistic ethos that had characterised Kenyatta's period and expressed [[populism
column38: populist]] tendencies by emphasizing a closer link to the poor.{{sfn
column41: p=34}} In 1982 he would amend the Kenyan constitution to create a ''de jure'' one-party state.{{sfn

column4: quote=""Kenyatta possessed the common touch and great leadership qualities. He was essentially a moderate trying to achieve the radical revolution of a nationalist victory in a colonialist society, and his ambivalence over many issues can best be explained by his need to contain or use his militants—and he had plenty of them. They were impatient and wanted to see effective action. Kenyatta certainly knew how to appeal to African sentiments.""
p=26}} and was committed to the belief that European colonial rule in Africa must end.{{sfn
column7: p=27}} Like other anti-colonialists, he believed that under colonialism, the human and natural resources of Africa had been used not for the benefit of Africa's population but for the enrichment of the colonisers and their European homelands.{{sfn
column10: p=27}} For Kenyatta, independence meant not just self-rule, but an end to [[Racial segregation
