column11: the colour bar]] and to the patronising attitudes and racist slang of Kenya's white minority.{{sfn
column14: p=306}} According to Murray-Brown, Kenyatta's ""basic philosophy"" throughout his life was that ""all men deserved the right to develop peacefully according to their own wishes"".{{sfn
column17: p=321}} Kenyatta expressed this in his statement that ""I have stood always for the purposes of human dignity in freedom, and for the values of tolerance and peace.""{{sfn
column20: p=322}} This approach was similar to the Zambian President Kenneth Kaunda's ideology of ""African humanism"".{{sfn

column1: Murray-Brown noted that ""Kenyatta had always kept himself free from ideological commitments"",{{sfn
column4: p=312}} while the historian William R. Ochieng observed that ""Kenyatta articulated no particular social philosophy"".{{sfn
column7: p=93}} Similarly, Assensoh noted that Kenyatta was ""not interested in social philosophies and slogans"".{{sfn
column10: p=25}} Several commentators and biographers described him as being politically [[Conservatism
column26: 5p=89}} an ideological viewpoint likely bolstered by his training in functionalist anthropology.{{sfn
column29: p=94}} He pursued, according to Maloba, ""a conservatism that worked in concert with imperial powers and was distinctly hostile to radical politics"".{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta biographer [[Guy Arnold]] described the Kenyan leader as ""a pragmatist and a moderate"", noting that his only ""radicalism"" came in the form of his ""nationalist attack"" on imperialism.{{sfn
column4: p=33}} Arnold also noted that Kenyatta ""absorbed a great deal of the British approach to politics: pragmatism, only dealing with problems when they become crises, [and] tolerance as long as the other side is only talking"".{{sfn
column7: p=32}} Donald Savage noted that Kenyatta believed in ""the importance of authority and tradition"", and that he displayed ""a remarkably consistent view of development through self-help and hard work"".{{sfn
column10: p=537}} Kenyatta was also an elitist and encouraged the emergence of an elite class in Kenya.{{sfn
column13: pp=190, 208}} He wrestled with a contradiction between his conservative desire for a renewal of traditional custom and his reformist urges to embrace Western modernity.{{sfn
column17: p=38}} He also faced a contradiction between his internal debates on Kikuyu ethics and belief in tribal identity with his need to create a non-tribalised Kenyan nationalism.{{sfn

column1: While in Britain, Kenyatta made political alliances with individuals committed to Marxism and to radical Pan-Africanism, the idea that African countries should politically unify;{{sfn
column4: p=47}} some commentators have posthumously characterised Kenyatta as a Pan-Africanist.{{sfnm
column10: 2p=10}} Maloba observed that during the colonial period Kenyatta had embraced ""radical Pan African activism"" which differed sharply from the ""deliberate conservative positions, especially on the question of African liberation"" that he espoused while Kenya's leader.{{sfn
column13: p=201}} As leader of Kenya, Kenyatta published two collected volumes of his speeches: ''Harambee'' and ''Suffering Without Bitterness''.{{sfn
column16: p=3}} The material included in these publications was carefully selected so as to avoid mention of the radicalism he exhibited while in Britain during the 1930s.{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta had been exposed to Marxist-Leninist ideas through his friendship with Padmore and the time spent in the Soviet Union,{{sfnm
column7: 2p=6}} but had also been exposed to Western forms of [[liberal democracy
column8: liberal democratic]] government through his many years in Britain.{{sfn
column11: p=312}} He appears to have had no further involvement with the communist movement after 1934.{{sfn
column15: p=29}} As Kenya's leader, Kenyatta rejected the idea that Marxism offered a useful framework for analysing his country's socio-economic situation.{{sfn
column18: p=83}} The academics Bruce J. Berman and John M. Lonsdale argued that Marxist frameworks for analysing society influenced some of his beliefs, such as his view that British colonialism had to be destroyed rather than simply reformed.{{sfn
column22: p=28}} Kenyatta nevertheless disagreed with the Marxist attitude that tribalism was backward and retrograde;{{sfn
column26: pp=28–29}} his positive attitude toward tribal society frustrated some of Kenyatta's Marxist Pan-Africanist friends in Britain, among them Padmore, James, and [[T. Ras Makonnen]], who regarded it as parochial and un-progressive.{{sfn

column1: Assensoh suggested that Kenyatta initially had socialist inclinations but ""became a victim of capitalist circumstances"";{{sfn
column4: p=4}} conversely, Savage stated that ""Kenyatta's direction was hardly towards the creation of a radical new socialist society"",{{sfn
column7: p=535}} and Ochieng called him ""an African capitalist"".{{sfn
column10: p=93}} When in power, Kenyatta displayed a preoccupation with individual and ''mbari'' land rights that were at odds with any socialist-oriented collectivisation.{{sfn
column13: p=535}} According to Maloba, Kenyatta's government ""sought to project capitalism as an African ideology, and communism (or socialism) as alien and dangerous"".{{sfn

column4: quote=""Ever a showman, [Kenyatta] could appear one moment in gaily coloured shirts, decorated with the cock of KANU, and the next in elegant suits from Savile Row, seldom without a rose in his buttonhole; he could be photographed in leopard-skin hat and cloak waving a silver fly-whisk or in old slacks on his farm tending his shrubs; he was equally at home in academic robes at a university function and in sandals and shorts on the beach at Mombasa. African exuberance and love of display found perfect expression in Kenyatta's flair alongside the dignity and respect due to 'His Excellency, the President, Mzee Jomo Kenyatta'.""

column7: p=74}} According to Murray-Brown, he ""liked being at the centre of life"",{{sfn
column10: p=184}} and was always ""a rebel at heart"" who enjoyed ""earthly pleasures"".{{sfn
column13: p=144}} One of Kenyatta's fellow LSE students, Elspeth Huxley, referred to him as ""a showman to his finger tips; jovial, a good companion, shrewd, fluent, quick, devious, subtle, [and] flesh-pot loving"".{{sfn
column16: p=189}} Kenyatta liked to dress elaborately; throughout most of his adult life, he wore finger rings and while studying at university in London took to wearing a [[Fez (hat)
column17: fez]] and cloak and carrying a silver-topped black cane.{{sfn
column20: p=184}} He adopted his surname, ""Kenyatta"", after the name of a beaded belt he often wore in early life.{{sfn
column23: p=17}} As President he collected a variety of expensive cars.{{sfn

column1: Murray-Brown noted that Kenyatta had the ability to ""appear all things to all men"",{{sfn
column4: p=233}} also displaying a ""consummate ability to keep his true purposes and abilities to himself"", for instance concealing his connections with communists and the Soviet Union both from members of the British Labour Party and from Kikuyu figures at home.{{sfn
column7: p=165}} This deviousness was sometimes interpreted as dishonesty by those who met him.{{sfn
column10: pp=215, 216}} Referring to Kenyatta's appearance in 1920s Kenya, Murray-Brown stated the leader presented himself to Europeans as ""an agreeable if somewhat seedy 'Europeanized' native"" and to indigenous Africans as ""a sophisticated man-about-town about whose political earnestness they had certain reservations"".{{sfn

column1: Simon Gikandi argued that Kenyatta, like some of his contemporaries in the Pan-African movement, was an ""Afro-Victorian"", someone whose identity had been shaped ""by the culture of colonialism and colonial institutions"", especially those of the [[Victorian era]].{{sfn
column4: p=3}} During the 1920s and 1930s, Kenyatta cultivated the image of a ""colonial gentleman"";{{sfn
column7: p=9}} in England, he displayed ""pleasant manners"" and a flexible attitude in adapting to urban situations dissimilar to the lands he had grown up in.{{sfn
column10: p=317}} A. R. Barlow, a member of the Church of Scotland Mission at Kikuyu, met with Kenyatta in Britain, later relating that he was impressed by how Kenyatta could ""mix on equal terms with Europeans and to hold his end up in spite of his handicaps, educationally and socially.""{{sfn
column13: p=316}} The South African [[Peter Abrahams]] met Kenyatta in London, noting that of all the black men involved in the city's Pan-Africanist movement, he was ""the most relaxed, sophisticated and 'westernized' of the lot of us"".{{sfn
column16: p=5}} As President, Kenyatta often reminisced nostalgically about his time in England, referring to it as ""home"" on several occasions.{{sfn
column19: p=320}} Berman and Lonsdale described his life as being preoccupied with ""a search for the reconciliation of the Western modernity he embraced and an equally valued Kikuyuness he could not discard"".{{sfn
column23: p=19}} Gikandi argued that Kenyatta's ""identification with Englishness was much more profound than both his friends and enemies have been willing to admit"".{{sfn

column1: Kenyatta has also been described as a talented orator, author, and editor.{{sfn
column5: p=19}} He had dictatorial and autocratic tendencies,{{sfn
column8: p=209}} as well as a fierce temper that could emerge as rage on occasion.{{sfnm
column14: 2p=209}} Murray-Brown noted that Kenyatta could be ""quite unscrupulous, even brutal"" in using others to get what he wanted,{{sfn
column17: p=215}} but he never displayed any physical cruelty or [[nihilism]].{{sfn
column20: p=216}} Kenyatta had no racist impulses regarding white Europeans, as can, for instance, be seen through his marriage to a white English woman.{{sfn
column23: p=216}} He told his daughter ""the English are wonderful people to live with in England.""{{sfn
column26: p=32}} He welcomed white support for his cause, so long as it was generous and unconditional, and spoke of a Kenya in which indigenous Africans, Europeans, Arabs, and Indians could all regard themselves as Kenyans, working and living alongside each other peacefully.{{sfn
column29: p=223}} Despite this, Kenyatta exhibited a general dislike of Indians, believing that they exploited indigenous Africans in Kenya.{{sfn

column4: quote=""I do not think I am—and have never been—an enemy of Europeans or the white people, because I have spent many years in England or in Europe, and even today I have many friends in various nations.""

p=23}} He viewed [[monogamy]] through an anthropological lens as an interesting Western phenomenon but did not adopt the practice himself, instead having sexual relations with a wide range of women throughout his life.{{sfn
column7: p=216}} Murray-Brown characterized Kenyatta as an ""affectionate father"" to his children, but one who was frequently absent.{{sfn
column10: p=110}} Kenyatta had two children from his first marriage with Grace Wahu: son Peter Muigai Kenyatta (born 1920), who later became a deputy minister; and daughter [[Margaret Kenyatta (born 1928)
column11: Margaret Kenyatta]] (born 1928). Margaret served as mayor of Nairobi between 1970 and 1976 and then as Kenya's ambassador to the United Nations from 1976 to 1986.<ref>{{cite news
column22: url-status=usurped}}</ref> Of these children, it was Margaret who was Kenyatta's closest confidante.{{sfnm

column1: During his trial, Kenyatta described himself as a Christian{{sfn
column4: p=265}} saying, ""I do not follow any particular denomination. I believe in Christianity as a whole.""{{sfn
column7: p=269}} Arnold stated that in England, Kenyatta's adherence to Christianity was ""desultory"".{{sfn
column10: p=27}} While in London, Kenyatta had taken an interest in the [[atheism
column11: atheist]] speakers at [[Speakers' Corner]] in [[Hyde Park, London
column15: p=130}} while an Irish Muslim friend had unsuccessfully urged Kenyatta to convert to [[Islam]].{{sfn
column18: p=130}} During his imprisonment, Kenyatta read up on Islam, [[Hinduism]], [[Buddhism]], and [[Confucianism]] through books supplied to him by Stock.{{sfnm
column24: 2p=138}} The Israeli diplomat Asher Naim visited him in this period, noting that although Kenyatta was ""not a religious man, he was appreciative of the Bible"".{{sfn
column27: p=77}} Despite portraying himself as a Christian, he found the attitudes of many European missionaries intolerable, in particular their readiness to see everything African as evil.{{sfn
column31: p=25}} In ''Facing Mount Kenya'', he challenged the missionaries' dismissive attitude toward [[ancestor veneration]], which he instead preferred to call ""ancestor communion"".{{sfn
column34: p=175}} In that book's dedication, Kenyatta invoked ""ancestral spirits"" as part of ""the Fight for African Freedom.""{{sfn

column4: A statue of Kenyatta (1971) by [[James Butler (artist)
column5: James Butler]] was erected at the [[Kenyatta International Conference Centre

column1: Within Kenya, Kenyatta came to be regarded as the ""Father of the Nation"",{{sfnm
column13: 4p=516}} and was given the unofficial title of ''[[Mzee]]'', a Swahili term meaning ""grand old man"".{{sfnm
column23: 3p=4}} From 1963 until his death, a [[cult of personality]] surrounded him in the country,{{sfn
column26: p=4}} one which deliberately interlinked Kenyan nationalism with Kenyatta's own personality.{{sfn
column29: p=4}} This use of Kenyatta as a popular symbol of the nation itself was furthered by the similarities between their names.{{sfn
column33: p=98}} He came to be regarded as a [[father figure]] not only by Kikuyu and Kenyans, but by Africans more widely.{{sfn

column1: After 1963, Maloba noted, Kenyatta became ""about the most admired post-independence African leader"" on the world stage, one who Western countries hailed as a ""beloved elder statesman.""{{sfn
column4: p=2}} His opinions were ""most valued"" both by conservative African politicians and by Western leaders.{{sfn
column7: p=196}} On becoming Kenya's leader, his anti-communist positions gained favour in the West,{{sfn
column10: p=26}} and some pro-Western governments gave him awards; in 1965 he, for instance, received medals from both [[Pope Paul VI]] and from the South Korean government.{{sfn

column1: In 1974, Arnold referred to Kenyatta as ""one of the outstanding African leaders now living"", someone who had become ""synonymous with Kenya"".{{sfn
column4: p=9}} He added that Kenyatta had been ""one of the shrewdest politicians"" on the continent,{{sfn
column7: p=209}} regarded as ""one of the great architects of African nationalist achievement since 1945"".{{sfn
column10: p=192}} Kenneth O. Nyangena characterised him as ""one of the greatest men of the twentieth century"", having been ""a beacon, a rallying point for suffering Kenyans to fight for their rights, justice and freedom"" whose ""brilliance gave strength and aspiration to people beyond the boundaries of Kenya"".{{sfn
column13: p=4}} In 2018, Maloba described him as ""one of the legendary pioneers of modern African nationalism"".{{sfn
column16: p=1}} In their examination of his writings, Berman and Lonsdale described him as a ""pioneer"" for being one of the first Kikuyu to write and publish; ""his representational achievement was unique"".{{sfn

column1: Maxon noted that in the areas of health and education, Kenya under Kenyatta ""achieved more in a decade and a half than the colonial state had accomplished in the preceding six decades.""{{sfn
column4: p=143}} By the time of Kenyatta's death, Kenya had gained higher life expectancy rates than most of Sub-Saharan Africa.{{sfn
column7: p=143}} The country had taken what Maxon called ""giant steps"" toward achieving its goal of universal primary education for Kenyan children.{{sfn
column10: p=143}} Another significant success had been in dismantling the colonial-era system of racial segregation in schools, public facilities, and social clubs peacefully and with minimal disruption.{{sfn

column1: During much of his life, Kenya's white settlers regarded Kenyatta as a malcontent and an agitator;{{sfn
column4: p=46}} for them, he was a figure of hatred and fear.{{sfn
column7: p=2}} As the historian Keith Kyle put it, for many whites Kenyatta was ""Satan Incarnate"".{{sfn
column10: p=43}} This white animosity reached its apogee between 1950 and 1952.{{sfn
column13: pp=197–198}} By 1964, this image had largely shifted, and many white settlers referred to him as ""Good Old Mzee"".{{sfn
column16: p=180}} Murray-Brown expressed the view that for many, Kenyatta's ""message of reconciliation, 'to forgive and forget', was perhaps his greatest contribution to his country and to history.""{{sfn

column1: To Ochieng, Kenyatta was ""a personification of conservative social forces and tendencies"" in Kenya.{{sfn
column4: p=93}} Towards the end of his presidency, many younger Kenyans—while respecting Kenyatta's role in attaining independence—regarded him as a [[reactionary]].{{sfn
column7: pp=192–193}} Those desiring a radical transformation of Kenyan society often compared Kenyatta's Kenya unfavourably with its southern neighbour, Julius Nyerere's Tanzania.{{sfn
column10: pp=519–520}} The criticisms that leftists like Odinga made of Kenyatta's leadership were similar to those that the intellectual [[Frantz Fanon]] had made of post-colonial leaders throughout Africa.{{sfn
column13: p=518}} Drawing upon Marxist theory, Jay O'Brien, for instance, argued that Kenyatta had come to power ""as a representative of a would-be bourgeoisie"", a coalition of ""relatively privileged petty bourgeois African elements"" who wanted simply to replace the British colonialists and ""Asian commercial bourgeoisie"" with themselves. He suggested that the British supported Kenyatta in this, seeing him as a bulwark against growing worker and peasant militancy who would ensure continued neo-colonial dominance.{{sfn

column1: Providing a similar leftist critique, the Marxist writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o stated that ""here was a black Moses who had been called by history to lead his people to the promised land of no exploitation, no oppression, but who failed to rise to the occasion"".{{sfn
column4: p=354}} Ngũgĩ saw Kenyatta as a ""twentieth-century tragic figure: he could have been a [[Vladimir Lenin
column5: Lenin]], a [[Mao Zedong]], or a [[Ho Chi Minh]]; but he ended up being a [[Chiang Kai-shek]], a [[Park Chung Hee]], or a [[Augusto Pinochet
column9: p=355}} Ngũgĩ was among Kenyan critics who claimed that Kenyatta treated Mau Mau veterans dismissively, leaving many of them impoverished and landless while seeking to remove them from the centre stage of national politics.{{sfn
column12: pp=350–351, 353}} In other areas Kenyatta's government also faced criticism; it for instance made little progress in advancing women's rights in Kenya.{{sfn

column1: In 1991, the Kenyan lawyer and human rights activist [[Gibson Kamau Kuria]] noted that in abolishing the federal system, banning independent candidates from standing in elections, setting up a unicameral legislature, and relaxing restrictions on the use of emergency powers, Kenyatta had laid ""the groundwork"" for Moi to further advance dictatorial power in Kenya during the late 1970s and 1980s.{{sfn
In its 2013 report, the [[The Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission of Kenya
column2: Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission of Kenya]] accused Kenyatta  of using his authority as president to allocate large tracts of land to himself and his family.<ref>{{Cite news
column4: title=Kenyatta Led Elite in Land Grabbing
column10: url-status=live}}</ref> The Kenyatta family is among Kenya's biggest landowners.<ref>{{Cite news
column12: title=Kenyatta Family Seeks Approval To For Its Dream City Outside Nairobi

column1: During the 1990s, there was still much frustration among tribal groups, namely in the Nandi, Nakuru, Uasin-Gishu, and Trans-Nzoia Districts, where under Kenyatta's government they had not regained the land taken by European settlers and more of it had been sold to those regarded as ""foreigners""—Kenyans from other tribes.{{sfn
column4: p=86}} Among these groups there were widespread calls for restitution and in 1991 and 1992 there were violent attacks against many of those who obtained land through Kenyatta's patronage. The violence continued sporadically until 1996, with an estimated 1500 killed and 300,000 displaced in the Rift Valley.{{sfn

column1: '''Jomo Kenyatta'''English: [[Help:IPA/English
column2: /ˈdʒoʊmoʊ kɛnˈjɑːtə/]]; Gikuyu: [[Help:IPA
column3: [⁽ᶮ⁾dʒɔ̄mɔ̄ kéɲàːtà]]][[Category:Pages with Gikuyu IPA]][[#CITEREFJones1940
column4: Jones 1940]], p. vi. (c. 1897 – 22 August 1978) was a Kenyan [[Anticolonial
column5: anti-colonial]] activist and politician who governed [[Kenya]] as its [[Prime Minister of Kenya
column6: Prime Minister]] from 1963 to 1964 and then as its first [[President of Kenya
column7: President]] from 1964 to his death in 1978. He played a significant role in the transformation of Kenya from [[Kenya Colony
column8: a colony]] of the [[British Empire]] into an independent republic. Ideologically an [[African nationalist]] and a [[conservative]], he led the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU) party from 1961 until his death. His government was responsible for numerous massacres of ethnic minorities in Kenya, particularly ethnic Somali civilians.

column2: Kikuyu]] farmers in [[Kiambu]], British East Africa. He was educated at a [[mission school]] and later on worked in various jobs before becoming politically engaged through the [[Kikuyu Central Association]]. In 1929, he travelled to [[London]] to lobby for Kikuyu land affairs. During the 1930s, he studied at [[Moscow]]'s [[Communist University of the Toilers of the East]], [[University College London]], and the [[London School of Economics]]. In 1938, he published [[Facing Mount Kenya
column3: an anthropological study of Kikuyu life]] before working as a [[Farmworker
column4: farm labourer]] in [[Sussex]] during the [[Second World War]]. Influenced by his friend [[George Padmore]], he embraced anti-colonialist and [[Pan-African]] ideas, co-organising the 1945 [[Pan-African Congress]] in [[Manchester]]. He returned to Kenya in 1946 and became a school principal. In 1947, he was elected President of the [[Kenya African Union]], through which he lobbied for independence from British colonial rule, attracting widespread indigenous support but animosity from [[White Kenyans
column5: white settlers]]. In 1952, he was among the [[Kapenguria Six]] arrested and charged with masterminding the anti-colonial [[Mau Mau Uprising]]. Although protesting his innocence—a view shared by later historians—he was convicted. He remained imprisoned at [[Lokitaung]] until 1959 and was then exiled to [[Lodwar]] until 1961.

column1: On his release, Kenyatta became President of KANU and led the party to victory in the [[1963 Kenyan general election
column2: 1963 general election]]. As Prime Minister, he oversaw the transition of the Kenya Colony into an independent republic, of which he became president in 1964. Desiring a [[one-party state]], he transferred regional powers to his central government, suppressed political dissent, and prohibited KANU's only rival—[[Jaramogi Oginga Odinga
column3: Oginga Odinga]]'s leftist [[Kenya People's Union]]—from competing in elections. He promoted reconciliation between the country's indigenous ethnic groups and its European minority, although his relations with the [[Indians in Kenya
column4: Kenyan Indians]] were strained and Kenya's army clashed with [[Somali-Kenyan conflict
column5: Somali separatists]] in the [[North Eastern Province (Kenya)
column6: North Eastern Province]] during the [[Shifta War]]. His government pursued [[capitalist]] economic policies and the ""Africanisation"" of the economy, prohibiting non-citizens from controlling key industries. Education and healthcare were expanded, while UK-funded land redistribution favoured KANU loyalists and exacerbated ethnic tensions. Under Kenyatta, Kenya joined the [[Organisation of African Unity]] and the [[Commonwealth of Nations]], espousing a pro-[[Western world
column8: anti-communist]] foreign policy amid the [[Cold War]]. Kenyatta died in office and was succeeded by [[Daniel arap Moi]]. Kenyatta's son [[Uhuru Kenyatta

column1: Kenyatta was a controversial figure. Prior to Kenyan independence, many of its white settlers regarded him as an agitator and malcontent, although across Africa he gained widespread respect as an anti-colonialist. During his presidency, he was given the honorary title of '''Mzee''' and lauded as the [[Father of the Nation]], securing support from both the black majority and the white minority with his message of reconciliation. Conversely, his rule was criticised as dictatorial, [[authoritarian]], and [[neocolonialism
column2: neocolonial]], of favouring Kikuyu over other ethnic groups, and of facilitating the growth of widespread [[Corruption in Kenya

column1: A member of the [[Kikuyu people]], Kenyatta was born with the name Kamau in the small rural village of Ngenda.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197434Assensoh199838"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Assensoh 1998]], p. 38.</ref> Birth records were not then kept among the Kikuyu, and Kenyatta's date of birth is not known.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197433Arnold197411Assensoh199838"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Assensoh 1998]], p. 38.</ref> One biographer, Jules Archer, suggested he was probably born in 1890 or 1891,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196911"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column7: Archer 1969]], p. 11. although a fuller analysis by Jeremy Murray-Brown suggested a birth c. 1897 or 1898.[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 323.</ref> Kenyatta's father was named Mūigai, and his mother Wambūi.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197434Assensoh199838"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Assensoh 1998]], p. 38.</ref> They lived in a homestead near River Thiririka, where they raised crops and bred sheep and goats.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197434Assensoh199838"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Assensoh 1998]], p. 38.</ref> Mūigai was sufficiently wealthy that he could afford to keep several wives, each living in a separate ''nyũmba'' (hut).<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196911, 14–15"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969

column1: Kenyatta was raised according to traditional Kikuyu custom and belief, and was taught the skills needed to herd the family flock.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196913–14, 16Murray-Brown197435–36"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 35–36.</ref> When he was 10 years old, his earlobes were pierced to mark his transition from childhood.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196917"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column4: Archer 1969]], p. 17.</ref> Wambūi subsequently bore another son, Kongo,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197435"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 35.</ref> shortly before Mūigai died.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197437"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 37.</ref> In keeping with Kikuyu tradition, Wambūi then married her late husband's younger brother, Ngengi.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197437"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 37.</ref> Kenyatta then took the name of Kamau wa Ngengi (""Kamau, son of Ngengi"").<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196911Murray-Brown197442Arnold197415"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column10: Arnold 1974]], p. 15.</ref> Wambūi bore her new husband a son, whom they also named Mūigai.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197437"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 37.</ref> Ngengi was harsh and resentful toward the three boys, and Wambūi decided to take her youngest son to live with her parental family further north.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197437"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 37.</ref> It was there that she died, and Kenyatta—who was very fond of the younger Mūigai—travelled to collect his infant half-brother.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197437"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column13: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 37.</ref> Kenyatta then moved in with his grandfather, Kongo wa Magana, and assisted the latter in his role as a [[Traditional medicine

column1: Missionaries have done a lot of good work because it was through the missionary that many of the Kikuyu got their first education ... and were able to learn how to read and write ... Also, the medical side of it: the missionary did very well. At the same time I think the missionaries ... did not understand the value of the African custom, and many of them tried to stamp out some of the customs without knowing the part they play in the life of the Kikuyu ... They upset the life of the people.""
<div style=""padding-bottom: 0; padding-top: 0.5em""><cite class=""left-aligned"" style="""">— Kenyatta, in a BBC interview, 1963<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196932"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969

In November 1909, Kenyatta left home and enrolled as a pupil at the [[Church of Scotland]] Mission (CSM) at [[Thogoto]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197440, 43"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 40, 43.</ref> The missionaries were zealous Christians who believed that bringing [[Christianity]] to the indigenous peoples of Eastern Africa was part of Britain's civilizing mission.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197446"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 46.</ref> While there, Kenyatta stayed at the small [[boarding school]], where he learnt stories from the [[Bible]],<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197445"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 45.</ref> and was taught to read and write in [[English language
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 45.</ref> He also performed chores for the mission, including washing the dishes and weeding the gardens.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197443"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 43.</ref> He was soon joined at the mission dormitory by his brother Kongo.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197450"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 50.</ref> The longer the pupils stayed, the more they came to resent the patronising way many of the British missionaries treated them.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197449"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Kenyatta's academic progress was unremarkable, and in July 1912 he became an apprentice to the mission's carpenter.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197448"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 48.</ref> That year, he professed his dedication to Christianity and began undergoing [[catechism]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197448"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 48.</ref> In 1913, he underwent the Kikuyu [[circumcision]] ritual; the missionaries generally disapproved of this custom, but it was an important aspect of Kikuyu tradition, allowing Kenyatta to be recognized as an adult.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197450–51Assensoh199839"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Assensoh 1998]], p. 39.</ref> Asked to take a [[Christian name]] for his upcoming baptism, he first chose both John and Peter after [[Apostles in the New Testament
column6: Jesus' apostles]]. Forced by the missionaries to choose just one, he chose Johnstone, the ''-stone'' chosen as a reference to Peter.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197452"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: baptized]] as Johnstone Kamau in August 1914.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197452Assensoh199839"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Assensoh 1998]], p. 39.</ref> After his baptism, Kenyatta moved out of the mission dormitory and lived with friends.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197453"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 53.</ref> Having completed his apprenticeship to the carpenter, Kenyatta requested that the mission allow him to be an apprentice stonemason, but they refused.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197453"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 53.</ref> He then requested that the mission recommend him for employment, but the head missionary refused because of an allegation of minor dishonesty.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197471"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Kenyatta moved to [[Thika]], where he worked for an engineering firm run by the Briton John Cook. In this position, he was tasked with fetching the company wages from a bank in Nairobi, 25 miles (40 km) away.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197471Assensoh199840–41"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Assensoh 1998]], pp. 40–41.</ref> Kenyatta left the job when he became seriously ill; he recuperated at a friend's house in the Tumutumu Presbyterian mission.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197471–72Assensoh199841"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Assensoh 1998]], p. 41.</ref> At the time, the [[British Empire]] was engaged in the [[First World War]], and the [[British Army]] had recruited many Kikuyu. One of those who joined was Kongo, who disappeared during the conflict; his family never learned of his fate.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197473"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 73.</ref> Kenyatta did not join the armed forces, and like other Kikuyu he moved to live among the [[Maasai people
column7: Maasai]], who had refused to fight for the British.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197473Assensoh199841"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Assensoh 1998]], p. 41.</ref> Kenyatta lived with the family of an aunt who had married a Maasai chief,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197474"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 74.</ref> adopting Maasai customs and wearing Maasai jewellery, including a beaded belt known as ''kĩnyata'' in the [[Kikuyu language]]. At some point, he took to calling himself ""Kĩnyata"" or ""Kenyatta"" after this garment.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197475"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: In 1917, Kenyatta moved to [[Narok]], where he was involved in transporting livestock to Nairobi,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197474"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 74.</ref> before relocating to Nairobi to work in a store selling farming and engineering equipment.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197474"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 74.</ref> In the evenings, he took classes in a church mission school.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197474"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 74.</ref> Several months later he returned to Thika before obtaining employment building houses for the Thogota Mission.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197474–75"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 74–75.</ref> He also lived for a time in [[Dagoretti]], where he became a retainer for a local sub-chief, Kioi; in 1919 he assisted Kioi in putting the latter's case in a land dispute before a Nairobi court.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196938–39Murray-Brown197479, 80"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 79, 80.</ref> Desiring a wife,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197479"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 79.</ref> Kenyatta entered a relationship with [[Grace Wahu]], who had attended the CMS School in [[Kabete]]; she initially moved into Kenyatta's family homestead,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197479"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 79.</ref> although she joined Kenyatta in Dagoretti when Ngengi drove her out.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197479"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 79.</ref> On 20 November 1920 she gave birth to Kenyatta's son, Peter Muigai.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197479, 96Assensoh199842"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Assensoh 1998]], p. 42.</ref> In October 1920, Kenyatta was called before the Thogota Kirk Session and suspended from taking [[Holy Communion]]; the suspension was in response to his drinking and his relations with Wahu out of wedlock.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197491Assensoh199842"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Assensoh 1998]], p. 42.</ref> The church insisted that a traditional Kikuyu wedding would be inadequate, and that he must undergo a Christian marriage;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197492"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column15: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 92.</ref> this took place on 8 November 1922.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197493"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column16: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 93.</ref> Kenyatta had initially refused to cease drinking,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197492"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column17: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 92.</ref> but in July 1923 officially renounced alcohol and was allowed to return to Holy Communion.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197493–94"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: In April 1922, Kenyatta began working as a stores clerk and meter reader for Cook, who had been appointed water superintendent for Nairobi's municipal council.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197494–95Assensoh199842"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Assensoh 1998]], p. 42.</ref> He earned [[East African shilling
column5: £12/10/–]], equivalent to £614 in 2025) a month, a particularly high wage for a native African, which brought him financial independence and a growing sense of self-confidence.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197494, 95"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 94, 95.</ref> Kenyatta lived in the [[Kilimani]] neighbourhood of Nairobi,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197495"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 95.</ref> although he financed the construction of a second home at Dagoretti; he referred to this latter hut as the Kinyata Stores for he used it to hold general provisions for the neighborhood.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197495, 96Assensoh199842"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Assensoh 1998]], p. 42.</ref> He had sufficient funds that he could lend money to European clerks in the offices,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197496"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 96.</ref> and could enjoy the lifestyle offered by Nairobi, which included cinemas, football matches, and imported British fashions.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197496"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column4: Kenyatta lobbied against many of the actions of Edward Grigg, Governor of Kenya. Grigg tried to suppress many of Kenyatta's activities.]]

column2: Anti-imperialist]] sentiment was on the rise among both native and Indian communities in Kenya following the [[Irish War of Independence]] and the Russian [[October Revolution]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974103"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 103.</ref> Many indigenous Africans resented having to carry ''[[kipande]]'' identity certificates at all times, being forbidden from growing coffee, and paying taxes without political representation.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197418–19"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column4: Arnold 1974]], pp. 18–19.</ref> Political upheavals occurred in Kikuyuland—the area inhabited largely by the Kikuyu—following World War I, among them the campaigns of [[Harry Thuku]] and the East African Association, resulting in the government massacre of 21 native protesters in March 1922.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197490Arnold197419–20"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Arnold 1974]], pp. 19–20.</ref> Kenyatta had not taken part in these events,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197490"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 90.</ref> perhaps so as not to disrupt his lucrative employment prospects.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197495"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Kenyatta's interest in politics stemmed from his friendship with [[James Beauttah]], a senior figure in the [[Kikuyu Central Association]] (KCA). Beauttah took Kenyatta to a political meeting in [[Pumwani]], although this led to no firm involvement at the time.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974101"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 101.</ref> In either 1925 or early 1926, Beauttah moved to Uganda, but remained in contact with Kenyatta.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974103"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 103.</ref> When the KCA wrote to Beauttah and asked him to travel to [[London]] as their representative, he declined, but recommended that Kenyatta—who had a good command of English—go in his place.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974105"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 105.</ref> Kenyatta accepted, probably on the condition that the Association matched his pre-existing wage.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974106"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 106.</ref> He thus became the group's secretary.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199842–43"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998

column1: It is likely that the KCA purchased a motorbike for Kenyatta,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974106"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 106.</ref> which he used to travel around Kikuyuland and neighbouring areas inhabited by the [[Meru people
column4: Embu]], helping to establish new KCA branches.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196943, 46Murray-Brown1974110"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 110.</ref> In February 1928, he was part of a KCA party that visited Government House in Nairobi to give evidence in front of the [[Hilton Young Commission]], which was then considering a federation between Kenya, Uganda, and [[Tanganyika (territory)
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 105, 106.</ref> In June, he was part of a KCA team which appeared before a [[select committee (parliamentary system)
column9: select committee]] of the [[Legislative Council of Kenya
column10: Kenyan Legislative Council]] to express concerns about the recent introduction of Land Boards. Introduced by the British [[Governor of Kenya]], [[Edward Grigg, 1st Baron Altrincham
column11: Edward Grigg]], these Land Boards would hold all land in native reserves in trust for each tribal group. Both the KCA and the Kikuyu Association opposed these Land Boards, which treated Kikuyu land as collectively owned rather than recognising individual Kikuyu land ownership.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974107–108"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 107–108.</ref> Also in February, his daughter, Wambui Margaret, was born.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974110"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: By this point he was increasingly using the name ""Kenyatta"", which had a more African appearance than ""Johnstone"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974107"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

In May 1928, the KCA launched a Kikuyu-language magazine, ''Mũigwithania'' (roughly translated as ""The Reconciler"" or ""The Unifier""), in which it published news, articles, and homilies.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196946Murray-Brown1974107, 109BermanLonsdale199817"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column4: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 17.</ref> Its purpose was to help unify the Kikuyu and raise funds for the KCA.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974109"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 109.</ref> Kenyatta was listed as the publication's editor,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974107"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 107.</ref> although Murray-Brown suggested that he was not the guiding hand behind it and that his duties were largely confined to translating into Kikuyu.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974109"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 109.</ref> Aware that Thuku had been exiled for his activism, Kenyatta's took a cautious approach to campaigning, and in ''Mũigwithania'' he expressed support for the churches, district commissioners, and chiefs.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974109Maloba20189"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Maloba 2018]], p. 9.</ref> He also praised the British Empire, stating that: ""The first thing [about the Empire] is that all people are governed justly, big or small—equally. The second thing is that nobody is regarded as a slave, everyone is free to do what he or she likes without being hindered.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974109"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 109.</ref> This did not prevent Grigg from writing to the authorities in London requesting permission to shut the magazine down.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974110"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: [[File:Jomo Kenyatta Apa Pant and Acheing Oneko.jpg

After the KCA raised sufficient funds, in February 1929 Kenyatta sailed from [[Mombasa]] to Britain.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196948Murray-Brown1974111–112BermanLonsdale199823Maloba20189"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column5: Maloba 2018]], p. 9.</ref> Grigg's administration could not stop Kenyatta's journey but asked London's [[Colonial Office]] not to meet with him.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974111–112"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 111–112.</ref> He initially stayed at the [[West African Students' Union]] premises in [[West London (sub region)
column7: West London]], where he met [[Ladipo Solanke]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974114"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 114.</ref> He then lodged with a prostitute; both this and Kenyatta's lavish spending brought concern from the Church Mission Society.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974118–119"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 118–119.</ref> His landlord subsequently impounded his belongings due to unpaid debt.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974119"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 119.</ref> In the city, Kenyatta met with W. McGregor Ross at the [[Royal Empire Society]], Ross briefing him on how to deal with the Colonial Office.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974115–116"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 115–116.</ref> Kenyatta became friends with Ross' family, and accompanied them to social events in [[Hampstead]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974125–126"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 125–126.</ref> He also contacted anti-imperialists active in Britain, including the [[League Against Imperialism]], [[Fenner Brockway]], and [[Kingsley Martin]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974117BermanLonsdale199824"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 24.</ref> Grigg was in London at the same time and, despite his opposition to Kenyatta's visit, agreed to meet with him at the [[Rhodes Trust]] headquarters in April. At the meeting, Kenyatta raised the land issue and Thuku's exile, the atmosphere between the two being friendly.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974116–117"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column15: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 116–117.</ref> In spite of this, following the meeting, Grigg convinced [[Special Branch (Metropolitan Police)
column16: Special Branch]] to monitor Kenyatta.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974117"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Kenyatta developed contacts with radicals to the left of the [[Labour Party (UK)
column4: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 27.</ref> In the summer of 1929, he left London and traveled by [[Berlin]] to [[Moscow]] before returning to London in October.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBeck1966318Murray-Brown1974118–119, 121Maloba201827"">[[#CITEREFBeck1966
column7: Maloba 2018]], p. 27.</ref> Kenyatta was strongly influenced by his time in the [[Soviet Union]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974120"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 120.</ref> Back in England, he wrote three articles on the Kenyan situation for the [[Communist Party of Great Britain]]'s newspapers, the ''[[Morning Star (British newspaper)
column9: Daily Worker]]'' and ''Sunday Worker''. In these, his criticism of British imperialism was far stronger than it had been in ''Muĩgwithania''.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974119, 120BermanLonsdale199817Assensoh199844"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Assensoh 1998]], p. 44.</ref> These communist links concerned many of Kenyatta's [[liberalism
column14: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 27.</ref> In January, Kenyatta met with [[Drummond Shiels]], the [[Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies]], at the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom
column15: House of Commons]]. Kenyatta told Shiels that he was not affiliated with communist circles and was unaware of the nature of the newspaper which published his articles.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974121–122, 124Maloba201822–23"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column17: Maloba 2018]], pp. 22–23.</ref> Shiels advised Kenyatta to return home to promote Kikuyu involvement in the constitutional process and discourage violence and extremism.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974122"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: After eighteen months in Europe, Kenyatta had run out of money. The [[Anti-Slavery International
column2: Anti-Slavery Society]] advanced him funds to pay off his debts and return to Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974131"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 131.</ref> Although Kenyatta enjoyed life in London and feared arrest if he returned home,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974125"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 125.</ref> he sailed back to Mombasa in September 1930.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974142Maloba201829"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 29.</ref> On his return, his prestige among the Kikuyu was high because of his time spent in Europe.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974144Maloba201829"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: In his absence, [[female genital mutilation]] (FGM) had become a topic of strong debate in Kikuyu society. The [[Protestantism
column2: Protestant]] churches, backed by European medics and the colonial authorities, [[Campaign against female genital mutilation in colonial Kenya
column3: supported the abolition of this traditional practice]], but the KCA rallied to its defence, claiming that its abolition would damage the structure of Kikuyu society.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBeck1966312Murray-Brown1974135–137Frederiksen200825"">[[#CITEREFBeck1966
column6: Frederiksen 2008]], p. 25.</ref> Anger between the two sides had heightened, several churches expelling KCA members from their congregations, and it was widely believed that the January 1930 killing of an American missionary, [[Hulda Stumpf]], had been due to the issue.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974134, 139"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 134, 139.</ref> As Secretary of the KCA, Kenyatta met with church representatives. He expressed the view that although personally opposing FGM, he regarded its legal abolition as counter-productive, and argued that the churches should focus on eradicating the practice through educating people about its harmful effects on women's health.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974143–144BermanLonsdale199825"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 25.</ref> The meeting ended without compromise, and [[John Arthur (missionary)
column10: John Arthur]]—the head of the Church of Scotland in Kenya—later expelled Kenyatta from the church, citing what he deemed dishonesty during the debate.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974145–146BermanLonsdale199825"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 25.</ref> In 1931, Kenyatta took his son out of the church school at Thogota and enrolled him in a KCA-approved, independent school.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974148"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: With the support of all revolutionary workers and peasants we must redouble our efforts to break the bonds that bind us. We must refuse to give any support to the British imperialists either by paying taxes or obeying any of their slave laws! We can fight in unity with the workers and toilers of the whole world, and for a Free Africa.""

<div style=""padding-bottom: 0; padding-top: 0.5em""><cite class=""left-aligned"" style="""">— Kenyatta in the ''Labour Monthly'', November 1933<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974178"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
In May 1931, Kenyatta and [[Parmenas Githendu Mukiri]] sailed for Britain, intent on representing the KCA at a [[Joint committee of the Parliament of the United Kingdom
column2: Joint Committee of Parliament]] on the future of East Africa.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974149–151Arnold197426Maloba201831"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Maloba 2018]], p. 31.</ref> Kenyatta would not return to Kenya for fifteen years.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196951Murray-Brown1974151"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 151.</ref> In Britain, he spent the summer attending an [[Independent Labour Party]] [[summer school]] and [[Fabian Society]] gatherings.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974153"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 153.</ref> In June, he visited [[Geneva]], Switzerland to attend a [[Save the Children]] conference on African children.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974153Assensoh199851"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Assensoh 1998]], p. 51.</ref> In November, he met the Indian independence leader [[Mohandas Gandhi]] while in London.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974157"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 157.</ref> That month, he enrolled in the [[Woodbrooke Quaker Study Centre
column12: Woodbrooke Quaker College]] in [[Birmingham]], where he remained until the spring of 1932, attaining a certificate in English writing.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196951Murray-Brown1974155BermanLonsdale199826Maloba201859"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969

column1: In Britain, Kenyatta befriended an Afro-Caribbean Marxist, [[George Padmore]], who was working for the Soviet-run [[Comintern]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974163–165BermanLonsdale199817Assensoh199844"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Assensoh 1998]], p. 44.</ref> Over time, he became Padmore's protégé.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974171"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 171.</ref> In late 1932, he joined Padmore in Germany.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974166"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 166.</ref> Before the end of the year, the duo relocated to Moscow, where Kenyatta studied at the [[Communist University of the Toilers of the East]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974167BermanLonsdale199827Maloba201869–71"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Maloba 2018]], pp. 69–71.</ref> There he was taught arithmetic, geography, natural science, and political economy, as well as [[Marxism-Leninism
column10: Marxist-Leninist]] doctrine and the history of the Marxist-Leninist movement.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201870"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column11: Maloba 2018]], p. 70.</ref> Many Africans and members of the African diaspora were attracted to the institution because it offered free education and the opportunity to study in an environment where they were treated with dignity, free from the [[institutionalised racism]] present in the U.S. and British Empire.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201871"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column12: Maloba 2018]], p. 71.</ref> Kenyatta complained about the food, accommodation, and poor quality of English instruction.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199827"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998
column13: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 27.</ref> There is no evidence that he joined the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]],<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201872"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column14: Maloba 2018]], p. 72.</ref> and one of his fellow students later characterised him as ""the biggest reactionary I have ever met.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201873"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column15: Maloba 2018]], p. 73.</ref> Kenyatta also visited [[Siberia]], probably as part of an official guided tour.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974168Assensoh199845"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column2: Nazi]] government shifted political allegiances in Europe; the Soviet Union pursued formal alliances with France and Czechoslovakia,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974169–170BermanLonsdale199827"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 27.</ref> and thus reduced its support for the movement against British and French colonial rule in Africa.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEPolsgrove20096"">[[#CITEREFPolsgrove2009
column5: Polsgrove 2009]], p. 6.</ref> As a result, Comintern disbanded the [[International Trade Union Committee of Negro Workers]], with which both Padmore and Kenyatta were affiliated. Padmore resigned from the Soviet Communist Party in protest, and was subsequently vilified in the Soviet press.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974171Assensoh199845"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Assensoh 1998]], p. 45.</ref> Both Padmore and Kenyatta left the Soviet Union, the latter returning to London in August 1933.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974171, 174BermanLonsdale199827"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 27.</ref> The British authorities were highly suspicious of Kenyatta's time in the Soviet Union, suspecting that he was a Marxist-Leninist, and following his return the [[MI5]] intelligence service intercepted and read all his mail.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201874–75"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018

column1: Kenyatta continued writing articles, reflecting Padmore's influence.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974176"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 176.</ref> Between 1931 and 1937 he wrote several articles for the ''Negro Worker'' and joined the newspaper's editorial board in 1933.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201866, 68"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column3: Maloba 2018]], pp. 66, 68.</ref> He also produced an article for a November 1933 issue of ''[[Labour Monthly]]'',<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974177"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 177.</ref> and in May 1934 had a letter published in ''[[The Guardian
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 64.</ref> He also wrote the entry on Kenya for ''Negro'', an anthology edited by [[Nancy Cunard]] and published in 1934.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974176BermanLonsdale199828Maloba201862"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Maloba 2018]], p. 62.</ref> In these, he took a more radical position than he had in the past, calling for complete self-rule in Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974175–176"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 175–176.</ref> In doing so he was virtually alone among political Kenyans; figures like Thuku and Jesse Kariuki were far more moderate in their demands.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974179"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 179.</ref> The pro-independence sentiments that he was able to express in Britain would not have been permitted in Kenya itself.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974178"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: ===University College London and the London School of Economics: 1933–1939===
Between 1935 and 1937, Kenyatta worked as a [[Informant (linguistics)
column2: linguistic informant]] for the Phonetics Department at [[University College London]] (UCL); his Kikuyu voice recordings assisted [[Lilias Armstrong]]'s production of ''The Phonetic and Tonal Structure of Kikuyu''.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974180Assensoh199846"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Assensoh 1998]], p. 46.</ref> The book was published under Armstrong's name, although Kenyatta claimed he should have been listed as co-author.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974180"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 180.</ref> He enrolled at UCL as a student, studying an English course between January and July 1935 and then a [[phonetics]] course from October 1935 to June 1936.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974181Assensoh199846"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Assensoh 1998]], p. 46.</ref> Enabled by a grant from the [[International African Institute]],<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196955Murray-Brown1974181Arnold197428Assensoh199846"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column11: Assensoh 1998]], p. 46.</ref> he also took a [[social anthropology]] course under [[Bronisław Malinowski]] at the [[London School of Economics]] (LSE). Kenyatta lacked the qualifications normally required to join the course, but Malinowski was keen to support the participation of indigenous peoples in anthropological research.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974180–181Arnold197428Maloba201859"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Maloba 2018]], p. 59.</ref> For Kenyatta, acquiring an advanced degree would bolster his status among Kenyans and display his intellectual equality with white Europeans in Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199830"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998

column1: Over the course of his studies, Kenyatta and Malinowski became close friends.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974187BermanLonsdale199830"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 30.</ref> Fellow course-mates included the anthropologists [[Audrey Richards]], [[Lucy Mair]], and [[Elspeth Huxley]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974189"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 189.</ref> Another of his fellow LSE students was [[Prince Peter of Greece and Denmark]], who invited Kenyatta to stay with him and his mother, [[Princess Marie Bonaparte]], in Paris during the spring of 1936.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974187Frederiksen200831"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: <templatestyles src=""Multiple image/styles.css"" wrapper="".tmulti""></templatestyles><div class=""thumb tmulti floatleft""><div class=""thumbinner multiimageinner"" style=""width:404px;max-width:404px""><div class=""trow""><div class=""tsingle"" style=""width:172px;max-width:172px""><div class=""thumbimage"">[[File:JOMO KENYATTA - 95 Cambridge Street Pimlico London SW1V 4PY.jpg
column3:
226px]]
95 Cambridge Street, London, where Kenyatta resided for much of his time in London; it is now marked by a [[blue plaque]].

column1: Kenyatta returned to his former dwellings at 95 Cambridge Street,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974181"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 181.</ref> but did not pay his landlady for over a year, owing over £100 in rent.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974182"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 182.</ref> This angered Ross and contributed to the breakdown of their friendship.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974181, 182"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 181, 182.</ref> He then rented a [[Camden Town]] flat with his friend Dinah Stock, whom he had met at an anti-imperialist rally in [[Trafalgar Square]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974199–200Maloba201863"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 63.</ref> Kenyatta socialised at the [[Student Movement House]] in [[Russell Square]], which he had joined in the spring of 1934,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974183"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 183.</ref> and befriended Africans in the city.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974185"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 185.</ref> To earn money, he worked as one of 250 black [[Extra (acting)
column9: extras]] in the film ''[[Sanders of the River]]'', filmed at [[Shepperton Studios]] in Autumn 1934.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974185"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 185.</ref> Several other Africans in London criticized him for doing so, arguing that the film degraded black people.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974186"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 186.</ref> Appearing in the film also allowed him to meet and befriend its star, the African-American [[Paul Robeson]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974187"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column2: Italy invaded Ethiopia (Abyssinia)]], incensing Kenyatta and other Africans in London; he became the honorary secretary of the [[International African Friends of Abyssinia]], a group established by Padmore and [[C. L. R. James]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974196–197Assensoh199853Maloba201855–56"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Maloba 2018]], pp. 55–56.</ref> When Ethiopia's monarch [[Haile Selassie]] fled to London in exile, Kenyatta personally welcomed him at [[London Waterloo station
column8: Maloba 2018]], p. 58.</ref> This group developed into a wider [[pan-Africanism
column9: pan-Africanist]] organisation, the [[International African Service Bureau]] (IASB), of which Kenyatta became one of the vice chairs.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974199Maloba201847–48"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Maloba 2018]], pp. 47–48.</ref> Kenyatta began giving anti-colonial lectures across Britain for groups like the IASB, the [[Workers' Educational Association]], [[British Committee of the Indian National Congress
column12: Indian National Congress of Great Britain]], and the [[League of Coloured Peoples]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974203Maloba201849, 53–55"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Maloba 2018]], pp. 49, 53–55.</ref> In October 1938, he gave a talk to the Manchester Fabian Society in which he described British colonial policy as [[fascism]] and compared the treatment of indigenous people in East Africa to the [[Anti-Jewish legislation in prewar Nazi Germany
column15: treatment of Jews]] in [[Nazi Germany]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974203"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column16: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 203.</ref> In response to these activities, the British Colonial Office reopened their file on him, although could not find any evidence that he was engaged in anything sufficiently seditious to warrant prosecution.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974204"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Kenyatta assembled the essays on Kikuyu society written for Malinowski's class and published them as ''[[Facing Mount Kenya]]'' in 1938.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974189–190BermanLonsdale199830Maloba201859"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Maloba 2018]], p. 59.</ref> Featuring an introduction written by Malinowski,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974190BermanLonsdale199832"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 32.</ref> the book reflected Kenyatta's desire to use anthropology as a weapon against colonialism.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974189"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 189.</ref> In it, Kenyatta challenged the Eurocentric view of history by presenting an image of a golden African past by emphasising the perceived order, virtue, and self-sufficiency of Kikuyu society.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974190–191"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Frederiksen 2008]], p. 36.</ref> he promoted the idea that traditional Kikuyu society had a cohesion and integrity that was better than anything offered by European colonialism.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974191"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 191.</ref> In this book, Kenyatta made clear his belief that the rights of the individual should be downgraded in favour of the interests of the group.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974193"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column13: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 193.</ref> The book also reflected his changing views on female genital mutilation; where once he opposed it, he now unequivocally supported the practice, downplaying the medical dangers that it posed to women.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197447192–193Assensoh1998Frederiksen200827"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: The book's jacket cover featured an image of Kenyatta in traditional dress, wearing a skin cloak over one shoulder and carrying a spear.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196956Murray-Brown1974194BermanLonsdale199831"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column4: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 31.</ref> The book was published under the name ""Jomo Kenyatta"", the first time that he had done so; the term ''Jomo'' was close to a Kikuyu word describing the removal of a sword from its scabbard.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974194, 196"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 194, 196.</ref> ''Facing Mount Kenya'' was a commercial failure, selling only 517 copies, but was generally well received;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974195"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 195.</ref> an exception was among white Kenyans, whose assumptions about the Kikuyu being primitive savages in need of European civilization it challenged.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBernardi1993168–169"">[[#CITEREFBernardi1993
column7: Bernardi 1993]], pp. 168–169.</ref> Murray-Brown later described it as ""a propaganda ''tour de force''. No other African had made such an uncompromising stand for tribal integrity.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974192"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 192.</ref> Bodil Folke Frederiksen, a scholar of [[development studies]], referred to it as ""probably the most well-known and influential African scholarly work of its time"",<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEFrederiksen200836"">[[#CITEREFFrederiksen2008
column9: Frederiksen 2008]], p. 36.</ref> while for fellow scholar Simon Gikandi, it was ""one of the major texts in what has come to be known as the invention of tradition in colonial Africa"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGikandi200010"">[[#CITEREFGikandi2000

column1: In the last war 300,000 of my people fought in the British Army to drive the Germans from East Africa and 60,000 of them lost their lives. In this war large numbers of my people have been fighting to smash fascist power in Africa and have borne some of the hardest fights against the Italians. Surely if we are considered fit enough to take our rifles and fight side by side with white men we have a right to a direct say in the running of our country and to education.""

<div style=""padding-bottom: 0; padding-top: 0.5em""><cite class=""left-aligned"" style="""">— Kenyatta, during World War II<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974211"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

After the United Kingdom entered [[World War II]] in September 1939, Kenyatta and Stock moved to the [[Sussex]] village of [[Storrington]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974209BermanLonsdale199835Maloba201881"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Maloba 2018]], p. 81.</ref> Kenyatta remained there for the duration of the war, renting a flat and a small plot of land to grow vegetables and raise chickens.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974210Maloba201881"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 81.</ref> He settled into rural Sussex life,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974214Maloba201881"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Maloba 2018]], p. 81.</ref> and became a regular at the village pub, where he gained the nickname ""Jumbo"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196958Arnold197430Maloba201881"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column11: Maloba 2018]], p. 81.</ref> In August 1940, he took a job at a local farm as an agricultural worker—allowing him to evade [[Conscription in the United Kingdom
column12: military conscription]]—before working in the tomato greenhouses at [[Lindfield, West Sussex
column16: Maloba 2018]], p. 81.</ref> He attempted to join the local [[Home Guard (United Kingdom)
column17: Home Guard]], but was turned down.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974211"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column18: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 211.</ref> On 11 May 1942 he married an English woman, Edna Grace Clarke, at [[Register office (United Kingdom)
column21: Maloba 2018]], p. 84.</ref> In August 1943, their son, Peter Magana, was born.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974214Maloba201884"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Intelligence services continued monitoring Kenyatta, noting that he was politically inactive between 1939 and 1944.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201885"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column2: Maloba 2018]], p. 85.</ref> In Sussex, he wrote an essay for the United Society for Christian Literature, ''My People of Kikuyu and the Life of Chief Wangombe'', in which he called for his tribe's political independence.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974212BermanLonsdale199835Lonsdale200695"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Lonsdale 2006]], p. 95.</ref> He also began—although never finished—a novel partly based on his life experiences.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974211BermanLonsdale199835"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 35.</ref> He continued to give lectures around the country, including to groups of East African soldiers stationed in Britain.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974211Maloba201883–84"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Maloba 2018]], pp. 83–84.</ref> He became frustrated by the distance between him and Kenya, telling Edna that he felt ""like a general separated by 5000 miles from his troops"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974216–217"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 216–217.</ref> While he was absent, Kenya's authorities banned the KCA in 1940.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974209–210"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Kenyatta and other senior IASB members began planning the fifth [[Pan-African Congress]], held in Manchester in October 1945.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974219Assensoh199854Maloba201885"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Maloba 2018]], p. 85.</ref> They were assisted by [[Kwame Nkrumah]], a [[Gold Coast (British colony)
column5: Gold Coast]] (Ghanaian) who arrived in Britain earlier that year.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974219Assensoh199853"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Assensoh 1998]], p. 53.</ref> Kenyatta spoke at the conference, although made no particular impact on the proceedings.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974220–221"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 220–221.</ref> Much of the debate that took place centred on whether indigenous Africans should continue pursuing a gradual campaign for independence or whether they should seek the military overthrow of the European imperialists.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974220"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 220.</ref> The conference ended with a statement declaring that while delegates desired a peaceful transition to African self-rule, Africans ""as a last resort, may have to appeal to force in the effort to achieve Freedom"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974220–221"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 220–221.</ref> Kenyatta supported this resolution, although was more cautious than other delegates and made no open commitment to violence.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974Assensoh199854–55"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Assensoh 1998]], pp. 54–55.</ref> He subsequently authored an IASB pamphlet, ''Kenya: The Land of Conflict'', in which he blended political calls for independence with romanticised descriptions of an idealised pre-colonial African past.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974221BermanLonsdale199837"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: [[File:Jomo Kenyatta. Nairobi. 1949. Photo by Gopal Singh of Star Studio.jpg

After British victory in World War II, Kenyatta received a request to return to Kenya in September 1946, sailing back that month.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196961Murray-Brown1974222–223Maloba2018106"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column4: Maloba 2018]], p. 106.</ref> He decided not to bring Edna—who was pregnant with a second child<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974223Maloba2018106"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 106.</ref>—with him, aware that if they joined him in Kenya their lives would be made very difficult by the colony's racial laws.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196960"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
column7: Archer 1969]], p. 60.</ref> On his arrival in Mombasa, Kenyatta was greeted by his first wife, Grace Wahu and their children.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974222–228"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 222–228.</ref> He built a bungalow at [[Gatundu]], near to where he was born, and began farming his 32-acre estate.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974230"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 230.</ref> Kenyatta met with the new Governor of Kenya, [[Philip Euen Mitchell]], and in March 1947 accepted a post on an African Land Settlement Board, holding the post for two years.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974232Archer196969Arnold197491Maloba2018114"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column13: Maloba 2018]], p. 114.</ref> He also met with [[Mbiyu Koinange]] to discuss the future of the Koinange Independent Teachers' College in Githungui, Koinange appointing Kenyatta as its Vice-Principal.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974229–230"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 229–230.</ref> In May 1947, Koinange moved to England, leaving Kenyatta to take full control of the college.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArcher196969Murray-Brown1974230"">[[#CITEREFArcher1969
