column16: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 230.</ref> Under Kenyatta's leadership, additional funds were raised for the construction of school buildings and the number of boys in attendance rose from 250 to 900.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974230–231"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column17: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 230–231.</ref> It was also beset with problems, including a decline in standards and teachers' strikes over non-payment of wages. Gradually, the number of enrolled pupils fell.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974231"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column18: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 231.</ref> Kenyatta built a friendship with Koinange's father, a Senior Chief, who gave Kenyatta one of his daughters to take as his third wife.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974229–230"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: They had another child, but she died in childbirth.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974243"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 243.</ref> In 1951, he married his fourth wife, [[Ngina Kenyatta
column3: Ngina]], who was one of the few female students at his college; she then gave birth to a daughter.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974247Archer196967"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column4: In October 1951 Kenyatta selected colors for the KAU flag: green for the land, black for the skin of the people, and red for the blood of liberty.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974242"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: In August 1944, the [[Kenya African Union]] (KAU) had been founded; at that time it was the only active political outlet for indigenous Africans in the colony.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974226Maloba2018113"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Maloba 2018]], p. 113.</ref> At its June 1947 [[annual general meeting]], KAU's President [[James Gichuru]] stepped down and Kenyatta was elected as his replacement.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974233Archer196970Arnold197499Maloba2018117"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Maloba 2018]], p. 117.</ref> Kenyatta began to draw large crowds wherever he travelled in Kikuyuland,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974233"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 233.</ref> and Kikuyu press began describing him as the ""Saviour"", ""Great Elder"", and ""Hero of Our Race"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974234"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 234.</ref> He was nevertheless aware that to achieve independence, KAU needed the support of other indigenous tribes and ethnic groups.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974225"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 225.</ref> This was made difficult by the fact that many Maasai and [[Luo people of Kenya and Tanzania
column11: Luo]]—tribes traditionally hostile to the Kikuyu—regarded him as an advocate of Kikuyu dominance.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974226"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 226.</ref> He insisted on intertribal representation on the KAU executive and ensured that party business was conducted in [[Swahili language
column13: Swahili]], the ''lingua franca'' of indigenous Kenyans.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974226"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: To attract support from Kenya's Indian community, he made contact with [[Jawaharlal Nehru]], the first [[Prime Minister of India
column2: Prime Minister]] of the new Indian republic. Nehru's response was supportive, sending a message to Kenya's Indian minority reminding them that they were the guests of the indigenous African population.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974233"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 233.</ref> Relations with the white minority remained strained; for most white Kenyans, Kenyatta was their principal enemy, an agitator with links to the Soviet Union who had the impertinence to marry a white woman.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974227"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 227.</ref> They too increasingly called for further Kenyan autonomy from the British government, but wanted continued white-minority rule and closer links to the white-minority governments of South Africa, [[Northern Rhodesia]], and [[Southern Rhodesia]]; they viewed Britain's [[Attlee ministry
column5: newly elected Labour government]] with great suspicion.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974226–227"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 226–227.</ref> The white Electors' Union put forward a ""Kenya Plan"" which proposed greater white settlement in Kenya, bringing Tanganyika into the British Empire, and incorporating it within their new British East African Dominion.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974237"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 237.</ref> In April 1950, Kenyatta was present at a joint meeting of KAU and the [[East African Indian National Congress]] in which they both expressed opposition to the Kenya Plan.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974241"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: By 1952, Kenyatta was widely recognized as a national leader, both by his supporters and by his opponents.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974181"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 181.</ref> As KAU leader, he was at pains to oppose all illegal activity, including workers' strikes.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974229"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 229.</ref> He called on his supporters to work hard, and to abandon laziness, theft, and crime.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974244Maloba2018119"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Maloba 2018]], p. 119.</ref> He also insisted that in an independent Kenya, all racial groups would be safeguarded.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974244"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 244.</ref> Kenyatta's gradualist and peaceful approach contrasted with the growth of the [[Mau Mau Uprising]], as armed guerrilla groups began targeting the white minority and members of the Kikuyu community who did not support them. By 1959, the Mau Mau had killed around 1,880 people.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTELeman201132"">[[#CITEREFLeman2011
column7: Leman 2011]], p. 32.</ref> For many young Mau Mau militants, Kenyatta was regarded as a hero,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTELonsdale200698"">[[#CITEREFLonsdale2006
column8: Lonsdale 2006]], p. 98.</ref> and they included his name in the oaths they gave to the organisation; such oathing was a Kikuyu custom by which individuals pledged allegiance to another.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018123"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column9: Maloba 2018]], p. 123.</ref> Kenyatta publicly distanced himself from the Mau Mau.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018121"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column10: Maloba 2018]], p. 121.</ref> In April 1952, he began a speaking tour in which he denounced the Mau Mau to assembled crowds, insisting that independence must be achieved through peaceful means.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974243Arnold1974115, 118Assensoh199858Maloba2018123"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Maloba 2018]], p. 123.</ref> In August he attended a much-publicised mass meeting in Kiambu where—in front of 30,000 people—he said that ""Mau Mau has spoiled the country. Let Mau Mau perish forever. All people should search for Mau Mau and kill it.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974248–249"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column15: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 248–249.</ref> Despite Kenyatta's vocal opposition to the Mau Mau, KAU had moved towards a position of greater militancy.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974241"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column16: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 241.</ref> At its 1951 AGM, more militant African nationalists had taken senior positions and the party officially announced its call for Kenyan independence within three years.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974242"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column17: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 242.</ref> In January 1952, KAU members formed a secret Central Committee devoted to direct action, formulated along a [[Clandestine cell system
column19: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 242.</ref> Whatever Kenyatta's views on these developments, he had little ability to control them.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974243"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column20: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 243.</ref> He was increasingly frustrated, and—without the intellectual companionship he experienced in Britain—felt lonely.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018124–125"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018

column1: We Africans are in the majority [in Kenya], and we should have self-government. That does not mean we should not take account of whites, provided we have the key position. We want to be friendly with whites. We don't want to be dominated by them.""

<div style=""padding-bottom: 0; padding-top: 0.5em""><cite class=""left-aligned"" style="""">— Kenyatta, quoted by the ''[[Daily Express]]'', September 1952<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018120–121"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018

In October 1952, Kenyatta was arrested and driven to Nairobi, where he was taken aboard a plane and flown to [[Lokitaung]], northwest Kenya, one of the most remote locations in the country.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974253–254, 257"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 253–254, 257.</ref> From there he wrote to his family to let them know of his situation.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974257"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 257.</ref> Kenya's authorities believed that detaining Kenyatta would help quell civil unrest.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974258"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 258.</ref> Many white settlers wanted him exiled, but the government feared this would turn him into a martyr for the anti-colonialist cause.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974257Arnold197460"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Arnold 1974]], p. 60.</ref> They thought it better that he be convicted and imprisoned, although at the time had nothing to charge him with, and so began searching his personal files for evidence of criminal activity.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974258"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 258.</ref> Eventually, they charged him and five senior KAU members with masterminding the Mau Mau, a proscribed group.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974259"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 259.</ref> The historian John M. Lonsdale stated that Kenyatta had been made a ""scapegoat"",<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTELonsdale1990403"">[[#CITEREFLonsdale1990
column9: Lonsdale 1990]], p. 403.</ref> while the historian A. B. Assensoh later suggested that the authorities ""knew very well"" that Kenyatta was not involved in the Mau Mau, but that they were nevertheless committed to silencing his calls for independence.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199862"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998

column1: The trial took place in [[Kapenguria]], a remote area near the Ugandan border that the authorities hoped would not attract crowds or attention.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974258Arnold1974134"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Arnold 1974]], p. 134.</ref> Together, Kenyatta, [[Bildad Kaggia]], [[Fred Kubai]], [[Paul Ngei]], [[Achieng Oneko]] and [[Kung'u Karumba]]—the ""[[Kapenguria Six]]""—were put on trial.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974258"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 258.</ref> The defendants assembled an international and multiracial team of defence lawyers, including [[Chaman Lall]], [[H. O. Davies]], [[Fitz Remedios Santana de Souza
column5: F. R. S. De Souza]], and [[Dudley Thompson]], led by British barrister and Member of Parliament [[Denis Nowell Pritt]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974259"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 259.</ref> Pritt's involvement brought much media attention;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974259"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 259.</ref> during the trial he faced government harassment and was sent death threats.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974260Arnold1974142"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Arnold 1974]], p. 142.</ref> The judge selected, [[Ransley Thacker]], had recently retired from the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]];<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974259"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 259.</ref> the government knew he would be sympathetic to their case and gave him £20,000 to oversee it.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018129"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column11: Maloba 2018]], p. 129.</ref> The trial lasted five months: [[Rawson Macharia]], the main prosecution witness, turned out to have perjured himself; the judge had only recently been awarded an unusually large pension and maintained secret contact with the then colonial Governor [[Evelyn Baring, 1st Baron Howick of Glendale
column13: Anderson 2005]], p. 65.</ref> The prosecution failed to produce any strong evidence that Kenyatta or the other accused had any involvement in managing the Mau Mau.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974262"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: In April 1953, Judge Thacker found the defendants guilty.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974274Arnold1974143Maloba2018129"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Maloba 2018]], p. 129.</ref> He sentenced them to seven years' [[hard labour]], to be followed by indefinite restriction preventing them from leaving a given area without permission.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974276Arnold1974143Maloba2018129"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Maloba 2018]], p. 129.</ref> In addressing the court, Kenyatta stated that he and the others did not recognise the judge's findings; they claimed that the government had used them as scapegoats as a pretext to shut down KAU.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESlater195614Murray-Brown1974274"">[[#CITEREFSlater1956
column9: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 274.</ref> The historian Wunyabari O. Maloba later characterised it as ""a rigged political trial with a predetermined outcome"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018129"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column10: Maloba 2018]], p. 129.</ref> The government followed the verdict with a wider crackdown, banning KAU in June 1953,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974255"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 255.</ref> and closing down most of the independent schools in the country, including Kenyatta's.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974255"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 255.</ref> It appropriated his land at Gatundu and demolished his house.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018136"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018

column1: Kenyatta and the others were returned to Lokitaung, where they resided on [[Remand (detention)
column2: remand]] while awaiting the results of the [[appeal]] process.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974278"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 278.</ref> Pritt pointed out that Thacker had been appointed magistrate for the wrong district, a technicality voiding the whole trial; the Supreme Court of Kenya concurred and Kenyatta and the others were freed in July 1953, only to be immediately re-arrested.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974278"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 278.</ref> The government took the case to the [[East African Court of Appeal]], which reversed the Supreme Court's decision in August.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974278"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 278.</ref> The appeals process resumed in October 1953, and in January 1954 the Supreme Court upheld the convictions against all but Oneko.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974279"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 279.</ref> Pritt finally took the case to the [[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
column7: Privy Council]] in London, but they refused his petition without providing an explanation. He later noted that this was despite the fact his case was one of the strongest he had ever presented during his career.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESlater195626, 252Murray-Brown1974279Arnold1974140Maloba2018135"">[[#CITEREFSlater1956
column11: Maloba 2018]], p. 135.</ref> According to Murray-Brown, it is likely that political, rather than legal considerations, informed their decision to reject the case.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974279"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column4: Tanganyikan children with signs demanding Kenyatta's release]]

column1: During the appeal process, a prison had been built at Lokitaung, where Kenyatta and the four others were then interned.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974280Maloba2018135"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Maloba 2018]], p. 135.</ref> The others were made to break rocks in the hot sun but Kenyatta, because of his age, was instead appointed their cook, preparing a daily diet of beans and [[posho]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974280Maloba2018136"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Maloba 2018]], p. 136.</ref> In 1955, P. de Robeck became the District Officer, after which Kenyatta and the other inmates were treated more leniently.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974283–284"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 283–284.</ref> In April 1954, they had been joined by a captured Mau Mau commander, [[Waruhiu Itote]]; Kenyatta befriended him, and gave him English lessons.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974283, 284Maloba2018139"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Maloba 2018]], p. 139.</ref> By 1957, the inmates had formed into two rival cliques, with Kenyatta and Itote on one side and the other KAU members—now calling themselves the ""National Democratic Party""—on the other.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974291Maloba2018138"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Maloba 2018]], p. 138.</ref> In one incident, one of his rivals made an unsuccessful attempt to stab Kenyatta at breakfast.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974294–295"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 294–295.</ref> Kenyatta's health had deteriorated in prison; manacles had caused problems for his feet and he had [[eczema]] across his body.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974289Maloba2018137"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Kenyatta's imprisonment transformed him into a political martyr for many Kenyans, further enhancing his status.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974181"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 181.</ref> A Luo anti-colonial activist, [[Jaramogi Oginga Odinga]], was the first to publicly call for Kenyatta's release, an issue that gained growing support among Kenya's anti-colonialists.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197493, 199"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Arnold 1974]], pp. 93, 199.</ref> In 1955, the British writer [[Montagu Slater]]—a socialist sympathetic to Kenyatta's plight—released ''The Trial of Jomo Kenyatta'', a book which raised the profile of the case.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974145Leman201127, 34"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column5: Leman 2011]], pp. 27, 34.</ref> In 1958, Rawson Macharia, the key witness in the state's prosecution of Kenyatta, signed an affidavit swearing that his evidence against Kenyatta had been false; this was widely publicised.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018161"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 161.</ref> By the late 1950s, the imprisoned Kenyatta had become a symbol of African nationalism across the continent.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197496"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column1: His sentence served, in April 1959 Kenyatta was released from Lokitaung.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974296Maloba2018140"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Maloba 2018]], p. 140.</ref> The administration then placed a restricting order on Kenyatta, forcing him to reside in the remote area of [[Lodwar]], where he had to report to the district commissioner twice a day.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974296Maloba2018140, 143"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Maloba 2018]], pp. 140, 143.</ref> There, he was joined by his wife Ngina.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974296"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 296.</ref> In October 1961, they had another son, [[Uhuru Kenyatta
column7: Uhuru]], and later on another daughter, Nyokabi, and a further son, Muhoho.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974320"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 320.</ref> Kenyatta spent two years in Lodwar.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974297"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 297.</ref> The Governor of Kenya, [[Patrick Muir Renison]], insisted that it was necessary; in a March 1961 speech, he described Kenyatta an ""African leader to darkness and death"" and stated that if he were released, violence would erupt.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018153–154"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018

column1: <templatestyles src=""Multiple image/styles.css"" wrapper="".tmulti""></templatestyles><div class=""thumb tmulti floatleft""><div class=""thumbinner multiimageinner"" style=""width:368px;max-width:368px""><div class=""trow""><div class=""tsingle"" style=""width:192px;max-width:192px""><div class=""thumbimage"">[[File:Julius Nyerere (1965).jpg
column3:
170px]]
Among those lobbying for Kenyatta's release from indefinite detention were Tanganyika's Julius Nyerere and Ghana's Kwame Nkrumah.

column1: This indefinite detention was widely interpreted internationally as a reflection of the cruelties of British imperialism.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018144"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column2: Maloba 2018]], p. 144.</ref> Calls for his release came from the Chinese government,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018145–146"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column4: Maloba 2018]], pp. 155–156.</ref> and Tanganyika's Prime Minister [[Julius Nyerere]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974204Maloba2018152"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 152.</ref> Kwame Nkrumah—whom Kenyatta had known since the 1940s and who was now President of a newly independent Ghana—personally raised the issue with British Prime Minister [[Harold Macmillan]] and other UK officials,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018147–149"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column7: Maloba 2018]], pp. 147–149.</ref> with the Ghanaian government offering Kenyatta asylum in the event of his release.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018147"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column8: Maloba 2018]], p. 147.</ref> Resolutions calling for his release were produced at the [[All-African Peoples' Conference]]s held in [[Tunis]] in 1960 and [[Cairo]] in 1961.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197496"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column9: Arnold 1974]], p. 96.</ref> Internal calls for his release came from Kenyan Asian activists in the [[Kenya Indian Congress]],<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974169"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column10: Arnold 1974]], p. 169.</ref> while a colonial government commissioned poll revealed that most of Kenya's indigenous Africans wanted this outcome.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018176"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018

column1: By this point, it was widely accepted that Kenyan independence was inevitable, the British Empire having been dismantled throughout much of Asia and Macmillan having made his ""[[Wind of Change (speech)
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 287–288.</ref> In January 1960, the British government made its intention to free Kenya apparent.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974299"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 299.</ref> It invited representatives of Kenya's anti-colonial movement to [[Lancaster House Conferences (Kenya)
column5: discuss the transition]] at London's [[Lancaster House]]. An agreement was reached that an election would be called for a new 65-seat Legislative Council, with 33 seats reserved for black Africans, 20 for other ethnic groups, and 12 as 'national members' elected by a pan-racial electorate.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199862"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column6: Assensoh 1998]], p. 62.</ref> It was clear to all concerned that Kenyatta was going to be the key to the future of Kenyan politics.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197451"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column1: After the Lancaster House negotiations, the anti-colonial movement had split into two parties, the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU), which was dominated by Kikuyu and Luo, and the [[Kenya African Democratic Union]] (KADU), which was led largely by members of smaller ethnic groups like the Kalenjin and Maasai.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974300Assensoh199859Maloba2018204"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Maloba 2018]], p. 204.</ref> In May 1960, KANU nominated Kenyatta as its president, although the government vetoed it, insisting that he had been an instigator of the Mau Mau.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974300"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 300.</ref> KANU then declared that it would refuse to take part in any government unless Kenyatta was freed.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974303"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 303.</ref> KANU campaigned on the issue of Kenyatta's detainment in the [[1961 Kenyan general election
column7: February 1961 election]], where it gained a majority of votes.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974303Kyle199749"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Kyle 1997]], p. 49.</ref> KANU nevertheless refused to form a government, which was instead created through a KADU-led coalition of smaller parties.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974303Arnold1974184Kyle199750Assensoh199859"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column13: Assensoh 1998]], p. 59.</ref> Kenyatta had kept abreast of these developments, although he had refused to back either KANU or KADU,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974304"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 304.</ref> instead insisting on unity between the two parties.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974304Arnold1974185"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Renison decided to release Kenyatta before Kenya achieved independence. He thought public exposure to Kenyatta prior to elections would make the populace less likely to vote for a man Renison regarded as a violent extremist.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018182"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column2: Maloba 2018]], p. 182.</ref> In April 1961, the government flew Kenyatta to [[Maralal]], where he maintained his innocence of the charges but told reporters that he bore no grudges.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974304–305Kyle199750Maloba2018182–183"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Maloba 2018]], pp. 182–183.</ref> He reiterated that he had never supported violence or the illegal oathing system used by the Mau Mau,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEKyle199750"">[[#CITEREFKyle1997
column6: Kyle 1997]], p. 50.</ref> and denied having ever been a Marxist, stating: ""I shall always remain an African Nationalist to the end"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974304–305"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 304–305.</ref> In August, he was moved to Gatundu in Kikuyuland, where he was greeted by a crowd of 10,000.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974306Kyle199751Maloba2018191"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Maloba 2018]], p. 191.</ref> There, the colonial government had built him a new house to replace that they had demolished.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018186"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column11: Maloba 2018]], p. 186.</ref> Now a free man, he travelled to cities like Nairobi and Mombasa to make public appearances.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974307"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: After his release, Kenyatta set about trying to ensure that he was the only realistic option as Kenya's future leader.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974149"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 149.</ref> In August he met with Renison at Kiambu,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974307Arnold1974152Maloba2018191"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Maloba 2018]], p. 191.</ref> and was interviewed by the [[BBC]]'s ''[[Face to Face (British TV series)
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 307.</ref> In October 1961, Kenyatta formally joined KANU and accepted its presidency.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974308Arnold1974159Maloba2018209"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Maloba 2018]], p. 209.</ref> In January 1962 he was elected unopposed as KANU's representative for the [[Murang'a
column11: Fort Hall]] constituency in the legislative council after its sitting member, Kariuki Njiiri, resigned.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974308Arnold1974151–152"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column4: Kenyatta became close friends with the last British Governor of Kenya, Malcolm MacDonald, who helped speed the process of independence.]]

column1: Kenyatta traveled elsewhere in Africa, visiting Tanganyika in October 1961 and Ethiopia in November at the invitation of their governments.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018192–193"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column2: Maloba 2018]], pp. 192–193.</ref> A key issue facing Kenya was a border dispute in [[North Eastern Province (Kenya)
column3: North East Province]], alongside Somalia. Ethnic Somalis inhabited this region and claimed it should be part of Somalia, not Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974175Kyle199752"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column5: Kyle 1997]], p. 52.</ref> Kenyatta disagreed, insisting the land remain Kenyan,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974174–175"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column6: Arnold 1974]], pp. 174–175.</ref> and stated that Somalis in Kenya should ""pack up [their] camels and go to Somalia"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBranch2017104"">[[#CITEREFBranch2017
column7: Branch 2017]], p. 104.</ref> In June 1962, Kenyatta travelled to [[Mogadishu]] to discuss the issue with the Somalian authorities, but the two sides could not reach an agreement.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974176"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column1: Kenyatta sought to gain the confidence of the white settler community. In 1962, the white minority had produced 80% of the country's exports and were a vital part of its economy, yet between 1962 and 1963 they were emigrating at a rate of 700 a month; Kenyatta feared that this white exodus would cause a [[brain drain]] and [[Labour shortage
column2: skills shortage]] that would be detrimental to the economy.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197466"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Arnold 1974]], p. 66.</ref> He was also aware that the confidence of the white minority would be crucial to securing Western investment in Kenya's economy.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974309"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 309.</ref> Kenyatta made it clear that when in power, he would not sack any white civil servants unless there were competent black individuals capable of replacing them.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974187"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column5: Arnold 1974]], p. 187.</ref> He was sufficiently successful that several prominent white Kenyans backed KANU in the subsequent election.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974308"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: In 1962 he returned to London to attend one of the Lancaster House conferences.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974159Kyle199755"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Kyle 1997]], p. 55.</ref> There, KANU and KADU representatives met with British officials to formulate a new constitution.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974152"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column4: Arnold 1974]], p. 152.</ref> KADU desired a federalist state organised on a system they called ''[[Majimbo]]'' with six largely autonomous regional authorities, a two-chamber legislature, and a central Federal Council of Ministers who would select a rotating chair to serve as head of government for a one-year term. Renison's administration and most white settlers favoured this system as it would prevent a strong central government implementing radical reform.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018209–213"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column5: Maloba 2018]], pp. 209–213.</ref> KANU opposed ''Majimbo'', believing that it served entrenched interests and denied equal opportunities across Kenya; they also insisted on an elected head of government.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018215"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 215.</ref> At Kenyatta's prompting, KANU conceded to some of KADU's demands; he was aware that he could amend the constitution when in office.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974152Maloba2018217–218"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column8: Maloba 2018]], pp. 217–218.</ref> The new constitution divided Kenya into six regions, each with a regional assembly, but also featured a strong central government and both an upper and a lower house.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974152"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column9: Arnold 1974]], p. 152.</ref> It was agreed that a temporary coalition government would be established until independence, several KANU politicians being given ministerial posts.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018220"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column10: Maloba 2018]], p. 220.</ref> Kenyatta accepted a minor position, that of the Minister of State for Constitutional Affairs and Economic Planning.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974308Arnold1974159Kyle199756Maloba2018220"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: The British government considered Renison too ill at ease with indigenous Africans to oversee the transition to independence and thus replaced him with [[Malcolm MacDonald]] as Governor of Kenya in January 1963.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018222–223"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column2: Maloba 2018]], pp. 222–223.</ref> MacDonald and Kenyatta developed a strong friendship;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018230"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column3: Maloba 2018]], p. 230.</ref> the Briton referred to the latter as ""the wisest and perhaps strongest as well as most popular potential Prime Minister of the independent nation to be"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018234"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column4: Maloba 2018]], p. 234.</ref> MacDonald sped up plans for Kenyan independence, believing that the longer the wait, the greater the opportunity for radicalisation among African nationalists.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018239"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column5: Maloba 2018]], p. 239.</ref> An election was scheduled for May, with self-government in June, followed by full independence in December 1964.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018240"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018

column2: May 1963 general election]] pitted Kenyatta's KANU against KADU, the Akamba People's Party, and various independent candidates.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974308Kuria1991120"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Kuria 1991]], p. 120.</ref> KANU was victorious with 83 seats out of 124 in the [[House of Representatives (Kenya)
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 308.</ref> a KANU majority government replaced the pre-existing coalition.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2018244"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column7: Maloba 2018]], p. 244.</ref> On 1 June 1963, Kenyatta was sworn in as prime minister of the autonomous Kenyan government.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974308Arnold1974156Kyle199758Maloba2018244, 245"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column11: Maloba 2018]], pp. 244, 245.</ref> Kenya remained a monarchy, with Queen [[Elizabeth II]] as its head of state.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTELonsdale200699"">[[#CITEREFLonsdale2006
column12: Lonsdale 2006]], p. 99.</ref> In November 1963, Kenyatta's government introduced a law making it a criminal offence to disrespect the Prime Minister, exile being the punishment.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974315"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column13: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 315.</ref> Kenyatta's personality became a central aspect of the creation of the new state.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974315"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 315.</ref> In December, Nairobi's Delamere Avenue was renamed Kenyatta Avenue,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974315Arnold1974155"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column16: Arnold 1974]], p. 155.</ref> and a bronze statue of him was erected beside the country's [[National Assembly (Kenya)
column18: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 315.</ref> Photographs of Kenyatta were widely displayed in shop windows,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974315"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column19: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 315.</ref> and his face was also printed on the new currency.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974315"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column20: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 315.</ref> In 1964, [[Oxford University Press]] published a collection of Kenyatta's speeches under the title of ''Harambee!''.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199824"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998

column4: Kenyatta initially agreed to merge Kenya with Tanganyika, Uganda and Zanzibar to form an [[East African Federation]].]]

column1: Kenya's first cabinet included not only Kikuyu but also members of the Luo, Kamba, Kisii, and Maragoli tribal groups.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974155"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 155.</ref> In June 1963, Kenyatta met with Julius Nyerere and Ugandan President [[Milton Obote]] in Nairobi. The trio discussed the possibility of merging their three nations (plus Zanzibar) into a single [[East African Federation]], agreeing that this would be accomplished by the end of the year.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974173Assensoh199855Kyle199758"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column5: Kyle 1997]], p. 58.</ref> Privately, Kenyatta was more reluctant regarding the arrangement and as 1964 came around the federation had not come to pass.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974174"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column6: Arnold 1974]], p. 174.</ref> Many radical voices in Kenya urged him to pursue the project;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199595"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column7: Ochieng 1995]], p. 95.</ref> in May 1964, Kenyatta rejected a back-benchers resolution calling for speedier federation.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974174"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column8: Arnold 1974]], p. 174.</ref> He publicly stated that talk of a federation had always been a ruse to hasten the pace of Kenyan independence from Britain, but Nyerere denied that this was true.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974174"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column1: Continuing to emphasize good relations with the white settlers, in August 1963 Kenyatta met with 300 white farmers at [[Nakuru]]. He reassured them that they would be safe and welcome in an independent Kenya, and more broadly talked of forgiving and forgetting the conflicts of the past.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974309Arnold197465, 67Maloba2018258–259"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Maloba 2018]], pp. 258–259.</ref> Despite his attempts at wooing white support, he did not do the same with the Indian minority.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974153"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column5: Arnold 1974]], p. 153.</ref> Like many indigenous Africans in Kenya, Kenyatta bore a sense of resentment towards this community, despite the role that many Indians had played in securing the country's independence.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974316"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 316.</ref> He also encouraged the remaining Mau Mau fighters to leave the forests and settle in society.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974309"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 309.</ref> Throughout Kenyatta's rule, many of these individuals remained out of work, unemployment being one of the most persistent problems facing his government.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974316"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: A celebration to mark independence was held in a specially constructed stadium on 12 December 1963. During the ceremony, [[Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh]]—representing the British monarchy—formally handed over control of the country to Kenyatta.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974309–310Assensoh199863"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Assensoh 1998]], p. 63.</ref> Also in attendance were leading figures from the Mau Mau.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEKyle199760"">[[#CITEREFKyle1997
column4: Kyle 1997]], p. 60.</ref> In a speech, Kenyatta described it as ""the greatest day in Kenya's history and the happiest day in my life.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974311"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 311.</ref> He had flown Edna and Peter over for the ceremony, and in Kenya they were welcomed into Kenyatta's family by his other wives.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974310–311"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Disputes with Somalia over the Northern Frontier District (NFD) continued; for much of Kenyatta's rule, Somalia remained the major threat to his government.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017153–154"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column2: Maloba 2017]], pp. 153–154.</ref> To deal with sporadic violence in the region by Somali ''[[shifta]]'' guerrillas, Kenyatta sent soldiers into the region in December 1963 and gave them broad powers of arrest and seizure in the NFD in September 1964.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017154"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column3: Maloba 2017]], p. 154.</ref> British troops were assigned to assist the Kenyan Army in the region.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017155"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column4: Maloba 2017]], p. 155.</ref> Kenyatta also faced domestic opposition: in January 1964, sections of the army launched a mutiny in Nairobi, and Kenyatta called on the British Army to put down the rebellion.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974157Maloba201751"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column6: Maloba 2017]], p. 51.</ref> Similar armed uprisings had taken place that month in neighboring Uganda and Tanganyika.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974157Maloba201751"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column8: Maloba 2017]], p. 51.</ref> Kenyatta was outraged and shaken by the mutiny.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201752"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column9: Maloba 2017]], p. 52.</ref> He publicly rebuked the mutineers, emphasising the need for law and order in Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974157"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column10: Arnold 1974]], p. 157.</ref> To prevent further military unrest, he brought in a review of the salaries of the army, police, and prison staff, leading to pay rises.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201752"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column11: Maloba 2017]], p. 52.</ref> Kenyatta also wanted to contain parliamentary opposition and at Kenyatta's prompting, in November 1964 KADU officially dissolved and its representatives joined KANU.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974314–315Arnold1974160Maloba2018265–266"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Maloba 2018]], pp. 265–266.</ref> Two of the senior members of KADU, [[Ronald Ngala]] and [[Daniel arap Moi]], subsequently became some of Kenyatta's most loyal supporters.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974160"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column15: Arnold 1974]], p. 160.</ref> Kenya therefore became a ''de facto'' one-party state.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel197034Arnold1974160"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970

column4: The presidential standard of Jomo Kenyatta, adopted in 1970]]

column1: In December 1964, Kenya was officially proclaimed a republic.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel197034"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970
column2: Gertzel 1970]], p. 34.</ref> Kenyatta became its executive president,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974166Kyle199760"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column4: Kyle 1997]], p. 60.</ref> combining the roles of [[head of state]] and [[head of government]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel197034Murray-Brown1974314–315Assensoh199863"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970
column7: Assensoh 1998]], p. 63.</ref> Over the course of 1965 and 1966, several constitutional amendments enhanced the president's power.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel197035"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970
column8: Gertzel 1970]], p. 35.</ref> For instance, a May 1966 amendment gave the president the ability to order the [[preventive detention]] of individuals without trial if he deemed them to be security risks.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199594Gertzel1970152"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column10: Gertzel 1970]], p. 152.</ref> Seeking the support of Kenya's second largest ethnic group, the Luo, Kenyatta appointed the Luo Oginga Odinga as his vice president.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199820"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column11: Assensoh 1998]], p. 20.</ref> The Kikuyu—who made up around 20 percent of population—still held most of the country's important government and administrative positions.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974316Maloba2017340"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column13: Maloba 2017]], p. 340.</ref> This contributed to a perception among many Kenyans that independence had simply seen the dominance of a British elite replaced by the dominance of a Kikuyu elite.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974316"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Kenyatta's calls to forgive and forget the past were a keystone of his government.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974313Assensoh199863"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Assensoh 1998]], p. 63.</ref> He preserved some elements of the old colonial order, particularly in relation to [[Law and order (politics)
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 312.</ref> The police and military structures were left largely intact.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974312"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 312.</ref> White Kenyans were left in senior positions within the judiciary, civil service, and parliament,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974312–313Assensoh199863"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Assensoh 1998]], p. 63.</ref> with the white Kenyans [[Bruce Mackenzie]] and [[Humphrey Slade]] being among Kenyatta's top officials.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974168Ochieng199593Assensoh199863"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column11: Assensoh 1998]], p. 63.</ref> Kenyatta's government nevertheless rejected the idea that the European and Asian minorities could be permitted [[dual citizenship]], expecting these communities to offer total loyalty to the independent Kenyan state.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995112"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column12: Maxon 1995]], p. 112.</ref> His administration pressured whites-only social clubs to adopt multi-racial entry policies,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995115"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column13: Maxon 1995]], p. 115.</ref> and in 1964 schools formerly reserved for European pupils were opened to Africans and Asians.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995115"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995

column1: Kenyatta's government believed it necessary to cultivate a united Kenyan national culture.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995138"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column2: Maxon 1995]], p. 138.</ref> To this end, it made efforts to assert the dignity of indigenous African cultures which missionaries and colonial authorities had belittled as ""primitive"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995139"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column3: Maxon 1995]], p. 139.</ref> An [[East African Literature Bureau]] was created to publish the work of indigenous writers.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995140"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column4: Maxon 1995]], p. 140.</ref> The Kenya Cultural Centre supported indigenous art and music, and hundreds of traditional music and dance groups were formed; Kenyatta personally insisted that such performances were held at all national celebrations.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995141"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column5: Maxon 1995]], p. 141.</ref> Support was given to the preservation of historic and cultural monuments, while street names referencing colonial figures were renamed and symbols of colonialism—like the statue of British settler [[Hugh Cholmondeley, 3rd Baron Delamere]] in Nairobi city centre—were removed.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995140"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column6: Maxon 1995]], p. 140.</ref> The government encouraged the use of Swahili as a national language, although English remained the main medium for parliamentary debates and the language of instruction in schools and universities.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995139"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column7: Maxon 1995]], p. 139.</ref> The historian Robert M. Maxon nevertheless suggested that ""no national culture emerged during the Kenyatta era"", most artistic and cultural expressions reflecting particular ethnic groups rather than a broader sense of Kenyanness, while Western culture remained heavily influential over the country's elites.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995142"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995

column1: Independent Kenya had an economy heavily molded by colonial rule; agriculture dominated while industry was limited, and there was a heavy reliance on exporting primary goods while importing capital and manufactured goods.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199583"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column2: Ochieng 1995]], p. 83.</ref> Under Kenyatta, the structure of this economy did not fundamentally change, remaining externally oriented and dominated by [[multinational corporation]]s and foreign capital.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199590, 91"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column3: Ochieng 1995]], pp. 90, 91.</ref> Kenyatta's economic policy was [[capitalism
column7: Maloba 2017]], p. 6.</ref> with no serious socialist policies being pursued;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974208"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column8: Arnold 1974]], p. 208.</ref> its focus was on achieving [[economic growth]] as opposed to equitable redistribution.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199585"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column9: Ochieng 1995]], p. 85.</ref> The government passed laws to encourage foreign investment, recognising that Kenya needed foreign-trained specialists in scientific and technical fields to aid its economic development.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974157–158"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column10: Arnold 1974]], pp. 157–158.</ref> Under Kenyatta, Western companies regarded Kenya as a safe and profitable place for investment;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974177"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column11: Arnold 1974]], p. 177.</ref> between 1964 and 1970, large-scale foreign investment and industry in Kenya nearly doubled.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199585"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995

column1: [[File:COLLECTIE TROPENMUSEUM President Jomo Kenyatta kijkt toe bij de keuring van stamboekvee tijdens de Eldoret Agricultural Show TMnr 20038663.jpg
column4: Kenyatta at an agricultural show in 1968]]

column1: In contrast to his economic policies, Kenyatta publicly claimed he would create a [[democratic socialism
column2: democratic socialist]] state with an equitable distribution of economic and social development.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199591"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column3: Ochieng 1995]], p. 91.</ref> In 1965, when [[Thomas Mboya]] was minister for economic planning and development, the government issued a session paper titled ""African Socialism and its Application to Planning in Kenya"", in which it officially declared its commitment to what it called an ""[[African socialism
column7: Maloba 2017]], p. 77.</ref> The session proposed a [[mixed economy]] with an important role for private capital,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970520Ochieng199584"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column9: Ochieng 1995]], p. 84.</ref> with Kenyatta's government specifying that it would only consider [[nationalisation]] in instances where national security was at risk.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199584Assensoh199864"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column11: Assensoh 1998]], p. 64.</ref> Left-wing critics highlighted that the image of ""African socialism"" portrayed in the document provided for no major shift away from the colonial economy.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199596"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995

column1: Kenya's agricultural and industrial sectors were dominated by Europeans and its commerce and trade by Asians; one of Kenyatta's most pressing issues was to bring the economy under indigenous control.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199585"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column2: Ochieng 1995]], p. 85.</ref> There was growing black resentment towards the Asian domination of the small business sector,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974171"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Arnold 1974]], p. 171.</ref> with Kenyatta's government putting pressure on Asian-owned businesses, intending to replace them with African-owned counterparts.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970521"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column4: Savage 1970]], p. 521.</ref> The 1965 session paper promised an ""Africanization"" of the Kenyan economy,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199864–65"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column5: Assensoh 1998]], pp. 64–65.</ref> with the government increasingly pushing for ""black capitalism"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970521"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column6: Savage 1970]], p. 521.</ref> The government established the [[Industrial and Commercial Development Corporation]] to provide loans for black-owned businesses,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970521"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column7: Savage 1970]], p. 521.</ref> and secured a 51% share in the Kenya National Assurance Company.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970522"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column8: Savage 1970]], p. 522.</ref> In 1965, the government established the Kenya National Trading Corporation to ensure indigenous control over the trade in essential commodities,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199864"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column9: Assensoh 1998]], p. 64.</ref> while the Trade Licensing Act of 1967 prohibited non-citizens from involvement in the rice, sugar, and maize trade.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970521Ochieng199585Maxon1995114Assensoh199864"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column13: Assensoh 1998]], p. 64.</ref> During the 1970s, this expanded to cover the trade in soap, cement, and textiles.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199864"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column14: Assensoh 1998]], p. 64.</ref> Many Asians who had retained British citizenship were affected by these measures.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974316Arnold1974170"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column16: Arnold 1974]], p. 170.</ref> Between late 1967 and early 1968, growing numbers of Kenyan Asians migrated to Britain;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974114"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column17: Arnold 1974]], p. 114.</ref> in February 1968 large numbers migrated quickly before [[Immigration Act 1971
column18: a legal change revoked their right to do so]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974172"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column19: Arnold 1974]], p. 172.</ref> Kenyatta was not sympathetic to those leaving: ""Kenya's identity as an African country is not going to be altered by the whims and malaises of groups of uncommitted individuals.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974172"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column1: Under Kenyatta, corruption became widespread throughout the government, civil service, and business community.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017215–216"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column2: Maloba 2017]], pp. 215–216.</ref> Kenyatta and his family were tied up with this corruption as they enriched themselves through the mass purchase of property after 1963.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017236–237"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column3: Maloba 2017]], pp. 236–237.</ref> Their acquisitions in the Central, Rift Valley, and Coast Provinces aroused great anger among landless Kenyans.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017241"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column4: Maloba 2017]], p. 241.</ref> His family used his presidential position to circumvent legal or administrative obstacles to acquiring property.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017238"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column5: Maloba 2017]], p. 238.</ref> The Kenyatta family also heavily invested in the coastal hotel business, Kenyatta personally owning the Leonard Beach Hotel.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017242"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column6: Maloba 2017]], p. 242.</ref> Other businesses they were involved with included ruby mining in [[Tsavo East National Park
column7: Tsavo National Park]], the casino business, the charcoal trade—which was causing significant deforestation—and the ivory trade.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017242–244"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column8: Maloba 2017]], pp. 242–244.</ref> The Kenyan press, which was largely loyal to Kenyatta, did not delve into this issue;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017236"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column9: Maloba 2017]], p. 236.</ref> it was only after his death that publications appeared revealing the scale of his personal enrichment.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017237–238"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column10: Maloba 2017]], pp. 237–238.</ref> Kenyan corruption and Kenyatta's role in it was better known in Britain, although many of his British friends—including McDonald and Brockway—chose to believe Kenyatta was not personally involved.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017246–247, 249"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017

column1: Despite Kenyatta's shortcomings on economic policy, compared with the economic performance of the vast majority of countries in independent Africa, Kenya's economic success during Kenyatta's tenure was outstanding. During the years following its independence in December, 1963, Kenya attained such a high rate of economic growth that it came to be widely regarded as something of an economic ""miracle."" According to World Bank figures, Kenya's economy attained an average growth rate of 6.4 percent per year from 1965 to 1980.<ref name="":0"">{{Cite journal
column13: url-access=subscription }}</ref> Among the 40 or more independent countries in sub-Saharan Africa, only 3 exceeded that growth rate; Nigeria, Ivory Coast, and Botswana. Kenyatta's success can be attributed to his focus on the agricultural sector, particularly on cash crops such as tea and coffee.<ref name="":0"" />

column1: [[File:Dr Banda of Malawi and Jomo Kenyatta of Kenya.jpg

The question of land ownership had deep emotional resonance in Kenya, having been a major grievance against the British colonialists.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974195"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 195.</ref> As part of the Lancaster House negotiations, Britain's government agreed to provide Kenya with £27 million with which to buy out white farmers and redistribute their land among the indigenous population.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974196"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Arnold 1974]], p. 196.</ref> To ease this transition, Kenyatta made [[Bruce McKenzie]], a white farmer, the Minister of Agriculture and Land.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974196"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column4: Arnold 1974]], p. 196.</ref> Kenyatta's government encouraged the establishment of private land-buying companies that were often headed by prominent politicians.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBoone201281"">[[#CITEREFBoone2012
column5: Boone 2012]], p. 81.</ref> The government sold or leased lands in the former White Highlands to these companies, which in turn subdivided them among individual shareholders.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBoone201281"">[[#CITEREFBoone2012
column6: Boone 2012]], p. 81.</ref> In this way, the land redistribution programs favoured the ruling party's chief constituency.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBoone201282"">[[#CITEREFBoone2012
column7: Boone 2012]], p. 82.</ref> Kenyatta himself expanded the land that he owned around Gatundu.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974316"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 316.</ref> Kenyans who made claims to land on the basis of ancestral ownership often found the land given to other people, including Kenyans from different parts of the country.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBoone201282"">[[#CITEREFBoone2012
column9: Boone 2012]], p. 82.</ref> Voices began to condemn the redistribution; in 1969, the MP [[Jean-Marie Seroney]] censured the sale of historically [[Nandi people
column10: Nandi]] lands in the Rift to non-Nandi, describing the settlement schemes as ""Kenyatta's colonization of the rift"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBoone201285Maloba2017251"">[[#CITEREFBoone2012

column1: In part fuelled by high rural unemployment, Kenya witnessed growing rural-to-urban migration under Kenyatta's government.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995124–125"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column2: Maxon 1995]], pp. 124–125.</ref> This exacerbated urban unemployment and housing shortages, with squatter settlements and slums growing up and urban crime rates rising.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995125–126"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column3: Maxon 1995]], pp. 125–126.</ref> Kenyatta was concerned by this, and promoted the reversal of this rural-to-urban migration, but in this was unsuccessful.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995126"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column4: Maxon 1995]], p. 126.</ref> Kenyatta's government was eager to control the country's trade unions, fearing their ability to disrupt the economy.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970522"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column5: Savage 1970]], p. 522.</ref> To this end it emphasised social welfare schemes over traditional industrial institutions,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970522"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column6: Savage 1970]], p. 522.</ref> and in 1965 transformed the Kenya Federation of Labour into the Central Organization of Trade (COT), a body which came under strong government influence.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970523Maloba201791"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column8: Maloba 2017]], p. 91.</ref> No strikes could be legally carried out in Kenya without COT's permission.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970523"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column9: Savage 1970]], p. 523.</ref> There were also measures to Africanise the civil service, which by mid-1967 had become 91% African.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995113"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column10: Maxon 1995]], p. 113.</ref> During the 1960s and 1970s the [[public sector]] grew faster than the private sector.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995118"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column11: Maxon 1995]], p. 118.</ref> The growth in the public sector contributed to the significant expansion of the indigenous [[middle class]] in Kenyatta's Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995120"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995

column4: The University of Nairobi, Kenya's first institution of higher education, was established under Kenyatta's administration.]]

column1: The government oversaw a massive expansion in education facilities.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995110"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column2: Maxon 1995]], p. 110.</ref> In June 1963, Kenyatta ordered the Ominda Commission to determine a framework for meeting Kenya's educational needs.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995126–127"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column3: Maxon 1995]], pp. 126–127.</ref> Their report set out the long-term goal of universal free primary education in Kenya but argued that the government's emphasis should be on secondary and higher education to facilitate the training of indigenous African personnel to take over the civil service and other jobs requiring such an education.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995127"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column4: Maxon 1995]], p. 127.</ref> Between 1964 and 1966, the number of primary schools grew by 11.6%, and the number of secondary schools by 80%.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995127"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column5: Maxon 1995]], p. 127.</ref> By the time of Kenyatta's death, Kenya's first universities—the [[University of Nairobi]] and [[Kenyatta University]]—had been established.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995127Assensoh1998147"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column7: Assensoh 1998]], p. 147.</ref> Although Kenyatta died without having attained the goal of free, universal primary education in Kenya, the country had made significant advances in that direction, with 85% of Kenyan children in primary education, and within a decade of independence had trained sufficient numbers of indigenous Africans to take over the civil service.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995128"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995

column1: Another priority for Kenyatta's government was improving access to healthcare services.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995132"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column2: Maxon 1995]], p. 132.</ref> It stated that its long-term goal was to establish a system of free, universal medical care.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995133"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column3: Maxon 1995]], p. 133.</ref> In the short-term, its emphasis was on increasing the overall number of doctors and registered nurses while decreasing the number of expatriates in those positions.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995132"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column4: Maxon 1995]], p. 132.</ref> In 1965, the government introduced free medical services for out-patients and children.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995133"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column5: Maxon 1995]], p. 133.</ref> By Kenyatta's death, the majority of Kenyans had access to significantly better healthcare than they had had in the colonial period.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995133"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column6: Maxon 1995]], p. 133.</ref> Before independence, the average life expectancy in Kenya was 45, but by the end of the 1970s it was 55, the second-highest in Sub-Saharan Africa.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995134"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column7: Maxon 1995]], p. 134.</ref> This improved medical care had resulted in declining mortality rates while birth rates remained high, resulting in a rapidly growing population; from 1962 to 1979, Kenya's population grew by just under 4% a year, the highest rate in the world at the time.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995122"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column8: Maxon 1995]], p. 122.</ref> This put a severe strain on social services; Kenyatta's government promoted [[family planning]] projects to stem the birth-rate, but these had little success.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995123–124"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995

column1: [[File:Roy Innis, Jomo Kenyatta, Doris Funnye Innis in Kenya Circa 1970.jpg
column4: Kenyatta meets an American delegation from the [[Congress of Racial Equality]], including [[Roy Innis]].]]

column1: In part due to his advanced years (he was already 66–67 years old at the time of independence), Kenyatta rarely traveled outside of Eastern Africa.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974167"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 167.</ref> Under Kenyatta, Kenya was largely uninvolved in the affairs of other states, including those in the [[East African Community]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974320"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 320.</ref> Despite his reservations about any immediate East African Federation, in June 1967 Kenyatta signed the Treaty for East African Co-operation.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974175"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column4: Arnold 1974]], p. 175.</ref> In December he attended a meeting with Tanzanian and Ugandan representatives to form the East African Economic Community, reflecting Kenyatta's cautious approach toward regional integration.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974175"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column5: Arnold 1974]], p. 175.</ref> He also took on a mediating role during the [[Congo Crisis]], heading the [[Organisation of African Unity]]'s Conciliation Commission on the Congo.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974178"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column1: Facing the pressures of the [[Cold War]],<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974188"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 188.</ref> Kenyatta officially pursued a policy of ""positive non-alignment"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016515"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column3: Cullen 2016]], p. 515.</ref> In reality, his foreign policy was pro-Western and in particular pro-British.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016515Maloba201796"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column5: Maloba 2017]], p. 96.</ref> Kenya became a member of the [[Commonwealth of Nations]],<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974313"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 313.</ref> using this as a vehicle to put pressure on the white-minority [[apartheid]] regimes in South Africa and Rhodesia.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974167–168"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column7: Arnold 1974]], pp. 167–168.</ref> Britain remained one of Kenya's foremost sources of foreign trade; British aid to Kenya was among the highest in Africa.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016515"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column8: Cullen 2016]], p. 515.</ref> In 1964, Kenya and the UK signed a Memorandum of Understanding, one of only two military alliances Kenyatta's government made;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016515"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column9: Cullen 2016]], p. 515.</ref> the British [[Special Air Service]] trained Kenyatta's own bodyguards.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201754"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column10: Maloba 2017]], p. 54.</ref> Commentators argued that Britain's relationship with Kenyatta's Kenya was a [[Neo-colonialism
column11: neo-colonial]] one, with the British having exchanged their position of political power for one of influence.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016514"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column12: Cullen 2016]], p. 514.</ref> The historian Poppy Cullen nevertheless noted that there was no ""dictatorial neo-colonial control"" in Kenyatta's Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016515"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016

column1: [[File:Bundesarchiv B 145 Bild-F021917-0014, Kenia, Staatsbesuch Bundespräsident Lübke.jpg
column4: Jomo Kenyatta and his son meet the [[President of Germany
column5: President of West Germany]] [[Heinrich Lübke]] in 1966.]]

column1: Although many white Kenyans accepted Kenyatta's rule, he remained opposed by white [[far right politics
column2: far-right]] activists; while in London at the [[1964 Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference
column3: July 1964 Commonwealth Conference]], he was assaulted by [[Martin Webster]], a British [[Neo-Nazism
column4: neo-Nazi]], at the [[London Hilton Hotel]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974296"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column5: Arnold 1974]], p. 296.</ref> Kenyatta's relationship with the United States was also warm; the [[United States Agency for International Development]] played a key role in helping respond to a maize shortage in [[Kamba people
column7: Maloba 2017]], pp. 63–65.</ref> Kenyatta also maintained a warm relationship with Israel, including when other East African nations endorsed Arab hostility to the state;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTENaim200579–80"">[[#CITEREFNaim2005
column8: Naim 2005]], pp. 79–80.</ref> he for instance permitted Israeli jets to refuel in Kenya on their way back from the [[Entebbe raid]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTENaim200579–80Maloba2017190–193"">[[#CITEREFNaim2005
column10: Maloba 2017]], pp. 190–193.</ref> In turn, in 1976 the Israelis warned of a plot by the [[Palestinian Liberation Army]] to assassinate him, a threat he took seriously.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017172–173"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017

column1: Kenyatta and his government were anti-communist,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974167Assensoh1998147"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Assensoh 1998]], p. 147.</ref> and in June 1965 he warned that ""it is naive to think that there is no danger of imperialism from the East. In world power politics the East has as much designs upon us as the West and would like to serve their own interests. That is why we reject Communism.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970527Maloba201776"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column5: Maloba 2017]], p. 76.</ref> His governance was often criticised by communists and other leftists, some of whom accused him of being a fascist.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974177"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column6: Arnold 1974]], p. 177.</ref> When Chinese Communist official [[Zhou Enlai]] visited Dar es Salaam, his statement that ""Africa is ripe for revolution"" was clearly aimed largely at Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974177"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column7: Arnold 1974]], p. 177.</ref> In 1964, Kenyatta impounded a secret shipment of Chinese armaments that passed through Kenyan territory on its way to Uganda. Obote personally visited Kenyatta to apologise.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974177Maloba201759–60"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column9: Maloba 2017]], pp. 59–60.</ref> In June 1967, Kenyatta declared the Chinese Chargé d'Affairs ''persona non grata'' in Kenya and recalled the Kenyan ambassador from [[Peking]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974177"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column10: Arnold 1974]], p. 177.</ref> Relations with the Soviet Union were also strained; Kenyatta shut down the Lumumba Institute—an educational organisation named after the Congolese independence leader [[Patrice Lumumba]]—on the basis that it was a front for Soviet influence in Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974160Maloba201793–94"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column1: [[File:COLLECTIE TROPENMUSEUM President Jomo Kenyatta staande in een landrover tijdens de opening van de Eldoret Agricultural Show TMnr 20038660.jpg
column4: Kenyatta at the Eldoret Agricultural Show, 1968]]

column1: Kenyatta made clear his desire for Kenya to become a one-party state, regarding this as a better expression of national unity than a multi-party system.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974314"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 314.</ref> In the first five years of independence, he consolidated control of the central government,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBoone201284"">[[#CITEREFBoone2012
column3: Boone 2012]], p. 84.</ref> removing the autonomy of Kenya's provinces to prevent the entrenchment of ethnic power bases.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199818"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column4: Assensoh 1998]], p. 18.</ref> He argued that centralised control of the government was needed to deal with the growth in demands for local services and to assist quicker economic development.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199818"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column5: Assensoh 1998]], p. 18.</ref> In 1966, it launched a commission to examine reforms to local government operations,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199818"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column6: Assensoh 1998]], p. 18.</ref> and in 1969 passed the Transfer of Functions Act, which terminated grants to local authorities and transferred major services from provincial to central control.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199819"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998

column1: A major focus for Kenyatta during the first three and a half years of Kenya's independence were the divisions within KANU itself.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel197032"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970
column2: Gertzel 1970]], p. 32.</ref> Opposition to Kenyatta's government grew, particularly following the assassination of [[Pio Pinto]] in February 1965.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974316"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 316.</ref> Kenyatta condemned the assassination of the prominent leftist politician, although UK intelligence agencies believed that his own bodyguard had orchestrated the murder.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201768"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column4: Maloba 2017]], p. 68.</ref> Relations between Kenyatta and Odinga were strained, and at the March 1966 party conference, Odinga's post—that of party vice president—was divided among eight different politicians, greatly limiting his power and ending his position as Kenyatta's automatic successor.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974161Maloba2017105–106"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column6: Maloba 2017]], p. 105–106.</ref> Between 1964 and 1966, Kenyatta and other KANU conservatives had been deliberately trying to push Odinga to resign from the party.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201770–71"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column7: Maloba 2017]], pp. 70–71.</ref> Under growing pressure, in 1966 Odinga stepped down as state vice president, claiming that Kenya had failed to achieve economic independence and needed to adopt socialist policies. Backed by several other senior KANU figures and trade unionists, he became head of the new [[Kenya Peoples Union]] (KPU).<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel197032Savage1970527Murray-Brown1974317Arnold1974164Assensoh199867Maloba2017108"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970
column13: Maloba 2017]], p. 108.</ref> In its manifesto, the KPU stated that it would pursue ""truly socialist policies"" like the nationalisation of public utilities; it claimed Kenyatta's government ""want[ed] to build a capitalist system in the image of Western capitalism but are too embarrassed or dishonest to call it that.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199599, 100"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column14: Ochieng 1995]], pp. 99, 100.</ref> The KPU were legally recognised as the [[official opposition]],<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel1970146"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970
column15: Gertzel 1970]], p. 146.</ref> thus restoring the country's [[two party system]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel1970144"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970

column1: The new party was a direct challenge to Kenyatta's rule,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel1970144"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970
column2: Gertzel 1970]], p. 144.</ref> and he regarded it as a communist-inspired plot to oust him.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199598"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column3: Ochieng 1995]], p. 98.</ref> Soon after the KPU's creation, the Kenyan Parliament amended the constitution to ensure that the defectors—who had originally been elected on the KANU ticket—could not automatically retain their seats and would have to stand for re-election.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel197035Maloba2017110–111"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970
