column5: Maloba 2017]], pp. 110–111.</ref> This resulted in the [[1966 Kenyan parliamentary by-elections
column8: Maloba 2017]], p. 111.</ref> The Luo increasingly rallied around the KPU,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974318"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column9: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 318.</ref> which experienced localized violence that hindered its ability to campaign, although Kenyatta's government officially disavowed this violence.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGertzel1970147"">[[#CITEREFGertzel1970
column10: Gertzel 1970]], p. 147.</ref> KANU retained the support of all national newspapers and the government-owned radio and television stations.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017119"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column11: Maloba 2017]], p. 119.</ref> Of the 29 defectors, only nine were re-elected on the KPU ticket;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970527Maloba2017125"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column13: Maloba 2017]], p. 125.</ref> Odinga was among them, having retained his Central Nyanza seat with a high majority.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974164"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column14: Arnold 1974]], p. 164.</ref> Odinga was replaced as vice president by [[Joseph Murumbi]],<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199867"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column15: Assensoh 1998]], p. 67.</ref> who in turn would be replaced by Moi.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199867Maloba2017138"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998

column5: A British newsreel about Kenyatta's rule, produced in 1973]]

column1: In July 1969, Mboya—a prominent and popular Luo KANU politician—was assassinated by a Kikuyu.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970529Murray-Brown1974317Arnold1974166Ochieng1995102Assensoh199867Maloba2017135"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column7: Maloba 2017]], p. 135.</ref> Kenyatta had reportedly been concerned that Mboya, with U.S. backing, could remove him from the presidency,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng1995101"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column8: Ochieng 1995]], p. 101.</ref> and across Kenya there were suspicions voiced that Kenyatta's government was responsible for Mboya's death.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199867"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column9: Assensoh 1998]], p. 67.</ref> The killing sparked tensions between the Kikuyu and other ethnic groups across the country,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970529Maloba2017137"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column11: Maloba 2017]], p. 137.</ref> with riots breaking out in Nairobi.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974318"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column12: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 318.</ref> In October 1969, Kenyatta visited [[Kisumu]], located in Luo territory, to open a hospital. On being greeted by a crowd shouting KPU slogans, he lost his temper. When members of the crowd started throwing stones, Kenyatta's bodyguards opened fire on them, killing and wounding several.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974319Maloba2017140–143"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column14: Maloba 2017]], pp. 140–143.</ref> In response to the rise of KPU, Kenyatta had introduced oathing, a Kikuyu cultural tradition in which individuals came to Gatundu to swear their loyalty to him.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970529–530Murray-Brown1974317Ochieng1995101–102Maloba2017138"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column18: Maloba 2017]], p. 138.</ref> Journalists were discouraged from reporting on the oathing system, and several were deported when they tried to do so.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974317"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column19: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 317.</ref> Many Kenyans were pressured or forced to swear oaths, something condemned by the country's Christian establishment.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974318Maloba2017139"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column21: Maloba 2017]], p. 139.</ref> In response to the growing condemnation, the oathing was terminated in September 1969,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974319Maloba2017139"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column23: Maloba 2017]], p. 139.</ref> and Kenyatta invited leaders from other ethnic groups to a meeting in Gatundu.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970531Maloba2017140"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970

column1: Kenyatta's government resorted to un-democratic measures to restrict the opposition.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199821"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column2: Assensoh 1998]], p. 21.</ref> It used laws on detention and deportation to perpetuate its political hold.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199823"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column3: Assensoh 1998]], p. 23.</ref> In 1966, it passed the Public Security (Detained and Restricted Persons) Regulations, allowing the authorities to arrest and detain anyone ""for the preservation of public security"" [[Indefinite detention without trial
column4: without putting them on trial]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199822, 67Maloba2017129"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column6: Maloba 2017]], p. 129.</ref> In October 1969 the government banned the KPU,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970531Arnold1974191Assensoh199867Maloba2017145"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column10: Maloba 2017]], p. 145.</ref> and arrested Odinga before putting him under indefinite detainment.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974191Assensoh199867Maloba2017145"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column13: Maloba 2017]], p. 145.</ref> With the organised opposition eliminated, from 1969, Kenya was once again a ''de facto'' one-party state.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970531Tamarkin197925Boone201284"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column16: Boone 2012]], p. 84.</ref> The [[1969 Kenyan general election
column17: December 1969 general election]]—in which all candidates were from the ruling KANU—resulted in Kenyatta's government remaining in power, but many members of his government lost their parliamentary seats to rivals from within the party.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970531Murray-Brown1974319"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column19: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 319.</ref> Over coming years, many other political and intellectual figures considered hostile to Kenyatta's rule were detained or imprisoned, including Seroney, Flomena Chelagat, [[George Anyona]], [[Martin Shikuku]], and [[Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng1995103–104Assensoh199867"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column21: Assensoh 1998]], p. 67.</ref> Other political figures who were critical of Kenyatta's administration, including Ronald Ngala and [[Josiah Mwangi Kariuki]], were killed in incidents that many speculated were government assassinations.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199868"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998

column4: Kenyatta in the last year of his life]]

column1: For many years, Kenyatta had suffered health problems. He had a mild stroke in 1966,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974320Maloba2017238"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Maloba 2017]], p. 238.</ref> and a second in May 1968.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016516"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column4: Cullen 2016]], p. 516.</ref> He suffered from [[gout]] and heart problems, all of which he sought to keep hidden from the public.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017239"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column5: Maloba 2017]], p. 239.</ref> By 1970, he was increasingly feeble and senile,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng1995103"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column6: Ochieng 1995]], p. 103.</ref> and by 1975 Kenyatta had—according to Maloba—""in effect ceased to actively govern"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017282"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column7: Maloba 2017]], p. 282.</ref> Four Kikuyu politicians—Koinange, James Gichuru, [[Njoroge Mungai]], and [[Charles Njonjo]]—formed his inner circle of associates, and he was rarely seen in public without one of them present.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng1995102"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column8: Ochieng 1995]], p. 102.</ref> This clique faced opposition from KANU back-benchers spearheaded by Josiah Mwangi Kariuki. In March 1975 Kariuki was kidnapped, tortured, and murdered, and his body was dumped in the [[Ngong Hills]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng1995103Maloba2017264–265"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column10: Maloba 2017]], pp. 264–265.</ref> After Kariuki's murder, Maloba noted, there was a ""noticeable erosion"" of support for Kenyatta and his government.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017274"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column11: Maloba 2017]], p. 274.</ref> Thenceforth, when the president spoke to crowds, they no longer applauded his statements.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017274–275"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017

column1: In 1977, Kenyatta had several further strokes or heart attacks.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017239"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column2: Maloba 2017]], p. 239.</ref> On 22 August 1978, he died of a heart attack in the State House, Mombasa.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTETamarkin197930Kuria1991121Maloba2017305"">[[#CITEREFTamarkin1979
column5: Maloba 2017]], p. 305.</ref> The Kenyan government had been preparing for Kenyatta's death since at least his 1968 stroke; it had requested British assistance in organising his [[state funeral]] as a result of the UK's longstanding experience in this area.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016514, 517Maloba2017311"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column7: Maloba 2017]], p. 311.</ref> McKenzie had been employed as a go-between,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016516"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column8: Cullen 2016]], p. 516.</ref> and the structure of the funeral was orchestrated to deliberately imitate that of deceased British Prime Minister [[Winston Churchill]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016524"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column9: Cullen 2016]], p. 524.</ref> In doing so, senior Kenyans sought to project an image of their country as a modern nation-state rather than one incumbent on tradition.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016516"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column10: Cullen 2016]], p. 516.</ref> The funeral took place at St. Andrew's Presbyterian Church, six days after Kenyatta's death.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016518"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column11: Cullen 2016]], p. 518.</ref> Britain's heir to the throne, [[Charles, Prince of Wales]], attended the event, a symbol of the value that the British government perceived in its relationship with Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016524, 526Maloba2017314"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column13: Maloba 2017]], p. 314.</ref> African heads of state also attended, including Nyerere, [[Idi Amin]], [[Kenneth Kaunda]], and [[Hastings Banda]], as did India's [[Morarji Desai]] and Pakistan's [[Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017316"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column14: Maloba 2017]], p. 316.</ref> His body was buried in a [[mausoleum]] in the grounds of the [[Parliament Buildings (Kenya)

column1: Kenyatta's succession had been an issue of debate since independence,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTETamarkin197922"">[[#CITEREFTamarkin1979
column2: Tamarkin 1979]], p. 22.</ref> and Kenyatta had not unreservedly nominated a successor.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTECullen2016516"">[[#CITEREFCullen2016
column3: Cullen 2016]], p. 516.</ref> The Kikuyu clique surrounding him had sought to amend the constitution to prevent vice president Moi—who was from the [[Kalenjin people]] rather than the Kikuyu—from automatically becoming acting president, but their attempts failed amid sustained popular and parliamentary opposition.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng1995104Maloba2017279, 281"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column5: Maloba 2017]], pp. 279, 281.</ref> After Kenyatta's death, the transition of power proved smooth,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTETamarkin197922"">[[#CITEREFTamarkin1979
column6: Tamarkin 1979]], p. 22.</ref> surprising many international commentators.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199829"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column7: Assensoh 1998]], p. 29.</ref> As vice president, Moi was sworn in as acting president for a 90-day interim period.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEKuria1991121Assensoh199867Cullen2016521Maloba2017308, 309"">[[#CITEREFKuria1991
column11: Maloba 2017]], pp. 308, 309.</ref> In October he was unanimously elected KANU President and subsequently declared President of Kenya itself.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTETamarkin197930–31"">[[#CITEREFTamarkin1979
column12: Tamarkin 1979]], pp. 30–31.</ref> Moi emphasised his loyalty to Kenyatta—""I followed and was faithful to him until his last day, even when his closest friends forsook him""—and there was much expectation that he would continue the policies inaugurated by Kenyatta.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTETamarkin197933–34"">[[#CITEREFTamarkin1979
column13: Tamarkin 1979]], pp. 33–34.</ref> He nevertheless criticised the corruption, [[land grabbing]], and capitalistic ethos that had characterised Kenyatta's period and expressed [[populism
column14: populist]] tendencies by emphasizing a closer link to the poor.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTETamarkin197934"">[[#CITEREFTamarkin1979
column15: Tamarkin 1979]], p. 34.</ref> In 1982 he would amend the Kenyan constitution to create a ''de jure'' one-party state.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEKuria1991117"">[[#CITEREFKuria1991

column1: Kenyatta possessed the common touch and great leadership qualities. He was essentially a moderate trying to achieve the radical revolution of a nationalist victory in a colonialist society, and his ambivalence over many issues can best be explained by his need to contain or use his militants—and he had plenty of them. They were impatient and wanted to see effective action. Kenyatta certainly knew how to appeal to African sentiments.""
<div style=""padding-bottom: 0; padding-top: 0.5em""><cite class=""left-aligned"" style="""">— Kenyatta biographer Guy Arnold<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974105"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
Kenyatta was an African nationalist,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199826"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column2: Assensoh 1998]], p. 26.</ref> and was committed to the belief that European colonial rule in Africa must end.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199827"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column3: Assensoh 1998]], p. 27.</ref> Like other anti-colonialists, he believed that under colonialism, the human and natural resources of Africa had been used not for the benefit of Africa's population but for the enrichment of the colonisers and their European homelands.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199827"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column4: Assensoh 1998]], p. 27.</ref> For Kenyatta, independence meant not just self-rule, but an end to [[Racial segregation
column5: the colour bar]] and to the patronising attitudes and racist slang of Kenya's white minority.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974306"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 306.</ref> According to Murray-Brown, Kenyatta's ""basic philosophy"" throughout his life was that ""all men deserved the right to develop peacefully according to their own wishes"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974321"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 321.</ref> Kenyatta expressed this in his statement that ""I have stood always for the purposes of human dignity in freedom, and for the values of tolerance and peace.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974322"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 322.</ref> This approach was similar to the Zambian President Kenneth Kaunda's ideology of ""African humanism"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974321"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Murray-Brown noted that ""Kenyatta had always kept himself free from ideological commitments"",<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974312"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 312.</ref> while the historian William R. Ochieng observed that ""Kenyatta articulated no particular social philosophy"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199593"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column3: Ochieng 1995]], p. 93.</ref> Similarly, Assensoh noted that Kenyatta was ""not interested in social philosophies and slogans"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199825"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column4: Assensoh 1998]], p. 25.</ref> Several commentators and biographers described him as being politically [[Conservatism
column10: Lonsdale 2006]], p. 89.</ref> an ideological viewpoint likely bolstered by his training in functionalist anthropology.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTELonsdale200694"">[[#CITEREFLonsdale2006
column11: Lonsdale 2006]], p. 94.</ref> He pursued, according to Maloba, ""a conservatism that worked in concert with imperial powers and was distinctly hostile to radical politics"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017209"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017

column1: Kenyatta biographer [[Guy Arnold]] described the Kenyan leader as ""a pragmatist and a moderate"", noting that his only ""radicalism"" came in the form of his ""nationalist attack"" on imperialism.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197433"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 33.</ref> Arnold also noted that Kenyatta ""absorbed a great deal of the British approach to politics: pragmatism, only dealing with problems when they become crises, [and] tolerance as long as the other side is only talking"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197432"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Arnold 1974]], p. 32.</ref> Donald Savage noted that Kenyatta believed in ""the importance of authority and tradition"", and that he displayed ""a remarkably consistent view of development through self-help and hard work"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970537"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column4: Savage 1970]], p. 537.</ref> Kenyatta was also an elitist and encouraged the emergence of an elite class in Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974190, 208"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column5: Arnold 1974]], pp. 190, 208.</ref> He wrestled with a contradiction between his conservative desire for a renewal of traditional custom and his reformist urges to embrace Western modernity.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199838"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998
column6: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 38.</ref> He also faced a contradiction between his internal debates on Kikuyu ethics and belief in tribal identity with his need to create a non-tribalised Kenyan nationalism.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199838"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998

column1: While in Britain, Kenyatta made political alliances with individuals committed to Marxism and to radical Pan-Africanism, the idea that African countries should politically unify;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201847"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column2: Maloba 2018]], p. 47.</ref> some commentators have posthumously characterised Kenyatta as a Pan-Africanist.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199827Nyangena200310"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column4: Nyangena 2003]], p. 10.</ref> Maloba observed that during the colonial period Kenyatta had embraced ""radical Pan African activism"" which differed sharply from the ""deliberate conservative positions, especially on the question of African liberation"" that he espoused while Kenya's leader.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017201"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column5: Maloba 2017]], p. 201.</ref> As leader of Kenya, Kenyatta published two collected volumes of his speeches: ''Harambee'' and ''Suffering Without Bitterness''.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba20183"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 3.</ref> The material included in these publications was carefully selected so as to avoid mention of the radicalism he exhibited while in Britain during the 1930s.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba20183–4"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018

column1: Kenyatta had been exposed to Marxist-Leninist ideas through his friendship with Padmore and the time spent in the Soviet Union,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974312Assensoh19986"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Assensoh 1998]], p. 6.</ref> but had also been exposed to Western forms of [[liberal democracy
column4: liberal democratic]] government through his many years in Britain.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974312"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 312.</ref> He appears to have had no further involvement with the communist movement after 1934.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199829"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998
column6: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 29.</ref> As Kenya's leader, Kenyatta rejected the idea that Marxism offered a useful framework for analysing his country's socio-economic situation.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201783"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column7: Maloba 2017]], p. 83.</ref> The academics Bruce J. Berman and John M. Lonsdale argued that Marxist frameworks for analysing society influenced some of his beliefs, such as his view that British colonialism had to be destroyed rather than simply reformed.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199828"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998
column8: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 28.</ref> Kenyatta nevertheless disagreed with the Marxist attitude that tribalism was backward and retrograde;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199828–29"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998
column9: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], pp. 28–29.</ref> his positive attitude toward tribal society frustrated some of Kenyatta's Marxist Pan-Africanist friends in Britain, among them Padmore, James, and [[T. Ras Makonnen]], who regarded it as parochial and un-progressive.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199834"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998

column1: Assensoh suggested that Kenyatta initially had socialist inclinations but ""became a victim of capitalist circumstances"";<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh19984"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998
column2: Assensoh 1998]], p. 4.</ref> conversely, Savage stated that ""Kenyatta's direction was hardly towards the creation of a radical new socialist society"",<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970535"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column3: Savage 1970]], p. 535.</ref> and Ochieng called him ""an African capitalist"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199593"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column4: Ochieng 1995]], p. 93.</ref> When in power, Kenyatta displayed a preoccupation with individual and ''mbari'' land rights that were at odds with any socialist-oriented collectivisation.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970535"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column5: Savage 1970]], p. 535.</ref> According to Maloba, Kenyatta's government ""sought to project capitalism as an African ideology, and communism (or socialism) as alien and dangerous"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba20176"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017

column1: Ever a showman, [Kenyatta] could appear one moment in gaily coloured shirts, decorated with the cock of KANU, and the next in elegant suits from Savile Row, seldom without a rose in his buttonhole; he could be photographed in leopard-skin hat and cloak waving a silver fly-whisk or in old slacks on his farm tending his shrubs; he was equally at home in academic robes at a university function and in sandals and shorts on the beach at Mombasa. African exuberance and love of display found perfect expression in Kenyatta's flair alongside the dignity and respect due to 'His Excellency, the President, Mzee Jomo Kenyatta'.""

<div style=""padding-bottom: 0; padding-top: 0.5em""><cite class=""left-aligned"" style="""">— Kenyatta biographer Jeremy Murray-Brown<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974315"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
Kenyatta was a flamboyant character,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974232"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 232.</ref> with an extroverted personality.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown197474"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 74.</ref> According to Murray-Brown, he ""liked being at the centre of life"",<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974184"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 184.</ref> and was always ""a rebel at heart"" who enjoyed ""earthly pleasures"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974144"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 144.</ref> One of Kenyatta's fellow LSE students, Elspeth Huxley, referred to him as ""a showman to his finger tips; jovial, a good companion, shrewd, fluent, quick, devious, subtle, [and] flesh-pot loving"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974189"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 189.</ref> Kenyatta liked to dress elaborately; throughout most of his adult life, he wore finger rings and while studying at university in London took to wearing a [[Fez (hat)
column7: fez]] and cloak and carrying a silver-topped black cane.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974184"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 184.</ref> He adopted his surname, ""Kenyatta"", after the name of a beaded belt he often wore in early life.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197417"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column9: Arnold 1974]], p. 17.</ref> As President he collected a variety of expensive cars.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974316"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Murray-Brown noted that Kenyatta had the ability to ""appear all things to all men"",<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974233"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 233.</ref> also displaying a ""consummate ability to keep his true purposes and abilities to himself"", for instance concealing his connections with communists and the Soviet Union both from members of the British Labour Party and from Kikuyu figures at home.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974165"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 165.</ref> This deviousness was sometimes interpreted as dishonesty by those who met him.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974215, 216"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], pp. 215, 216.</ref> Referring to Kenyatta's appearance in 1920s Kenya, Murray-Brown stated the leader presented himself to Europeans as ""an agreeable if somewhat seedy 'Europeanized' native"" and to indigenous Africans as ""a sophisticated man-about-town about whose political earnestness they had certain reservations"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974107"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: Simon Gikandi argued that Kenyatta, like some of his contemporaries in the Pan-African movement, was an ""Afro-Victorian"", someone whose identity had been shaped ""by the culture of colonialism and colonial institutions"", especially those of the [[Victorian era]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGikandi20003"">[[#CITEREFGikandi2000
column2: Gikandi 2000]], p. 3.</ref> During the 1920s and 1930s, Kenyatta cultivated the image of a ""colonial gentleman"";<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGikandi20009"">[[#CITEREFGikandi2000
column3: Gikandi 2000]], p. 9.</ref> in England, he displayed ""pleasant manners"" and a flexible attitude in adapting to urban situations dissimilar to the lands he had grown up in.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBeck1966317"">[[#CITEREFBeck1966
column4: Beck 1966]], p. 317.</ref> A. R. Barlow, a member of the Church of Scotland Mission at Kikuyu, met with Kenyatta in Britain, later relating that he was impressed by how Kenyatta could ""mix on equal terms with Europeans and to hold his end up in spite of his handicaps, educationally and socially.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBeck1966316"">[[#CITEREFBeck1966
column5: Beck 1966]], p. 316.</ref> The South African [[Peter Abrahams]] met Kenyatta in London, noting that of all the black men involved in the city's Pan-Africanist movement, he was ""the most relaxed, sophisticated and 'westernized' of the lot of us"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGikandi20005"">[[#CITEREFGikandi2000
column6: Gikandi 2000]], p. 5.</ref> As President, Kenyatta often reminisced nostalgically about his time in England, referring to it as ""home"" on several occasions.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974320"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 320.</ref> Berman and Lonsdale described his life as being preoccupied with ""a search for the reconciliation of the Western modernity he embraced and an equally valued Kikuyuness he could not discard"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199819"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998
column8: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 19.</ref> Gikandi argued that Kenyatta's ""identification with Englishness was much more profound than both his friends and enemies have been willing to admit"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEGikandi20006"">[[#CITEREFGikandi2000

column1: Kenyatta has also been described as a talented orator, author, and editor.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199819"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998
column2: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 19.</ref> He had dictatorial and autocratic tendencies,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974209"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Arnold 1974]], p. 209.</ref> as well as a fierce temper that could emerge as rage on occasion.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974215Arnold1974209"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Arnold 1974]], p. 209.</ref> Murray-Brown noted that Kenyatta could be ""quite unscrupulous, even brutal"" in using others to get what he wanted,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974215"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column6: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 215.</ref> but he never displayed any physical cruelty or [[nihilism]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974216"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 216.</ref> Kenyatta had no racist impulses regarding white Europeans, as can, for instance, be seen through his marriage to a white English woman.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974216"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 216.</ref> He told his daughter ""the English are wonderful people to live with in England.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197432"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column9: Arnold 1974]], p. 32.</ref> He welcomed white support for his cause, so long as it was generous and unconditional, and spoke of a Kenya in which indigenous Africans, Europeans, Arabs, and Indians could all regard themselves as Kenyans, working and living alongside each other peacefully.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974223"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 223.</ref> Despite this, Kenyatta exhibited a general dislike of Indians, believing that they exploited indigenous Africans in Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974188–189"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: I do not think I am—and have never been—an enemy of Europeans or the white people, because I have spent many years in England or in Europe, and even today I have many friends in various nations.""
<div style=""padding-bottom: 0; padding-top: 0.5em""><cite class=""left-aligned"" style="""">— Kenyatta, April 1961<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197465"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column2: Maloba 2017]], p. 23.</ref> He viewed [[monogamy]] through an anthropological lens as an interesting Western phenomenon but did not adopt the practice himself, instead having sexual relations with a wide range of women throughout his life.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974216"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 216.</ref> Murray-Brown characterized Kenyatta as an ""affectionate father"" to his children, but one who was frequently absent.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974110"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column4: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 110.</ref> Kenyatta had two children from his first marriage with Grace Wahu: son Peter Muigai Kenyatta (born 1920), who later became a deputy minister; and daughter [[Margaret Kenyatta (born 1928)
column5: Margaret Kenyatta]] (born 1928). Margaret served as mayor of Nairobi between 1970 and 1976 and then as Kenya's ambassador to the United Nations from 1976 to 1986.<ref>{{cite news
column16: url-status=usurped}}</ref> Of these children, it was Margaret who was Kenyatta's closest confidante.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974110Maloba2018137"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: During his trial, Kenyatta described himself as a Christian<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974265"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column2: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 265.</ref> saying, ""I do not follow any particular denomination. I believe in Christianity as a whole.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974269"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column3: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 269.</ref> Arnold stated that in England, Kenyatta's adherence to Christianity was ""desultory"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197427"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column4: Arnold 1974]], p. 27.</ref> While in London, Kenyatta had taken an interest in the [[atheism
column5: atheist]] speakers at [[Speakers' Corner]] in [[Hyde Park, London
column7: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 130.</ref> while an Irish Muslim friend had unsuccessfully urged Kenyatta to convert to [[Islam]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974130"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column8: Murray-Brown 1974]], p. 130.</ref> During his imprisonment, Kenyatta read up on Islam, [[Hinduism]], [[Buddhism]], and [[Confucianism]] through books supplied to him by Stock.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974285Maloba2018138"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column10: Maloba 2018]], p. 138.</ref> The Israeli diplomat Asher Naim visited him in this period, noting that although Kenyatta was ""not a religious man, he was appreciative of the Bible"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTENaim200577"">[[#CITEREFNaim2005
column11: Naim 2005]], p. 77.</ref> Despite portraying himself as a Christian, he found the attitudes of many European missionaries intolerable, in particular their readiness to see everything African as evil.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199825"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998
column12: Berman & Lonsdale 1998]], p. 25.</ref> In ''Facing Mount Kenya'', he challenged the missionaries' dismissive attitude toward [[ancestor veneration]], which he instead preferred to call ""ancestor communion"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBernardi1993175"">[[#CITEREFBernardi1993
column13: Bernardi 1993]], p. 175.</ref> In that book's dedication, Kenyatta invoked ""ancestral spirits"" as part of ""the Fight for African Freedom.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197470"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column4: A statue of Kenyatta (1971) by [[James Butler (artist)
column5: James Butler]] was erected at the [[Kenyatta International Conference Centre

column1: Within Kenya, Kenyatta came to be regarded as the ""Father of the Nation"",<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974315Arnold1974166Bernardi1993168Cullen2016516"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974
column5: Cullen 2016]], p. 516.</ref> and was given the unofficial title of ''[[Mzee]]'', a Swahili term meaning ""grand old man"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEJacksonRosberg198298Assensoh19983Nyangena20034"">[[#CITEREFJacksonRosberg1982
column8: Nyangena 2003]], p. 4.</ref> From 1963 until his death, a [[cult of personality]] surrounded him in the country,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba20184"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column9: Maloba 2018]], p. 4.</ref> one which deliberately interlinked Kenyan nationalism with Kenyatta's own personality.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba20184"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column10: Maloba 2018]], p. 4.</ref> This use of Kenyatta as a popular symbol of the nation itself was furthered by the similarities between their names.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEJacksonRosberg198298"">[[#CITEREFJacksonRosberg1982
column11: Jackson & Rosberg 1982]], p. 98.</ref> He came to be regarded as a [[father figure]] not only by Kikuyu and Kenyans, but by Africans more widely.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974192, 195"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974

column1: After 1963, Maloba noted, Kenyatta became ""about the most admired post-independence African leader"" on the world stage, one who Western countries hailed as a ""beloved elder statesman.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba20182"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column2: Maloba 2018]], p. 2.</ref> His opinions were ""most valued"" both by conservative African politicians and by Western leaders.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017196"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column3: Maloba 2017]], p. 196.</ref> On becoming Kenya's leader, his anti-communist positions gained favour in the West,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201726"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column4: Maloba 2017]], p. 26.</ref> and some pro-Western governments gave him awards; in 1965 he, for instance, received medals from both [[Pope Paul VI]] and from the South Korean government.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba201725"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017

column1: In 1974, Arnold referred to Kenyatta as ""one of the outstanding African leaders now living"", someone who had become ""synonymous with Kenya"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold19749"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 9.</ref> He added that Kenyatta had been ""one of the shrewdest politicians"" on the continent,<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974209"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Arnold 1974]], p. 209.</ref> regarded as ""one of the great architects of African nationalist achievement since 1945"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974192"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column4: Arnold 1974]], p. 192.</ref> Kenneth O. Nyangena characterised him as ""one of the greatest men of the twentieth century"", having been ""a beacon, a rallying point for suffering Kenyans to fight for their rights, justice and freedom"" whose ""brilliance gave strength and aspiration to people beyond the boundaries of Kenya"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTENyangena20034"">[[#CITEREFNyangena2003
column5: Nyangena 2003]], p. 4.</ref> In 2018, Maloba described him as ""one of the legendary pioneers of modern African nationalism"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba20181"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column6: Maloba 2018]], p. 1.</ref> In their examination of his writings, Berman and Lonsdale described him as a ""pioneer"" for being one of the first Kikuyu to write and publish; ""his representational achievement was unique"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBermanLonsdale199817"">[[#CITEREFBermanLonsdale1998

column1: Maxon noted that in the areas of health and education, Kenya under Kenyatta ""achieved more in a decade and a half than the colonial state had accomplished in the preceding six decades.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995143"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column2: Maxon 1995]], p. 143.</ref> By the time of Kenyatta's death, Kenya had gained higher life expectancy rates than most of Sub-Saharan Africa.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995143"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column3: Maxon 1995]], p. 143.</ref> The country had taken what Maxon called ""giant steps"" toward achieving its goal of universal primary education for Kenyan children.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995143"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995
column4: Maxon 1995]], p. 143.</ref> Another significant success had been in dismantling the colonial-era system of racial segregation in schools, public facilities, and social clubs peacefully and with minimal disruption.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaxon1995143"">[[#CITEREFMaxon1995

column1: During much of his life, Kenya's white settlers regarded Kenyatta as a malcontent and an agitator;<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold197446"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column2: Arnold 1974]], p. 46.</ref> for them, he was a figure of hatred and fear.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba20182"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2018
column3: Maloba 2018]], p. 2.</ref> As the historian Keith Kyle put it, for many whites Kenyatta was ""Satan Incarnate"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEKyle199743"">[[#CITEREFKyle1997
column4: Kyle 1997]], p. 43.</ref> This white animosity reached its apogee between 1950 and 1952.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974197–198"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column5: Arnold 1974]], pp. 197–198.</ref> By 1964, this image had largely shifted, and many white settlers referred to him as ""Good Old Mzee"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974180"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column6: Arnold 1974]], p. 180.</ref> Murray-Brown expressed the view that for many, Kenyatta's ""message of reconciliation, 'to forgive and forget', was perhaps his greatest contribution to his country and to history.""<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMurray-Brown1974322"">[[#CITEREFMurray-Brown1974

column1: To Ochieng, Kenyatta was ""a personification of conservative social forces and tendencies"" in Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEOchieng199593"">[[#CITEREFOchieng1995
column2: Ochieng 1995]], p. 93.</ref> Towards the end of his presidency, many younger Kenyans—while respecting Kenyatta's role in attaining independence—regarded him as a [[reactionary]].<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEArnold1974192–193"">[[#CITEREFArnold1974
column3: Arnold 1974]], pp. 192–193.</ref> Those desiring a radical transformation of Kenyan society often compared Kenyatta's Kenya unfavourably with its southern neighbour, Julius Nyerere's Tanzania.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970519–520"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column4: Savage 1970]], pp. 519–520.</ref> The criticisms that leftists like Odinga made of Kenyatta's leadership were similar to those that the intellectual [[Frantz Fanon]] had made of post-colonial leaders throughout Africa.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTESavage1970518"">[[#CITEREFSavage1970
column5: Savage 1970]], p. 518.</ref> Drawing upon Marxist theory, Jay O'Brien, for instance, argued that Kenyatta had come to power ""as a representative of a would-be bourgeoisie"", a coalition of ""relatively privileged petty bourgeois African elements"" who wanted simply to replace the British colonialists and ""Asian commercial bourgeoisie"" with themselves. He suggested that the British supported Kenyatta in this, seeing him as a bulwark against growing worker and peasant militancy who would ensure continued neo-colonial dominance.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEO'Brien197692–93"">[[#CITEREFO'Brien1976

column1: Providing a similar leftist critique, the Marxist writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o stated that ""here was a black Moses who had been called by history to lead his people to the promised land of no exploitation, no oppression, but who failed to rise to the occasion"".<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017354"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column2: Maloba 2017]], p. 354.</ref> Ngũgĩ saw Kenyatta as a ""twentieth-century tragic figure: he could have been a [[Vladimir Lenin
column3: Lenin]], a [[Mao Zedong]], or a [[Ho Chi Minh]]; but he ended up being a [[Chiang Kai-shek]], a [[Park Chung Hee]], or a [[Augusto Pinochet
column5: Maloba 2017]], p. 355.</ref> Ngũgĩ was among Kenyan critics who claimed that Kenyatta treated Mau Mau veterans dismissively, leaving many of them impoverished and landless while seeking to remove them from the centre stage of national politics.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEMaloba2017350–351, 353"">[[#CITEREFMaloba2017
column6: Maloba 2017]], pp. 350–351, 353.</ref> In other areas Kenyatta's government also faced criticism; it for instance made little progress in advancing women's rights in Kenya.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEAssensoh199865"">[[#CITEREFAssensoh1998

column1: In 1991, the Kenyan lawyer and human rights activist [[Gibson Kamau Kuria]] noted that in abolishing the federal system, banning independent candidates from standing in elections, setting up a unicameral legislature, and relaxing restrictions on the use of emergency powers, Kenyatta had laid ""the groundwork"" for Moi to further advance dictatorial power in Kenya during the late 1970s and 1980s.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEKuria1991120–21"">[[#CITEREFKuria1991
In its 2013 report, the [[The Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission of Kenya
column2: Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission of Kenya]] accused Kenyatta  of using his authority as president to allocate large tracts of land to himself and his family.<ref>{{Cite news
column4: title=Kenyatta Led Elite in Land Grabbing
column10: url-status=live}}</ref> The Kenyatta family is among Kenya's biggest landowners.<ref>{{Cite news
column12: title=Kenyatta Family Seeks Approval To For Its Dream City Outside Nairobi

column1: During the 1990s, there was still much frustration among tribal groups, namely in the Nandi, Nakuru, Uasin-Gishu, and Trans-Nzoia Districts, where under Kenyatta's government they had not regained the land taken by European settlers and more of it had been sold to those regarded as ""foreigners""—Kenyans from other tribes.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBoone201286"">[[#CITEREFBoone2012
column2: Boone 2012]], p. 86.</ref> Among these groups there were widespread calls for restitution and in 1991 and 1992 there were violent attacks against many of those who obtained land through Kenyatta's patronage. The violence continued sporadically until 1996, with an estimated 1500 killed and 300,000 displaced in the Rift Valley.<ref group="""" name=""FOOTNOTEBoone201286–87"">[[#CITEREFBoone2012

column106: anti-colonial]] activist and politician who governed [[Kenya]] as its [[Prime Minister of Kenya
column107: Prime Minister]] from 1963 to 1964 and then as its first [[President of Kenya
column108: President]] from 1964 to his death in 1978. He played a significant role in the transformation of Kenya from [[Kenya Colony
column109:
a colony]] of the [[British Empire]] into an independent republic. Ideologically an [[African nationalist]] and a [[conservative]], he led the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU) party from 1961 until his death. His government was responsible for numerous massacres of ethnic minorities in Kenya, particularly ethnic Somali civilians.

<!--Early life, childhood through to imprisonment-->
Kenyatta was born to [[Kikuyu people
column110: Kikuyu]] farmers in [[Kiambu]], British East Africa. He was educated at a [[mission school]] and later on worked in various jobs before becoming politically engaged through the [[Kikuyu Central Association]]. In 1929, he travelled to [[London]] to lobby for Kikuyu land affairs. During the 1930s, he studied at [[Moscow]]\'s [[Communist University of the Toilers of the East]], [[University College London]], and the [[London School of Economics]]. In 1938, he published [[Facing Mount Kenya
column111: an anthropological study of Kikuyu life]] before working as a [[Farmworker
column112: farm labourer]] in [[Sussex]] during the [[Second World War]]. Influenced by his friend [[George Padmore]], he embraced anti-colonialist and [[Pan-African]] ideas, co-organising the 1945 [[Pan-African Congress]] in [[Manchester]]. He returned to Kenya in 1946 and became a school principal. In 1947, he was elected President of the [[Kenya African Union]], through which he lobbied for independence from British colonial rule, attracting widespread indigenous support but animosity from [[White Kenyans
column113:
white settlers]]. In 1952, he was among the [[Kapenguria Six]] arrested and charged with masterminding the anti-colonial [[Mau Mau Uprising]]. Although protesting his innocence—a view shared by later historians—he was convicted. He remained imprisoned at [[Lokitaung]] until 1959 and was then exiled to [[Lodwar]] until 1961.

<!--Later life; premiership and presidency-->
On his release, Kenyatta became President of KANU and led the party to victory in the [[1963 Kenyan general election
column114: 1963 general election]]. As Prime Minister, he oversaw the transition of the Kenya Colony into an independent republic, of which he became president in 1964. Desiring a [[one-party state]], he transferred regional powers to his central government, suppressed political dissent, and prohibited KANU\'s only rival—[[Jaramogi Oginga Odinga
column115: Oginga Odinga]]\'s leftist [[Kenya People\'s Union]]—from competing in elections. He promoted reconciliation between the country\'s indigenous ethnic groups and its European minority, although his relations with the [[Indians in Kenya
column116: Kenyan Indians]] were strained and Kenya\'s army clashed with [[Somali-Kenyan conflict
column117: Somali separatists]] in the [[North Eastern Province (Kenya)
column118: North Eastern Province]] during the [[Shifta War]]. His government pursued [[capitalist]] economic policies and the ""Africanisation"" of the economy, prohibiting non-citizens from controlling key industries. Education and healthcare were expanded, while UK-funded land redistribution favoured KANU loyalists and exacerbated ethnic tensions. Under Kenyatta, Kenya joined the [[Organisation of African Unity]] and the [[Commonwealth of Nations]], espousing a pro-[[Western world
column120: anti-communist]] foreign policy amid the [[Cold War]]. Kenyatta died in office and was succeeded by [[Daniel arap Moi]]. Kenyatta\'s son [[Uhuru Kenyatta
column121:
Uhuru]] later also became president.

<!--Reception and legacy-->
Kenyatta was a controversial figure. Prior to Kenyan independence, many of its white settlers regarded him as an agitator and malcontent, although across Africa he gained widespread respect as an anti-colonialist. During his presidency, he was given the honorary title of '''Mzee''' and lauded as the [[Father of the Nation]], securing support from both the black majority and the white minority with his message of reconciliation. Conversely, his rule was criticised as dictatorial, [[authoritarian]], and [[neocolonialism
column122: neocolonial]], of favouring Kikuyu over other ethnic groups, and of facilitating the growth of widespread [[Corruption in Kenya
column123:
corruption]].

[[File:Kikuyu village 02.jpg
column126: A traditional Kikuyu house, similar to that in which Kenyatta would have lived in Ngenda]]\n\nA member of the [[Kikuyu people]], Kenyatta was born with the name Kamau in the small rural village of Ngenda.{{sfnm
column132: 2p=38}} Birth records were not then kept among the Kikuyu, and Kenyatta\'s date of birth is not known.{{sfnm
column141: 3p=38}} One biographer, Jules Archer, suggested he was probably born in 1890 or 1891,{{sfn
column144: p=11}} although a fuller analysis by Jeremy Murray-Brown suggested a birth {{Circa
column148: p=323}} Kenyatta\'s father was named Mūigai, and his mother Wambūi.{{sfnm
column154: 2p=38}} They lived in a homestead near River Thiririka, where they raised crops and bred sheep and goats.{{sfnm
column160: 2p=38}} Mūigai was sufficiently wealthy that he could afford to keep several wives, each living in a separate \'\'nyũmba\'\' (hut).{{sfn
column163: pp=11, 14–15}}\n\nKenyatta was raised according to traditional Kikuyu custom and belief, and was taught the skills needed to herd the family flock.{{sfnm
column169: 2pp=35–36}} When he was 10 years old, his earlobes were pierced to mark his transition from childhood.{{sfn
column172: p=17}} Wambūi subsequently bore another son, Kongo,{{sfn
column178: p=37}} In keeping with Kikuyu tradition, Wambūi then married her late husband\'s younger brother, Ngengi.{{sfn
column181: p=37}} Kenyatta then took the name of Kamau wa Ngengi (""Kamau, son of Ngengi"").{{sfnm
column190: 3p=15}} Wambūi bore her new husband a son, whom they also named Mūigai.{{sfn
column193: p=37}} Ngengi was harsh and resentful toward the three boys, and Wambūi decided to take her youngest son to live with her parental family further north.{{sfn
column196: p=37}} It was there that she died, and Kenyatta—who was very fond of the younger Mūigai—travelled to collect his infant half-brother.{{sfn
column199: p=37}} Kenyatta then moved in with his grandfather, Kongo wa Magana, and assisted the latter in his role as a [[Traditional medicine
column209: quote=""Missionaries have done a lot of good work because it was through the missionary that many of the Kikuyu got their first education ... and were able to learn how to read and write ... Also, the medical side of it: the missionary did very well. At the same time I think the missionaries ... did not understand the value of the African custom, and many of them tried to stamp out some of the customs without knowing the part they play in the life of the Kikuyu ... They upset the life of the people.""
column213: p=32}} }}\n\nIn November 1909, Kenyatta left home and enrolled as a pupil at the [[Church of Scotland]] Mission (CSM) at [[Thogoto]].{{sfn
column216: pp=40, 43}} The missionaries were zealous Christians who believed that bringing [[Christianity]] to the indigenous peoples of Eastern Africa was part of Britain\'s civilizing mission.{{sfn
column219: p=46}} While there, Kenyatta stayed at the small [[boarding school]], where he learnt stories from the [[Bible]],{{sfn
column222: p=45}} and was taught to read and write in [[English language
column229: 2p=45}} He also performed chores for the mission, including washing the dishes and weeding the gardens.{{sfn
column232: p=43}} He was soon joined at the mission dormitory by his brother Kongo.{{sfn
column235: p=50}} The longer the pupils stayed, the more they came to resent the patronising way many of the British missionaries treated them.{{sfn
column238: p=49}}\n\nKenyatta\'s academic progress was unremarkable, and in July 1912 he became an apprentice to the mission\'s carpenter.{{sfn
column241: p=48}} That year, he professed his dedication to Christianity and began undergoing [[catechism]].{{sfn
column244: p=48}} In 1913, he underwent the Kikuyu [[circumcision]] ritual; the missionaries generally disapproved of this custom, but it was an important aspect of Kikuyu tradition, allowing Kenyatta to be recognized as an adult.{{sfnm
column250: 2p=39}} Asked to take a [[Christian name]] for his upcoming baptism, he first chose both John and Peter after [[Apostles in the New Testament
column251: Jesus\' apostles]]. Forced by the missionaries to choose just one, he chose Johnstone, the \'\'-stone\'\' chosen as a reference to Peter.{{sfn
column255: baptized]] as Johnstone Kamau in August 1914.{{sfnm
column261: 2p=39}} After his baptism, Kenyatta moved out of the mission dormitory and lived with friends.{{sfn
column264: p=53}} Having completed his apprenticeship to the carpenter, Kenyatta requested that the mission allow him to be an apprentice stonemason, but they refused.{{sfn
column267: p=53}} He then requested that the mission recommend him for employment, but the head missionary refused because of an allegation of minor dishonesty.{{sfn
column278: 2pp=40–41}} Kenyatta left the job when he became seriously ill; he recuperated at a friend\'s house in the Tumutumu Presbyterian mission.{{sfnm
column284: 2p=41}} At the time, the [[British Empire]] was engaged in the [[First World War]], and the [[British Army]] had recruited many Kikuyu. One of those who joined was Kongo, who disappeared during the conflict; his family never learned of his fate.{{sfn
column287: p=73}} Kenyatta did not join the armed forces, and like other Kikuyu he moved to live among the [[Maasai people
column288: Maasai]], who had refused to fight for the British.{{sfnm
column294: 2p=41}} Kenyatta lived with the family of an aunt who had married a Maasai chief,{{sfn
column297: p=74}} adopting Maasai customs and wearing Maasai jewellery, including a beaded belt known as \'\'kĩnyata\'\' in the [[Kikuyu language]]. At some point, he took to calling himself ""Kĩnyata"" or ""Kenyatta"" after this garment.{{sfn
column300: p=75}}\n\nIn 1917, Kenyatta moved to [[Narok]], where he was involved in transporting livestock to Nairobi,{{sfn
column303: p=74}} before relocating to Nairobi to work in a store selling farming and engineering equipment.{{sfn
column306: p=74}} In the evenings, he took classes in a church mission school.{{sfn
column309: p=74}} Several months later he returned to Thika before obtaining employment building houses for the Thogota Mission.{{sfn
column312: pp=74–75}} He also lived for a time in [[Dagoretti]], where he became a retainer for a local sub-chief, Kioi; in 1919 he assisted Kioi in putting the latter\'s case in a land dispute before a Nairobi court.{{sfnm
column321: p=79}} Kenyatta entered a relationship with [[Grace Wahu]], who had attended the CMS School in [[Kabete]]; she initially moved into Kenyatta\'s family homestead,{{sfn
column324: p=79}} although she joined Kenyatta in Dagoretti when Ngengi drove her out.{{sfn
column327: p=79}} On 20 November 1920 she gave birth to Kenyatta\'s son, Peter Muigai.{{sfnm
column333: 2p=42}} In October 1920, Kenyatta was called before the Thogota Kirk Session and suspended from taking [[Holy Communion]]; the suspension was in response to his drinking and his relations with Wahu out of wedlock.{{sfnm
column339: 2p=42}} The church insisted that a traditional Kikuyu wedding would be inadequate, and that he must undergo a Christian marriage;{{sfn
column345: p=93}} Kenyatta had initially refused to cease drinking,{{sfn
column348: p=92}} but in July 1923 officially renounced alcohol and was allowed to return to Holy Communion.{{sfn
column351: pp=93–94}}\n\nIn April 1922, Kenyatta began working as a stores clerk and meter reader for Cook, who had been appointed water superintendent for Nairobi\'s municipal council.{{sfnm
column364: cursign=£}}) a month, a particularly high wage for a native African, which brought him financial independence and a growing sense of self-confidence.{{sfn
column367: pp=94, 95}} Kenyatta lived in the [[Kilimani]] neighbourhood of Nairobi,{{sfn
column370: p=95}} although he financed the construction of a second home at Dagoretti; he referred to this latter hut as the Kinyata Stores for he used it to hold general provisions for the neighborhood.{{sfnm
column376: 2p=42}} He had sufficient funds that he could lend money to European clerks in the offices,{{sfn
column379: p=96}} and could enjoy the lifestyle offered by Nairobi, which included cinemas, football matches, and imported British fashions.{{sfn
column385: Kenyatta lobbied against many of the actions of Edward Grigg, Governor of Kenya. Grigg tried to suppress many of Kenyatta\'s activities.]]\n\n[[Anti-imperialism
column386: Anti-imperialist]] sentiment was on the rise among both native and Indian communities in Kenya following the [[Irish War of Independence]] and the Russian [[October Revolution]].{{sfn
column389: p=103}} Many indigenous Africans resented having to carry \'\'[[kipande]]\'\' identity certificates at all times, being forbidden from growing coffee, and paying taxes without political representation.{{sfn
column392: pp=18–19}} Political upheavals occurred in Kikuyuland—the area inhabited largely by the Kikuyu—following World War I, among them the campaigns of [[Harry Thuku]] and the East African Association, resulting in the government massacre of 21 native protesters in March 1922.{{sfnm
column398: 2pp=19–20}} Kenyatta had not taken part in these events,{{sfn
column401: p=90}} perhaps so as not to disrupt his lucrative employment prospects.{{sfn
column404: p=95}}\n\nKenyatta\'s interest in politics stemmed from his friendship with [[James Beauttah]], a senior figure in the [[Kikuyu Central Association]] (KCA). Beauttah took Kenyatta to a political meeting in [[Pumwani]], although this led to no firm involvement at the time.{{sfn
column407: p=101}} In either 1925 or early 1926, Beauttah moved to Uganda, but remained in contact with Kenyatta.{{sfn
column410: p=103}} When the KCA wrote to Beauttah and asked him to travel to [[London]] as their representative, he declined, but recommended that Kenyatta—who had a good command of English—go in his place.{{sfn
column413: p=105}} Kenyatta accepted, probably on the condition that the Association matched his pre-existing wage.{{sfn
column416: p=106}} He thus became the group\'s secretary.{{sfn
column419: pp=42–43}}\n\nIt is likely that the KCA purchased a motorbike for Kenyatta,{{sfn
column422: p=106}} which he used to travel around Kikuyuland and neighbouring areas inhabited by the [[Meru people
column424: Embu]], helping to establish new KCA branches.{{sfnm
column430: 2p=110}} In February 1928, he was part of a KCA party that visited Government House in Nairobi to give evidence in front of the [[Hilton Young Commission]], which was then considering a federation between Kenya, Uganda, and [[Tanganyika (territory)
column434: pp=105, 106}} In June, he was part of a KCA team which appeared before a [[select committee (parliamentary system)
column435: select committee]] of the [[Legislative Council of Kenya
column436: Kenyan Legislative Council]] to express concerns about the recent introduction of Land Boards. Introduced by the British [[Governor of Kenya]], [[Edward Grigg, 1st Baron Altrincham
column437: Edward Grigg]], these Land Boards would hold all land in native reserves in trust for each tribal group. Both the KCA and the Kikuyu Association opposed these Land Boards, which treated Kikuyu land as collectively owned rather than recognising individual Kikuyu land ownership.{{sfn
column440: pp=107–108}} Also in February, his daughter, Wambui Margaret, was born.{{sfn
column443: p=110}}\nBy this point he was increasingly using the name ""Kenyatta"", which had a more African appearance than ""Johnstone"".{{sfn
column446: p=107}}\n\nIn May 1928, the KCA launched a Kikuyu-language magazine, \'\'Mũigwithania\'\' (roughly translated as ""The Reconciler"" or ""The Unifier""), in which it published news, articles, and homilies.{{sfnm
column456: 3p=17}} Its purpose was to help unify the Kikuyu and raise funds for the KCA.{{sfn
column459: p=109}} Kenyatta was listed as the publication\'s editor,{{sfn
column462: p=107}} although Murray-Brown suggested that he was not the guiding hand behind it and that his duties were largely confined to translating into Kikuyu.{{sfn
column465: p=109}} Aware that Thuku had been exiled for his activism, Kenyatta\'s took a cautious approach to campaigning, and in \'\'Mũigwithania\'\' he expressed support for the churches, district commissioners, and chiefs.{{sfnm
column471: 2p=9}} He also praised the British Empire, stating that: ""The first thing [about the Empire] is that all people are governed justly, big or small—equally. The second thing is that nobody is regarded as a slave, everyone is free to do what he or she likes without being hindered.""{{sfn
column474: p=109}} This did not prevent Grigg from writing to the authorities in London requesting permission to shut the magazine down.{{sfn
column477:
p=110}}
