[[File:Jomo Kenyatta Apa Pant and Acheing Oneko.jpg
column479: (l-r) Jomo Kenyatta, [[Apa Pant]], and [[Achieng Oneko]]]]\nAfter the KCA raised sufficient funds, in February 1929 Kenyatta sailed from [[Mombasa]] to Britain.{{sfnm
column492: 4p=9}} Grigg's administration could not stop Kenyatta's journey but asked London's [[Colonial Office]] not to meet with him.{{sfn
column495: pp=111–112}} He initially stayed at the [[West African Students' Union]] premises in [[West London (sub region)
column496: West London]], where he met [[Ladipo Solanke]].{{sfn
column499: p=114}} He then lodged with a prostitute; both this and Kenyatta's lavish spending brought concern from the Church Mission Society.{{sfn
column502: pp=118–119}} His landlord subsequently impounded his belongings due to unpaid debt.{{sfn
column505: p=119}} In the city, Kenyatta met with W. McGregor Ross at the [[Royal Empire Society]], Ross briefing him on how to deal with the Colonial Office.{{sfn
column508: pp=115–116}} Kenyatta became friends with Ross' family, and accompanied them to social events in [[Hampstead]].{{sfn
column511: pp=125–126}} He also contacted anti-imperialists active in Britain, including the [[League Against Imperialism]], [[Fenner Brockway]], and [[Kingsley Martin]].{{sfnm
column518: 2p=24}} Grigg was in London at the same time and, despite his opposition to Kenyatta's visit, agreed to meet with him at the [[Rhodes Trust]] headquarters in April. At the meeting, Kenyatta raised the land issue and Thuku's exile, the atmosphere between the two being friendly.{{sfn
column521: pp=116–117}} In spite of this, following the meeting, Grigg convinced [[Special Branch (Metropolitan Police)
column525: p=117}}\n\nKenyatta developed contacts with radicals to the left of the [[Labour Party (UK)
column531: p=27}} In the summer of 1929, he left London and traveled by [[Berlin]] to [[Moscow]] before returning to London in October.{{sfnm
column540: 3p=27}} Kenyatta was strongly influenced by his time in the [[Soviet Union]].{{sfn
column543: p=120}} Back in England, he wrote three articles on the Kenyan situation for the [[Communist Party of Great Britain]]'s newspapers, the ''[[Morning Star (British newspaper)
column544: Daily Worker]]'' and ''Sunday Worker''. In these, his criticism of British imperialism was far stronger than it had been in ''Muĩgwithania''.{{sfnm
column554: 3p=44}} These communist links concerned many of Kenyatta's [[liberalism
column559: p=27}} In January, Kenyatta met with [[Drummond Shiels]], the [[Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies]], at the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom
column560: House of Commons]]. Kenyatta told Shiels that he was not affiliated with communist circles and was unaware of the nature of the newspaper which published his articles.{{sfnm
column566: 2pp=22–23}} Shiels advised Kenyatta to return home to promote Kikuyu involvement in the constitutional process and discourage violence and extremism.{{sfn
column569: p=122}}\nAfter eighteen months in Europe, Kenyatta had run out of money. The [[Anti-Slavery International
column570: Anti-Slavery Society]] advanced him funds to pay off his debts and return to Kenya.{{sfn
column573: p=131}} Although Kenyatta enjoyed life in London and feared arrest if he returned home,{{sfn
column576: p=125}} he sailed back to Mombasa in September 1930.{{sfnm
column582: 2p=29}} On his return, his prestige among the Kikuyu was high because of his time spent in Europe.{{sfnm
column588: 2p=29}}\n\nIn his absence, [[female genital mutilation]] (FGM) had become a topic of strong debate in Kikuyu society. The [[Protestantism
column589: Protestant]] churches, backed by European medics and the colonial authorities, [[Campaign against female genital mutilation in colonial Kenya
column590: supported the abolition of this traditional practice]], but the KCA rallied to its defence, claiming that its abolition would damage the structure of Kikuyu society.{{sfnm
column599: 3p=25}} Anger between the two sides had heightened, several churches expelling KCA members from their congregations, and it was widely believed that the January 1930 killing of an American missionary, [[Hulda Stumpf]], had been due to the issue.{{sfn
column602: pp=134, 139}} As Secretary of the KCA, Kenyatta met with church representatives. He expressed the view that although personally opposing FGM, he regarded its legal abolition as counter-productive, and argued that the churches should focus on eradicating the practice through educating people about its harmful effects on women's health.{{sfnm
column609: 2p=25}} The meeting ended without compromise, and [[John Arthur (missionary)
column610: John Arthur]]—the head of the Church of Scotland in Kenya—later expelled Kenyatta from the church, citing what he deemed dishonesty during the debate.{{sfnm
column617: 2p=25}} In 1931, Kenyatta took his son out of the church school at Thogota and enrolled him in a KCA-approved, independent school.{{sfn
column623: quote=""With the support of all revolutionary workers and peasants we must redouble our efforts to break the bonds that bind us. We must refuse to give any support to the British imperialists either by paying taxes or obeying any of their slave laws! We can fight in unity with the workers and toilers of the whole world, and for a Free Africa.""
column627: p=178}} }}\n\nIn May 1931, Kenyatta and [[Parmenas Githendu Mukiri]] sailed for Britain, intent on representing the KCA at a [[Joint committee of the Parliament of the United Kingdom
column628: Joint Committee of Parliament]] on the future of East Africa.{{sfnm
column637: 3p=31}} Kenyatta would not return to Kenya for fifteen years.{{sfnm
column643: 2p=151}} In Britain, he spent the summer attending an [[Independent Labour Party]] [[summer school]] and [[Fabian Society]] gatherings.{{sfn
column646: p=153}} In June, he visited [[Geneva]], Switzerland to attend a [[Save the Children]] conference on African children.{{sfnm
column652: 2p=51}} In November, he met the Indian independence leader [[Mohandas Gandhi]] while in London.{{sfn
column655: p=157}} That month, he enrolled in the [[Woodbrooke Quaker Study Centre
column656: Woodbrooke Quaker College]] in [[Birmingham]], where he remained until the spring of 1932, attaining a certificate in English writing.{{sfnm
column669: 4p=59}}\n\nIn Britain, Kenyatta befriended an Afro-Caribbean Marxist, [[George Padmore]], who was working for the Soviet-run [[Comintern]].{{sfnm
column679: 3p=44}} Over time, he became Padmore\'s protégé.{{sfn
column682: p=171}} In late 1932, he joined Padmore in Germany.{{sfn
column685: p=166}} Before the end of the year, the duo relocated to Moscow, where Kenyatta studied at the [[Communist University of the Toilers of the East]].{{sfnm
column695: 3pp=69–71}} There he was taught arithmetic, geography, natural science, and political economy, as well as [[Marxism-Leninism
column696: Marxist-Leninist]] doctrine and the history of the Marxist-Leninist movement.{{sfn
column699: p=70}} Many Africans and members of the African diaspora were attracted to the institution because it offered free education and the opportunity to study in an environment where they were treated with dignity, free from the [[institutionalised racism]] present in the U.S. and British Empire.{{sfn
column702: p=71}} Kenyatta complained about the food, accommodation, and poor quality of English instruction.{{sfn
column706: p=27}} There is no evidence that he joined the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]],{{sfn
column709: p=72}} and one of his fellow students later characterised him as ""the biggest reactionary I have ever met.""{{sfn
column712: p=73}} Kenyatta also visited [[Siberia]], probably as part of an official guided tour.{{sfnm
column719: Nazi]] government shifted political allegiances in Europe; the Soviet Union pursued formal alliances with France and Czechoslovakia,{{sfnm
column726: 2p=27}} and thus reduced its support for the movement against British and French colonial rule in Africa.{{sfn
column729: p=6}} As a result, Comintern disbanded the [[International Trade Union Committee of Negro Workers]], with which both Padmore and Kenyatta were affiliated. Padmore resigned from the Soviet Communist Party in protest, and was subsequently vilified in the Soviet press.{{sfnm
column735: 2p=45}} Both Padmore and Kenyatta left the Soviet Union, the latter returning to London in August 1933.{{sfnm
column742: 2p=27}} The British authorities were highly suspicious of Kenyatta\'s time in the Soviet Union, suspecting that he was a Marxist-Leninist, and following his return the [[MI5]] intelligence service intercepted and read all his mail.{{sfn
column745: pp=74–75}}\n\nKenyatta continued writing articles, reflecting Padmore\'s influence.{{sfn
column748: p=176}} Between 1931 and 1937 he wrote several articles for the \'\'Negro Worker\'\' and joined the newspaper\'s editorial board in 1933.{{sfn
column751: pp=66, 68}} He also produced an article for a November 1933 issue of \'\'[[Labour Monthly]]\'\',{{sfn
column754: p=177}} and in May 1934 had a letter published in \'\'[[The Guardian
column758: p=64}} He also wrote the entry on Kenya for \'\'Negro\'\', an anthology edited by [[Nancy Cunard]] and published in 1934.{{sfnm
column768: 3p=62}} In these, he took a more radical position than he had in the past, calling for complete self-rule in Kenya.{{sfn
column771: pp=175–176}} In doing so he was virtually alone among political Kenyans; figures like Thuku and Jesse Kariuki were far more moderate in their demands.{{sfn
column774: p=179}} The pro-independence sentiments that he was able to express in Britain would not have been permitted in Kenya itself.{{sfn
column778: linguistic informant]] for the Phonetics Department at [[University College London]] (UCL); his Kikuyu voice recordings assisted [[Lilias Armstrong]]\'s production of \'\'The Phonetic and Tonal Structure of Kikuyu\'\'.{{sfnm
column784: 2p=46}} The book was published under Armstrong\'s name, although Kenyatta claimed he should have been listed as co-author.{{sfn
column787: p=180}} He enrolled at UCL as a student, studying an English course between January and July 1935 and then a [[phonetics]] course from October 1935 to June 1936.{{sfnm
column793: 2p=46}} Enabled by a grant from the [[International African Institute]],{{sfnm
column805: 4p=46}} he also took a [[social anthropology]] course under [[Bronisław Malinowski]] at the [[London School of Economics]] (LSE). Kenyatta lacked the qualifications normally required to join the course, but Malinowski was keen to support the participation of indigenous peoples in anthropological research.{{sfnm
column814: 3p=59}} For Kenyatta, acquiring an advanced degree would bolster his status among Kenyans and display his intellectual equality with white Europeans in Kenya.{{sfn
column818: p=30}}\nOver the course of his studies, Kenyatta and Malinowski became close friends.{{sfnm
column825: 2p=30}} Fellow course-mates included the anthropologists [[Audrey Richards]], [[Lucy Mair]], and [[Elspeth Huxley]].{{sfn
column828: p=189}} Another of his fellow LSE students was [[Prince Peter of Greece and Denmark]], who invited Kenyatta to stay with him and his mother, [[Princess Marie Bonaparte]], in Paris during the spring of 1936.{{sfnm
column836: image1 = JOMO KENYATTA - 95 Cambridge Street Pimlico London SW1V 4PY.jpg\n
column847: p=181}} but did not pay his landlady for over a year, owing over £100 in rent.{{sfn
column850: p=182}} This angered Ross and contributed to the breakdown of their friendship.{{sfn
column853: pp=181, 182}} He then rented a [[Camden Town]] flat with his friend Dinah Stock, whom he had met at an anti-imperialist rally in [[Trafalgar Square]].{{sfnm
column859: 2p=63}} Kenyatta socialised at the [[Student Movement House]] in [[Russell Square]], which he had joined in the spring of 1934,{{sfn
column862: p=183}} and befriended Africans in the city.{{sfn
column865: p=185}} To earn money, he worked as one of 250 black [[Extra (acting)
column866: extras]] in the film \'\'[[Sanders of the River]]\'\', filmed at [[Shepperton Studios]] in Autumn 1934.{{sfn
column869: p=185}} Several other Africans in London criticized him for doing so, arguing that the film degraded black people.{{sfn
column872: p=186}} Appearing in the film also allowed him to meet and befriend its star, the African-American [[Paul Robeson]].{{sfn
column876: Italy invaded Ethiopia (Abyssinia)]], incensing Kenyatta and other Africans in London; he became the honorary secretary of the [[International African Friends of Abyssinia]], a group established by Padmore and [[C. L. R. James]].{{sfnm
column885: 3pp=55–56}} When Ethiopia\'s monarch [[Haile Selassie]] fled to London in exile, Kenyatta personally welcomed him at [[London Waterloo station
column892: 2p=58}} This group developed into a wider [[pan-Africanism
column893: pan-Africanist]] organisation, the [[International African Service Bureau]] (IASB), of which Kenyatta became one of the vice chairs.{{sfnm
column899: 2pp=47–48}} Kenyatta began giving anti-colonial lectures across Britain for groups like the IASB, the [[Workers\' Educational Association]], [[British Committee of the Indian National Congress
column900: Indian National Congress of Great Britain]], and the [[League of Coloured Peoples]].{{sfnm
column906: 2pp=49, 53–55}} In October 1938, he gave a talk to the Manchester Fabian Society in which he described British colonial policy as [[fascism]] and compared the treatment of indigenous people in East Africa to the [[Anti-Jewish legislation in prewar Nazi Germany
column910: p=203}} In response to these activities, the British Colonial Office reopened their file on him, although could not find any evidence that he was engaged in anything sufficiently seditious to warrant prosecution.{{sfn
column913: p=204}}\n\nKenyatta assembled the essays on Kikuyu society written for Malinowski\'s class and published them as \'\'[[Facing Mount Kenya]]\'\' in 1938.{{sfnm
column923: 3p=59}} Featuring an introduction written by Malinowski,{{sfnm
column930: 2p=32}} the book reflected Kenyatta\'s desire to use anthropology as a weapon against colonialism.{{sfn
column933: p=189}} In it, Kenyatta challenged the Eurocentric view of history by presenting an image of a golden African past by emphasising the perceived order, virtue, and self-sufficiency of Kikuyu society.{{sfn
column944: 2p=36}} he promoted the idea that traditional Kikuyu society had a cohesion and integrity that was better than anything offered by European colonialism.{{sfn
column947: p=191}} In this book, Kenyatta made clear his belief that the rights of the individual should be downgraded in favour of the interests of the group.{{sfn
column950: p=193}} The book also reflected his changing views on female genital mutilation; where once he opposed it, he now unequivocally supported the practice, downplaying the medical dangers that it posed to women.{{sfnm
column959: 3p=27}}\n\nThe book\'s jacket cover featured an image of Kenyatta in traditional dress, wearing a skin cloak over one shoulder and carrying a spear.{{sfnm
column969: 3p=31}} The book was published under the name ""Jomo Kenyatta"", the first time that he had done so; the term \'\'Jomo\'\' was close to a Kikuyu word describing the removal of a sword from its scabbard.{{sfn
column972: pp=194, 196}} \'\'Facing Mount Kenya\'\' was a commercial failure, selling only 517 copies, but was generally well received;{{sfn
column975: p=195}} an exception was among white Kenyans, whose assumptions about the Kikuyu being primitive savages in need of European civilization it challenged.{{sfn
column978: pp=168–169}} Murray-Brown later described it as ""a propaganda \'\'tour de force\'\'. No other African had made such an uncompromising stand for tribal integrity.""{{sfn
column981: p=192}} Bodil Folke Frederiksen, a scholar of [[development studies]], referred to it as ""probably the most well-known and influential African scholarly work of its time"",{{sfn
column984: p=36}} while for fellow scholar Simon Gikandi, it was ""one of the major texts in what has come to be known as the invention of tradition in colonial Africa"".{{sfn
column990: quote=""In the last war 300,000 of my people fought in the British Army to drive the Germans from East Africa and 60,000 of them lost their lives. In this war large numbers of my people have been fighting to smash fascist power in Africa and have borne some of the hardest fights against the Italians. Surely if we are considered fit enough to take our rifles and fight side by side with white men we have a right to a direct say in the running of our country and to education.""
column994: p=211}} }}\n\nAfter the United Kingdom entered [[World War II]] in September 1939, Kenyatta and Stock moved to the [[Sussex]] village of [[Storrington]].{{sfnm
column1004: 3p=81}} Kenyatta remained there for the duration of the war, renting a flat and a small plot of land to grow vegetables and raise chickens.{{sfnm
column1010: 2p=81}} He settled into rural Sussex life,{{sfnm
column1016: 2p=81}} and became a regular at the village pub, where he gained the nickname ""Jumbo"".{{sfnm
column1025: 3p=81}} In August 1940, he took a job at a local farm as an agricultural worker—allowing him to evade [[Conscription in the United Kingdom
column1026: military conscription]]—before working in the tomato greenhouses at [[Lindfield, West Sussex
column1036: 3p=81}} He attempted to join the local [[Home Guard (United Kingdom)
column1037: Home Guard]], but was turned down.{{sfn
column1040: p=211}} On 11 May 1942 he married an English woman, Edna Grace Clarke, at [[Register office (United Kingdom)
column1047: 2p=84}} In August 1943, their son, Peter Magana, was born.{{sfnm
column1053: 2p=84}}\n\nIntelligence services continued monitoring Kenyatta, noting that he was politically inactive between 1939 and 1944.{{sfn
column1056: p=85}} In Sussex, he wrote an essay for the United Society for Christian Literature, \'\'My People of Kikuyu and the Life of Chief Wangombe\'\', in which he called for his tribe\'s political independence.{{sfnm
column1066: 3p=95}} He also began—although never finished—a novel partly based on his life experiences.{{sfnm
column1073: 2p=35}} He continued to give lectures around the country, including to groups of East African soldiers stationed in Britain.{{sfnm
column1079: 2pp=83–84}} He became frustrated by the distance between him and Kenya, telling Edna that he felt ""like a general separated by 5000 miles from his troops"".{{sfn
column1082: pp=216–217}} While he was absent, Kenya\'s authorities banned the KCA in 1940.{{sfn
column1085: pp=209–210}}\n\nKenyatta and other senior IASB members began planning the fifth [[Pan-African Congress]], held in Manchester in October 1945.{{sfnm
column1094: 3p=85}} They were assisted by [[Kwame Nkrumah]], a [[Gold Coast (British colony)
column1095: Gold Coast]] (Ghanaian) who arrived in Britain earlier that year.{{sfnm
column1101: 2p=53}} Kenyatta spoke at the conference, although made no particular impact on the proceedings.{{sfn
column1104: pp=220–221}} Much of the debate that took place centred on whether indigenous Africans should continue pursuing a gradual campaign for independence or whether they should seek the military overthrow of the European imperialists.{{sfn
column1107: p=220}} The conference ended with a statement declaring that while delegates desired a peaceful transition to African self-rule, Africans ""as a last resort, may have to appeal to force in the effort to achieve Freedom"".{{sfn
column1110: pp=220–221}} Kenyatta supported this resolution, although was more cautious than other delegates and made no open commitment to violence.{{sfnm
column1116: 2pp=54–55}} He subsequently authored an IASB pamphlet, \'\'Kenya: The Land of Conflict\'\', in which he blended political calls for independence with romanticised descriptions of an idealised pre-colonial African past.{{sfnm
column1123:
2p=37}}

[[File:Jomo Kenyatta. Nairobi. 1949. Photo by Gopal Singh of Star Studio.jpg
column1125: Jomo Kenyatta in Nairobi in 1949]]\nAfter British victory in World War II, Kenyatta received a request to return to Kenya in September 1946, sailing back that month.{{sfnm
column1134: 3p=106}} He decided not to bring Edna—who was pregnant with a second child{{sfnm
column1140: 2p=106}}—with him, aware that if they joined him in Kenya their lives would be made very difficult by the colony\'s racial laws.{{sfn
column1143: p=60}} On his arrival in Mombasa, Kenyatta was greeted by his first wife, Grace Wahu and their children.{{sfn
column1146: pp=222–228}} He built a bungalow at [[Gatundu]], near to where he was born, and began farming his 32-acre estate.{{sfn
column1149: p=230}} Kenyatta met with the new Governor of Kenya, [[Philip Euen Mitchell]], and in March 1947 accepted a post on an African Land Settlement Board, holding the post for two years.{{sfnm
column1161: 4p=114}} He also met with [[Mbiyu Koinange]] to discuss the future of the Koinange Independent Teachers\' College in Githungui, Koinange appointing Kenyatta as its Vice-Principal.{{sfn
column1164: pp=229–230}} In May 1947, Koinange moved to England, leaving Kenyatta to take full control of the college.{{sfnm
column1170: 2p=230}} Under Kenyatta\'s leadership, additional funds were raised for the construction of school buildings and the number of boys in attendance rose from 250 to 900.{{sfn
column1173: pp=230–231}} It was also beset with problems, including a decline in standards and teachers\' strikes over non-payment of wages. Gradually, the number of enrolled pupils fell.{{sfn
column1176: p=231}} Kenyatta built a friendship with Koinange\'s father, a Senior Chief, who gave Kenyatta one of his daughters to take as his third wife.{{sfn
column1179: pp=229–230}}\nThey had another child, but she died in childbirth.{{sfn
column1182: p=243}} In 1951, he married his fourth wife, [[Ngina Kenyatta
column1183: Ngina]], who was one of the few female students at his college; she then gave birth to a daughter.{{sfnm
column1192: In October 1951 Kenyatta selected colors for the KAU flag: green for the land, black for the skin of the people, and red for the blood of liberty.{{sfn
column1195: p=242}}]]\n\nIn August 1944, the [[Kenya African Union]] (KAU) had been founded; at that time it was the only active political outlet for indigenous Africans in the colony.{{sfnm
column1201: 2p=113}} At its June 1947 [[annual general meeting]], KAU\'s President [[James Gichuru]] stepped down and Kenyatta was elected as his replacement.{{sfnm
column1213: 4p=117}} Kenyatta began to draw large crowds wherever he travelled in Kikuyuland,{{sfn
column1216: p=233}} and Kikuyu press began describing him as the ""Saviour"", ""Great Elder"", and ""Hero of Our Race"".{{sfn
column1219: p=234}} He was nevertheless aware that to achieve independence, KAU needed the support of other indigenous tribes and ethnic groups.{{sfn
column1222: p=225}} This was made difficult by the fact that many Maasai and [[Luo people of Kenya and Tanzania
column1223: Luo]]—tribes traditionally hostile to the Kikuyu—regarded him as an advocate of Kikuyu dominance.{{sfn
column1226: p=226}} He insisted on intertribal representation on the KAU executive and ensured that party business was conducted in [[Swahili language
column1227: Swahili]], the \'\'lingua franca\'\' of indigenous Kenyans.{{sfn
column1230: p=226}}\n\nTo attract support from Kenya\'s Indian community, he made contact with [[Jawaharlal Nehru]], the first [[Prime Minister of India
column1231: Prime Minister]] of the new Indian republic. Nehru\'s response was supportive, sending a message to Kenya\'s Indian minority reminding them that they were the guests of the indigenous African population.{{sfn
column1234: p=233}} Relations with the white minority remained strained; for most white Kenyans, Kenyatta was their principal enemy, an agitator with links to the Soviet Union who had the impertinence to marry a white woman.{{sfn
column1237: p=227}} They too increasingly called for further Kenyan autonomy from the British government, but wanted continued white-minority rule and closer links to the white-minority governments of South Africa, [[Northern Rhodesia]], and [[Southern Rhodesia]]; they viewed Britain\'s [[Attlee ministry
column1238: newly elected Labour government]] with great suspicion.{{sfn
column1241: pp=226–227}} The white Electors\' Union put forward a ""Kenya Plan"" which proposed greater white settlement in Kenya, bringing Tanganyika into the British Empire, and incorporating it within their new British East African Dominion.{{sfn
column1244: p=237}} In April 1950, Kenyatta was present at a joint meeting of KAU and the [[East African Indian National Congress]] in which they both expressed opposition to the Kenya Plan.{{sfn
column1247: p=241}}\n\nBy 1952, Kenyatta was widely recognized as a national leader, both by his supporters and by his opponents.{{sfn
column1250: p=181}} As KAU leader, he was at pains to oppose all illegal activity, including workers\' strikes.{{sfn
column1253: p=229}} He called on his supporters to work hard, and to abandon laziness, theft, and crime.{{sfnm
column1259: 2p=119}} He also insisted that in an independent Kenya, all racial groups would be safeguarded.{{sfn
column1262: p=244}} Kenyatta\'s gradualist and peaceful approach contrasted with the growth of the [[Mau Mau Uprising]], as armed guerrilla groups began targeting the white minority and members of the Kikuyu community who did not support them. By 1959, the Mau Mau had killed around 1,880 people.{{sfn
column1265: p=32}} For many young Mau Mau militants, Kenyatta was regarded as a hero,{{sfn
column1268: p=98}} and they included his name in the oaths they gave to the organisation; such oathing was a Kikuyu custom by which individuals pledged allegiance to another.{{sfn
column1271: p=123}} Kenyatta publicly distanced himself from the Mau Mau.{{sfn
column1274: p=121}} In April 1952, he began a speaking tour in which he denounced the Mau Mau to assembled crowds, insisting that independence must be achieved through peaceful means.{{sfnm
column1286: 4p=123}} In August he attended a much-publicised mass meeting in Kiambu where—in front of 30,000 people—he said that ""Mau Mau has spoiled the country. Let Mau Mau perish forever. All people should search for Mau Mau and kill it.""{{sfn
column1289: pp=248–249}} Despite Kenyatta\'s vocal opposition to the Mau Mau, KAU had moved towards a position of greater militancy.{{sfn
column1292: p=241}} At its 1951 AGM, more militant African nationalists had taken senior positions and the party officially announced its call for Kenyan independence within three years.{{sfn
column1295: p=242}} In January 1952, KAU members formed a secret Central Committee devoted to direct action, formulated along a [[Clandestine cell system
column1299: p=242}} Whatever Kenyatta\'s views on these developments, he had little ability to control them.{{sfn
column1302: p=243}} He was increasingly frustrated, and—without the intellectual companionship he experienced in Britain—felt lonely.{{sfn
column1308: quote=""We Africans are in the majority [in Kenya], and we should have self-government. That does not mean we should not take account of whites, provided we have the key position. We want to be friendly with whites. We don\'t want to be dominated by them.""
column1309: source= —Kenyatta, quoted by the \'\'[[Daily Express]]\'\', September 1952{{sfn
column1312: pp=120–121}} }}\n\nIn October 1952, Kenyatta was arrested and driven to Nairobi, where he was taken aboard a plane and flown to [[Lokitaung]], northwest Kenya, one of the most remote locations in the country.{{sfn
column1315: pp=253–254, 257}} From there he wrote to his family to let them know of his situation.{{sfn
column1318: p=257}} Kenya\'s authorities believed that detaining Kenyatta would help quell civil unrest.{{sfn
column1321: p=258}} Many white settlers wanted him exiled, but the government feared this would turn him into a martyr for the anti-colonialist cause.{{sfnm
column1327: 2p=60}} They thought it better that he be convicted and imprisoned, although at the time had nothing to charge him with, and so began searching his personal files for evidence of criminal activity.{{sfn
column1330: p=258}} Eventually, they charged him and five senior KAU members with masterminding the Mau Mau, a proscribed group.{{sfn
column1333: p=259}} The historian John M. Lonsdale stated that Kenyatta had been made a ""scapegoat"",{{sfn
column1336: p=403}} while the historian A. B. Assensoh later suggested that the authorities ""knew very well"" that Kenyatta was not involved in the Mau Mau, but that they were nevertheless committed to silencing his calls for independence.{{sfn
column1339: p=62}}\n\nThe trial took place in [[Kapenguria]], a remote area near the Ugandan border that the authorities hoped would not attract crowds or attention.{{sfnm
column1345: 2p=134}} Together, Kenyatta, [[Bildad Kaggia]], [[Fred Kubai]], [[Paul Ngei]], [[Achieng Oneko]] and [[Kung\'u Karumba]]—the ""[[Kapenguria Six]]""—were put on trial.{{sfn
column1348: p=258}} The defendants assembled an international and multiracial team of defence lawyers, including [[Chaman Lall]], [[H. O. Davies]], [[Fitz Remedios Santana de Souza
column1349: F. R. S. De Souza]], and [[Dudley Thompson]], led by British barrister and Member of Parliament [[Denis Nowell Pritt]].{{sfn
column1352: p=259}} Pritt\'s involvement brought much media attention;{{sfn
column1355: p=259}} during the trial he faced government harassment and was sent death threats.{{sfnm
column1361: 2p=142}} The judge selected, [[Ransley Thacker]], had recently retired from the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]];{{sfn
column1364: p=259}} the government knew he would be sympathetic to their case and gave him £20,000 to oversee it.{{sfn
column1367: p=129}} The trial lasted five months: [[Rawson Macharia]], the main prosecution witness, turned out to have perjured himself; the judge had only recently been awarded an unusually large pension and maintained secret contact with the then colonial Governor [[Evelyn Baring, 1st Baron Howick of Glendale
column1371: p=65}} The prosecution failed to produce any strong evidence that Kenyatta or the other accused had any involvement in managing the Mau Mau.{{sfn
column1374: p=262}}\n\nIn April 1953, Judge Thacker found the defendants guilty.{{sfnm
column1383: 3p=129}} He sentenced them to seven years\' [[hard labour]], to be followed by indefinite restriction preventing them from leaving a given area without permission.{{sfnm
column1392: 3p=129}} In addressing the court, Kenyatta stated that he and the others did not recognise the judge\'s findings; they claimed that the government had used them as scapegoats as a pretext to shut down KAU.{{sfnm
column1398: 2p=274}} The historian Wunyabari O. Maloba later characterised it as ""a rigged political trial with a predetermined outcome"".{{sfn
column1401: p=129}} The government followed the verdict with a wider crackdown, banning KAU in June 1953,{{sfn
column1404: p=255}} and closing down most of the independent schools in the country, including Kenyatta\'s.{{sfn
column1407: p=255}} It appropriated his land at Gatundu and demolished his house.{{sfn
column1410: p=136}}\n\nKenyatta and the others were returned to Lokitaung, where they resided on [[Remand (detention)
column1411: remand]] while awaiting the results of the [[appeal]] process.{{sfn
column1414: p=278}} Pritt pointed out that Thacker had been appointed magistrate for the wrong district, a technicality voiding the whole trial; the Supreme Court of Kenya concurred and Kenyatta and the others were freed in July 1953, only to be immediately re-arrested.{{sfn
column1417: p=278}} The government took the case to the [[East African Court of Appeal]], which reversed the Supreme Court\'s decision in August.{{sfn
column1420: p=278}} The appeals process resumed in October 1953, and in January 1954 the Supreme Court upheld the convictions against all but Oneko.{{sfn
column1423: p=279}} Pritt finally took the case to the [[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
column1424: Privy Council]] in London, but they refused his petition without providing an explanation. He later noted that this was despite the fact his case was one of the strongest he had ever presented during his career.{{sfnm
column1436: 4p=135}} According to Murray-Brown, it is likely that political, rather than legal considerations, informed their decision to reject the case.{{sfn
column1442: Tanganyikan children with signs demanding Kenyatta\'s release]]\n\nDuring the appeal process, a prison had been built at Lokitaung, where Kenyatta and the four others were then interned.{{sfnm
column1448: 2p=135}} The others were made to break rocks in the hot sun but Kenyatta, because of his age, was instead appointed their cook, preparing a daily diet of beans and [[posho]].{{sfnm
column1454: 2p=136}} In 1955, P. de Robeck became the District Officer, after which Kenyatta and the other inmates were treated more leniently.{{sfn
column1457: pp=283–284}} In April 1954, they had been joined by a captured Mau Mau commander, [[Waruhiu Itote]]; Kenyatta befriended him, and gave him English lessons.{{sfnm
column1463: 2p=139}} By 1957, the inmates had formed into two rival cliques, with Kenyatta and Itote on one side and the other KAU members—now calling themselves the ""National Democratic Party""—on the other.{{sfnm
column1469: 2p=138}} In one incident, one of his rivals made an unsuccessful attempt to stab Kenyatta at breakfast.{{sfn
column1472: pp=294–295}} Kenyatta\'s health had deteriorated in prison; manacles had caused problems for his feet and he had [[eczema]] across his body.{{sfnm
column1478: 2p=137}}\n\nKenyatta\'s imprisonment transformed him into a political martyr for many Kenyans, further enhancing his status.{{sfn
column1481: p=181}} A Luo anti-colonial activist, [[Jaramogi Oginga Odinga]], was the first to publicly call for Kenyatta\'s release, an issue that gained growing support among Kenya\'s anti-colonialists.{{sfn
column1484: pp=93, 199}} In 1955, the British writer [[Montagu Slater]]—a socialist sympathetic to Kenyatta\'s plight—released \'\'The Trial of Jomo Kenyatta\'\', a book which raised the profile of the case.{{sfnm
column1490: 2pp=27, 34}} In 1958, Rawson Macharia, the key witness in the state\'s prosecution of Kenyatta, signed an affidavit swearing that his evidence against Kenyatta had been false; this was widely publicised.{{sfn
column1493: p=161}} By the late 1950s, the imprisoned Kenyatta had become a symbol of African nationalism across the continent.{{sfn
column1496: p=96}}\n\nHis sentence served, in April 1959 Kenyatta was released from Lokitaung.{{sfnm
column1502: 2p=140}} The administration then placed a restricting order on Kenyatta, forcing him to reside in the remote area of [[Lodwar]], where he had to report to the district commissioner twice a day.{{sfnm
column1508: 2pp=140, 143}} There, he was joined by his wife Ngina.{{sfn
column1511: p=296}} In October 1961, they had another son, [[Uhuru Kenyatta
column1512: Uhuru]], and later on another daughter, Nyokabi, and a further son, Muhoho.{{sfn
column1515: p=320}} Kenyatta spent two years in Lodwar.{{sfn
column1518: p=297}} The Governor of Kenya, [[Patrick Muir Renison]], insisted that it was necessary; in a March 1961 speech, he described Kenyatta an ""African leader to darkness and death"" and stated that if he were released, violence would erupt.{{sfn
column1534: p=144}} Calls for his release came from the Chinese government,{{sfn
column1540: pp=155–156}} and Tanganyika\'s Prime Minister [[Julius Nyerere]].{{sfnm
column1546: 2p=152}} Kwame Nkrumah—whom Kenyatta had known since the 1940s and who was now President of a newly independent Ghana—personally raised the issue with British Prime Minister [[Harold Macmillan]] and other UK officials,{{sfn
column1549: pp=147–149}} with the Ghanaian government offering Kenyatta asylum in the event of his release.{{sfn
column1552: p=147}} Resolutions calling for his release were produced at the [[All-African Peoples\' Conference]]s held in [[Tunis]] in 1960 and [[Cairo]] in 1961.{{sfn
column1555: p=96}} Internal calls for his release came from Kenyan Asian activists in the [[Kenya Indian Congress]],{{sfn
column1558: p=169}} while a colonial government commissioned poll revealed that most of Kenya\'s indigenous Africans wanted this outcome.{{sfn
column1561: p=176}}\n\nBy this point, it was widely accepted that Kenyan independence was inevitable, the British Empire having been dismantled throughout much of Asia and Macmillan having made his ""[[Wind of Change (speech)
column1565: pp=287–288}} In January 1960, the British government made its intention to free Kenya apparent.{{sfn
column1568: p=299}} It invited representatives of Kenya\'s anti-colonial movement to [[Lancaster House Conferences (Kenya)
column1569: discuss the transition]] at London\'s [[Lancaster House]]. An agreement was reached that an election would be called for a new 65-seat Legislative Council, with 33 seats reserved for black Africans, 20 for other ethnic groups, and 12 as \'national members\' elected by a pan-racial electorate.{{sfn
column1572: p=62}} It was clear to all concerned that Kenyatta was going to be the key to the future of Kenyan politics.{{sfn
column1575: p=51}}\n\nAfter the Lancaster House negotiations, the anti-colonial movement had split into two parties, the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU), which was dominated by Kikuyu and Luo, and the [[Kenya African Democratic Union]] (KADU), which was led largely by members of smaller ethnic groups like the Kalenjin and Maasai.{{sfnm
column1584: 3p=204}} In May 1960, KANU nominated Kenyatta as its president, although the government vetoed it, insisting that he had been an instigator of the Mau Mau.{{sfn
column1587: p=300}} KANU then declared that it would refuse to take part in any government unless Kenyatta was freed.{{sfn
column1590: p=303}} KANU campaigned on the issue of Kenyatta\'s detainment in the [[1961 Kenyan general election
column1591: February 1961 election]], where it gained a majority of votes.{{sfnm
column1597: 2p=49}} KANU nevertheless refused to form a government, which was instead created through a KADU-led coalition of smaller parties.{{sfnm
column1609: 4p=59}} Kenyatta had kept abreast of these developments, although he had refused to back either KANU or KADU,{{sfn
column1612: p=304}} instead insisting on unity between the two parties.{{sfnm
column1621: p=182}} In April 1961, the government flew Kenyatta to [[Maralal]], where he maintained his innocence of the charges but told reporters that he bore no grudges.{{sfnm
column1630: 3pp=182–183}} He reiterated that he had never supported violence or the illegal oathing system used by the Mau Mau,{{sfn
column1633: p=50}} and denied having ever been a Marxist, stating: ""I shall always remain an African Nationalist to the end"".{{sfn
column1636: pp=304–305}} In August, he was moved to Gatundu in Kikuyuland, where he was greeted by a crowd of 10,000.{{sfnm
column1645: 3p=191}} There, the colonial government had built him a new house to replace that they had demolished.{{sfn
column1648: p=186}} Now a free man, he travelled to cities like Nairobi and Mombasa to make public appearances.{{sfn
column1651: p=307}}\nAfter his release, Kenyatta set about trying to ensure that he was the only realistic option as Kenya\'s future leader.{{sfn
column1654: p=149}} In August he met with Renison at Kiambu,{{sfnm
column1663: 3p=191}} and was interviewed by the [[BBC]]\'s \'\'[[Face to Face (British TV series)
column1667: p=307}} In October 1961, Kenyatta formally joined KANU and accepted its presidency.{{sfnm
column1676: 3p=209}} In January 1962 he was elected unopposed as KANU\'s representative for the [[Murang\'a
column1677: Fort Hall]] constituency in the legislative council after its sitting member, Kariuki Njiiri, resigned.{{sfnm
column1686: Kenyatta became close friends with the last British Governor of Kenya, Malcolm MacDonald, who helped speed the process of independence.]]\n\nKenyatta traveled elsewhere in Africa, visiting Tanganyika in October 1961 and Ethiopia in November at the invitation of their governments.{{sfn
column1689: pp=192–193}} A key issue facing Kenya was a border dispute in [[North Eastern Province (Kenya)
column1690: North East Province]], alongside Somalia. Ethnic Somalis inhabited this region and claimed it should be part of Somalia, not Kenya.{{sfnm
column1696: 2p=52}} Kenyatta disagreed, insisting the land remain Kenyan,{{sfn
column1699: pp=174–175}} and stated that Somalis in Kenya should ""pack up [their] camels and go to Somalia"".{{sfn
column1702: p=104}} In June 1962, Kenyatta travelled to [[Mogadishu]] to discuss the issue with the Somalian authorities, but the two sides could not reach an agreement.{{sfn
column1705: p=176}}\n\nKenyatta sought to gain the confidence of the white settler community. In 1962, the white minority had produced 80% of the country\'s exports and were a vital part of its economy, yet between 1962 and 1963 they were emigrating at a rate of 700 a month; Kenyatta feared that this white exodus would cause a [[brain drain]] and [[Labour shortage
column1706: skills shortage]] that would be detrimental to the economy.{{sfn
column1709: p=66}} He was also aware that the confidence of the white minority would be crucial to securing Western investment in Kenya\'s economy.{{sfn
column1712: p=309}} Kenyatta made it clear that when in power, he would not sack any white civil servants unless there were competent black individuals capable of replacing them.{{sfn
column1715: p=187}} He was sufficiently successful that several prominent white Kenyans backed KANU in the subsequent election.{{sfn
column1718: p=308}}\n\nIn 1962 he returned to London to attend one of the Lancaster House conferences.{{sfnm
column1724: 2p=55}} There, KANU and KADU representatives met with British officials to formulate a new constitution.{{sfn
column1727: p=152}} KADU desired a federalist state organised on a system they called \'\'[[Majimbo]]\'\' with six largely autonomous regional authorities, a two-chamber legislature, and a central Federal Council of Ministers who would select a rotating chair to serve as head of government for a one-year term. Renison\'s administration and most white settlers favoured this system as it would prevent a strong central government implementing radical reform.{{sfn
column1730: pp=209–213}} KANU opposed \'\'Majimbo\'\', believing that it served entrenched interests and denied equal opportunities across Kenya; they also insisted on an elected head of government.{{sfn
column1733: p=215}} At Kenyatta\'s prompting, KANU conceded to some of KADU\'s demands; he was aware that he could amend the constitution when in office.{{sfnm
column1739: 2pp=217–218}} The new constitution divided Kenya into six regions, each with a regional assembly, but also featured a strong central government and both an upper and a lower house.{{sfn
column1742: p=152}} It was agreed that a temporary coalition government would be established until independence, several KANU politicians being given ministerial posts.{{sfn
column1745: p=220}} Kenyatta accepted a minor position, that of the Minister of State for Constitutional Affairs and Economic Planning.{{sfnm
column1757: 4p=220}}\n\nThe British government considered Renison too ill at ease with indigenous Africans to oversee the transition to independence and thus replaced him with [[Malcolm MacDonald]] as Governor of Kenya in January 1963.{{sfn
column1760: pp=222–223}} MacDonald and Kenyatta developed a strong friendship;{{sfn
column1763: p=230}} the Briton referred to the latter as ""the wisest and perhaps strongest as well as most popular potential Prime Minister of the independent nation to be"".{{sfn
column1766: p=234}} MacDonald sped up plans for Kenyan independence, believing that the longer the wait, the greater the opportunity for radicalisation among African nationalists.{{sfn
column1769: p=239}} An election was scheduled for May, with self-government in June, followed by full independence in December 1964.{{sfn
column1772:
p=240}}
