The [[1963 Kenyan general election
column1773: May 1963 general election]] pitted Kenyatta\'s KANU against KADU, the Akamba People\'s Party, and various independent candidates.{{sfnm
column1779: 2p=120}} KANU was victorious with 83 seats out of 124 in the [[House of Representatives (Kenya)
column1783: p=308}} a KANU majority government replaced the pre-existing coalition.{{sfn
column1786: p=244}} On 1 June 1963, Kenyatta was sworn in as prime minister of the autonomous Kenyan government.{{sfnm
column1798: 4pp=244, 245}} Kenya remained a monarchy, with Queen [[Elizabeth II]] as its head of state.{{sfn
column1801: p=99}} In November 1963, Kenyatta\'s government introduced a law making it a criminal offence to disrespect the Prime Minister, exile being the punishment.{{sfn
column1804: p=315}} Kenyatta\'s personality became a central aspect of the creation of the new state.{{sfn
column1807: p=315}} In December, Nairobi\'s Delamere Avenue was renamed Kenyatta Avenue,{{sfnm
column1813: 2p=155}} and a bronze statue of him was erected beside the country\'s [[National Assembly (Kenya)
column1817: p=315}} Photographs of Kenyatta were widely displayed in shop windows,{{sfn
column1820: p=315}} and his face was also printed on the new currency.{{sfn
column1823: p=315}} In 1964, [[Oxford University Press]] published a collection of Kenyatta\'s speeches under the title of \'\'Harambee!\'\'.{{sfn
column1829: Kenyatta initially agreed to merge Kenya with Tanganyika, Uganda and Zanzibar to form an [[East African Federation]].]]\n\nKenya\'s first cabinet included not only Kikuyu but also members of the Luo, Kamba, Kisii, and Maragoli tribal groups.{{sfn
column1832: p=155}} In June 1963, Kenyatta met with Julius Nyerere and Ugandan President [[Milton Obote]] in Nairobi. The trio discussed the possibility of merging their three nations (plus Zanzibar) into a single [[East African Federation]], agreeing that this would be accomplished by the end of the year.{{sfnm
column1841: 3p=58}} Privately, Kenyatta was more reluctant regarding the arrangement and as 1964 came around the federation had not come to pass.{{sfn
column1844: p=174}} Many radical voices in Kenya urged him to pursue the project;{{sfn
column1847: p=95}} in May 1964, Kenyatta rejected a back-benchers resolution calling for speedier federation.{{sfn
column1850: p=174}} He publicly stated that talk of a federation had always been a ruse to hasten the pace of Kenyan independence from Britain, but Nyerere denied that this was true.{{sfn
column1853: p=174}}\n\nContinuing to emphasize good relations with the white settlers, in August 1963 Kenyatta met with 300 white farmers at [[Nakuru]]. He reassured them that they would be safe and welcome in an independent Kenya, and more broadly talked of forgiving and forgetting the conflicts of the past.{{sfnm
column1862: 3pp=258–259}} Despite his attempts at wooing white support, he did not do the same with the Indian minority.{{sfn
column1865: p=153}} Like many indigenous Africans in Kenya, Kenyatta bore a sense of resentment towards this community, despite the role that many Indians had played in securing the country\'s independence.{{sfn
column1868: p=316}} He also encouraged the remaining Mau Mau fighters to leave the forests and settle in society.{{sfn
column1871: p=309}} Throughout Kenyatta\'s rule, many of these individuals remained out of work, unemployment being one of the most persistent problems facing his government.{{sfn
column1874: p=316}}\n\nA celebration to mark independence was held in a specially constructed stadium on 12 December 1963. During the ceremony, [[Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh]]—representing the British monarchy—formally handed over control of the country to Kenyatta.{{sfnm
column1880: 2p=63}} Also in attendance were leading figures from the Mau Mau.{{sfn
column1883: p=60}} In a speech, Kenyatta described it as ""the greatest day in Kenya\'s history and the happiest day in my life.""{{sfn
column1886: p=311}} He had flown Edna and Peter over for the ceremony, and in Kenya they were welcomed into Kenyatta\'s family by his other wives.{{sfn
column1889: pp=310–311}}\n\nDisputes with Somalia over the Northern Frontier District (NFD) continued; for much of Kenyatta\'s rule, Somalia remained the major threat to his government.{{sfn
column1892: pp=153–154}} To deal with sporadic violence in the region by Somali \'\'[[shifta]]\'\' guerrillas, Kenyatta sent soldiers into the region in December 1963 and gave them broad powers of arrest and seizure in the NFD in September 1964.{{sfn
column1895: p=154}} British troops were assigned to assist the Kenyan Army in the region.{{sfn
column1898: p=155}} Kenyatta also faced domestic opposition: in January 1964, sections of the army launched a mutiny in Nairobi, and Kenyatta called on the British Army to put down the rebellion.{{sfnm
column1904: 2p=51}} Similar armed uprisings had taken place that month in neighboring Uganda and Tanganyika.{{sfnm
column1910: 2p=51}} Kenyatta was outraged and shaken by the mutiny.{{sfn
column1913: p=52}} He publicly rebuked the mutineers, emphasising the need for law and order in Kenya.{{sfn
column1916: p=157}} To prevent further military unrest, he brought in a review of the salaries of the army, police, and prison staff, leading to pay rises.{{sfn
column1919: p=52}} Kenyatta also wanted to contain parliamentary opposition and at Kenyatta\'s prompting, in November 1964 KADU officially dissolved and its representatives joined KANU.{{sfnm
column1928: 3pp=265–266}} Two of the senior members of KADU, [[Ronald Ngala]] and [[Daniel arap Moi]], subsequently became some of Kenyatta\'s most loyal supporters.{{sfn
column1931: p=160}} Kenya therefore became a \'\'de facto\'\' one-party state.{{sfnm
column1940: The presidential standard of Jomo Kenyatta, adopted in 1970]]\n\nIn December 1964, Kenya was officially proclaimed a republic.{{sfn
column1943: p=34}} Kenyatta became its executive president,{{sfnm
column1949: 2p=60}} combining the roles of [[head of state]] and [[head of government]].{{sfnm
column1958: 3p=63}} Over the course of 1965 and 1966, several constitutional amendments enhanced the president\'s power.{{sfn
column1961: p=35}} For instance, a May 1966 amendment gave the president the ability to order the [[preventive detention]] of individuals without trial if he deemed them to be security risks.{{sfnm
column1967: 2p=152}} Seeking the support of Kenya\'s second largest ethnic group, the Luo, Kenyatta appointed the Luo Oginga Odinga as his vice president.{{sfn
column1970: p=20}} The Kikuyu—who made up around 20 percent of population—still held most of the country\'s important government and administrative positions.{{sfnm
column1976: 2p=340}} This contributed to a perception among many Kenyans that independence had simply seen the dominance of a British elite replaced by the dominance of a Kikuyu elite.{{sfn
column1979: p=316}}\n\nKenyatta\'s calls to forgive and forget the past were a keystone of his government.{{sfnm
column1985: 2p=63}} He preserved some elements of the old colonial order, particularly in relation to [[Law and order (politics)
column1989: p=312}} The police and military structures were left largely intact.{{sfn
column1992: p=312}} White Kenyans were left in senior positions within the judiciary, civil service, and parliament,{{sfnm
column1998: 2p=63}} with the white Kenyans [[Bruce Mackenzie]] and [[Humphrey Slade]] being among Kenyatta\'s top officials.{{sfnm
column2007: 3p=63}} Kenyatta\'s government nevertheless rejected the idea that the European and Asian minorities could be permitted [[dual citizenship]], expecting these communities to offer total loyalty to the independent Kenyan state.{{sfn
column2010: p=112}} His administration pressured whites-only social clubs to adopt multi-racial entry policies,{{sfn
column2013: p=115}} and in 1964 schools formerly reserved for European pupils were opened to Africans and Asians.{{sfn
column2016: p=115}}\n\nKenyatta\'s government believed it necessary to cultivate a united Kenyan national culture.{{sfn
column2019: p=138}} To this end, it made efforts to assert the dignity of indigenous African cultures which missionaries and colonial authorities had belittled as ""primitive"".{{sfn
column2022: p=139}} An [[East African Literature Bureau]] was created to publish the work of indigenous writers.{{sfn
column2025: p=140}} The Kenya Cultural Centre supported indigenous art and music, and hundreds of traditional music and dance groups were formed; Kenyatta personally insisted that such performances were held at all national celebrations.{{sfn
column2028: p=141}} Support was given to the preservation of historic and cultural monuments, while street names referencing colonial figures were renamed and symbols of colonialism—like the statue of British settler [[Hugh Cholmondeley, 3rd Baron Delamere]] in Nairobi city centre—were removed.{{sfn
column2031: p=140}} The government encouraged the use of Swahili as a national language, although English remained the main medium for parliamentary debates and the language of instruction in schools and universities.{{sfn
column2034: p=139}} The historian Robert M. Maxon nevertheless suggested that ""no national culture emerged during the Kenyatta era"", most artistic and cultural expressions reflecting particular ethnic groups rather than a broader sense of Kenyanness, while Western culture remained heavily influential over the country\'s elites.{{sfn
column2040: p=83}} Under Kenyatta, the structure of this economy did not fundamentally change, remaining externally oriented and dominated by [[multinational corporation]]s and foreign capital.{{sfn
column2053: 3p=6}} with no serious socialist policies being pursued;{{sfn
column2056: p=208}} its focus was on achieving [[economic growth]] as opposed to equitable redistribution.{{sfn
column2059: p=85}} The government passed laws to encourage foreign investment, recognising that Kenya needed foreign-trained specialists in scientific and technical fields to aid its economic development.{{sfn
column2062: pp=157–158}} Under Kenyatta, Western companies regarded Kenya as a safe and profitable place for investment;{{sfn
column2065: p=177}} between 1964 and 1970, large-scale foreign investment and industry in Kenya nearly doubled.{{sfn
column2068: p=85}}\n[[File:COLLECTIE TROPENMUSEUM President Jomo Kenyatta kijkt toe bij de keuring van stamboekvee tijdens de Eldoret Agricultural Show TMnr 20038663.jpg
column2071: Kenyatta at an agricultural show in 1968]]\n\nIn contrast to his economic policies, Kenyatta publicly claimed he would create a [[democratic socialism
column2072: democratic socialist]] state with an equitable distribution of economic and social development.{{sfn
column2075: p=91}} In 1965, when [[Thomas Mboya]] was minister for economic planning and development, the government issued a session paper titled ""African Socialism and its Application to Planning in Kenya"", in which it officially declared its commitment to what it called an ""[[African socialism
column2085: 3p=77}} The session proposed a [[mixed economy]] with an important role for private capital,{{sfnm
column2091: 2p=84}} with Kenyatta\'s government specifying that it would only consider [[nationalisation]] in instances where national security was at risk.{{sfnm
column2097: 2p=64}} Left-wing critics highlighted that the image of ""African socialism"" portrayed in the document provided for no major shift away from the colonial economy.{{sfn
column2100: p=96}}\n\nKenya\'s agricultural and industrial sectors were dominated by Europeans and its commerce and trade by Asians; one of Kenyatta\'s most pressing issues was to bring the economy under indigenous control.{{sfn
column2103: p=85}} There was growing black resentment towards the Asian domination of the small business sector,{{sfn
column2106: p=171}} with Kenyatta\'s government putting pressure on Asian-owned businesses, intending to replace them with African-owned counterparts.{{sfn
column2109: p=521}} The 1965 session paper promised an ""Africanization"" of the Kenyan economy,{{sfn
column2112: pp=64–65}} with the government increasingly pushing for ""black capitalism"".{{sfn
column2115: p=521}} The government established the [[Industrial and Commercial Development Corporation]] to provide loans for black-owned businesses,{{sfn
column2118: p=521}} and secured a 51% share in the Kenya National Assurance Company.{{sfn
column2121: p=522}} In 1965, the government established the Kenya National Trading Corporation to ensure indigenous control over the trade in essential commodities,{{sfn
column2124: p=64}} while the Trade Licensing Act of 1967 prohibited non-citizens from involvement in the rice, sugar, and maize trade.{{sfnm
column2136: 4p=64}} During the 1970s, this expanded to cover the trade in soap, cement, and textiles.{{sfn
column2139: p=64}} Many Asians who had retained British citizenship were affected by these measures.{{sfnm
column2145: 2p=170}} Between late 1967 and early 1968, growing numbers of Kenyan Asians migrated to Britain;{{sfn
column2148: p=114}} in February 1968 large numbers migrated quickly before [[Immigration Act 1971
column2149: a legal change revoked their right to do so]].{{sfn
column2152: p=172}} Kenyatta was not sympathetic to those leaving: ""Kenya\'s identity as an African country is not going to be altered by the whims and malaises of groups of uncommitted individuals.""{{sfn
column2155: p=172}}\n\nUnder Kenyatta, corruption became widespread throughout the government, civil service, and business community.{{sfn
column2158: pp=215–216}} Kenyatta and his family were tied up with this corruption as they enriched themselves through the mass purchase of property after 1963.{{sfn
column2161: pp=236–237}} Their acquisitions in the Central, Rift Valley, and Coast Provinces aroused great anger among landless Kenyans.{{sfn
column2164: p=241}} His family used his presidential position to circumvent legal or administrative obstacles to acquiring property.{{sfn
column2167: p=238}} The Kenyatta family also heavily invested in the coastal hotel business, Kenyatta personally owning the Leonard Beach Hotel.{{sfn
column2170: p=242}} Other businesses they were involved with included ruby mining in [[Tsavo East National Park
column2171: Tsavo National Park]], the casino business, the charcoal trade—which was causing significant deforestation—and the ivory trade.{{sfn
column2174: pp=242–244}} The Kenyan press, which was largely loyal to Kenyatta, did not delve into this issue;{{sfn
column2177: p=236}} it was only after his death that publications appeared revealing the scale of his personal enrichment.{{sfn
column2180: pp=237–238}} Kenyan corruption and Kenyatta\'s role in it was better known in Britain, although many of his British friends—including McDonald and Brockway—chose to believe Kenyatta was not personally involved.{{sfn
column2183: pp=246–247, 249}}\n\nDespite Kenyatta\'s shortcomings on economic policy, compared with the economic performance of the vast majority of countries in independent Africa, Kenya\'s economic success during Kenyatta\'s tenure was outstanding. During the years following its independence in December, 1963, Kenya attained such a high rate of economic growth that it came to be widely regarded as something of an economic ""miracle."" According to World Bank figures, Kenya\'s economy attained an average growth rate of 6.4 percent per year from 1965 to 1980.<ref name="":0"">{{Cite journal
column2195:
url-access=subscription }}</ref> Among the 40 or more independent countries in sub-Saharan Africa, only 3 exceeded that growth rate; Nigeria, Ivory Coast, and Botswana. Kenyatta's success can be attributed to his focus on the agricultural sector, particularly on cash crops such as tea and coffee.<ref name="":0"" />

'), Section(title='====Land, healthcare, and education reform====', content='

[[File:Dr Banda of Malawi and Jomo Kenyatta of Kenya.jpg
column2198: Kenyatta with Malawian President [[Hastings Banda]]]]\n\nThe question of land ownership had deep emotional resonance in Kenya, having been a major grievance against the British colonialists.{{sfn
column2201: p=195}} As part of the Lancaster House negotiations, Britain\'s government agreed to provide Kenya with £27 million with which to buy out white farmers and redistribute their land among the indigenous population.{{sfn
column2204: p=196}} To ease this transition, Kenyatta made [[Bruce McKenzie]], a white farmer, the Minister of Agriculture and Land.{{sfn
column2207: p=196}} Kenyatta\'s government encouraged the establishment of private land-buying companies that were often headed by prominent politicians.{{sfn
column2210: p=81}} The government sold or leased lands in the former White Highlands to these companies, which in turn subdivided them among individual shareholders.{{sfn
column2213: p=81}} In this way, the land redistribution programs favoured the ruling party\'s chief constituency.{{sfn
column2216: p=82}} Kenyatta himself expanded the land that he owned around Gatundu.{{sfn
column2219: p=316}} Kenyans who made claims to land on the basis of ancestral ownership often found the land given to other people, including Kenyans from different parts of the country.{{sfn
column2222: p=82}} Voices began to condemn the redistribution; in 1969, the MP [[Jean-Marie Seroney]] censured the sale of historically [[Nandi people
column2223: Nandi]] lands in the Rift to non-Nandi, describing the settlement schemes as ""Kenyatta\'s colonization of the rift"".{{sfnm
column2229: 2p=251}}\n\nIn part fuelled by high rural unemployment, Kenya witnessed growing rural-to-urban migration under Kenyatta\'s government.{{sfn
column2232: pp=124–125}} This exacerbated urban unemployment and housing shortages, with squatter settlements and slums growing up and urban crime rates rising.{{sfn
column2235: pp=125–126}} Kenyatta was concerned by this, and promoted the reversal of this rural-to-urban migration, but in this was unsuccessful.{{sfn
column2238: p=126}} Kenyatta\'s government was eager to control the country\'s trade unions, fearing their ability to disrupt the economy.{{sfn
column2241: p=522}} To this end it emphasised social welfare schemes over traditional industrial institutions,{{sfn
column2244: p=522}} and in 1965 transformed the Kenya Federation of Labour into the Central Organization of Trade (COT), a body which came under strong government influence.{{sfnm
column2250: 2p=91}} No strikes could be legally carried out in Kenya without COT\'s permission.{{sfn
column2253: p=523}} There were also measures to Africanise the civil service, which by mid-1967 had become 91% African.{{sfn
column2256: p=113}} During the 1960s and 1970s the [[public sector]] grew faster than the private sector.{{sfn
column2259: p=118}} The growth in the public sector contributed to the significant expansion of the indigenous [[middle class]] in Kenyatta\'s Kenya.{{sfn
column2265: The University of Nairobi, Kenya\'s first institution of higher education, was established under Kenyatta\'s administration.]]\n\nThe government oversaw a massive expansion in education facilities.{{sfn
column2268: p=110}} In June 1963, Kenyatta ordered the Ominda Commission to determine a framework for meeting Kenya\'s educational needs.{{sfn
column2271: pp=126–127}} Their report set out the long-term goal of universal free primary education in Kenya but argued that the government\'s emphasis should be on secondary and higher education to facilitate the training of indigenous African personnel to take over the civil service and other jobs requiring such an education.{{sfn
column2274: p=127}} Between 1964 and 1966, the number of primary schools grew by 11.6%, and the number of secondary schools by 80%.{{sfn
column2277: p=127}} By the time of Kenyatta\'s death, Kenya\'s first universities—the [[University of Nairobi]] and [[Kenyatta University]]—had been established.{{sfnm
column2283: 2p=147}} Although Kenyatta died without having attained the goal of free, universal primary education in Kenya, the country had made significant advances in that direction, with 85% of Kenyan children in primary education, and within a decade of independence had trained sufficient numbers of indigenous Africans to take over the civil service.{{sfn
column2286: p=128}}\n\nAnother priority for Kenyatta\'s government was improving access to healthcare services.{{sfn
column2289: p=132}} It stated that its long-term goal was to establish a system of free, universal medical care.{{sfn
column2292: p=133}} In the short-term, its emphasis was on increasing the overall number of doctors and registered nurses while decreasing the number of expatriates in those positions.{{sfn
column2295: p=132}} In 1965, the government introduced free medical services for out-patients and children.{{sfn
column2298: p=133}} By Kenyatta\'s death, the majority of Kenyans had access to significantly better healthcare than they had had in the colonial period.{{sfn
column2301: p=133}} Before independence, the average life expectancy in Kenya was 45, but by the end of the 1970s it was 55, the second-highest in Sub-Saharan Africa.{{sfn
column2304: p=134}} This improved medical care had resulted in declining mortality rates while birth rates remained high, resulting in a rapidly growing population; from 1962 to 1979, Kenya\'s population grew by just under 4% a year, the highest rate in the world at the time.{{sfn
column2307: p=122}} This put a severe strain on social services; Kenyatta\'s government promoted [[family planning]] projects to stem the birth-rate, but these had little success.{{sfn
column2313: Kenyatta meets an American delegation from the [[Congress of Racial Equality]], including [[Roy Innis]].]]\n\nIn part due to his advanced years (he was already 66–67 years old at the time of independence), Kenyatta rarely traveled outside of Eastern Africa.{{sfn
column2316: p=167}} Under Kenyatta, Kenya was largely uninvolved in the affairs of other states, including those in the [[East African Community]].{{sfn
column2319: p=320}} Despite his reservations about any immediate East African Federation, in June 1967 Kenyatta signed the Treaty for East African Co-operation.{{sfn
column2322: p=175}} In December he attended a meeting with Tanzanian and Ugandan representatives to form the East African Economic Community, reflecting Kenyatta\'s cautious approach toward regional integration.{{sfn
column2325: p=175}} He also took on a mediating role during the [[Congo Crisis]], heading the [[Organisation of African Unity]]\'s Conciliation Commission on the Congo.{{sfn
column2328: p=178}}\n\nFacing the pressures of the [[Cold War]],{{sfn
column2331: p=188}} Kenyatta officially pursued a policy of ""positive non-alignment"".{{sfn
column2334: p=515}} In reality, his foreign policy was pro-Western and in particular pro-British.{{sfnm
column2340: 2p=96}} Kenya became a member of the [[Commonwealth of Nations]],{{sfn
column2343: p=313}} using this as a vehicle to put pressure on the white-minority [[apartheid]] regimes in South Africa and Rhodesia.{{sfn
column2346: pp=167–168}} Britain remained one of Kenya\'s foremost sources of foreign trade; British aid to Kenya was among the highest in Africa.{{sfn
column2349: p=515}} In 1964, Kenya and the UK signed a Memorandum of Understanding, one of only two military alliances Kenyatta\'s government made;{{sfn
column2352: p=515}} the British [[Special Air Service]] trained Kenyatta\'s own bodyguards.{{sfn
column2355: p=54}} Commentators argued that Britain\'s relationship with Kenyatta\'s Kenya was a [[Neo-colonialism
column2356: neo-colonial]] one, with the British having exchanged their position of political power for one of influence.{{sfn
column2359: p=514}} The historian Poppy Cullen nevertheless noted that there was no ""dictatorial neo-colonial control"" in Kenyatta\'s Kenya.{{sfn
column2362: p=515}}\n[[File:Bundesarchiv B 145 Bild-F021917-0014, Kenia, Staatsbesuch Bundespräsident Lübke.jpg
column2365: Jomo Kenyatta and his son meet the [[President of Germany
column2366: President of West Germany]] [[Heinrich Lübke]] in 1966.]]\n\nAlthough many white Kenyans accepted Kenyatta\'s rule, he remained opposed by white [[far right politics
column2367: far-right]] activists; while in London at the [[1964 Commonwealth Prime Ministers\' Conference
column2368: July 1964 Commonwealth Conference]], he was assaulted by [[Martin Webster]], a British [[Neo-Nazism
column2372: p=296}} Kenyatta\'s relationship with the United States was also warm; the [[United States Agency for International Development]] played a key role in helping respond to a maize shortage in [[Kamba people
column2376: pp=63–65}} Kenyatta also maintained a warm relationship with Israel, including when other East African nations endorsed Arab hostility to the state;{{sfn
column2379: pp=79–80}} he for instance permitted Israeli jets to refuel in Kenya on their way back from the [[Entebbe raid]].{{sfnm
column2385: 2pp=190–193}} In turn, in 1976 the Israelis warned of a plot by the [[Palestinian Liberation Army]] to assassinate him, a threat he took seriously.{{sfn
column2388: pp=172–173}}\n\nKenyatta and his government were anti-communist,{{sfnm
column2394: 2p=147}} and in June 1965 he warned that ""it is naive to think that there is no danger of imperialism from the East. In world power politics the East has as much designs upon us as the West and would like to serve their own interests. That is why we reject Communism.""{{sfnm
column2400: 2p=76}} His governance was often criticised by communists and other leftists, some of whom accused him of being a fascist.{{sfn
column2403: p=177}} When Chinese Communist official [[Zhou Enlai]] visited Dar es Salaam, his statement that ""Africa is ripe for revolution"" was clearly aimed largely at Kenya.{{sfn
column2406: p=177}} In 1964, Kenyatta impounded a secret shipment of Chinese armaments that passed through Kenyan territory on its way to Uganda. Obote personally visited Kenyatta to apologise.{{sfnm
column2412: 2pp=59–60}} In June 1967, Kenyatta declared the Chinese Chargé d\'Affairs \'\'persona non grata\'\' in Kenya and recalled the Kenyan ambassador from [[Peking]].{{sfn
column2415: p=177}} Relations with the Soviet Union were also strained; Kenyatta shut down the Lumumba Institute—an educational organisation named after the Congolese independence leader [[Patrice Lumumba]]—on the basis that it was a front for Soviet influence in Kenya.{{sfnm
column2424: Kenyatta at the Eldoret Agricultural Show, 1968]]\n\nKenyatta made clear his desire for Kenya to become a one-party state, regarding this as a better expression of national unity than a multi-party system.{{sfn
column2427: p=314}} In the first five years of independence, he consolidated control of the central government,{{sfn
column2430: p=84}} removing the autonomy of Kenya\'s provinces to prevent the entrenchment of ethnic power bases.{{sfn
column2433: p=18}} He argued that centralised control of the government was needed to deal with the growth in demands for local services and to assist quicker economic development.{{sfn
column2436: p=18}} In 1966, it launched a commission to examine reforms to local government operations,{{sfn
column2439: p=18}} and in 1969 passed the Transfer of Functions Act, which terminated grants to local authorities and transferred major services from provincial to central control.{{sfn
column2442: p=19}}\n\nA major focus for Kenyatta during the first three and a half years of Kenya\'s independence were the divisions within KANU itself.{{sfn
column2445: p=32}} Opposition to Kenyatta\'s government grew, particularly following the assassination of [[Pio Pinto]] in February 1965.{{sfn
column2448: p=316}} Kenyatta condemned the assassination of the prominent leftist politician, although UK intelligence agencies believed that his own bodyguard had orchestrated the murder.{{sfn
column2451: p=68}} Relations between Kenyatta and Odinga were strained, and at the March 1966 party conference, Odinga\'s post—that of party vice president—was divided among eight different politicians, greatly limiting his power and ending his position as Kenyatta\'s automatic successor.{{sfnm
column2457: 2p=105–106}} Between 1964 and 1966, Kenyatta and other KANU conservatives had been deliberately trying to push Odinga to resign from the party.{{sfn
column2460: pp=70–71}} Under growing pressure, in 1966 Odinga stepped down as state vice president, claiming that Kenya had failed to achieve economic independence and needed to adopt socialist policies. Backed by several other senior KANU figures and trade unionists, he became head of the new [[Kenya Peoples Union]] (KPU).{{sfnm
column2478: 6p=108}} In its manifesto, the KPU stated that it would pursue ""truly socialist policies"" like the nationalisation of public utilities; it claimed Kenyatta\'s government ""want[ed] to build a capitalist system in the image of Western capitalism but are too embarrassed or dishonest to call it that.""{{sfn
column2481: pp=99, 100}} The KPU were legally recognised as the [[official opposition]],{{sfn
column2484: p=146}} thus restoring the country\'s [[two party system]].{{sfn
column2487: p=144}}\n\nThe new party was a direct challenge to Kenyatta\'s rule,{{sfn
column2490: p=144}} and he regarded it as a communist-inspired plot to oust him.{{sfn
column2493: p=98}} Soon after the KPU\'s creation, the Kenyan Parliament amended the constitution to ensure that the defectors—who had originally been elected on the KANU ticket—could not automatically retain their seats and would have to stand for re-election.{{sfnm
column2499: 2pp=110–111}} This resulted in the [[1966 Kenyan parliamentary by-elections
column2506: 2p=111}} The Luo increasingly rallied around the KPU,{{sfn
column2509: p=318}} which experienced localized violence that hindered its ability to campaign, although Kenyatta\'s government officially disavowed this violence.{{sfn
column2512: p=147}} KANU retained the support of all national newspapers and the government-owned radio and television stations.{{sfn
column2515: p=119}} Of the 29 defectors, only nine were re-elected on the KPU ticket;{{sfnm
column2521: 2p=125}} Odinga was among them, having retained his Central Nyanza seat with a high majority.{{sfn
column2524: p=164}} Odinga was replaced as vice president by [[Joseph Murumbi]],{{sfn
column2527: p=67}} who in turn would be replaced by Moi.{{sfnm
column2537: A British newsreel about Kenyatta\'s rule, produced in 1973]]\n\nIn July 1969, Mboya—a prominent and popular Luo KANU politician—was assassinated by a Kikuyu.{{sfnm
column2555: 6p=135}} Kenyatta had reportedly been concerned that Mboya, with U.S. backing, could remove him from the presidency,{{sfn
column2558: p=101}} and across Kenya there were suspicions voiced that Kenyatta\'s government was responsible for Mboya\'s death.{{sfn
column2561: p=67}} The killing sparked tensions between the Kikuyu and other ethnic groups across the country,{{sfnm
column2567: 2p=137}} with riots breaking out in Nairobi.{{sfn
column2570: p=318}} In October 1969, Kenyatta visited [[Kisumu]], located in Luo territory, to open a hospital. On being greeted by a crowd shouting KPU slogans, he lost his temper. When members of the crowd started throwing stones, Kenyatta\'s bodyguards opened fire on them, killing and wounding several.{{sfnm
column2576: 2pp=140–143}} In response to the rise of KPU, Kenyatta had introduced oathing, a Kikuyu cultural tradition in which individuals came to Gatundu to swear their loyalty to him.{{sfnm
column2588: 4p=138}} Journalists were discouraged from reporting on the oathing system, and several were deported when they tried to do so.{{sfn
column2591: p=317}} Many Kenyans were pressured or forced to swear oaths, something condemned by the country\'s Christian establishment.{{sfnm
column2597: 2p=139}} In response to the growing condemnation, the oathing was terminated in September 1969,{{sfnm
column2603: 2p=139}} and Kenyatta invited leaders from other ethnic groups to a meeting in Gatundu.{{sfnm
column2609: 2p=140}}\n\nKenyatta\'s government resorted to un-democratic measures to restrict the opposition.{{sfn
column2612: p=21}} It used laws on detention and deportation to perpetuate its political hold.{{sfn
column2615: p=23}} In 1966, it passed the Public Security (Detained and Restricted Persons) Regulations, allowing the authorities to arrest and detain anyone ""for the preservation of public security"" [[Indefinite detention without trial
column2622: 2p=129}} In October 1969 the government banned the KPU,{{sfnm
column2634: 4p=145}} and arrested Odinga before putting him under indefinite detainment.{{sfnm
column2643: 3p=145}} With the organised opposition eliminated, from 1969, Kenya was once again a \'\'de facto\'\' one-party state.{{sfnm
column2653: December 1969 general election]]—in which all candidates were from the ruling KANU—resulted in Kenyatta\'s government remaining in power, but many members of his government lost their parliamentary seats to rivals from within the party.{{sfnm
column2659: 2p=319}} Over coming years, many other political and intellectual figures considered hostile to Kenyatta\'s rule were detained or imprisoned, including Seroney, Flomena Chelagat, [[George Anyona]], [[Martin Shikuku]], and [[Ngũgĩ wa Thiong\'o]].{{sfnm
column2665: 2p=67}} Other political figures who were critical of Kenyatta\'s administration, including Ronald Ngala and [[Josiah Mwangi Kariuki]], were killed in incidents that many speculated were government assassinations.{{sfn
column2671: Kenyatta in the last year of his life]]\n\nFor many years, Kenyatta had suffered health problems. He had a mild stroke in 1966,{{sfnm
column2680: p=516}} He suffered from [[gout]] and heart problems, all of which he sought to keep hidden from the public.{{sfn
column2683: p=239}} By 1970, he was increasingly feeble and senile,{{sfn
column2686: p=103}} and by 1975 Kenyatta had—according to Maloba—""in effect ceased to actively govern"".{{sfn
column2689: p=282}} Four Kikuyu politicians—Koinange, James Gichuru, [[Njoroge Mungai]], and [[Charles Njonjo]]—formed his inner circle of associates, and he was rarely seen in public without one of them present.{{sfn
column2692: p=102}} This clique faced opposition from KANU back-benchers spearheaded by Josiah Mwangi Kariuki. In March 1975 Kariuki was kidnapped, tortured, and murdered, and his body was dumped in the [[Ngong Hills]].{{sfnm
column2698: 2pp=264–265}} After Kariuki\'s murder, Maloba noted, there was a ""noticeable erosion"" of support for Kenyatta and his government.{{sfn
column2701: p=274}} Thenceforth, when the president spoke to crowds, they no longer applauded his statements.{{sfn
column2704: pp=274–275}}\n\nIn 1977, Kenyatta had several further strokes or heart attacks.{{sfn
column2707: p=239}} On 22 August 1978, he died of a heart attack in the State House, Mombasa.{{sfnm
column2716: 3p=305}} The Kenyan government had been preparing for Kenyatta\'s death since at least his 1968 stroke; it had requested British assistance in organising his [[state funeral]] as a result of the UK\'s longstanding experience in this area.{{sfnm
column2722: 2p=311}} McKenzie had been employed as a go-between,{{sfn
column2725: p=516}} and the structure of the funeral was orchestrated to deliberately imitate that of deceased British Prime Minister [[Winston Churchill]].{{sfn
column2728: p=524}} In doing so, senior Kenyans sought to project an image of their country as a modern nation-state rather than one incumbent on tradition.{{sfn
column2731: p=516}} The funeral took place at St. Andrew\'s Presbyterian Church, six days after Kenyatta\'s death.{{sfn
column2734: p=518}} Britain\'s heir to the throne, [[Charles, Prince of Wales]], attended the event, a symbol of the value that the British government perceived in its relationship with Kenya.{{sfnm
column2740: 2p=314}} African heads of state also attended, including Nyerere, [[Idi Amin]], [[Kenneth Kaunda]], and [[Hastings Banda]], as did India\'s [[Morarji Desai]] and Pakistan\'s [[Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq]].{{sfn
column2743: p=316}} His body was buried in a [[mausoleum]] in the grounds of the [[Parliament Buildings (Kenya)
column2747: pp=311–312}}\n\nKenyatta\'s succession had been an issue of debate since independence,{{sfn
column2750: p=22}} and Kenyatta had not unreservedly nominated a successor.{{sfn
column2753: p=516}} The Kikuyu clique surrounding him had sought to amend the constitution to prevent vice president Moi—who was from the [[Kalenjin people]] rather than the Kikuyu—from automatically becoming acting president, but their attempts failed amid sustained popular and parliamentary opposition.{{sfnm
column2759: 2pp=279, 281}} After Kenyatta\'s death, the transition of power proved smooth,{{sfn
column2765: p=29}} As vice president, Moi was sworn in as acting president for a 90-day interim period.{{sfnm
column2777: 4pp=308, 309}} In October he was unanimously elected KANU President and subsequently declared President of Kenya itself.{{sfn
column2780: pp=30–31}} Moi emphasised his loyalty to Kenyatta—""I followed and was faithful to him until his last day, even when his closest friends forsook him""—and there was much expectation that he would continue the policies inaugurated by Kenyatta.{{sfn
column2783: pp=33–34}} He nevertheless criticised the corruption, [[land grabbing]], and capitalistic ethos that had characterised Kenyatta\'s period and expressed [[populism
column2784: populist]] tendencies by emphasizing a closer link to the poor.{{sfn
column2787: p=34}} In 1982 he would amend the Kenyan constitution to create a \'\'de jure\'\' one-party state.{{sfn
column2793: quote=""Kenyatta possessed the common touch and great leadership qualities. He was essentially a moderate trying to achieve the radical revolution of a nationalist victory in a colonialist society, and his ambivalence over many issues can best be explained by his need to contain or use his militants—and he had plenty of them. They were impatient and wanted to see effective action. Kenyatta certainly knew how to appeal to African sentiments.""
column2800: p=26}} and was committed to the belief that European colonial rule in Africa must end.{{sfn
column2803: p=27}} Like other anti-colonialists, he believed that under colonialism, the human and natural resources of Africa had been used not for the benefit of Africa\'s population but for the enrichment of the colonisers and their European homelands.{{sfn
column2806: p=27}} For Kenyatta, independence meant not just self-rule, but an end to [[Racial segregation
column2807: the colour bar]] and to the patronising attitudes and racist slang of Kenya\'s white minority.{{sfn
column2810: p=306}} According to Murray-Brown, Kenyatta\'s ""basic philosophy"" throughout his life was that ""all men deserved the right to develop peacefully according to their own wishes"".{{sfn
column2813: p=321}} Kenyatta expressed this in his statement that ""I have stood always for the purposes of human dignity in freedom, and for the values of tolerance and peace.""{{sfn
column2816: p=322}} This approach was similar to the Zambian President Kenneth Kaunda\'s ideology of ""African humanism"".{{sfn
column2819: p=321}}\n\nMurray-Brown noted that ""Kenyatta had always kept himself free from ideological commitments"",{{sfn
column2822: p=312}} while the historian William R. Ochieng observed that ""Kenyatta articulated no particular social philosophy"".{{sfn
column2825: p=93}} Similarly, Assensoh noted that Kenyatta was ""not interested in social philosophies and slogans"".{{sfn
column2828: p=25}} Several commentators and biographers described him as being politically [[Conservatism
column2844: 5p=89}} an ideological viewpoint likely bolstered by his training in functionalist anthropology.{{sfn
column2847: p=94}} He pursued, according to Maloba, ""a conservatism that worked in concert with imperial powers and was distinctly hostile to radical politics"".{{sfn
column2850: p=209}}\n\nKenyatta biographer [[Guy Arnold]] described the Kenyan leader as ""a pragmatist and a moderate"", noting that his only ""radicalism"" came in the form of his ""nationalist attack"" on imperialism.{{sfn
column2853: p=33}} Arnold also noted that Kenyatta ""absorbed a great deal of the British approach to politics: pragmatism, only dealing with problems when they become crises, [and] tolerance as long as the other side is only talking"".{{sfn
column2856: p=32}} Donald Savage noted that Kenyatta believed in ""the importance of authority and tradition"", and that he displayed ""a remarkably consistent view of development through self-help and hard work"".{{sfn
column2859: p=537}} Kenyatta was also an elitist and encouraged the emergence of an elite class in Kenya.{{sfn
column2862: pp=190, 208}} He wrestled with a contradiction between his conservative desire for a renewal of traditional custom and his reformist urges to embrace Western modernity.{{sfn
column2866: p=38}} He also faced a contradiction between his internal debates on Kikuyu ethics and belief in tribal identity with his need to create a non-tribalised Kenyan nationalism.{{sfn
column2873: p=47}} some commentators have posthumously characterised Kenyatta as a Pan-Africanist.{{sfnm
column2879: 2p=10}} Maloba observed that during the colonial period Kenyatta had embraced ""radical Pan African activism"" which differed sharply from the ""deliberate conservative positions, especially on the question of African liberation"" that he espoused while Kenya\'s leader.{{sfn
column2882: p=201}} As leader of Kenya, Kenyatta published two collected volumes of his speeches: \'\'Harambee\'\' and \'\'Suffering Without Bitterness\'\'.{{sfn
column2885: p=3}} The material included in these publications was carefully selected so as to avoid mention of the radicalism he exhibited while in Britain during the 1930s.{{sfn
column2888: pp=3–4}}\n\nKenyatta had been exposed to Marxist-Leninist ideas through his friendship with Padmore and the time spent in the Soviet Union,{{sfnm
column2894: 2p=6}} but had also been exposed to Western forms of [[liberal democracy
column2895: liberal democratic]] government through his many years in Britain.{{sfn
column2898: p=312}} He appears to have had no further involvement with the communist movement after 1934.{{sfn
column2902: p=29}} As Kenya\'s leader, Kenyatta rejected the idea that Marxism offered a useful framework for analysing his country\'s socio-economic situation.{{sfn
column2905: p=83}} The academics Bruce J. Berman and John M. Lonsdale argued that Marxist frameworks for analysing society influenced some of his beliefs, such as his view that British colonialism had to be destroyed rather than simply reformed.{{sfn
column2909: p=28}} Kenyatta nevertheless disagreed with the Marxist attitude that tribalism was backward and retrograde;{{sfn
column2913: pp=28–29}} his positive attitude toward tribal society frustrated some of Kenyatta\'s Marxist Pan-Africanist friends in Britain, among them Padmore, James, and [[T. Ras Makonnen]], who regarded it as parochial and un-progressive.{{sfn
column2917: p=34}}\n\nAssensoh suggested that Kenyatta initially had socialist inclinations but ""became a victim of capitalist circumstances"";{{sfn
column2920: p=4}} conversely, Savage stated that ""Kenyatta\'s direction was hardly towards the creation of a radical new socialist society"",{{sfn
column2923: p=535}} and Ochieng called him ""an African capitalist"".{{sfn
column2926: p=93}} When in power, Kenyatta displayed a preoccupation with individual and \'\'mbari\'\' land rights that were at odds with any socialist-oriented collectivisation.{{sfn
column2929: p=535}} According to Maloba, Kenyatta\'s government ""sought to project capitalism as an African ideology, and communism (or socialism) as alien and dangerous"".{{sfn
column2936: quote=""Ever a showman, [Kenyatta] could appear one moment in gaily coloured shirts, decorated with the cock of KANU, and the next in elegant suits from Savile Row, seldom without a rose in his buttonhole; he could be photographed in leopard-skin hat and cloak waving a silver fly-whisk or in old slacks on his farm tending his shrubs; he was equally at home in academic robes at a university function and in sandals and shorts on the beach at Mombasa. African exuberance and love of display found perfect expression in Kenyatta\'s flair alongside the dignity and respect due to \'His Excellency, the President, Mzee Jomo Kenyatta\'.""
column2946: p=74}} According to Murray-Brown, he ""liked being at the centre of life"",{{sfn
column2949: p=184}} and was always ""a rebel at heart"" who enjoyed ""earthly pleasures"".{{sfn
column2952: p=144}} One of Kenyatta\'s fellow LSE students, Elspeth Huxley, referred to him as ""a showman to his finger tips; jovial, a good companion, shrewd, fluent, quick, devious, subtle, [and] flesh-pot loving"".{{sfn
column2955: p=189}} Kenyatta liked to dress elaborately; throughout most of his adult life, he wore finger rings and while studying at university in London took to wearing a [[Fez (hat)
column2956: fez]] and cloak and carrying a silver-topped black cane.{{sfn
column2959: p=184}} He adopted his surname, ""Kenyatta"", after the name of a beaded belt he often wore in early life.{{sfn
column2962: p=17}} As President he collected a variety of expensive cars.{{sfn
column2965: p=316}}\n\nMurray-Brown noted that Kenyatta had the ability to ""appear all things to all men"",{{sfn
column2968: p=233}} also displaying a ""consummate ability to keep his true purposes and abilities to himself"", for instance concealing his connections with communists and the Soviet Union both from members of the British Labour Party and from Kikuyu figures at home.{{sfn
column2971: p=165}} This deviousness was sometimes interpreted as dishonesty by those who met him.{{sfn
column2974: pp=215, 216}} Referring to Kenyatta\'s appearance in 1920s Kenya, Murray-Brown stated the leader presented himself to Europeans as ""an agreeable if somewhat seedy \'Europeanized\' native"" and to indigenous Africans as ""a sophisticated man-about-town about whose political earnestness they had certain reservations"".{{sfn
column2977: p=107}}\n\nSimon Gikandi argued that Kenyatta, like some of his contemporaries in the Pan-African movement, was an ""Afro-Victorian"", someone whose identity had been shaped ""by the culture of colonialism and colonial institutions"", especially those of the [[Victorian era]].{{sfn
column2980: p=3}} During the 1920s and 1930s, Kenyatta cultivated the image of a ""colonial gentleman"";{{sfn
column2983: p=9}} in England, he displayed ""pleasant manners"" and a flexible attitude in adapting to urban situations dissimilar to the lands he had grown up in.{{sfn
column2986: p=317}} A. R. Barlow, a member of the Church of Scotland Mission at Kikuyu, met with Kenyatta in Britain, later relating that he was impressed by how Kenyatta could ""mix on equal terms with Europeans and to hold his end up in spite of his handicaps, educationally and socially.""{{sfn
column2989: p=316}} The South African [[Peter Abrahams]] met Kenyatta in London, noting that of all the black men involved in the city\'s Pan-Africanist movement, he was ""the most relaxed, sophisticated and \'westernized\' of the lot of us"".{{sfn
column2992: p=5}} As President, Kenyatta often reminisced nostalgically about his time in England, referring to it as ""home"" on several occasions.{{sfn
column2995: p=320}} Berman and Lonsdale described his life as being preoccupied with ""a search for the reconciliation of the Western modernity he embraced and an equally valued Kikuyuness he could not discard"".{{sfn
column2999: p=19}} Gikandi argued that Kenyatta\'s ""identification with Englishness was much more profound than both his friends and enemies have been willing to admit"".{{sfn
column3002: p=6}}\n\nKenyatta has also been described as a talented orator, author, and editor.{{sfn
column3006: p=19}} He had dictatorial and autocratic tendencies,{{sfn
column3009: p=209}} as well as a fierce temper that could emerge as rage on occasion.{{sfnm
column3015: 2p=209}} Murray-Brown noted that Kenyatta could be ""quite unscrupulous, even brutal"" in using others to get what he wanted,{{sfn
column3018: p=215}} but he never displayed any physical cruelty or [[nihilism]].{{sfn
column3021: p=216}} Kenyatta had no racist impulses regarding white Europeans, as can, for instance, be seen through his marriage to a white English woman.{{sfn
column3024: p=216}} He told his daughter ""the English are wonderful people to live with in England.""{{sfn
column3027: p=32}} He welcomed white support for his cause, so long as it was generous and unconditional, and spoke of a Kenya in which indigenous Africans, Europeans, Arabs, and Indians could all regard themselves as Kenyans, working and living alongside each other peacefully.{{sfn
column3030: p=223}} Despite this, Kenyatta exhibited a general dislike of Indians, believing that they exploited indigenous Africans in Kenya.{{sfn
column3036: quote=""I do not think I am—and have never been—an enemy of Europeans or the white people, because I have spent many years in England or in Europe, and even today I have many friends in various nations.""
column3043: p=23}} He viewed [[monogamy]] through an anthropological lens as an interesting Western phenomenon but did not adopt the practice himself, instead having sexual relations with a wide range of women throughout his life.{{sfn
column3046: p=216}} Murray-Brown characterized Kenyatta as an ""affectionate father"" to his children, but one who was frequently absent.{{sfn
column3049: p=110}} Kenyatta had two children from his first marriage with Grace Wahu: son Peter Muigai Kenyatta (born 1920), who later became a deputy minister; and daughter [[Margaret Kenyatta (born 1928)
column3050: Margaret Kenyatta]] (born 1928). Margaret served as mayor of Nairobi between 1970 and 1976 and then as Kenya\'s ambassador to the United Nations from 1976 to 1986.<ref>{{cite news
column3061: url-status=usurped}}</ref> Of these children, it was Margaret who was Kenyatta\'s closest confidante.{{sfnm
column3067: 2p=137}}\n\nDuring his trial, Kenyatta described himself as a Christian{{sfn
column3070: p=265}} saying, ""I do not follow any particular denomination. I believe in Christianity as a whole.""{{sfn
column3073: p=269}} Arnold stated that in England, Kenyatta\'s adherence to Christianity was ""desultory"".{{sfn
column3076: p=27}} While in London, Kenyatta had taken an interest in the [[atheism
column3077: atheist]] speakers at [[Speakers\' Corner]] in [[Hyde Park, London
column3081: p=130}} while an Irish Muslim friend had unsuccessfully urged Kenyatta to convert to [[Islam]].{{sfn
column3084: p=130}} During his imprisonment, Kenyatta read up on Islam, [[Hinduism]], [[Buddhism]], and [[Confucianism]] through books supplied to him by Stock.{{sfnm
column3090: 2p=138}} The Israeli diplomat Asher Naim visited him in this period, noting that although Kenyatta was ""not a religious man, he was appreciative of the Bible"".{{sfn
column3093: p=77}} Despite portraying himself as a Christian, he found the attitudes of many European missionaries intolerable, in particular their readiness to see everything African as evil.{{sfn
column3097: p=25}} In \'\'Facing Mount Kenya\'\', he challenged the missionaries\' dismissive attitude toward [[ancestor veneration]], which he instead preferred to call ""ancestor communion"".{{sfn
column3100: p=175}} In that book\'s dedication, Kenyatta invoked ""ancestral spirits"" as part of ""the Fight for African Freedom.""{{sfn
column3106: A statue of Kenyatta (1971) by [[James Butler (artist)
column3107: James Butler]] was erected at the [[Kenyatta International Conference Centre
column3108: KICC]] in Nairobi.]]\n\nWithin Kenya, Kenyatta came to be regarded as the ""Father of the Nation"",{{sfnm
column3120: 4p=516}} and was given the unofficial title of \'\'[[Mzee]]\'\', a Swahili term meaning ""grand old man"".{{sfnm
column3130: 3p=4}} From 1963 until his death, a [[cult of personality]] surrounded him in the country,{{sfn
column3133: p=4}} one which deliberately interlinked Kenyan nationalism with Kenyatta\'s own personality.{{sfn
column3136: p=4}} This use of Kenyatta as a popular symbol of the nation itself was furthered by the similarities between their names.{{sfn
column3140: p=98}} He came to be regarded as a [[father figure]] not only by Kikuyu and Kenyans, but by Africans more widely.{{sfn
column3143: pp=192, 195}}\n\nAfter 1963, Maloba noted, Kenyatta became ""about the most admired post-independence African leader"" on the world stage, one who Western countries hailed as a ""beloved elder statesman.""{{sfn
column3146: p=2}} His opinions were ""most valued"" both by conservative African politicians and by Western leaders.{{sfn
column3149: p=196}} On becoming Kenya\'s leader, his anti-communist positions gained favour in the West,{{sfn
column3152: p=26}} and some pro-Western governments gave him awards; in 1965 he, for instance, received medals from both [[Pope Paul VI]] and from the South Korean government.{{sfn
column3155: p=25}}\n\nIn 1974, Arnold referred to Kenyatta as ""one of the outstanding African leaders now living"", someone who had become ""synonymous with Kenya"".{{sfn
column3158: p=9}} He added that Kenyatta had been ""one of the shrewdest politicians"" on the continent,{{sfn
column3161: p=209}} regarded as ""one of the great architects of African nationalist achievement since 1945"".{{sfn
column3164: p=192}} Kenneth O. Nyangena characterised him as ""one of the greatest men of the twentieth century"", having been ""a beacon, a rallying point for suffering Kenyans to fight for their rights, justice and freedom"" whose ""brilliance gave strength and aspiration to people beyond the boundaries of Kenya"".{{sfn
column3167: p=4}} In 2018, Maloba described him as ""one of the legendary pioneers of modern African nationalism"".{{sfn
column3170: p=1}} In their examination of his writings, Berman and Lonsdale described him as a ""pioneer"" for being one of the first Kikuyu to write and publish; ""his representational achievement was unique"".{{sfn
column3177: p=143}} By the time of Kenyatta\'s death, Kenya had gained higher life expectancy rates than most of Sub-Saharan Africa.{{sfn
column3180: p=143}} The country had taken what Maxon called ""giant steps"" toward achieving its goal of universal primary education for Kenyan children.{{sfn
column3183: p=143}} Another significant success had been in dismantling the colonial-era system of racial segregation in schools, public facilities, and social clubs peacefully and with minimal disruption.{{sfn
column3189: Kenyatta\'s [[Mausoleum]] in Nairobi]]\nDuring much of his life, Kenya\'s white settlers regarded Kenyatta as a malcontent and an agitator;{{sfn
column3192: p=46}} for them, he was a figure of hatred and fear.{{sfn
column3195: p=2}} As the historian Keith Kyle put it, for many whites Kenyatta was ""Satan Incarnate"".{{sfn
column3198: p=43}} This white animosity reached its apogee between 1950 and 1952.{{sfn
column3201: pp=197–198}} By 1964, this image had largely shifted, and many white settlers referred to him as ""Good Old Mzee"".{{sfn
column3204: p=180}} Murray-Brown expressed the view that for many, Kenyatta\'s ""message of reconciliation, \'to forgive and forget\', was perhaps his greatest contribution to his country and to history.""{{sfn
column3207: p=322}}\n\nTo Ochieng, Kenyatta was ""a personification of conservative social forces and tendencies"" in Kenya.{{sfn
column3210: p=93}} Towards the end of his presidency, many younger Kenyans—while respecting Kenyatta\'s role in attaining independence—regarded him as a [[reactionary]].{{sfn
column3213: pp=192–193}} Those desiring a radical transformation of Kenyan society often compared Kenyatta\'s Kenya unfavourably with its southern neighbour, Julius Nyerere\'s Tanzania.{{sfn
column3216: pp=519–520}} The criticisms that leftists like Odinga made of Kenyatta\'s leadership were similar to those that the intellectual [[Frantz Fanon]] had made of post-colonial leaders throughout Africa.{{sfn
column3219: p=518}} Drawing upon Marxist theory, Jay O\'Brien, for instance, argued that Kenyatta had come to power ""as a representative of a would-be bourgeoisie"", a coalition of ""relatively privileged petty bourgeois African elements"" who wanted simply to replace the British colonialists and ""Asian commercial bourgeoisie"" with themselves. He suggested that the British supported Kenyatta in this, seeing him as a bulwark against growing worker and peasant militancy who would ensure continued neo-colonial dominance.{{sfn
column3222: pp=92–93}}\n\nProviding a similar leftist critique, the Marxist writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong\'o stated that ""here was a black Moses who had been called by history to lead his people to the promised land of no exploitation, no oppression, but who failed to rise to the occasion"".{{sfn
column3225: p=354}} Ngũgĩ saw Kenyatta as a ""twentieth-century tragic figure: he could have been a [[Vladimir Lenin
column3226: Lenin]], a [[Mao Zedong]], or a [[Ho Chi Minh]]; but he ended up being a [[Chiang Kai-shek]], a [[Park Chung Hee]], or a [[Augusto Pinochet
column3230: p=355}} Ngũgĩ was among Kenyan critics who claimed that Kenyatta treated Mau Mau veterans dismissively, leaving many of them impoverished and landless while seeking to remove them from the centre stage of national politics.{{sfn
column3233: pp=350–351, 353}} In other areas Kenyatta\'s government also faced criticism; it for instance made little progress in advancing women\'s rights in Kenya.{{sfn
column3236: p=65}}\n\nIn 1991, the Kenyan lawyer and human rights activist [[Gibson Kamau Kuria]] noted that in abolishing the federal system, banning independent candidates from standing in elections, setting up a unicameral legislature, and relaxing restrictions on the use of emergency powers, Kenyatta had laid ""the groundwork"" for Moi to further advance dictatorial power in Kenya during the late 1970s and 1980s.{{sfn
column3239: pp=120–21}}\n\nIn its 2013 report, the [[The Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission of Kenya
column3240: Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission of Kenya]] accused Kenyatta  of using his authority as president to allocate large tracts of land to himself and his family.<ref>{{Cite news
column3242: title=Kenyatta Led Elite in Land Grabbing
column3248: url-status=live}}</ref> The Kenyatta family is among Kenya\'s biggest landowners.<ref>{{Cite news

column1: '''George Thuo''' (14 February 1967 – 17 November 2013) was a Kenyan politician. He belonged to the [[Party of National Unity (Kenya)
column2: Party of National Unity]]. In the [[2007 Kenyan parliamentary election]] he was elected to the [[National Assembly of Kenya]] to represent the [[Juja Constituency]].<ref>[http://www.bunge.go.ke/members.php Members Of The 10th Parliament] {{webarchive
column4: date=16 June 2008 }}. Parliament of Kenya. Accessed 19 June 2008.</ref>

column1: He was the Chief Whip of the ruling PNU party in Parliament.

In April 2010 he lost the parliamentary seat after a court nullified the 2007 election results of Juja Constituency citing irregularities <ref>Daily Nation, 16 April 2010: [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/Kenya%20MP%20loses%20seat/-/1056/900546/-/1501gjfz/-/index.html Kenya MP loses seat]</ref>

A by-election was subsequently held on 20 September 2010, but Thuo was left third after [[William Kabogo Gitau]] ([[NARC-Kenya]]) and  Alice Wambui of [[Kenya National Congress]].<ref>Daily Nation, 20 September 2010: [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/politics/PNU+trounced+in+Juja+as+ODM+wins+Starehe+/-/1064/1015044/-/14y823k/-/index.html PNU trounced in Juja as ODM wins Starehe]</ref>

Previously, George Thuo (GT) worked as an Accountant and later Managing Director of Kenya Bus Services. He left KBS to start his own Nairobi city metro transport company, City Hopper Ltd, which was a 100% family owned business. In the meantime, he was Managing Director of Trendsetters tyre company, a position he left to join politics in 2007.
GT who was an outgoing, loud speaking, direct, open minded and regarded as having a larger than life personality, left behind his wife Judy Thuo and three children, a son and two daughters.
He died on 17 November 2013 at Porkies Pub in Thika town, Kiambu county, Kenya.<ref>{{cite news
column2: title=Former Juja MP George Thuo dies in Kiambu
column4: accessdate=18 November 2013}}</ref> According to several news sources, he collapsed while having drinks with friends.<ref>{{cite news
column5: title=Former Juja MP George Thuo dies in Kiambu

column1: '''Githu Muigai''' (born 31 January 1960) is a [[Demographics of Kenya
column2: Kenyan]] lawyer who was the [[Attorney General of Kenya
column3: Attorney General]] of the Republic of Kenya from 2011  until 13 February 2018, when he resigned.<ref>{{cite web
column10: title=Githu: I'll transform State Law office

column1: He holds a bachelor's degree in law from the [[University of Nairobi]], a master's degree in international law from [[Columbia Law School
column2: Columbia University School of Law]],<ref>{{cite web
column4: title=Politics and policy | Parliament to vet three nominees for top public offices
column9: title=Mohammed Muigai Advocates | The Chambers Global Guide 2011
column14: archivedate=2011-08-11 }}</ref> and was awarded a doctoral degree in law in November 2002.<ref>[http://allafrica.com/stories/200211050543.html ""Kenya: Moi Presides At His Last Graduation Ceremony""]. AllAfrica, 2 November 2002.</ref>

column1: Prior to becoming Attorney General Githu Muigai served in the defunct [[Constitution of Kenya Review Commission]] and at the United Nations as Special Rapporteur on contemporary forms of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance.<ref>{{cite web
column3: title=Graduate Named Attorney General in Kenya
column6: accessdate=2011-10-08}}</ref><ref>[http://www2.ohchr.org/english/issues/racism/rapporteur/ ""Special Rapporteur on contemporary forms of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance""]. Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.</ref>

column1: When the first round of the presidential election took place on 4 March 2013, [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] was declared the [[president-elect]] of Kenya by the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission]]. [[Raila Odinga]] challenged this in the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]].

He was allowed by the court to be ''[[amicus curiae]]''. In his presentation he told the court that the constitution is not clear on what ""fresh elections"" would entail. He further stated that that if court declare the voters register as having substantial defects as the petition is asking them to, it may mean that the legality of the elections for senators, governors and other elective posts may be questioned since they were elected using the same registers.<ref>{{Cite news
column4: title=Githu: Law vague on what ‘fresh polls’ means

column1: Although he was meant to be a non-partisan friend of the court, some believed his submissions were biased towards the winning party.
The court [[The Kenya Presidential Election Petition 2013
column2: dismissed Raila Odinga's petition on 30 March 2013]].

When the first round of the presidential election took place on 4 March 2013, [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] was declared the [[president-elect]] of Kenya by the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission]]. [[Raila Odinga]] challenged this in the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]].

He was allowed by the court to be ''[[amicus curiae]]''. In his presentation he told the court that the constitution is not clear on what ""fresh elections"" would entail. He further stated that that if court declare the voters register as having substantial defects as the petition is asking them to, it may mean that the legality of the elections for senators, governors and other elective posts may be questioned since they were elected using the same registers.<ref>{{Cite news
column94: title=Githu: Law vague on what ‘fresh polls’ means
column99: archive-date=28 March 2013}}</ref>\nAlthough he was meant to be a non-partisan friend of the court, some believed his submissions were biased towards the winning party.\nThe court [[The Kenya Presidential Election Petition 2013
column100:
dismissed Raila Odinga's petition on 30 March 2013]].

column1: '''Franklin Kipn'getich Bett''' alias (''Chepkooit'') (born 23 March 1953) is a Kenyan politician. He is the chairman of the Agricultural Finance Corporation (AFC) after President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] appointed him to the position. He belongs to the Jubilee Alliance Party and was elected to represent the [[Bureti Constituency]] in the [[National Assembly (Kenya)
column2: National Assembly of Kenya]] in the Kenyan parliamentary election, 2007.<ref>[http://www.bunge.go.ke/members.php Members Of The 10th Parliament] {{webarchive
column4: date=16 June 2008 }}. Parliament of Kenya. Accessed 19 June 2008.</ref>

column1: Franklin Kipng’etich Bett, also known as Chepkooit to his supporters, was born on 23 March 1953 in [[Kiptiriri Village,]] Cheborge, in the larger [[Kericho District]]. He was enrolled in Cheborge Primary School in 1960 and later moved to Korongoi Primary School in 1963 where he graduated top of his class in 1968.

He was selected to join Tenwek High School in 1969, then a mission school under the auspices of the World Gospel Missionaries. Some of Bett's notable co-alumni of Tenwek High School include Mark Kipkemoi Bor, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Public Health and Sanitation, his close friend and predecessor at the Ministry of Roads [[Kipkalya Kones]], Dr. Bishop Rono, Ambassador [[John Koech]], [[Josphat Nanok
column2: Josephat Nanok]] and many other leaders in business, politics and academia.

column1: Bett graduated from Tenwek High School in 1972 with Division 1, the highest grade possible in the then Kenya Certificates of Examination (O-level).

In 1973, he proceeded to Shimo la Tewa High School in [[Mombasa]] for his Kenya Advanced Certificate of Education (KACE) where he attained three principals in history, geography, economics and a subsidiary in general paper upon graduation from the school in 1974.

After graduation, Bett went back home where he founded Tebesonik Secondary School and served briefly as its first head teacher before joining the [[University of Nairobi]] to pursue an undergraduate degree in commerce (accounting). He graduated in 1979.

After graduating, Bett joined the civil service where he built a career that culminated in his appointment as an Assistant Secretary at the [[Treasury]] in 1987. His seniors at the time included [[Simeon Nyachae]], a one-time finance minister, Chief Secretary and businessman; and Jeremiah Kiereini who too was once a Chief Secretary, Head of the Civil Service and Secretary to the Cabinet.

After his resignation, he worked briefly with the Federation of Kenya. Employers before the then president [[Daniel arap Moi]] recalled him back to government and assigned him the Supplies Branch of the Ministry of Roads and Public Works. Soon after, Moi once again tapped him for the position of Deputy State House Comptroller. His main duties were speech and report writing.

He worked in the position until 1996 when he was promoted to the position of State House Comptroller upon the retirement of Abraham Kiptanui, for whom he was a deputy. He held this role for two years until, in 1998, he was demoted to a Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Environmental Conservation.
In early 2002, Bett was approached by [[Raila Odinga]] to join him in a new political party - the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Kenya)
column2: Liberal Democratic Party]] (LDP) and he acquiesced.

column1: When LDP joined hands with the [[Mwai Kibaki]]-led NAK to form [[National Rainbow Coalition – Kenya
column2: NARC]], Bett was entrusted with the responsibility of coordinating its activities in the South Rift. In spite of the fact that South Rift had been a KANU bastion for the four decades since independence, Bett's team was able to claw back substantial ground for NARC. As the historic 2002 election votes trickled in, his input was manifest in the numerous civic seats, impressive performance by parliamentary candidates on its ticket and thousands of votes for its presidential candidate Kibaki who eventually was declared the winner. Unlike many leaders from the region, Bett's judgment carried the day. The NARC government nominated him as a member of parliament in 2003 and was subsequently elected to chair the Parliamentary Select Committee on Agriculture, Land and Natural Resources. With him at the helm, the committee sponsored many bills and motions with the Forest Act of 2005 being its most remarkable. The committee is remembered for vehemently opposing the introduction of [[Genetically modified organism

column1: The year 2005 saw Bett and [[Henry Kosgey]] leading the people of [[Rift Valley Province
column2: Rift Valley]] to join the rest of the country in rejecting a what they termed a 'watered-down' draft constitution in that year's referendum. In 2007, Bett contested the [[Bureti Constituency
column3: Buret Constituency]] parliamentary seat on an ODM ticket and won. He garnered 43,000 votes against his nearest competitor Paul Sang of [[Kenya African National Union

column1: From his contributions on the floor of the House, he was able to nudge the government into putting up a pineapple processing plant in Roret and the Tiriitab-Moita-based Bureti Technical Institute, both projects are still underway. Other projects are Kapkatet Stadium that is being modernised alongside the Sotik-Cheborge-Roret-Sigowet and Litein-Kibugat roads that are being upgraded with bitumen.

Following the demise of [[Kipkalya Kones]], he was appointed to replace him as Minister for Roads in February 2009. His stewardship at the Ministry of Roads has seen a rapid expansion of roads infrastructure in all parts of the country. The [[Thika Road
column2: Thika Superhighway]] became a reality under his charge.

column1: Bett is fond of travelling for business and leisure. He has visited over 70 countries and has close business and political contacts in Australia, United States and United Kingdom. He has five daughters and four sons.

column1: '''Franklin Kipn'getich Bett''' alias (''Chepkooit'') (born 23 March 1953) is a Kenyan politician. He is the chairman of the Agricultural Finance Corporation (AFC) after President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] appointed him to the position. He belongs to the Jubilee Alliance Party and was elected to represent the [[Bureti Constituency]] in the [[National Assembly (Kenya)
column2: National Assembly of Kenya]] in the Kenyan parliamentary election, 2007.<ref>[http://www.bunge.go.ke/members.php Members Of The 10th Parliament] {{webarchive
column4: date=16 June 2008 }}. Parliament of Kenya. Accessed 19 June 2008.</ref>

column1: Franklin Kipng’etich Bett, also known as Chepkooit to his supporters, was born on 23 March 1953 in [[Kiptiriri Village,]] Cheborge, in the larger [[Kericho District]]. He was enrolled in Cheborge Primary School in 1960 and later moved to Korongoi Primary School in 1963 where he graduated top of his class in 1968.

He was selected to join Tenwek High School in 1969, then a mission school under the auspices of the World Gospel Missionaries. Some of Bett's notable co-alumni of Tenwek High School include Mark Kipkemoi Bor, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Public Health and Sanitation, his close friend and predecessor at the Ministry of Roads [[Kipkalya Kones]], Dr. Bishop Rono, Ambassador [[John Koech]], [[Josphat Nanok
column2: Josephat Nanok]] and many other leaders in business, politics and academia.

column1: Bett graduated from Tenwek High School in 1972 with Division 1, the highest grade possible in the then Kenya Certificates of Examination (O-level).

In 1973, he proceeded to Shimo la Tewa High School in [[Mombasa]] for his Kenya Advanced Certificate of Education (KACE) where he attained three principals in history, geography, economics and a subsidiary in general paper upon graduation from the school in 1974.

After graduation, Bett went back home where he founded Tebesonik Secondary School and served briefly as its first head teacher before joining the [[University of Nairobi]] to pursue an undergraduate degree in commerce (accounting). He graduated in 1979.

After graduating, Bett joined the civil service where he built a career that culminated in his appointment as an Assistant Secretary at the [[Treasury]] in 1987. His seniors at the time included [[Simeon Nyachae]], a one-time finance minister, Chief Secretary and businessman; and Jeremiah Kiereini who too was once a Chief Secretary, Head of the Civil Service and Secretary to the Cabinet.

After his resignation, he worked briefly with the Federation of Kenya. Employers before the then president [[Daniel arap Moi]] recalled him back to government and assigned him the Supplies Branch of the Ministry of Roads and Public Works. Soon after, Moi once again tapped him for the position of Deputy State House Comptroller. His main duties were speech and report writing.

He worked in the position until 1996 when he was promoted to the position of State House Comptroller upon the retirement of Abraham Kiptanui, for whom he was a deputy. He held this role for two years until, in 1998, he was demoted to a Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Environmental Conservation.
In early 2002, Bett was approached by [[Raila Odinga]] to join him in a new political party - the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Kenya)
column2: Liberal Democratic Party]] (LDP) and he acquiesced.

column1: When LDP joined hands with the [[Mwai Kibaki]]-led NAK to form [[National Rainbow Coalition – Kenya
column2: NARC]], Bett was entrusted with the responsibility of coordinating its activities in the South Rift. In spite of the fact that South Rift had been a KANU bastion for the four decades since independence, Bett's team was able to claw back substantial ground for NARC. As the historic 2002 election votes trickled in, his input was manifest in the numerous civic seats, impressive performance by parliamentary candidates on its ticket and thousands of votes for its presidential candidate Kibaki who eventually was declared the winner. Unlike many leaders from the region, Bett's judgment carried the day. The NARC government nominated him as a member of parliament in 2003 and was subsequently elected to chair the Parliamentary Select Committee on Agriculture, Land and Natural Resources. With him at the helm, the committee sponsored many bills and motions with the Forest Act of 2005 being its most remarkable. The committee is remembered for vehemently opposing the introduction of [[Genetically modified organism

column1: From his contributions on the floor of the House, he was able to nudge the government into putting up a pineapple processing plant in Roret and the Tiriitab-Moita-based Bureti Technical Institute, both projects are still underway. Other projects are Kapkatet Stadium that is being modernised alongside the Sotik-Cheborge-Roret-Sigowet and Litein-Kibugat roads that are being upgraded with bitumen.

Following the demise of [[Kipkalya Kones]], he was appointed to replace him as Minister for Roads in February 2009. His stewardship at the Ministry of Roads has seen a rapid expansion of roads infrastructure in all parts of the country. The [[Thika Road
column2: Thika Superhighway]] became a reality under his charge.

column1: After Imanyara spent more than two years in Maximum Security Prison on charges associated with his work as a human rights lawyer, he founded the ''[[Nairobi Law Monthly]]'' in 1987.<ref name=ned>{{Cite web
column7: url-status=dead }}</ref> It was not supportive of [[Daniel Arap Moi]]'s one party policy and Imanyara was arrested for not registering the magazine.<ref name=ned/> He was again arrested in 1990 after writing a special issue entitled ""The Historic Debate: Law, Democracy, and Multi-Party Politics in Kenya.""<ref name=ned/> At one point he was held in a prison psychiatric ward, though he re-released the issue following his own release.<ref name=ned/>

column1: Receiving the International Editor of the Year by the ''[[World Press Review]]'' while in prison, he was called ""the boldest voice for a free press in a country whose intolerant government does not hesitate to shut down publications and where most journalists practice self censorship.""<ref name=""ned"" />
Imanyara was arrested for a third time in April 1991 after police confiscated the current issue of his journal.<ref name=""nyt"">{{cite news
column2: title=Topics of the Times; High 'Crimes' in Kenya
column6: access-date=2008-05-21 }}</ref> The offending information was about the formation of an opposition political party, and Imanyara was unable to notify his family or lawyer.<ref name=""nyt"" /> His papers were ransacked without a warrant.<ref name=""nyt"" />

column1: While in custody, Imanyara developed a brain tumor which was treated.<ref name=""health"" /> Kenyan aid money went down significantly after the arrest, and the [[U.S. State Department]] called it ""another denial of freedom of expression in Kenya.""<ref name=""health"" /> He was awarded the [[World Association of Newspapers' Golden Pen of Freedom Award]] later that year, but due to authorities not allowing him to leave the country for it, Liberal International President [[Otto Lambsdorff]] brought it personally to [[Nairobi]] in early 1992.<ref name=""li"">{{Cite web

At the Kenyan general elections in December 1997, he won a regional landslide victory and was elected MP for [[Central Imenti Constituency]].<ref name=""li"" /> He continued to publish his newspaper, which was renamed the Africa Law Review.<ref name=""li"" /> Imanyara is a member of the International Board of Article XIX, a member of the Advisory Board of the Urban Morgan Institute for Human Rights, and also a member of the Media Institute for the advancement of the freedom of expression.<ref name=""li"" />
In January 2008, Imanyara accused the Kenyan first lady [[Lucy Kibaki]] of assault and threatened to sue Kibaki over the alleged incident.<ref name=""stan"">{{cite news
column2: title=Lawyer Imanyara in trouble with Kibaki’s wife refutes allegations that he is dead
column4: date=2008-02-05 }}</ref> The first lady was swift to deny the allegations, accusing Imanyara of blackmail after failing to secure the deputy Speaker's seat during the elections in Parliament.<ref name=""stan"" />
