column1: '''Richard Erskine Frere Leakey''' (19 December 1944 – 2 January 2022) was a Kenyan [[paleoanthropologist]], [[conservation movement
column11: issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Leakey held a number of official positions in Kenya, mostly in institutions of [[archaeology]] and [[wildlife conservation]]. He was director of the [[National Museum of Kenya]],<ref name="":0""/> founded the NGO [[WildlifeDirect]], and was the chairman of the [[Kenya Wildlife Service]].<ref>{{Cite book
column16: access-date=28 May 2020}}</ref> Leakey served in the powerful office of cabinet secretary and head of public service during the tail end of President [[Daniel Toroitich Arap Moi]]'s government.

column1: Leakey co-founded the ""Turkana Basin Institute"" in an academic partnership with [[Stony Brook University]], where he was an anthropology professor. He served as the chair of the Turkana Basin Institute until his death.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Richard Leakey, trailblazing conservationist and fossil hunter, dies at 77
column16: title=Richard Leakey, Kenyan Fossil Hunter and Conservationist, Dies at 77

column1: Richard Erskine Frere Leakey was born on 19 December 1944 in [[Nairobi]].<ref name="":2""/> As a small boy, Leakey lived in Nairobi with his parents: [[Louis Leakey]], curator of the Coryndon Museum, and [[Mary Leakey]], director of the Leakey excavations at [[Olduvai Gorge
column2: Olduvai]], and his two brothers, Jonathan and [[Philip Leakey
column4: title=Richard E. Leakey Biography and Interview
column6: url=https://achievement.org/achiever/richard-leakey/}}</ref> The Leakey brothers had a very active childhood. All the boys had ponies and belonged to the Langata Pony Club.<ref>{{cite web
column9: title=Kenyan Paleoanthropologist Richard Leakey Passed Away at 77 Family
column16: url-status=dead }}</ref> Sometimes the whole club were guests at the Leakeys' for holidays and vacations. Leakey's parents founded the Dalmatian Club of East Africa and won a prize in 1957.{{cn
column17: date=February 2026}} Dogs and many other pets shared the Leakey home.{{cn
column18: date=February 2026}} The Leakey boys participated in games conducted by both adults and children, in which they tried to imitate early humans, catching [[springhare]] and small antelope by hand on the [[Serengeti]]. They drove lions and [[jackal]]s from the kill to see if they could do it.<ref name=""ancestralpassions18"">{{cite book

column1: In 1956, aged eleven, Leakey fell from his horse, fracturing his skull and nearly dying as a result.<ref name=""natgeo-obit"">{{cite web
column4: title=Richard Leakey, trailblazing conservationist and fossil hunter, dies at 77
column12: date=2 January 2022}}</ref> Incidentally, it was this incident that saved his parents' marriage.<ref name=""natgeo-obit""/> Louis was seriously considering leaving Mary for his secretary, Rosalie Osborn. As the battle with Mary raged in the household, Leakey begged his father from his sickbed not to leave. That was the deciding factor. Louis broke up with Rosalie and the family lived in happy harmony for a few years more.<ref name=""morell"">Morell, Virginia (1995). Chapter 17, ""Chimpanzees and Other Loves"", in ''Ancestral Passions: The Leakey Family and the Quest for Humankind's Beginnings''. {{ISBN

column1: Leakey chose to support himself, borrowed £500 from his parents for a [[Land Rover]] and went into the trapping and skeleton supply business with [[Kamoya Kimeu]].<ref name=""finders"">{{cite web
column6: date=13 April 2018}}</ref> Already a skilled horseman, outdoorsman, Land Rover mechanic, amateur archaeologist, and expedition leader,<ref name=""wapo"">{{cite news
column9: title=Drive, Luck and the Leakey Genes
column13: date=3 October 1978}}</ref> he learned to identify bones, skills which all pointed to a path he did not yet wish to take, simply because his father was on it.<ref>Richard E. Leakey in ''The Making of Mankind'' (1981), chapter 1, p. 1, says he wished to be ""free"" of his parents' world, a sentiment both Louis and Mary must have understood very well, even though they opposed his freedom.</ref>

column1: The bone business turned into a safari business in 1961.<ref>{{cite web
column6: date=9 October 2001}}</ref> In 1962, he obtained a private pilot licence and took tours to the [[Olduvai Gorge]].<ref>{{cite journal
column9: title=The Old Man of Olduvai Gorge
column19: author-link=Roger Lewin}}</ref> It was from a casual aerial survey that he noted the potential of [[Lake Natron]]'s shores for palaeontology. He went looking for fossils in a Land Rover, but could find none, until his parents assigned [[Glynn Isaac]] to go with him.<ref>{{cite web
column24: website=Center for the Advanced Study of Human Paleobiology
column27: date=5 October 2015}}</ref> Louis was so impressed with their finds that he gave them [[National Geographic Society
column28: National Geographic]] money for a month's expedition.<ref>Morell, 1995, Chapter 18, ""Richard Makes his Move."" Besides Leakey and Glynn, the roster included Barbara Isaac, [[Philip Leakey]], [[Hugo van Lawick]] and six of Mary's African assistants.</ref> They explored in the vicinity of Peninj near the lake, where Leakey was in charge of the administrative details. Bored, he returned to Nairobi temporarily, but at that moment, Kamoya Kimeu discovered a fossil of ''[[Australopithecus boisei]]''.<ref name=""finders""/> A second expedition left Leakey feeling that he was being excluded from the most significant part of the operation, the scientific analysis.<ref name=""finders""/>

column1: In 1964, on his second Lake Natron expedition, Leakey met an archaeologist named Margaret Cropper.<ref>{{cite web
column5: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> When Margaret returned to England, Leakey decided to follow suit to study for a degree and become better acquainted with her. He completed his high school requirements in six months; meanwhile Margaret obtained her degree at the [[University of Edinburgh]].<ref name="":0""/> He passed the entrance exams for admission to college, but in 1965 he and Margaret decided to marry and return to Kenya. His father offered him a job at the Centre for Prehistory and Palaeontology.<ref>{{cite web
column11: language=en-gb}}</ref> He worked excavating at [[Lake Baringo]] and continued his photographic safari business, making enough money to buy a house in [[Karen, Kenya
column12: Karen]], a pleasant suburb of Nairobi.<ref>{{cite web
column15: title=A taste of paradise in the Kenyan wilderness
column19: date=8 June 1984}}</ref> Their daughter Anna was born in 1969, the same year that Leakey and Margaret divorced. He married his colleague [[Meave Leakey
column20: Meave Epps]] in 1970 and they had two daughters, [[Louise Leakey

column1: Richard formed the Kenya Museum Associates (now Kenya Museum Society) with influential Kenyans in 1955.<ref name=""kenyamuseum"">{{cite web
column5: access-date=4 January 2022}}</ref> They aimed to ""Kenyanise"" and improve the [[National Museums of Kenya
column6: National Museum]].<ref name=""kenyamuseum""/> They offered the museum £5000, one-third of its yearly budget, if it would place Leakey in a responsible position, and he became an observer on the board of directors.<ref>{{cite web
column9: title=A Protective Legislation, Policy and Practice of Archaeological Heritage Management in Kenya
column14: date=27 November 2013}}</ref> Joel Ojal, the government official in charge of the museum, and a member of the Associates, directed the chairman of the board to start placing Kenyans on it.<ref>{{cite book
column17: title=Ancestral Passions: The Leakey Family and the Quest for Humankind's Beginnings

column1: Plans for the museum had not matured when Louis, intentionally or not, found a way to remove his confrontational son from the scene. Louis attended a lunch with [[Emperor of Ethiopia
column6: title=Skulls crown Ethiopia's place in evolutionary studies
column10: date=22 February 2005}}</ref> The conversation turned to fossils, and the Emperor wanted to know why none had been found in [[Ethiopia]]. Louis developed this inquiry into permission to excavate on the [[Omo River (Ethiopia)

column1: The expedition consisted of three contingents: French, under [[Camille Arambourg]], American, under [[F. Clark Howell]], and Kenyan, led by Richard.<ref>{{cite journal
column4: title=Camille Arambourg et Louis Leakey ou un 1/2 siècle de paléontologie africaine
column6: journal=Bulletin de la Société préhistorique française
column15: url-access=subscription }}</ref> Louis could not go because of his arthritis. Crossing the Omo in 1967, Leakey's contingent was attacked by [[crocodiles]], which destroyed their wooden boat.<ref name=""wapo""/> Expedition members barely escaped with their lives. Richard radioed Louis for a new, aluminium boat, which the [[National Geographic Society]] was happy to supply.<ref name=""wapo""/>

column1: On site, Kamoya Kimeu found a hominid fossil. Leakey took it to be ''[[Homo erectus]]'', but Louis identified it as ''Homo sapiens''.<ref>{{cite web
column5: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> It was the oldest of the species found at that time, dating to 160,000 years, and was the first find contemporaneous with ''[[Homo neanderthalensis]]''. During the identification process, Leakey came to feel that the college men were patronising him.<ref>This section is based on Morell, 1995, Chapter 20, ""To the Omo"".</ref>

column1: During the Omo expedition of 1967, Leakey visited Nairobi and on the return flight the pilot flew over [[Lake Rudolph]] (renamed Lake Turkana from 1975) to avoid a thunderstorm.<ref name=""stonybrook"">{{cite web
column9: date=Spring 2016}}</ref> The map led Leakey to expect volcanic rock below him but he saw sediments. Visiting the region with Howell by helicopter, he saw tools and fossils everywhere. In his mind, he started formulating a new enterprise.<ref name=""stonybrook""/>

column1: In 1968 Louis and Richard attended a meeting of the Research and Exploration Committee of the National Geographic Society to ask for money for Omo.<ref name=""alive"">{{cite web
column11: url-status=dead }}</ref> Catching Louis by surprise, Richard asked the committee to divert the $25,000 intended for Omo to new excavations to be conducted under his leadership at Koobi Fora. Richard won, but chairman [[Leonard Carmichael]] told him he had better find something or never ""come begging at our door again"".<ref name=""alive""/> Louis graciously congratulated Richard.<ref name=""alive""/>

column1: By that time the board of the [[National Museums of Kenya
column2: National Museum]] was packed with Kenyan supporters of Richard. They appointed him administrative director.<ref>{{cite web
column5: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> The curator, Robert Carcasson, resigned in protest,<ref name=""alive""/> and Leakey was left with the museum at his command, which he, like Louis before him, used as a base of operations.<ref>Morell, 1995, Chapter 21, ""Breaking Away.""</ref> Although there was friendly rivalry and contention between Louis and Richard, relations remained good. Each took over for the other when one was busy with something else or incapacitated, and Richard continued to inform his father immediately of hominid finds.<ref name=""alive""/>

column1: In the first expedition to Allia Bay on Lake Turkana, where the Koobi Fora camp came to be located, Leakey hired primarily young researchers. The students included John Harris and Bernard Wood.<ref>{{cite journal
column10: title=Early Homo erectus skeleton from west Lake Turkana, Kenya
column23: url-access=subscription }}</ref> Also present was a team of Africans under Kamoya: a geochemist, Paul Abel, and a photographer, [[Bob Campbell (photographer)
column25: title=Paul Abel and Richard Leakey Walking the Shores of Lake Turkana
column33: date=3 February 2018}}</ref> Margaret was the archaeologist. In contrast to his father, Richard ran a disciplined and tidy camp, although, in order to find fossils, he did push the expedition harder than it wished.<ref name=""aoa"">{{cite web
column34: title=Richard Leakey, Academy Class of 2007, Part 2

column1: In 1969 the discovery of a cranium of ''[[Paranthropus boisei]]'' caused great excitement.<ref>{{cite web
column6: language=en}}</ref> A ''[[Homo rudolfensis]]'' skull ([[KNM ER 1470]]) and a ''[[Homo erectus]]'' skull ([[KNM ER 3733]]), discovered in 1972 and 1975, respectively, were among the most significant finds of Leakey's earlier expeditions.<ref>{{cite web
column9: website=The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program
column11: language=en}}</ref> In 1978 an intact cranium of ''Homo erectus'' ([[KNM ER 3883]]) was discovered.<ref name=""aoa""/>

column1: [[Donald Johanson]] and Leakey held different views about human evolution. They held a debate on ''Cronkite's Universe'', a talk show hosted by [[Walter Cronkite]], in 1981.<ref>{{Cite book
column4: title=Bones of Contention: Controversies in the Search for Human Origins

column1: [[File:Turkana boy - steps of forensic facial reconstruction.jpg
column3: Turkana Boy – steps of forensic facial reconstruction/approximation]]

column1: [[Turkana Boy]], discovered by [[Kamoya Kimeu]], a member of the Leakeys' team, in 1984, was the nearly complete skeleton of a ''[[Homo ergaster]]'' (though some, including Leakey, call it ''erectus'') who died 1.6 million years ago at about age 9–12.<ref name=""bloomberg"">{{cite web
column2: title=Richard Leakey, Who Found 'Turkana Boy' Fossil, Dies at 77
column8: first=Eric}}</ref> Leakey and [[Roger Lewin]] describe the experience of this find and their interpretation of it, in their book ''Origins Reconsidered'' (1992).<ref>{{cite web
column13: title=Origins Reconsidered: In Search of What Makes Us Human
column18: author-link2=Roger Lewin}}</ref> Shortly after the discovery of Turkana Boy, Leakey and his team made the discovery of a skull ([[KNM WT 17000]], known as ""Black Skull"") of a new species, ''[[Australopithecus aethiopicus]]'' (or ''Paranthropus aethiopicus'').<ref>{{cite web
column21: title=Skull Piece Takes Man a Step Back

column1: Richard shifted away from palaeontology in 1989, but his wife [[Meave Leakey]] and daughter [[Louise Leakey]] continue to conduct palaeontological research in Northern Kenya.<ref>{{cite web

In 1989 Richard Leakey was appointed the head of the Wildlife Conservation and Management Department (WMCD) by President [[Daniel Arap Moi]] in response to the international outcry over the [[poaching of elephants]] and the impact it was having on the wildlife of Kenya.<ref>{{Cite web
column4: title='Kenya's wildlife – Predictions for the next decade' with Dr Richard Leakey
column6: access-date=5 November 2016}}</ref> The department was replaced by the [[Kenya Wildlife Service]] (KWS) in 1990, and Leakey became its first chairman.<ref>{{cite web
column13: url-status=dead }}</ref> With characteristically bold steps Leakey created special, well-armed anti-poaching units that were authorised to shoot poachers on sight.<ref>{{Cite book
column24: isbn=9781743213063}}</ref> The poaching menace was dramatically reduced. Impressed by Leakey's transformation of the Kenya Wildlife Service, the [[World Bank]] approved grants worth $140 million.<ref>{{cite web
column25: title=Dr Richard Leakey: A swashbuckler with intent
column29: language=en}}</ref> Richard Leakey, President Moi, and the WMCD made the international news headlines when a stockpile of 12 tons of [[ivory]] was [[destruction of ivory
column30: burned in 1989]] in [[Nairobi National Park]].<ref>{{cite web
column33: title=Kenya, In Gesture, Burns Ivory Tusks

column3: video1 = [https://www.c-span.org/video/?17614-1/wildlife-policy-kenya Presentation by Leakey to the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., ""New Wildlife Policy for Kenya"", April 18, 1991], [[C-SPAN]]}}

column1: Richard Leakey's confrontational approach to the issue of human–wildlife conflict in [[national park]]s did not win him friends. His view was that parks were self-contained ecosystems that had to be fenced in and the humans kept out. Leakey's bold and incorruptible nature also offended many local politicians.<ref>{{Cite news
In 2016, Leakey was named Conservationist of the Year by [[The Perfect World Foundation]] and won ""The Fragile Rhino"" prize at the Elephant Ball in [[Gothenburg]], Sweden.<ref>{{cite web
column2: title=Another great legend awarded the world's most prestigious conservation prize

column1: In 1993, a small propeller-driven plane piloted by Richard Leakey crashed, crushing his lower legs, both of which were later amputated.<ref name=""natgeo-obit""/> Sabotage was suspected but never proven.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Richard Leakey Tries to Save the Elephants—Again
column9: access-date=25 May 2020}}</ref> While in the hospital, Leakey told President Moi, a religious man, not to pray for him, but act on matters pending for the Kenya Wildlife Service.<ref name=humanistinterview>Ryan Shaffer, [http://thehumanist.com/july-august-2012/evolution-humanism-and-conservation-the-humanist-interview-with-richard-leakey/ ""Evolution, Humanism, and Conservation: The Humanist Interview with Richard Leakey""], ''The Humanist'', 29 June 2012.</ref> Thereafter, Richard Leakey walked on [[artificial limb]]s.<ref name=""guardian2001""/> Around this time the Kenyan government announced that a secret probe had found evidence of corruption and mismanagement in the Kenya Wildlife Service. An annoyed Leakey resigned publicly in a press conference in January 1994.<ref>{{cite web
column12: title=Noted Kenya Conservationist Resigning in a Political Storm
column16: date=15 January 1994}}</ref> He was replaced by David Western as the head of the Kenya Wildlife Service.<ref>{{cite web

column1: Richard Leakey wrote about his experiences at the Kenya Wildlife Service in his book ''[[Wildlife Wars
column2: Wildlife Wars: My Fight to Save Africa's Natural Treasures]]'' (2001).<ref>{{cite book
column7: title=Wildlife Wars: My Fight to Save Africa's Natural Treasures

column1: In May 1995, Richard Leakey joined some Kenyan intellectuals in launching a new political party—the [[Safina Party]],<ref name=""reuters"">{{cite web
column2: title=Richard Leakey, Kenyan conservationist who campaigned against ivory trade, has died
column7: date=3 January 2022}}</ref> which in Swahili means ""[[Noah's Ark]]"".<ref name=""reuters""/> The Safina party was routinely harassed and even its application to become an official political party was not approved until 1997.<ref>{{cite web
column8: title=Kenya: Current information on Safina Party, especially on arrests of its members in 1995
column10: website=Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada

column3: video1 = [https://www.c-span.org/video/?67504-1/origins-politics Presentation by Leakey to the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., ""Origins and Politics"", October 6, 1995], [[C-SPAN]]}}

column1: In 1997, international donor institutions froze their aid to Kenya because of widespread corruption.<ref>{{cite web
column4: title=Time for Zuma to read his obituary - OPINION
column9: date=7 February 2020}}</ref> To placate the donors, Moi appointed Richard Leakey as Cabinet Secretary and head of the civil service in 1999. Leakey's second stint in the civil service lasted two years.<ref>{{cite web
column14: date=10 January 2019}}</ref> He sacked 25,000 civil servants and obtained £250 million of funds from the [[International Monetary Fund]] and the [[World Bank]].<ref>{{cite web
column20: date=3 January 2022}}</ref> However, Leakey found himself sidelined after the money arrived, and his reforms were blocked in the courts. He was sacked from his cabinet post in 2001.<ref name=""guardian2001"">{{cite news

column1: Leakey left Kenya for the U.S. in 2002 and became a professor of anthropology at [[Stony Brook University]], New York.<ref>Stony Brook University, Press release, 27 March 2007: [http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/General_University_News_2/World-Renowned_Anthropologist_Richard_Leakey_to_be_Honored_at_Stony_Brook_University_s_50th_Anniversary_Gala_April_11.shtml ""World-Renowned Anthropologist Richard Leakey to be Honored at Stony Brook University's 50th Anniversary Gala April 11"".] {{webarchive
column3: date=8 June 2010 }}</ref> He was also Chair of the Turkana Basin Institute.<ref>{{cite web
column10: date=8 August 2016}}</ref> In 2004, Leakey founded and chaired [[WildlifeDirect]], a Kenya-based charitable organisation.<ref>{{cite web
column14: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> The charity was established to provide support to conservationists in Africa directly on the ground via the use of blogs. This enables individuals anywhere to play a direct and interactive role in the survival of some of the world's most precious species. The organisation played a significant role in the saving of the [[Democratic Republic of Congo]]'s [[mountain gorillas]] in [[Virunga National Park]] in January 2007 after a rebel uprising threatened to eliminate the highly vulnerable population.<ref name=""natgeo-obit""/>

column1: In April 2007, he was appointed interim chairman of [[Transparency International]]'s Kenya branch.<ref name=""bloomberg""/> The same year, Leakey was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]]<ref>{{cite web
column5: access-date = 8 March 2012}}</ref> and received the [[Academy of Achievement#Notable recipients of the Golden Plate Award
column6: Golden Plate Award]] of the [[Academy of Achievement
column8: title=Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement
column10: url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref> In June 2013, Leakey was awarded the [[Isaac Asimov]] Science Award from the [[American Humanist Association]].<ref>SmashPipe, 5 June 2013: [https://archive.today/20130624234603/http://science.smashpipe.com/?f=XeGlhASFV4M%23stop ''Humanist Awards Banquet of the 2013 American Humanist Conference'']</ref>

column1: Leakey's groundbreaking work contributed to the recognition of Africa as the birthplace of humankind, that contributed as evidence that the earliest humans had lived on the African continent. He was known to have spearheaded campaigns to stop poaching in Kenya.<ref name="":1""/> Aside from his contributions to public service, he was known to have contributed immensely to the civil service; ""Besides his distinguished career in public service, Dr Leakey is celebrated for his prominent role in Kenya's civil society where he founded and successfully ran a number of institutions,"" Mr Kenyatta said.<ref name="":1"">{{Cite news
column3: title=Richard Leakey: Kenyan conservationist dies aged 77
Sketch of Richard Leakey (2014), by Patrick L. Gallegos]]

column1: In 2015, President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] appointed Leakey chairman of the board of the Kenya Wildlife Service. Although he was chairman rather than director, Leakey played an active role in KWS policies.<ref name=""guardian2001""/> He brokered a deal on the extension of the [[Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway]], allowing the railway to pass over [[Nairobi National Park]] on an 18-metre-tall [[viaduct]].<ref>{{cite news
column4: title=Kenya: SGR to Pass Over the Nairobi National Park
column7: date=14 September 2016}}</ref> Leakey felt that the viaduct would set an example for the rest of Africa in balancing economic development with environmental protection. However, other Kenyan conservationists have opposed railway construction in the park.<ref>{{cite news
column10: title=Opposing camps to hold dialogue on railway through Nairobi National Park

column1: [[Angelina Jolie]] was to direct a film about Leakey's life, with Leakey in early 2016 expressing his confidence that the film would be shot in Kenya.<ref>{{cite news
column4: title=Richard Leakey: What does Angelina Jolie see in this man?

column1: Leakey spoke fluent [[Kiswahili]] and moved effortlessly between white and black communities. While he rarely talked about race in public, racism and gender inequality infuriated him.<ref>{{Cite journal
column16: doi-access=free}}</ref> Leakey stated that he was an [[atheist]]<ref>{{cite book
column19: title=One Life: Richard E. Leakey: An Autobiography

column1: Leakey came from a family of renowned archeologists. His mother, Mary Leakey, discovered evidence in 1978 that man walked upright much earlier than had been thought. She and her husband, Louis Leakey, unearthed skulls of ape-like early humans, shedding fresh light on our ancestors.<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=World-renowned Kenyan conservationist Richard Leakey dies at 77

column1: Leakey was diagnosed with a terminal [[kidney]] disease in 1969. Ten years later he became seriously ill but received a [[kidney transplant]] from his brother, Philip, and recovered to full health.<ref>{{cite web
column5: title=Famed fossil hunter and conservationist Richard Leakey dies at 77

column1: He died at his home outside Nairobi, on 2 January 2022,<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Richard Leakey's Legacy in Science, Conservation and Politics
column10: author-link=Virginia Morell}}</ref> less than a month after his 77th birthday.<ref>{{cite web
column12: title=Message of Condolence from H.E Hon. Uhuru Kenyatta following the death of former Head of Public Service Dr Richard Leakey
column22: title=Renowned Kenyan conservationist Richard Leakey dies aged 77
column28: title=Fossil hunter Richard Leakey who showed humans evolved in Africa dies at 77
column33: first=Jane}}</ref> In accordance with his wishes, he was buried on a hill along the Rift Valley.<ref>{{Cite web
column35: title=Richard Leakey Laid To Rest On A Hill Along Rift Valley

column1: '''Richard Erskine Frere Leakey''' (19 December 1944 – 2 January 2022) was a Kenyan [[paleoanthropologist]], [[conservation movement
column11: issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Leakey held a number of official positions in Kenya, mostly in institutions of [[archaeology]] and [[wildlife conservation]]. He was director of the [[National Museum of Kenya]],<ref name="":0""/> founded the NGO [[WildlifeDirect]], and was the chairman of the [[Kenya Wildlife Service]].<ref>{{Cite book
column16: access-date=28 May 2020}}</ref> Leakey served in the powerful office of cabinet secretary and head of public service during the tail end of President [[Daniel Toroitich Arap Moi]]'s government.

column1: Leakey co-founded the ""Turkana Basin Institute"" in an academic partnership with [[Stony Brook University]], where he was an anthropology professor. He served as the chair of the Turkana Basin Institute until his death.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Richard Leakey, trailblazing conservationist and fossil hunter, dies at 77
column16: title=Richard Leakey, Kenyan Fossil Hunter and Conservationist, Dies at 77

column1: Richard Erskine Frere Leakey was born on 19 December 1944 in [[Nairobi]].<ref name="":2""/> As a small boy, Leakey lived in Nairobi with his parents: [[Louis Leakey]], curator of the Coryndon Museum, and [[Mary Leakey]], director of the Leakey excavations at [[Olduvai Gorge
column2: Olduvai]], and his two brothers, Jonathan and [[Philip Leakey
column4: title=Richard E. Leakey Biography and Interview
column6: url=https://achievement.org/achiever/richard-leakey/}}</ref> The Leakey brothers had a very active childhood. All the boys had ponies and belonged to the Langata Pony Club.<ref>{{cite web
column9: title=Kenyan Paleoanthropologist Richard Leakey Passed Away at 77 Family
column16: url-status=dead }}</ref> Sometimes the whole club were guests at the Leakeys' for holidays and vacations. Leakey's parents founded the Dalmatian Club of East Africa and won a prize in 1957.[[Category:All articles with unsourced statements]][[Category:Articles with unsourced statements from February 2026]]<sup class=""noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact"" style=""white-space:nowrap;"">[<i>[[Wikipedia:Citation needed
column17: citation needed]]] Dogs and many other pets shared the Leakey home.[[Category:All articles with unsourced statements]][[Category:Articles with unsourced statements from February 2026]][[[Wikipedia:Citation needed
column18: citation needed]]] The Leakey boys participated in games conducted by both adults and children, in which they tried to imitate early humans, catching [[springhare]] and small antelope by hand on the [[Serengeti]]. They drove lions and [[jackal]]s from the kill to see if they could do it.{{cite book

column1: In 1956, aged eleven, Leakey fell from his horse, fracturing his skull and nearly dying as a result.<ref name=""natgeo-obit"">{{cite web
column4: title=Richard Leakey, trailblazing conservationist and fossil hunter, dies at 77
column12: date=2 January 2022}}</ref> Incidentally, it was this incident that saved his parents' marriage.<ref name=""natgeo-obit""/> Louis was seriously considering leaving Mary for his secretary, Rosalie Osborn. As the battle with Mary raged in the household, Leakey begged his father from his sickbed not to leave. That was the deciding factor. Louis broke up with Rosalie and the family lived in happy harmony for a few years more.<ref name=""morell"">Morell, Virginia (1995). Chapter 17, ""Chimpanzees and Other Loves"", in ''Ancestral Passions: The Leakey Family and the Quest for Humankind's Beginnings''. {{ISBN

column28: National Geographic]] money for a month's expedition.<ref>Morell, 1995, Chapter 18, ""Richard Makes his Move."" Besides Leakey and Glynn, the roster included Barbara Isaac, [[Philip Leakey]], [[Hugo van Lawick]] and six of Mary's African assistants.</ref> They explored in the vicinity of Peninj near the lake, where Leakey was in charge of the administrative details. Bored, he returned to Nairobi temporarily, but at that moment, Kamoya Kimeu discovered a fossil of ''[[Australopithecus boisei]]''.<ref name=""finders""/> A second expedition left Leakey feeling that he was being excluded from the most significant part of the operation, the scientific analysis.<ref name=""finders""/>

column1: In 1964, on his second Lake Natron expedition, Leakey met an archaeologist named Margaret Cropper.<ref>{{cite web
column5: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> When Margaret returned to England, Leakey decided to follow suit to study for a degree and become better acquainted with her. He completed his high school requirements in six months; meanwhile Margaret obtained her degree at the [[University of Edinburgh]].<ref name="":0""/> He passed the entrance exams for admission to college, but in 1965 he and Margaret decided to marry and return to Kenya. His father offered him a job at the Centre for Prehistory and Palaeontology.<ref>{{cite web
column11: language=en-gb}}</ref> He worked excavating at [[Lake Baringo]] and continued his photographic safari business, making enough money to buy a house in [[Karen, Kenya
column12: Karen]], a pleasant suburb of Nairobi.<ref>{{cite web
column15: title=A taste of paradise in the Kenyan wilderness
column19: date=8 June 1984}}</ref> Their daughter Anna was born in 1969, the same year that Leakey and Margaret divorced. He married his colleague [[Meave Leakey
column20: Meave Epps]] in 1970 and they had two daughters, [[Louise Leakey

column1: Richard formed the Kenya Museum Associates (now Kenya Museum Society) with influential Kenyans in 1955.<ref name=""kenyamuseum"">{{cite web
column5: access-date=4 January 2022}}</ref> They aimed to ""Kenyanise"" and improve the [[National Museums of Kenya
column6: National Museum]].<ref name=""kenyamuseum""/> They offered the museum £5000, one-third of its yearly budget, if it would place Leakey in a responsible position, and he became an observer on the board of directors.<ref>{{cite web
column9: title=A Protective Legislation, Policy and Practice of Archaeological Heritage Management in Kenya
column14: date=27 November 2013}}</ref> Joel Ojal, the government official in charge of the museum, and a member of the Associates, directed the chairman of the board to start placing Kenyans on it.<ref>{{cite book
column17: title=Ancestral Passions: The Leakey Family and the Quest for Humankind's Beginnings

column1: Plans for the museum had not matured when Louis, intentionally or not, found a way to remove his confrontational son from the scene. Louis attended a lunch with [[Emperor of Ethiopia
column6: title=Skulls crown Ethiopia's place in evolutionary studies
column10: date=22 February 2005}}</ref> The conversation turned to fossils, and the Emperor wanted to know why none had been found in [[Ethiopia]]. Louis developed this inquiry into permission to excavate on the [[Omo River (Ethiopia)

column1: The expedition consisted of three contingents: French, under [[Camille Arambourg]], American, under [[F. Clark Howell]], and Kenyan, led by Richard.<ref>{{cite journal
column4: title=Camille Arambourg et Louis Leakey ou un 1/2 siècle de paléontologie africaine
column6: journal=Bulletin de la Société préhistorique française
column15: url-access=subscription }}</ref> Louis could not go because of his arthritis. Crossing the Omo in 1967, Leakey's contingent was attacked by [[crocodiles]], which destroyed their wooden boat.<ref name=""wapo""/> Expedition members barely escaped with their lives. Richard radioed Louis for a new, aluminium boat, which the [[National Geographic Society]] was happy to supply.<ref name=""wapo""/>

column1: On site, Kamoya Kimeu found a hominid fossil. Leakey took it to be ''[[Homo erectus]]'', but Louis identified it as ''Homo sapiens''.<ref>{{cite web
column5: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> It was the oldest of the species found at that time, dating to 160,000 years, and was the first find contemporaneous with ''[[Homo neanderthalensis]]''. During the identification process, Leakey came to feel that the college men were patronising him.<ref>This section is based on Morell, 1995, Chapter 20, ""To the Omo"".</ref>

column1: During the Omo expedition of 1967, Leakey visited Nairobi and on the return flight the pilot flew over [[Lake Rudolph]] (renamed Lake Turkana from 1975) to avoid a thunderstorm.<ref name=""stonybrook"">{{cite web
column9: date=Spring 2016}}</ref> The map led Leakey to expect volcanic rock below him but he saw sediments. Visiting the region with Howell by helicopter, he saw tools and fossils everywhere. In his mind, he started formulating a new enterprise.<ref name=""stonybrook""/>

column1: In 1968 Louis and Richard attended a meeting of the Research and Exploration Committee of the National Geographic Society to ask for money for Omo.<ref name=""alive"">{{cite web
column11: url-status=dead }}</ref> Catching Louis by surprise, Richard asked the committee to divert the $25,000 intended for Omo to new excavations to be conducted under his leadership at Koobi Fora. Richard won, but chairman [[Leonard Carmichael]] told him he had better find something or never ""come begging at our door again"".<ref name=""alive""/> Louis graciously congratulated Richard.<ref name=""alive""/>

column1: By that time the board of the [[National Museums of Kenya
column2: National Museum]] was packed with Kenyan supporters of Richard. They appointed him administrative director.<ref>{{cite web
column5: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> The curator, Robert Carcasson, resigned in protest,<ref name=""alive""/> and Leakey was left with the museum at his command, which he, like Louis before him, used as a base of operations.<ref>Morell, 1995, Chapter 21, ""Breaking Away.""</ref> Although there was friendly rivalry and contention between Louis and Richard, relations remained good. Each took over for the other when one was busy with something else or incapacitated, and Richard continued to inform his father immediately of hominid finds.<ref name=""alive""/>

column1: In the first expedition to Allia Bay on Lake Turkana, where the Koobi Fora camp came to be located, Leakey hired primarily young researchers. The students included John Harris and Bernard Wood.<ref>{{cite journal
column10: title=Early Homo erectus skeleton from west Lake Turkana, Kenya
column23: url-access=subscription }}</ref> Also present was a team of Africans under Kamoya: a geochemist, Paul Abel, and a photographer, [[Bob Campbell (photographer)
column25: title=Paul Abel and Richard Leakey Walking the Shores of Lake Turkana
column33: date=3 February 2018}}</ref> Margaret was the archaeologist. In contrast to his father, Richard ran a disciplined and tidy camp, although, in order to find fossils, he did push the expedition harder than it wished.<ref name=""aoa"">{{cite web
column34: title=Richard Leakey, Academy Class of 2007, Part 2

column1: In 1969 the discovery of a cranium of ''[[Paranthropus boisei]]'' caused great excitement.<ref>{{cite web
column6: language=en}}</ref> A ''[[Homo rudolfensis]]'' skull ([[KNM ER 1470]]) and a ''[[Homo erectus]]'' skull ([[KNM ER 3733]]), discovered in 1972 and 1975, respectively, were among the most significant finds of Leakey's earlier expeditions.<ref>{{cite web
column9: website=The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program
column11: language=en}}</ref> In 1978 an intact cranium of ''Homo erectus'' ([[KNM ER 3883]]) was discovered.<ref name=""aoa""/>

column1: [[Donald Johanson]] and Leakey held different views about human evolution. They held a debate on ''Cronkite's Universe'', a talk show hosted by [[Walter Cronkite]], in 1981.<ref>{{Cite book
column4: title=Bones of Contention: Controversies in the Search for Human Origins

column1: [[File:Turkana boy - steps of forensic facial reconstruction.jpg
column3: Turkana Boy – steps of forensic facial reconstruction/approximation]]

column1: [[Turkana Boy]], discovered by [[Kamoya Kimeu]], a member of the Leakeys' team, in 1984, was the nearly complete skeleton of a ''[[Homo ergaster]]'' (though some, including Leakey, call it ''erectus'') who died 1.6 million years ago at about age 9–12.<ref name=""bloomberg"">{{cite web
column2: title=Richard Leakey, Who Found 'Turkana Boy' Fossil, Dies at 77
column8: first=Eric}}</ref> Leakey and [[Roger Lewin]] describe the experience of this find and their interpretation of it, in their book ''Origins Reconsidered'' (1992).<ref>{{cite web
column13: title=Origins Reconsidered: In Search of What Makes Us Human
column18: author-link2=Roger Lewin}}</ref> Shortly after the discovery of Turkana Boy, Leakey and his team made the discovery of a skull ([[KNM WT 17000]], known as ""Black Skull"") of a new species, ''[[Australopithecus aethiopicus]]'' (or ''Paranthropus aethiopicus'').<ref>{{cite web
column21: title=Skull Piece Takes Man a Step Back

column1: Richard shifted away from palaeontology in 1989, but his wife [[Meave Leakey]] and daughter [[Louise Leakey]] continue to conduct palaeontological research in Northern Kenya.<ref>{{cite web

In 1989 Richard Leakey was appointed the head of the Wildlife Conservation and Management Department (WMCD) by President [[Daniel Arap Moi]] in response to the international outcry over the [[poaching of elephants]] and the impact it was having on the wildlife of Kenya.<ref>{{Cite web
column4: title='Kenya's wildlife – Predictions for the next decade' with Dr Richard Leakey
column6: access-date=5 November 2016}}</ref> The department was replaced by the [[Kenya Wildlife Service]] (KWS) in 1990, and Leakey became its first chairman.<ref>{{cite web
column13: url-status=dead }}</ref> With characteristically bold steps Leakey created special, well-armed anti-poaching units that were authorised to shoot poachers on sight.<ref>{{Cite book
column24: isbn=9781743213063}}</ref> The poaching menace was dramatically reduced. Impressed by Leakey's transformation of the Kenya Wildlife Service, the [[World Bank]] approved grants worth $140 million.<ref>{{cite web
column25: title=Dr Richard Leakey: A swashbuckler with intent
column29: language=en}}</ref> Richard Leakey, President Moi, and the WMCD made the international news headlines when a stockpile of 12 tons of [[ivory]] was [[destruction of ivory
column30: burned in 1989]] in [[Nairobi National Park]].<ref>{{cite web
column33: title=Kenya, In Gesture, Burns Ivory Tusks

column4: class=noviewer]] [https://www.c-span.org/video/?17614-1/wildlife-policy-kenya Presentation by Leakey to the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., ""New Wildlife Policy for Kenya"", April 18, 1991], [[C-SPAN]]

column1: Richard Leakey's confrontational approach to the issue of human–wildlife conflict in [[national park]]s did not win him friends. His view was that parks were self-contained ecosystems that had to be fenced in and the humans kept out. Leakey's bold and incorruptible nature also offended many local politicians.<ref>{{Cite news
In 2016, Leakey was named Conservationist of the Year by [[The Perfect World Foundation]] and won ""The Fragile Rhino"" prize at the Elephant Ball in [[Gothenburg]], Sweden.<ref>{{cite web
column2: title=Another great legend awarded the world's most prestigious conservation prize

column1: In 1993, a small propeller-driven plane piloted by Richard Leakey crashed, crushing his lower legs, both of which were later amputated.<ref name=""natgeo-obit""/> Sabotage was suspected but never proven.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Richard Leakey Tries to Save the Elephants—Again
column9: access-date=25 May 2020}}</ref> While in the hospital, Leakey told President Moi, a religious man, not to pray for him, but act on matters pending for the Kenya Wildlife Service.<ref name=humanistinterview>Ryan Shaffer, [http://thehumanist.com/july-august-2012/evolution-humanism-and-conservation-the-humanist-interview-with-richard-leakey/ ""Evolution, Humanism, and Conservation: The Humanist Interview with Richard Leakey""], ''The Humanist'', 29 June 2012.</ref> Thereafter, Richard Leakey walked on [[artificial limb]]s.<ref name=""guardian2001""/> Around this time the Kenyan government announced that a secret probe had found evidence of corruption and mismanagement in the Kenya Wildlife Service. An annoyed Leakey resigned publicly in a press conference in January 1994.<ref>{{cite web
column12: title=Noted Kenya Conservationist Resigning in a Political Storm
column16: date=15 January 1994}}</ref> He was replaced by David Western as the head of the Kenya Wildlife Service.<ref>{{cite web

column1: Richard Leakey wrote about his experiences at the Kenya Wildlife Service in his book ''[[Wildlife Wars
column2: Wildlife Wars: My Fight to Save Africa's Natural Treasures]]'' (2001).<ref>{{cite book
column7: title=Wildlife Wars: My Fight to Save Africa's Natural Treasures

column1: In May 1995, Richard Leakey joined some Kenyan intellectuals in launching a new political party—the [[Safina Party]],<ref name=""reuters"">{{cite web
column2: title=Richard Leakey, Kenyan conservationist who campaigned against ivory trade, has died
column7: date=3 January 2022}}</ref> which in Swahili means ""[[Noah's Ark]]"".<ref name=""reuters""/> The Safina party was routinely harassed and even its application to become an official political party was not approved until 1997.<ref>{{cite web
column8: title=Kenya: Current information on Safina Party, especially on arrests of its members in 1995
column10: website=Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada

column1: <templatestyles src=""Module:Infobox/styles.css""></templatestyles><table class=""infobox"" style=""clear: left; float:left;margin:0 1.5em 1.5em 0;""><tr><th colspan=""2"" class=""infobox-above"" style=""font-size:115%"">External videos</th></tr><tr><td colspan=""2"" class=""infobox-full-data"" style=""text-align: left"">[[file:Nuvola apps kaboodle.svg
column4: class=noviewer]] [https://www.c-span.org/video/?67504-1/origins-politics Presentation by Leakey to the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., ""Origins and Politics"", October 6, 1995], [[C-SPAN]]

column1: In 1997, international donor institutions froze their aid to Kenya because of widespread corruption.<ref>{{cite web
column4: title=Time for Zuma to read his obituary - OPINION
column9: date=7 February 2020}}</ref> To placate the donors, Moi appointed Richard Leakey as Cabinet Secretary and head of the civil service in 1999. Leakey's second stint in the civil service lasted two years.<ref>{{cite web
column14: date=10 January 2019}}</ref> He sacked 25,000 civil servants and obtained £250 million of funds from the [[International Monetary Fund]] and the [[World Bank]].<ref>{{cite web
column20: date=3 January 2022}}</ref> However, Leakey found himself sidelined after the money arrived, and his reforms were blocked in the courts. He was sacked from his cabinet post in 2001.<ref name=""guardian2001"">{{cite news

column1: Leakey left Kenya for the U.S. in 2002 and became a professor of anthropology at [[Stony Brook University]], New York.<ref>Stony Brook University, Press release, 27 March 2007: [http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/General_University_News_2/World-Renowned_Anthropologist_Richard_Leakey_to_be_Honored_at_Stony_Brook_University_s_50th_Anniversary_Gala_April_11.shtml ""World-Renowned Anthropologist Richard Leakey to be Honored at Stony Brook University's 50th Anniversary Gala April 11"".] {{webarchive
column3: date=8 June 2010 }}</ref> He was also Chair of the Turkana Basin Institute.<ref>{{cite web
column10: date=8 August 2016}}</ref> In 2004, Leakey founded and chaired [[WildlifeDirect]], a Kenya-based charitable organisation.<ref>{{cite web
column14: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> The charity was established to provide support to conservationists in Africa directly on the ground via the use of blogs. This enables individuals anywhere to play a direct and interactive role in the survival of some of the world's most precious species. The organisation played a significant role in the saving of the [[Democratic Republic of Congo]]'s [[mountain gorillas]] in [[Virunga National Park]] in January 2007 after a rebel uprising threatened to eliminate the highly vulnerable population.<ref name=""natgeo-obit""/>

column1: In April 2007, he was appointed interim chairman of [[Transparency International]]'s Kenya branch.<ref name=""bloomberg""/> The same year, Leakey was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]]<ref>{{cite web
column5: access-date = 8 March 2012}}</ref> and received the [[Academy of Achievement#Notable recipients of the Golden Plate Award
column6: Golden Plate Award]] of the [[Academy of Achievement
column8: title=Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement
column10: url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref> In June 2013, Leakey was awarded the [[Isaac Asimov]] Science Award from the [[American Humanist Association]].<ref>SmashPipe, 5 June 2013: [https://archive.today/20130624234603/http://science.smashpipe.com/?f=XeGlhASFV4M%23stop ''Humanist Awards Banquet of the 2013 American Humanist Conference'']</ref>

column1: Leakey's groundbreaking work contributed to the recognition of Africa as the birthplace of humankind, that contributed as evidence that the earliest humans had lived on the African continent. He was known to have spearheaded campaigns to stop poaching in Kenya.<ref name="":1""/> Aside from his contributions to public service, he was known to have contributed immensely to the civil service; ""Besides his distinguished career in public service, Dr Leakey is celebrated for his prominent role in Kenya's civil society where he founded and successfully ran a number of institutions,"" Mr Kenyatta said.<ref name="":1"">{{Cite news
column3: title=Richard Leakey: Kenyan conservationist dies aged 77
Sketch of Richard Leakey (2014), by Patrick L. Gallegos]]

column1: In 2015, President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] appointed Leakey chairman of the board of the Kenya Wildlife Service. Although he was chairman rather than director, Leakey played an active role in KWS policies.<ref name=""guardian2001""/> He brokered a deal on the extension of the [[Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway]], allowing the railway to pass over [[Nairobi National Park]] on an 18-metre-tall [[viaduct]].<ref>{{cite news
column4: title=Kenya: SGR to Pass Over the Nairobi National Park
column7: date=14 September 2016}}</ref> Leakey felt that the viaduct would set an example for the rest of Africa in balancing economic development with environmental protection. However, other Kenyan conservationists have opposed railway construction in the park.<ref>{{cite news
column10: title=Opposing camps to hold dialogue on railway through Nairobi National Park

column1: [[Angelina Jolie]] was to direct a film about Leakey's life, with Leakey in early 2016 expressing his confidence that the film would be shot in Kenya.<ref>{{cite news
column4: title=Richard Leakey: What does Angelina Jolie see in this man?

column1: Leakey spoke fluent [[Kiswahili]] and moved effortlessly between white and black communities. While he rarely talked about race in public, racism and gender inequality infuriated him.<ref>{{Cite journal
column16: doi-access=free}}</ref> Leakey stated that he was an [[atheist]]<ref>{{cite book
column19: title=One Life: Richard E. Leakey: An Autobiography

column1: Leakey came from a family of renowned archeologists. His mother, Mary Leakey, discovered evidence in 1978 that man walked upright much earlier than had been thought. She and her husband, Louis Leakey, unearthed skulls of ape-like early humans, shedding fresh light on our ancestors.<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=World-renowned Kenyan conservationist Richard Leakey dies at 77

column1: Leakey was diagnosed with a terminal [[kidney]] disease in 1969. Ten years later he became seriously ill but received a [[kidney transplant]] from his brother, Philip, and recovered to full health.<ref>{{cite web
column5: title=Famed fossil hunter and conservationist Richard Leakey dies at 77

column1: He died at his home outside Nairobi, on 2 January 2022,<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Richard Leakey's Legacy in Science, Conservation and Politics
column10: author-link=Virginia Morell}}</ref> less than a month after his 77th birthday.<ref>{{cite web
column12: title=Message of Condolence from H.E Hon. Uhuru Kenyatta following the death of former Head of Public Service Dr Richard Leakey
column22: title=Renowned Kenyan conservationist Richard Leakey dies aged 77
column28: title=Fossil hunter Richard Leakey who showed humans evolved in Africa dies at 77
column33: first=Jane}}</ref> In accordance with his wishes, he was buried on a hill along the Rift Valley.<ref>{{Cite web
column35: title=Richard Leakey Laid To Rest On A Hill Along Rift Valley

column67: issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Leakey held a number of official positions in Kenya, mostly in institutions of [[archaeology]] and [[wildlife conservation]]. He was director of the [[National Museum of Kenya]],<ref name="":0""/> founded the NGO [[WildlifeDirect]], and was the chairman of the [[Kenya Wildlife Service]].<ref>{{Cite book
column72: access-date=28 May 2020}}</ref> Leakey served in the powerful office of cabinet secretary and head of public service during the tail end of President [[Daniel Toroitich Arap Moi]]\'s government.\n\nLeakey co-founded the ""Turkana Basin Institute"" in an academic partnership with [[Stony Brook University]], where he was an anthropology professor. He served as the chair of the Turkana Basin Institute until his death.<ref>{{Cite web
column74: title=Richard Leakey, trailblazing conservationist and fossil hunter, dies at 77
column87: title=Richard Leakey, Kenyan Fossil Hunter and Conservationist, Dies at 77
column93:
name-list-style=and}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===Earliest years===', content='
Richard Erskine Frere Leakey was born on 19 December 1944 in [[Nairobi]].<ref name="":2""/> As a small boy, Leakey lived in Nairobi with his parents: [[Louis Leakey]], curator of the Coryndon Museum, and [[Mary Leakey]], director of the Leakey excavations at [[Olduvai Gorge
column94: Olduvai]], and his two brothers, Jonathan and [[Philip Leakey
column96: title=Richard E. Leakey Biography and Interview
column98: url=https://achievement.org/achiever/richard-leakey/}}</ref> The Leakey brothers had a very active childhood. All the boys had ponies and belonged to the Langata Pony Club.<ref>{{cite web
column101: title=Kenyan Paleoanthropologist Richard Leakey Passed Away at 77 Family
column108: url-status=dead }}</ref> Sometimes the whole club were guests at the Leakeys\' for holidays and vacations. Leakey\'s parents founded the Dalmatian Club of East Africa and won a prize in 1957.{{cn
column109: date=February 2026}} Dogs and many other pets shared the Leakey home.{{cn
column110: date=February 2026}} The Leakey boys participated in games conducted by both adults and children, in which they tried to imitate early humans, catching [[springhare]] and small antelope by hand on the [[Serengeti]]. They drove lions and [[jackal]]s from the kill to see if they could do it.<ref name=""ancestralpassions18"">{{cite book
column116:
chapter=18: Richard Makes his Move}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===Fractured skull===', content='
In 1956, aged eleven, Leakey fell from his horse, fracturing his skull and nearly dying as a result.<ref name=""natgeo-obit"">{{cite web
column119: title=Richard Leakey, trailblazing conservationist and fossil hunter, dies at 77
column127: date=2 January 2022}}</ref> Incidentally, it was this incident that saved his parents\' marriage.<ref name=""natgeo-obit""/> Louis was seriously considering leaving Mary for his secretary, Rosalie Osborn. As the battle with Mary raged in the household, Leakey begged his father from his sickbed not to leave. That was the deciding factor. Louis broke up with Rosalie and the family lived in happy harmony for a few years more.<ref name=""morell"">Morell, Virginia (1995). Chapter 17, ""Chimpanzees and Other Loves"", in \'\'Ancestral Passions: The Leakey Family and the Quest for Humankind\'s Beginnings\'\'. {{ISBN
column128:
978-0684824703}}.</ref>

'), Section(title='===Teenage entrepreneur===', content='
Leakey chose to support himself, borrowed £500 from his parents for a [[Land Rover]] and went into the trapping and skeleton supply business with [[Kamoya Kimeu]].<ref name=""finders"">{{cite web
column133: date=13 April 2018}}</ref> Already a skilled horseman, outdoorsman, Land Rover mechanic, amateur archaeologist, and expedition leader,<ref name=""wapo"">{{cite news
column136: title=Drive, Luck and the Leakey Genes
column140: date=3 October 1978}}</ref> he learned to identify bones, skills which all pointed to a path he did not yet wish to take, simply because his father was on it.<ref>Richard E. Leakey in \'\'The Making of Mankind\'\' (1981), chapter 1, p. 1, says he wished to be ""free"" of his parents\' world, a sentiment both Louis and Mary must have understood very well, even though they opposed his freedom.</ref>\n\nThe bone business turned into a safari business in 1961.<ref>{{cite web
column145: date=9 October 2001}}</ref> In 1962, he obtained a private pilot licence and took tours to the [[Olduvai Gorge]].<ref>{{cite journal
column148: title=The Old Man of Olduvai Gorge
column158: author-link=Roger Lewin}}</ref> It was from a casual aerial survey that he noted the potential of [[Lake Natron]]\'s shores for palaeontology. He went looking for fossils in a Land Rover, but could find none, until his parents assigned [[Glynn Isaac]] to go with him.<ref>{{cite web
column163: website=Center for the Advanced Study of Human Paleobiology
column166: date=5 October 2015}}</ref> Louis was so impressed with their finds that he gave them [[National Geographic Society
column167:
National Geographic]] money for a month's expedition.<ref>Morell, 1995, Chapter 18, ""Richard Makes his Move."" Besides Leakey and Glynn, the roster included Barbara Isaac, [[Philip Leakey]], [[Hugo van Lawick]] and six of Mary's African assistants.</ref> They explored in the vicinity of Peninj near the lake, where Leakey was in charge of the administrative details. Bored, he returned to Nairobi temporarily, but at that moment, Kamoya Kimeu discovered a fossil of ''[[Australopithecus boisei]]''.<ref name=""finders""/> A second expedition left Leakey feeling that he was being excluded from the most significant part of the operation, the scientific analysis.<ref name=""finders""/>

'), Section(title='===Marriage===', content='
In 1964, on his second Lake Natron expedition, Leakey met an archaeologist named Margaret Cropper.<ref>{{cite web
column171: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> When Margaret returned to England, Leakey decided to follow suit to study for a degree and become better acquainted with her. He completed his high school requirements in six months; meanwhile Margaret obtained her degree at the [[University of Edinburgh]].<ref name="":0""/> He passed the entrance exams for admission to college, but in 1965 he and Margaret decided to marry and return to Kenya. His father offered him a job at the Centre for Prehistory and Palaeontology.<ref>{{cite web
column177: language=en-gb}}</ref> He worked excavating at [[Lake Baringo]] and continued his photographic safari business, making enough money to buy a house in [[Karen, Kenya
column178: Karen]], a pleasant suburb of Nairobi.<ref>{{cite web
column181: title=A taste of paradise in the Kenyan wilderness
column185: date=8 June 1984}}</ref> Their daughter Anna was born in 1969, the same year that Leakey and Margaret divorced. He married his colleague [[Meave Leakey
column186: Meave Epps]] in 1970 and they had two daughters, [[Louise Leakey
column187:
Louise]] (born 1972) and Samira (1974).<ref name="":2""/>

'), Section(title='== Palaeontology ==', content='
Richard formed the Kenya Museum Associates (now Kenya Museum Society) with influential Kenyans in 1955.<ref name=""kenyamuseum"">{{cite web
column191: access-date=4 January 2022}}</ref> They aimed to ""Kenyanise"" and improve the [[National Museums of Kenya
column192: National Museum]].<ref name=""kenyamuseum""/> They offered the museum £5000, one-third of its yearly budget, if it would place Leakey in a responsible position, and he became an observer on the board of directors.<ref>{{cite web
column195: title=A Protective Legislation, Policy and Practice of Archaeological Heritage Management in Kenya
column200: date=27 November 2013}}</ref> Joel Ojal, the government official in charge of the museum, and a member of the Associates, directed the chairman of the board to start placing Kenyans on it.<ref>{{cite book
column203: title=Ancestral Passions: The Leakey Family and the Quest for Humankind\'s Beginnings
column209:
isbn=9781439143872 }}</ref>

'), Section(title='===The Omo===', content='
Plans for the museum had not matured when Louis, intentionally or not, found a way to remove his confrontational son from the scene. Louis attended a lunch with [[Emperor of Ethiopia
column214: title=Skulls crown Ethiopia\'s place in evolutionary studies
column218: date=22 February 2005}}</ref> The conversation turned to fossils, and the Emperor wanted to know why none had been found in [[Ethiopia]]. Louis developed this inquiry into permission to excavate on the [[Omo River (Ethiopia)
column219: Omo River]].<ref name=""slt""/>\n\nThe expedition consisted of three contingents: French, under [[Camille Arambourg]], American, under [[F. Clark Howell]], and Kenyan, led by Richard.<ref>{{cite journal
column222: title=Camille Arambourg et Louis Leakey ou un 1/2 siècle de paléontologie africaine
column224: journal=Bulletin de la Société préhistorique française
column233: url-access=subscription }}</ref> Louis could not go because of his arthritis. Crossing the Omo in 1967, Leakey\'s contingent was attacked by [[crocodiles]], which destroyed their wooden boat.<ref name=""wapo""/> Expedition members barely escaped with their lives. Richard radioed Louis for a new, aluminium boat, which the [[National Geographic Society]] was happy to supply.<ref name=""wapo""/>\n\nOn site, Kamoya Kimeu found a hominid fossil. Leakey took it to be \'\'[[Homo erectus]]\'\', but Louis identified it as \'\'Homo sapiens\'\'.<ref>{{cite web
column237:
access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> It was the oldest of the species found at that time, dating to 160,000 years, and was the first find contemporaneous with ''[[Homo neanderthalensis]]''. During the identification process, Leakey came to feel that the college men were patronising him.<ref>This section is based on Morell, 1995, Chapter 20, ""To the Omo"".</ref>

'), Section(title='===Koobi Fora===', content='
During the Omo expedition of 1967, Leakey visited Nairobi and on the return flight the pilot flew over [[Lake Rudolph]] (renamed Lake Turkana from 1975) to avoid a thunderstorm.<ref name=""stonybrook"">{{cite web
column245: date=Spring 2016}}</ref> The map led Leakey to expect volcanic rock below him but he saw sediments. Visiting the region with Howell by helicopter, he saw tools and fossils everywhere. In his mind, he started formulating a new enterprise.<ref name=""stonybrook""/>\n\nIn 1968 Louis and Richard attended a meeting of the Research and Exploration Committee of the National Geographic Society to ask for money for Omo.<ref name=""alive"">{{cite web
column255: url-status=dead }}</ref> Catching Louis by surprise, Richard asked the committee to divert the $25,000 intended for Omo to new excavations to be conducted under his leadership at Koobi Fora. Richard won, but chairman [[Leonard Carmichael]] told him he had better find something or never ""come begging at our door again"".<ref name=""alive""/> Louis graciously congratulated Richard.<ref name=""alive""/>\n\nBy that time the board of the [[National Museums of Kenya
column256: National Museum]] was packed with Kenyan supporters of Richard. They appointed him administrative director.<ref>{{cite web
column259: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> The curator, Robert Carcasson, resigned in protest,<ref name=""alive""/> and Leakey was left with the museum at his command, which he, like Louis before him, used as a base of operations.<ref>Morell, 1995, Chapter 21, ""Breaking Away.""</ref> Although there was friendly rivalry and contention between Louis and Richard, relations remained good. Each took over for the other when one was busy with something else or incapacitated, and Richard continued to inform his father immediately of hominid finds.<ref name=""alive""/>\n\nIn the first expedition to Allia Bay on Lake Turkana, where the Koobi Fora camp came to be located, Leakey hired primarily young researchers. The students included John Harris and Bernard Wood.<ref>{{cite journal
column268: title=Early Homo erectus skeleton from west Lake Turkana, Kenya
column281: url-access=subscription }}</ref> Also present was a team of Africans under Kamoya: a geochemist, Paul Abel, and a photographer, [[Bob Campbell (photographer)
column283: title=Paul Abel and Richard Leakey Walking the Shores of Lake Turkana
column291: date=3 February 2018}}</ref> Margaret was the archaeologist. In contrast to his father, Richard ran a disciplined and tidy camp, although, in order to find fossils, he did push the expedition harder than it wished.<ref name=""aoa"">{{cite web
column292: title=Richard Leakey, Academy Class of 2007, Part 2
column295: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref>\n\nIn 1969 the discovery of a cranium of \'\'[[Paranthropus boisei]]\'\' caused great excitement.<ref>{{cite web
column300: language=en}}</ref> A \'\'[[Homo rudolfensis]]\'\' skull ([[KNM ER 1470]]) and a \'\'[[Homo erectus]]\'\' skull ([[KNM ER 3733]]), discovered in 1972 and 1975, respectively, were among the most significant finds of Leakey\'s earlier expeditions.<ref>{{cite web
column303: website=The Smithsonian Institution\'s Human Origins Program
column305: language=en}}</ref> In 1978 an intact cranium of \'\'Homo erectus\'\' ([[KNM ER 3883]]) was discovered.<ref name=""aoa""/>\n\n[[Donald Johanson]] and Leakey held different views about human evolution. They held a debate on \'\'Cronkite\'s Universe\'\', a talk show hosted by [[Walter Cronkite]], in 1981.<ref>{{Cite book
column308: title=Bones of Contention: Controversies in the Search for Human Origins
column315:
author-link=Roger Lewin}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===West Turkana===', content='
[[File:Turkana boy - steps of forensic facial reconstruction.jpg
column317: Turkana Boy – steps of forensic facial reconstruction/approximation]]\n[[Turkana Boy]], discovered by [[Kamoya Kimeu]], a member of the Leakeys\' team, in 1984, was the nearly complete skeleton of a \'\'[[Homo ergaster]]\'\' (though some, including Leakey, call it \'\'erectus\'\') who died 1.6 million years ago at about age 9–12.<ref name=""bloomberg"">{{cite web
column318: title=Richard Leakey, Who Found \'Turkana Boy\' Fossil, Dies at 77
column324: first=Eric}}</ref> Leakey and [[Roger Lewin]] describe the experience of this find and their interpretation of it, in their book \'\'Origins Reconsidered\'\' (1992).<ref>{{cite web
column329: title=Origins Reconsidered: In Search of What Makes Us Human
column334: author-link2=Roger Lewin}}</ref> Shortly after the discovery of Turkana Boy, Leakey and his team made the discovery of a skull ([[KNM WT 17000]], known as ""Black Skull"") of a new species, \'\'[[Australopithecus aethiopicus]]\'\' (or \'\'Paranthropus aethiopicus\'\').<ref>{{cite web
column337: title=Skull Piece Takes Man a Step Back
column342: date=14 November 1986}}</ref>\n\nRichard shifted away from palaeontology in 1989, but his wife [[Meave Leakey]] and daughter [[Louise Leakey]] continue to conduct palaeontological research in Northern Kenya.<ref>{{cite web
column356:
date=4 April 2012}}</ref>

'), Section(title='== Conservation ==', content='
[[File:Richard Leakey cropped.jpg
column359: Leakey in 2010]]\nIn 1989 Richard Leakey was appointed the head of the Wildlife Conservation and Management Department (WMCD) by President [[Daniel Arap Moi]] in response to the international outcry over the [[poaching of elephants]] and the impact it was having on the wildlife of Kenya.<ref>{{Cite web
column362: title=\'Kenya\'s wildlife – Predictions for the next decade\' with Dr Richard Leakey
column364: access-date=5 November 2016}}</ref> The department was replaced by the [[Kenya Wildlife Service]] (KWS) in 1990, and Leakey became its first chairman.<ref>{{cite web
column371: url-status=dead }}</ref> With characteristically bold steps Leakey created special, well-armed anti-poaching units that were authorised to shoot poachers on sight.<ref>{{Cite book
column382: isbn=9781743213063}}</ref> The poaching menace was dramatically reduced. Impressed by Leakey\'s transformation of the Kenya Wildlife Service, the [[World Bank]] approved grants worth $140 million.<ref>{{cite web
column383: title=Dr Richard Leakey: A swashbuckler with intent
column387: language=en}}</ref> Richard Leakey, President Moi, and the WMCD made the international news headlines when a stockpile of 12 tons of [[ivory]] was [[destruction of ivory
column388: burned in 1989]] in [[Nairobi National Park]].<ref>{{cite web
column391: title=Kenya, In Gesture, Burns Ivory Tusks
column398: video1 = [https://www.c-span.org/video/?17614-1/wildlife-policy-kenya Presentation by Leakey to the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., ""New Wildlife Policy for Kenya"", April 18, 1991], [[C-SPAN]]}} \nRichard Leakey\'s confrontational approach to the issue of human–wildlife conflict in [[national park]]s did not win him friends. His view was that parks were self-contained ecosystems that had to be fenced in and the humans kept out. Leakey\'s bold and incorruptible nature also offended many local politicians.<ref>{{Cite news
column408: author-link=Jane Perlez}}</ref>\n\nIn 2016, Leakey was named Conservationist of the Year by [[The Perfect World Foundation]] and won ""The Fragile Rhino"" prize at the Elephant Ball in [[Gothenburg]], Sweden.<ref>{{cite web
column409: title=Another great legend awarded the world\'s most prestigious conservation prize
column418:
access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===Plane crash===', content='
In 1993, a small propeller-driven plane piloted by Richard Leakey crashed, crushing his lower legs, both of which were later amputated.<ref name=""natgeo-obit""/> Sabotage was suspected but never proven.<ref>{{Cite web
column419: title=Richard Leakey Tries to Save the Elephants—Again
column426: access-date=25 May 2020}}</ref> While in the hospital, Leakey told President Moi, a religious man, not to pray for him, but act on matters pending for the Kenya Wildlife Service.<ref name=humanistinterview>Ryan Shaffer, [http://thehumanist.com/july-august-2012/evolution-humanism-and-conservation-the-humanist-interview-with-richard-leakey/ ""Evolution, Humanism, and Conservation: The Humanist Interview with Richard Leakey""], \'\'The Humanist\'\', 29 June 2012.</ref> Thereafter, Richard Leakey walked on [[artificial limb]]s.<ref name=""guardian2001""/> Around this time the Kenyan government announced that a secret probe had found evidence of corruption and mismanagement in the Kenya Wildlife Service. An annoyed Leakey resigned publicly in a press conference in January 1994.<ref>{{cite web
column429: title=Noted Kenya Conservationist Resigning in a Political Storm
column433: date=15 January 1994}}</ref> He was replaced by David Western as the head of the Kenya Wildlife Service.<ref>{{cite web
column439: date=1 January 1998}}</ref>\n\nRichard Leakey wrote about his experiences at the Kenya Wildlife Service in his book \'\'[[Wildlife Wars
column440: Wildlife Wars: My Fight to Save Africa\'s Natural Treasures]]\'\' (2001).<ref>{{cite book
column445: title=Wildlife Wars: My Fight to Save Africa\'s Natural Treasures
column452:
author-link2=Virginia Morell}}</ref>

'), Section(title='== Politics ==', content='
[[File:Richard Leakey 2015 (cropped).jpg
column455: Leakey in 2015]]\nIn May 1995, Richard Leakey joined some Kenyan intellectuals in launching a new political party—the [[Safina Party]],<ref name=""reuters"">{{cite web
column456: title=Richard Leakey, Kenyan conservationist who campaigned against ivory trade, has died
column461: date=3 January 2022}}</ref> which in Swahili means ""[[Noah\'s Ark]]"".<ref name=""reuters""/> The Safina party was routinely harassed and even its application to become an official political party was not approved until 1997.<ref>{{cite web
column462: title=Kenya: Current information on Safina Party, especially on arrests of its members in 1995
column464: website=Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada
column469: video1 = [https://www.c-span.org/video/?67504-1/origins-politics Presentation by Leakey to the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., ""Origins and Politics"", October 6, 1995], [[C-SPAN]]}} \nIn 1997, international donor institutions froze their aid to Kenya because of widespread corruption.<ref>{{cite web
column472: title=Time for Zuma to read his obituary - OPINION
column477: date=7 February 2020}}</ref> To placate the donors, Moi appointed Richard Leakey as Cabinet Secretary and head of the civil service in 1999. Leakey\'s second stint in the civil service lasted two years.<ref>{{cite web
column482: date=10 January 2019}}</ref> He sacked 25,000 civil servants and obtained £250 million of funds from the [[International Monetary Fund]] and the [[World Bank]].<ref>{{cite web
column488: date=3 January 2022}}</ref> However, Leakey found himself sidelined after the money arrived, and his reforms were blocked in the courts. He was sacked from his cabinet post in 2001.<ref name=""guardian2001"">{{cite news
column495:
language=en}}</ref>

'), Section(title='== United States ==', content='
Leakey left Kenya for the U.S. in 2002 and became a professor of anthropology at [[Stony Brook University]], New York.<ref>Stony Brook University, Press release, 27 March 2007: [http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/General_University_News_2/World-Renowned_Anthropologist_Richard_Leakey_to_be_Honored_at_Stony_Brook_University_s_50th_Anniversary_Gala_April_11.shtml ""World-Renowned Anthropologist Richard Leakey to be Honored at Stony Brook University's 50th Anniversary Gala April 11"".] {{webarchive
column497: date=8 June 2010 }}</ref> He was also Chair of the Turkana Basin Institute.<ref>{{cite web
column504: date=8 August 2016}}</ref> In 2004, Leakey founded and chaired [[WildlifeDirect]], a Kenya-based charitable organisation.<ref>{{cite web
column508: access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref> The charity was established to provide support to conservationists in Africa directly on the ground via the use of blogs. This enables individuals anywhere to play a direct and interactive role in the survival of some of the world\'s most precious species. The organisation played a significant role in the saving of the [[Democratic Republic of Congo]]\'s [[mountain gorillas]] in [[Virunga National Park]] in January 2007 after a rebel uprising threatened to eliminate the highly vulnerable population.<ref name=""natgeo-obit""/>\n\nIn April 2007, he was appointed interim chairman of [[Transparency International]]\'s Kenya branch.<ref name=""bloomberg""/> The same year, Leakey was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]]<ref>{{cite web
column512: access-date = 8 March 2012}}</ref> and received the [[Academy of Achievement#Notable recipients of the Golden Plate Award
column513: Golden Plate Award]] of the [[Academy of Achievement
column515: title=Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement
column517:
url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref> In June 2013, Leakey was awarded the [[Isaac Asimov]] Science Award from the [[American Humanist Association]].<ref>SmashPipe, 5 June 2013: [https://archive.today/20130624234603/http://science.smashpipe.com/?f=XeGlhASFV4M%23stop ''Humanist Awards Banquet of the 2013 American Humanist Conference'']</ref>

'), Section(title='==Contribution==', content='
Leakey's groundbreaking work contributed to the recognition of Africa as the birthplace of humankind, that contributed as evidence that the earliest humans had lived on the African continent. He was known to have spearheaded campaigns to stop poaching in Kenya.<ref name="":1""/> Aside from his contributions to public service, he was known to have contributed immensely to the civil service; ""Besides his distinguished career in public service, Dr Leakey is celebrated for his prominent role in Kenya's civil society where he founded and successfully ran a number of institutions,"" Mr Kenyatta said.<ref name="":1"">{{Cite news
column519: title=Richard Leakey: Kenyan conservationist dies aged 77
column523:
access-date=2023-04-29}}</ref>

'), Section(title='== Return to Kenya ==', content='
[[File:RichardLeakeyELA.jpg
column525: Sketch of Richard Leakey (2014), by Patrick L. Gallegos]]\nIn 2015, President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] appointed Leakey chairman of the board of the Kenya Wildlife Service. Although he was chairman rather than director, Leakey played an active role in KWS policies.<ref name=""guardian2001""/> He brokered a deal on the extension of the [[Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway]], allowing the railway to pass over [[Nairobi National Park]] on an 18-metre-tall [[viaduct]].<ref>{{cite news
column528: title=Kenya: SGR to Pass Over the Nairobi National Park
column531: date=14 September 2016}}</ref> Leakey felt that the viaduct would set an example for the rest of Africa in balancing economic development with environmental protection. However, other Kenyan conservationists have opposed railway construction in the park.<ref>{{cite news
column534: title=Opposing camps to hold dialogue on railway through Nairobi National Park
column538: language=en}}</ref>\n\n[[Angelina Jolie]] was to direct a film about Leakey\'s life, with Leakey in early 2016 expressing his confidence that the film would be shot in Kenya.<ref>{{cite news
column541: title=Richard Leakey: What does Angelina Jolie see in this man?
column544:
date=23 September 2014}}</ref>

'), Section(title='==Personal life and death==', content='
Leakey spoke fluent [[Kiswahili]] and moved effortlessly between white and black communities. While he rarely talked about race in public, racism and gender inequality infuriated him.<ref>{{Cite journal
column559: doi-access=free}}</ref> Leakey stated that he was an [[atheist]]<ref>{{cite book
column562: title=One Life: Richard E. Leakey: An Autobiography
column566: page=38}}</ref> and a [[humanist]].<ref name=""humanistinterview""/> \n\nLeakey came from a family of renowned archeologists. His mother, Mary Leakey, discovered evidence in 1978 that man walked upright much earlier than had been thought. She and her husband, Louis Leakey, unearthed skulls of ape-like early humans, shedding fresh light on our ancestors.<ref>{{Cite web
column570: title=World-renowned Kenyan conservationist Richard Leakey dies at 77
column574: language=en}}</ref>\n\nLeakey was diagnosed with a terminal [[kidney]] disease in 1969. Ten years later he became seriously ill but received a [[kidney transplant]] from his brother, Philip, and recovered to full health.<ref>{{cite web
column578: title=Famed fossil hunter and conservationist Richard Leakey dies at 77
column582: language=en}}</ref>\n\nHe died at his home outside Nairobi, on 2 January 2022,<ref>{{Cite web
column583: title=Richard Leakey\'s Legacy in Science, Conservation and Politics
column591: author-link=Virginia Morell}}</ref> less than a month after his 77th birthday.<ref>{{cite web
column593: title=Message of Condolence from H.E Hon. Uhuru Kenyatta following the death of former Head of Public Service Dr Richard Leakey
column603: title=Renowned Kenyan conservationist Richard Leakey dies aged 77
column609: title=Fossil hunter Richard Leakey who showed humans evolved in Africa dies at 77
column614: first=Jane}}</ref> In accordance with his wishes, he was buried on a hill along the Rift Valley.<ref>{{Cite web

column1: Duale received his Certificate of Primary Education from Garissa Primary School in 1981. He then enrolled in Garissa High School where he received his [[Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education]] in 1985, and later joined [[Moi Forces Academy, Nairobi]] for his Kenya Advanced Certificate of Secondary Education, which he completed in 1987. He enrolled in [[Moi University]] for his undergraduate studies in education before transferring to [[Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology]] for his master's degree in business administration (MBA).<ref>{{Cite web

In 1992, Duale began his teaching career as a graduate teacher at Sankuri Secondary School. He did, however, leave after two months and thereafter worked for six months as a clerical officer at the office of the provincial commissioner in Garissa.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Aden Duale Profile: Education Background, Family & Career
