Bondo]], [[Kenya Colony]] – 27 April 2010) was a Kenyan politician. He was a [[cabinet minister
column3: minister]] for Agriculture, Minister for Environment and Natural Resources<ref name=""KenyaGazette4"">{{cite magazine
column4: title=The Constitution of Kenya: Appointment of a Minister
column9: accessdate=11 April 2014}}</ref> and a [[National Assembly of Kenya
column10: member of parliament]] for the [[Bondo Constituency]] and [[Muhoroni Constituency]].<ref name="":0"">{{Cite web
column14: title=Ex Kenyan MP Odongo Omamo is dead » Capital News
column18: language=en-US}}</ref> Omamo had two wives, Joyce Acholla and Anne Audia, and 16 children. One of the most prominent is [[Raychelle Omamo]], a former [[Law Society of Kenya]] chairperson and former ambassador to France who was selected as Cabinet Secretary of Defence in April 2013.<ref name="":1"">{{Cite web
column19: title=William Odongo Omamo – Man with elephantine humour {{!}} Kenya Yearbook

column1: Omamo was also a large-scale farmer in Bondo and Muhoroni. He farmed many different crops, but was most noted for operating the largest privately owned sugar plantation in Kenya. After Kenya gained independence he became the first African principal of [[Egerton University
column2: Egerton College]], which has since become a university.

column1: Omamo was born on 27 March 1928, in [[Bondo, Kenya
column2: Bondo]] (then ruled as part of the [[British Empire
column3: British]] [[Kenya Colony]]) in a family of eight children, two boys and six girls. His father married eight other women and had scores of children. He went to Maranda Sector School, five kilometres from his home, in 1936. He once described his first day in school as follows: ""I was half naked, with only a [[Goatskin (material)
column4: goat skin]] strip to cover the private parts and buttocks.""<ref name="":1"" />

column1: By the time Omamo finished secondary school at Maseno College, he had developed a passion for agriculture. He then received a scholarship to study in India in 1951. He graduated from the [[University of Agriculture, Faisalabad
column2: Punjab Agricultural College]] in 1955 with a Bachelor of Science in Agriculture.<ref name="":1"" /> He also earned a Doctorate, and studied at [[Oregon State University]].{{Clarify
column3: reason=Did he attain his doctorate at Oregon?

column1: Omamo's career in politics began in 1969 and he successfully vied for the Bondo seat. It was previously [[Jaramogi Oginga Odinga]]’s, but after falling out with the administration in place he was detained just before the elections. Omamo's political career spanned almost four decades and saw him represent the Bondo and Muhoroni constituencies in Kenya. Starting on 10 August 1982, he was Minister for Environment and Natural Resources. Omamo also served as Minister for; Agriculture and Livestock development and Science and Technology.<ref name="":2"">{{Cite news
column5: access-date = 9 February 2016}}</ref> Omamo and Odinga partook in a political rivalry that would last for years. column1: '''Kenneth Makelo Lusaka''' (born 18 September 1963) is the current governor of Bungoma County. Previously, he served as the speaker of Senate [2017 -2022] and was the 1st Governor of Bungoma County in Kenya, a term he served between 4 March 2013 to 8 August 2017 where he was defeated by Wycliffe Wafula Wangamati in the 2017 General Elections. Ken Lusaka Was born on (18 September 1963) in Bungoma County. He attended Kamukuywa Primary School, then Kibabii High School<ref>{{Cite web
column5: access-date=2020-05-12}}</ref> for his 'O' Levels and later Chesamisi High School and [[Friends School Kamusinga]] for his 'A' levels. column1: In 2013, Ken Lusaka ran successfully for the position of Bungoma governor, alongside Alfred Khangati, Maurice Makhanu, Jack Tumwa and Wabwoba Walinywa.<ref>{{cite web

column1: In September 2015, the county government of Bungoma was audited and it was discovered that the county had spent Kshs 1,093,200 (approximately $10,881) on 10 wheelbarrows for the Bungoma slaughterhouse, suggesting that the wheelbarrows cost Kshs 109,320 ($1,088) each. In response to the outrage sparked by Kenyans over what appeared to be massive waste of taxpayer money by the government, Governor Lusaka said that, ""The information that I am getting from the veterinary department is that these are not the ordinary wheelbarrows that we know. These are wheelbarrows that are made of stainless, non-carcinogenic material and are used in the food industry."" However, he later said that he had begun investigations and ordered the tender and evaluation committees to justify the purchases.<ref>{{cite web

column5: CGH}} (born 21 December 1966) is a Kenyan politician who is the fifth and current [[president of Kenya]] since 13 September 2022. Prior to becoming president, he served as the first elected [[Deputy President of Kenya
column6: deputy president of Kenya]] from 2013 to 2022.<ref>{{Cite web
column8: title=Kenya's deputy president Ruto declared election winner
column17: title=The Office Of The Deputy President, Kenya
column39: work=iebc.or.ke}}</ref> He previously served in three [[Cabinet of Kenya
column41: portfolios]] as the [[Minister for Home Affairs]], the [[Ministry of Agriculture (Kenya)
column42: Minister of Agriculture]] and as [[Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (Kenya)

column2: Member of Parliament]] for [[Eldoret North Constituency
column3: Eldoret North]] constituency from 1997 to 2007 under the [[Kenya African National Union
column4: KANU]], and from 2007 to 2013 through the [[Orange Democratic Movement
column5: ODM]] party. He was the [[Minister for Home Affairs]] in the [[Daniel arap Moi]] administration from August to December 2002.

column1: Under the [[Mwai Kibaki]] administration, he was the [[Ministry of Agriculture (Kenya)
column2: Minister for Agriculture]] from 2008 to 2010 and [[Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (Kenya)
column3: Minister for Higher Education]] from April to October 2010. Ruto first contested for the presidency during the [[2007 Kenyan general election
column4: 2007 election]], but lost to [[Raila Odinga]] on the [[Orange Democratic Movement
column5: ODM]] party primaries; together with [[Musalia Mudavadi]], who finished second, he then supported the candidature of Odinga. He again ran for the presidency on the [[2013 Kenyan general election
column6: 2013 election]], but withdrew his candidature in favour of [[Uhuru Kenyatta]].

column1: He was later nominated to run for the deputy presidency in the [[2013 Kenyan general election
column3: United Republican Party]], becoming the [[running mate]] of [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] from [[The National Alliance]] (TNA). He was re-elected to the deputy presidency under the [[Jubilee Party]] in the [[2017 Kenyan general election]]. Following a political fallout, [[Uhuru Kenyatta
column4: Kenyatta]] endorsed [[Raila Odinga]] as his preferred successor.

column1: Ruto, now running under the [[United Democratic Alliance (Kenya)
column2: United Democratic Alliance]] (UDA), defeated Odinga for the [[President of Kenya
column3: presidency]] in the [[2022 Kenyan general election
column4: 2022 election]]. While the election was largely described as fair by the [[African Union]] and other international missions, it was contested by Odinga's allies, who alleged electoral fraud. However, the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]] upheld the results, ruling that the allegations lacked sufficient evidence to invalidate the outcome.<ref>{{Cite news
column5: title=Kenya Supreme Court upholds Ruto's presidential victory
column14: title=Four IEBC Commissioners distance themselves from final stage of presidential poll tallying

column2: geopolitical]] profile, positioning the country as a strategic partner for Western powers while championing pan-African interests. Under his leadership, Kenya became the first [[sub-Saharan Africa]]n nation to be designated as a [[Major non-NATO ally
column3: Major Non-NATO Ally]] by the [[United States]].<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=US names Kenya as major ally in face of growing Russian influence
column11: title=Designation of Kenya as a Major Non-NATO Ally
column15: language=en}}</ref> He is also an advocate for climate justice and global financial reform, chairing the inaugural Africa [[Climate Summit]] in 2023, which resulted in the Nairobi Declaration, a call for a global carbon tax and a more equitable international debt system.<ref>{{Cite web
column23: title=African Climate Summit issues unanimous call for world leaders to support global carbon tax on fossil fuels
column28: title=Nairobi Declaration makes strong push for accelerated climate action and financing mechanisms

column1: Regionally, Ruto has played a key role as a mediator in [[East Africa]]n conflicts, through the Nairobi Process<ref>{{Cite web
column5: website=www.eac.int}}</ref> aimed at ending the insurgency in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and his involvement in the Sudan peace talks. Domestically, his administration has built the [[Talanta Sports City]] stadium project and spearheaded the [[National Tree Growing Day
column6: National Tree Growing]] Restoration campaign, which aims to plant 15 billion trees by 2032 to combat climate change and restore Kenya's [[forest cover]].<ref>{{Cite web
column8: title=Kenya Invites CAF Inspection After Criticism Over Infrastructure Readiness for AFCON 2027 - Kenyans.co.ke
column12: language=en}}</ref> In June 2024, Ruto's proposed [[Kenya Finance Bill 2024
column13: finance bill]] was the subject of [[Kenya Finance Bill protests
column14: protests]] in which at least 22 people were killed, causing Ruto to back down and withdraw the bill.

column1: A member of the [[Kalenjin people]] from the [[Rift Valley Province
column8: language=en}}</ref> William Ruto is of mixed [[Kipsigis people
column10: Nandi]] heritage. His father, Daniel Cheruiyot, hailed from the ''Kapkomoseek'' clan of the Kipsigis in [[Kericho County
column11: Kericho]], while his mother, Sarah Cheruiyot, (familiarly known as '''Mama Sarah''{{'}}) of Nandi descent.<ref>{{cite web
column20: title=The President of the Republic of Kenya and Commander-in-Chief of the Defence Forces
column31: title=William Ruto's rise from chicken seller to Kenya's president-elect

column1: Ruto started his education at Kamagut Primary School, then transferred to Kerotet Primary School—both situated within the Uasin Gishu County; and he sat for his [[8-4-4 Curriculum in Kenya
column2: Certificate of Primary Education]] at the latter. He then proceeded to Wareng Secondary School, still in [[Uasin Gishu County]], and later [[Kapsabet High School]] in [[Nandi County]], where he obtained his [[Ordinary Level]] and [[Advanced Level]] education respectively.<ref>{{Cite web

column1: He then enrolled at the [[University of Nairobi]] to pursue [[Botany]] and [[Zoology]], graduating in 1990 with a [[Bachelor of Science
column5: title=For first time in Kenya, two PhD holders are at helm of military command
column9: language=en}}</ref> He went on to complete an [[Master of Science
column10: MSc]] in Plant Ecology, also from the [[University of Nairobi]].<ref>{{Cite web
column12: title=Biological and physico-chemical status of two wetlands in the Nairobi National Park, Kenya
column19: language=en}}</ref> The year after his graduation, he enrolled for a [[Doctor of Philosophy
column20: Ph.D.]] at the same university, and after several setbacks,<ref>{{Cite web
column22: title=I failed Ph.D. exam, admits DP William Ruto
column28: website=Business Today}}</ref> he completed and graduated on 21 December 2018.

column1: Ruto authored several papers, including one titled ''Plant Species Diversity and Composition of Two Wetlands in the Nairobi National Park, Kenya''.<ref>{{Cite journal
column5: title=Plant Species Diversity and Composition of Two Wetlands in the Nairobi National Park, Kenya

column1: During his time in the campus for his [[undergraduate education]], Ruto was an active member of the Christian Union. He also served as the Chairman of the University of Nairobi's choir.<ref name=""k24profile"">{{cite web
column5: title=A brief profile of DP William Ruto: PHOTOS
column11: website=K24}}</ref> Through his church activities at the University of Nairobi, he met President [[Daniel arap Moi]], who would later introduce him to politics during the [[1992 Kenyan general election
column16: title=How shy Ruto rose from a CU leader to money, power

column1: After graduating from the University of Nairobi in 1990, Ruto was employed as a temporary teacher in the North Rift region of Kenya from 1990 to 1992, where he was also a leader of the local church choir, the Africa Inland Church (AIC).<ref name=""auto2""/>
Ruto began his political career when he became the treasurer of the [[Youth for Kanu '92
column2: YK'92]] campaign group that was lobbying for the re-election of President Moi in 1992, from which he learned the basics of Kenyan politics.<ref name=""k24profile""/><ref name=""auto1"">{{Cite news
column6: title=Ghost of Moi surfaces in Kenya's violence
column12: url-status=live }}</ref> He is also believed to have accumulated some wealth in this period.<ref name=""auto4"">{{Cite news
column20: url-status=live }}</ref> After the 1992 elections, President Moi disbanded [[Youth for Kanu '92
column21: YK'92]] and Ruto unsuccessfully vied for various branch-level positions in [[Kenya African National Union
column22: KANU]], which was at that time Kenya's ruling party.<ref>{{cite web
column24: title = How Moi created then decimated youth lobby

column1: Ruto ran for a parliamentary seat in the [[1997 Kenyan general election
column2: 1997 general election]]. He surprisingly beat the incumbent, [[Reuben Chesire]], Moi's preferred candidate, as well as the [[Uasin Gishu]] KANU branch chairman and assistant minister.<ref>Courting the Kalenjin: The Failure of Dynasticism and the Strength of the ODM Wave in Kenya's Rift Valley Province, Gabrielle Lynch, African Affairs, Vol. 107, No. 429 (Oct. 2008), pp. 541–568</ref><ref>{{Cite web
column4: title=Mzee Moi was 'vicious', interesting fellow – DP Ruto
column9: url-status=live}}</ref> He later gained favour with Moi and was appointed [[Kenya African National Union
column10: KANU]] Director of Elections.<ref name=""auto"">{{Cite web
column12: title=How Ruto rose to be influential personality in Kenyan politics
column19: url-status=live}}</ref> His strong support in 2002 for Moi's preferred successor, [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], saw him get a place as assistant minister in the Home Affairs (Interior) ministry. Later in that [[2002 Kenyan general election
column20: election]], when some government ministers resigned to join the opposition, he was promoted to full [[Cabinet of Kenya
column21: Cabinet Minister]].<ref name=""auto4""/> KANU lost the election but he retained his parliamentary seat. Ruto was elected KANU Secretary General in 2005, with [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] elected as chairman.<ref name=""auto""/>

column2: held a referendum on a new constitution]], which KANU opposed.<ref name=""k24profile""/> Some members of the ruling NARC coalition government, mainly former KANU ministers who had joined the opposition coalition in 2002 under the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Kenya)
column3: LDP]] banner and who were disgruntled as President [[Mwai Kibaki]] had not honored a pre-election MoU<ref>{{cite web
column7: title=Matere Kerri: Why we broke the famous MoU with Raila
column14: url-status=live }}</ref> on power-sharing and creation of a Prime Minister post, joined KANU to oppose the proposed constitution.<ref>{{Cite news
column16: title=Kenyans say no to new constitution
column25: first1=David }}</ref> Since the symbol of the ""No"" vote was an Orange, this new grouping named their movement the [[Orange Democratic Movement]] (ODM). Ruto was part of its top brass, dubbed the Pentagon. He solidified his voter base in the [[Rift Valley Province]]. ODM was victorious in the referendum.<ref>{{Cite journal
column27: title=Of Oranges and Bananas: The 2005 Kenya Referendum on the Constitution

column1: In January 2006, Ruto declared publicly that he would vie for the presidency in the next [[2007 Kenyan general election
column2: general election (2007)]]. His statement was condemned by some of his KANU colleagues, including former president Moi. By this time, ODM had morphed into a political party.<ref name=""k24profile""/> Ruto sought the nomination of the [[Orange Democratic Movement]] (ODM) as its presidential candidate, but on 1 September 2007, he placed third with 368 votes. The winner was [[Raila Odinga]] with 2,656 votes and the runner-up was [[Musalia Mudavadi]] with 391.<ref>{{cite news
column9: archive-date=26 September 2007}}</ref> Ruto expressed his support for Odinga after the vote.<ref>{{cite news
column11: title=Kenya: ODM 'Pentagon' Promises to Keep the Team Intact
column18: access-date=11 June 2023}}</ref> As KANU under Uhuru Kenyatta moved to support Kibaki,<ref name=""auto3"">{{Cite web
column20: title=Nation – Breaking News, Kenya, Africa, Politics, Business, Sports | HOME
column25: url-status=live}}</ref> he resigned from his post as KANU secretary general on 6 October 2007.<ref>{{cite news
column27: title=Kenya: Ruto Abandons Kanu's Top Post

column4: U.S. Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]] (center) walks with Minister of Agriculture William Ruto (left) and environmental and political activist [[Wangari Maathai]] (right) during a tour of the Kenyan Agricultural Research Institute (KARI) near Nairobi, 5 August 2009.]]

column1: The presidential election of December 2007 ended in an impasse. Kenya's electoral commission declared Kibaki the winner, but Raila and ODM claimed the victory. Mwai Kibaki was hurriedly sworn in as the president of the [[2007 Kenyan presidential election
column2: December 2007 presidential election]]. Following the election and the dispute over the result, Kenya was engulfed by a [[Kenyan crisis, 2007-2008
column3: violent political crisis]]. Kibaki and Odinga agreed to form a power-sharing government.<ref name=PM>{{Cite news
column4: title=Odinga sworn in as Kenya PM
column11: archive-date=26 May 2008}}</ref><ref name=Names>Anthony Kariuki, [http://politics.nationmedia.com/inner.asp?pcat=NEWS&cat=TOP&sid=1787 ""Kibaki names Raila PM in new Cabinet""]{{dead link
column14: fix-attempted=yes }}, nationmedia.com, 13 April 2008.</ref> In the grand coalition Cabinet named on 13 April 2008<ref name=Names/> and sworn in on 17 April,<ref name=PM/> Ruto was appointed as Minister for Agriculture.<ref name=Names/> Ruto also became the [[Eldoret North Constituency
column15: Eldoret North's]] Member of Parliament from 2008 to 4 March 2013.<ref>{{Cite web

column1: Ruto was among the list of people who were indicted to stand trial at the ICC for their involvement in Kenya's 2007/2008 political violence. However, the ICC case was faced with challenges, especially concerning the withdrawal of key prosecution witnesses. In April 2016, the Court dropped the charges against Ruto.<ref name=""theguardian1"">{{cite news
column3: title=International criminal court abandons case against William Ruto

column1: On 21 April 2010, Ruto was transferred from the Agriculture Ministry and posted to the Higher Education Ministry, swapping posts with [[Sally Kosgei]].<ref>{{Cite web
column8: access-date=11 June 2023}}</ref> On 24 August 2011, Ruto was relieved of his ministerial duties but remained a member of parliament. He joined with Uhuru Kenyatta to form the Jubilee alliance for the 2013 presidential election.<ref>{{Cite news
column10: title=Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto confirm Kenyan alliance

column1: [[File:The Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi being seen off by the Deputy President of Kenya, Mr. William Ruto, at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, in Nairobi, Kenya on July 11, 2016.jpg
column4: Ruto with Indian Prime Minister [[Narendra Modi]] in 2016]]

column1: On 6 October 2014, Ruto was appointed acting president of Kenya by the then President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] following his summons to appear before the ICC. He served in the role between 6 and 9 October 2014 while President Kenyatta was away at The Hague. When he officially handed over power to Ruto at the Parliament on 6 October, Uhuru explained, ""To protect the sovereignty of the Republic of Kenya, I will sign a legal notice appointing Hon William Ruto as acting president while I attend the status conference.""<ref>{{Cite news
column2: title=The day William Ruto was president for 48 hours

column1: In the August [[2017 Kenyan general election
column2: 2017 General Elections]], Uhuru and Ruto were declared victors after garnering 54% of the total votes cast. However, the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]] nullified the election, and a fresh [[October 2017 Kenyan presidential election
column3: election]] was held in October 2017. The opposition boycotted the fresh election and Uhuru and Ruto were re-elected with 98% of the total votes cast. The [[Supreme Court of Kenya
column4: Supreme Court]] upheld the results of this second election.<ref>{{Cite web
column6: title=Kenya's Supreme Court upholds repeat presidential vote

column1: In December 2020 Ruto announced his alliance with the newly formed [[United Democratic Alliance (Kenya)
column4: title=Kenya: Has Deputy President Ruto joined the new UDA Party?
column14: title=Rift MPs: Ruto will use UDA to contest for presidency in 2022
column21: url-status=live}}</ref> He was the only presidential candidate to attend the second part of the 2022 presidential debate.<ref>{{Cite web
column27: title=Moderators place DP William Ruto between a rock and a hard place during debate
column31: quote=United Democratic Alliance presidential candidate William Ruto was the only candidate who took part in the second tier of the debate, after his main rival, Raila Odinga, of the Azimio la Umoja-One Kenya coalition skipped.

column1: On 15 August 2022, six days after the [[2022 Kenyan general election
column2: general election held on 9 August]], the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission]] chair [[Wafula Chebukati]] announced that Ruto had won the presidential election, defeating candidate [[Raila Odinga]] of the [[Azimio La Umoja]] party. Ruto received 50.49% of the valid votes cast, while Odinga received 48.85%.<ref>{{cite news
column9: title= Kenya's top court confirms William Ruto's victory in presidential vote

column1: Odinga disputed the presidential election results announced by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission, and he challenged the results with the [[Supreme Court of Kenya
column6: title= Kenya election: Raila Odinga challenges William Ruto win in Supreme Court
column8: url= https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-62631193 }}</ref> On 5 September, the Supreme Court judges unanimously found that evidence presented by Odinga's campaign inconclusive and upheld the election of Ruto as the winner of the election.<ref>{{cite news
column11: title= Kenya's Supreme Court upholds Ruto's narrow presidential win
column14: url= https://apnews.com/article/africa-elections-presidential-kenya-uhuru-kenyatta-c9f2ccef66f2267fe4aee0afdb8c9acc }}</ref> In response to the ruling, Odinga said he respected the Supreme Court's decision even though he strongly disagreed with it.<ref>{{cite news
column19: title= William Ruto's election victory upheld by Kenya's supreme court

column1: After taking office Ruto pledged to address climate change and end the use of fossil fuels in Kenya's electricity production by 2030.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Kenya's new president promises ambitious climate plan

column1: On 18 September 2022 President Ruto made his first foreign trip as head of state to the [[United Kingdom]], during which he attended the state funeral of the late [[Queen Elizabeth II]]<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Ruto among the 500 leaders attending Queen Elizabeth's State Funeral
column7: language=en}}</ref> on 19 September 2022 at [[Westminster Abbey]] in London.<ref>{{Cite web
column9: title=Ruto arrives in London for Queen Elizabeth's burial

column1: Two days later, on 21 September 2022, President Ruto made his debut address as head of state to the [[United Nations General Assembly]] ([[UNGA]]) in New York. He nodded to President [[Joe Biden
column3: Build Back Better]]''"" domestic plan, proposing a global effort toward ""building back better from the bottom upward."" The goal, he said, should be ""including the marginalized, working majority in the economic mainstream."" Other themes he addressed were the expansion of the representation of Africa on the [[U.N. Security Council]],<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=Ruto Joins Biden In Rooting For An Expanded Security Council As Part Of UN Reforms
column9: language=en}}</ref> increased investment in the African continent, ""moving Africa from aid to investment"", tapping ""the ever-bustling"" human capital for economic prosperity and a concerted effort towards tackling climate change in the world.<ref>{{Cite web
column11: title=Kenya's president pitches for investment and warns about climate change.

column1: In September 2022, he said that the Horn of Africa was experiencing its worst [[drought]] in 40 years, adding that ""3.1 million people are facing severe drought"" in Kenya alone.<ref name=""france24""/>

Asked about the ongoing [[Tigray War]] in northern [[Ethiopia]] between government forces and Tigray rebels, Ruto said that ''""''whatever happens in Ethiopia gets to Kenya''""''.<ref name=""france24"">{{cite news
column2: title=Kenya's Ruto warns of 'starvation in Horn of Africa' due to climate change
Somali Civil War]], he said that ''""''Kenyan troops will come back home as soon as we're done with the assignment that we have in Somalia''.""''<ref name=""france24""/>

column1: In November 2022 Ruto's government launched the [[Hustler Fund]], a loan program to grant immediate loans to Kenyan citizens.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Kenya's Ruto launches 'hustler fund' small loan scheme

column2: privatisation]] of public enterprises, noting that it is not economically viable to keep pumping government resources into sustaining those corporations.<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=President Ruto to privatise up to 10 State corporations within one year

column1: On 29 September 2023, Ruto joined the Advisory Board of the [[Global Center on Adaptation]] following the Africa Climate Summit in Nairobi, Kenya.<ref>{{cite web
column2: title=William Ruto President Of Kenya Joins GCA Advisory Board

column1: On 25 June 2024 at least five people were killed when public order broke down over tax protests. Ruto proposed several tax rises because more than half of its annual tax revenues are spent to service debt. The increased taxes are proposed ""on everything from car ownership and financial transactions to sanitary pads.""<ref name=""bbc6"">{{cite news
column3: title=Kenya's president faces tough choices after day of bloodshed

column1: On 11 July Ruto sacked most of his cabinet save for the deputy president and prime cabinet secretary, and the next day the police chief Japhet Koome resigned after 40 people died over the past month in the [[Kenya Finance Bill protests]]. Koome was held responsible for police violence against protesters. It was noted that ""[a]bout 60% of Kenya's collected revenues goes to servicing debt.""<ref name=""bbc2"">{{cite news
column3: title=Japhet Koome: Kenya's police chief resigns amid deadly anti-tax protests }}</ref>

column1: In September 2024, Ruto and German Chancellor [[Olaf Scholz]] signed an agreement that opened the German labor market to up to 250,000 skilled and semi-skilled [[Gastarbeiter
column3: title=Germany opens its doors to Kenyan workers in controlled migration deal
column6: date=14 September 2024}}</ref> The agreement will also simplify the [[deportation]] of Kenyans from Germany. There are concerns about [[brain drain]] in Kenya, as professionals such as doctors and nurses could leave for better-paying jobs in Germany.<ref>{{Cite news
column8: title=Germany to welcome Kenyans in labour deal
column11: work=[[BBC]]}}</ref> The deal was made at a time when the [[Opposition to immigration
column13: AfD]] party is growing in popularity in Germany.<ref>{{cite news
column14: title=Germany to welcome Kenyans in labour deal

column1: Since 2015, the Weston Hotel, a business associated with Ruto, has been the subject of a legal dispute regarding the acquisition of its 0.773-acre site opposite Wilson Airport. The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) alleged that the land was public property and was illegally excised in 2002. In January 2019, the National Land Commission (NLC) determined the allotment was irregular but recommended that Ruto compensate the KCAA at market value. Ruto subsequently stated he was a bona fide purchaser who had no knowledge of the original illegality. The matter moved to the High Court after the KCAA rejected the compensation offer, demanding the hotel's demolition.<ref>{{Cite news
column2: title=Kenya: Weston Hotel Refuses to Vacate Lang'ata Land, Pay Kcaa
column9: title=How Weston Hotel land was grabbed from KCAA

column3: Ruto at the 54th Regular Session of the IAEA General Conference]]

column1: In 2004, Ruto was charged with defrauding the Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) of approximately Sh272 million through the sale of plots allegedly hived off from the Ngong Forest. Following a Constitutional Court ruling in 2010 that he must face trial, Ruto was suspended from his position as Minister for Higher Education. In April 2011, he was acquitted<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Ruto acquitted in Sh43m fraud case
column7: language=en}}</ref> after the court found that the prosecution had failed to provide sufficient evidence that he or his co-accused received the funds from KPC.<ref>{{Cite web
column9: title=Accused Kenyan minister William Ruto is suspended

column1: In early 2020, the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) reopened the investigation to trace the money trail of the Sh272 million transaction. Ruto maintained that the renewed probe was politically motivated. Since his assumption of the presidency in 2022, no further charges have been brought forward in this matter, and the case remains part of his historical political discourse.<ref>{{Cite news
column6: title=DCI reopens Ruto land fraud case nine years after acquittal

column1: In June 2013, a court ordered Ruto to pay a victim of 2007/08 post-election violence 5 million shillings for illegally taking away his land during the post-election violence.<ref name=""headon"">{{cite news
column4: title=End of an era for the man who took DP Ruto head-on for grabbing his land
column14: title=How claims of dubious land deals are hurting DP's image
column21: language=en}}</ref> In the same judgement, Ruto was evicted from the grabbed land in [[Uasin Gishu]]. Adrian Muteshi had accused Ruto of grabbing<ref name=""dubious""/> and trespassing on his 100-acre piece of land in Uasin Gishu after he, Adrian, had fled his land for safety during the post-election violence of 2007/08.<ref name=""headon""/> In February 2014, Ruto appealed the court order to pay the 5 million shilling fine. In 2017, Ruto withdrew the appeal against the judgment. In October 2020, Adrian Muteshi died at the age of 86.<ref name=""headon""/>

column1: In October 2019, the ''[[Daily Nation]]'' reported that Ruto's acquisition of a 900-acre piece of land of another former deputy president, [[Joseph Murumbi]], haunted Ruto because he had been involved in the irregular acquisition of the land.<ref>{{cite news
column2: title=Ruto sucked into controversy over purchase of 900 acres
column10: url-status=live }}</ref> In the same month, Ruto claimed that the articles were persistent, and obviously sponsored [[fake news]]. Later that month, a human rights lobby activist, Trusted Society of Human Rights Alliance, called for an investigation into the mysterious acquisition of a 900-acre piece of land that formerly belonged to former vice-president Murumbi.<ref name=""murumbi"">{{cite news
column13: title=How taxpayers lost Sh180m in former VP Murumbi land sale
column21: url-status=live }}</ref> According to the allegations, Murumbi had been involved in a dispute over loan defaults with a state corporation, AFC, against the land that was pledged as a security for the loan.<ref name=""murumbi""/> It is alleged that Murumbi defaulted the loan and AFC took over ownership of the land that was eventually sold to Ruto after he paid off the loan owed to the state corporation.<ref name=""murumbi""/>

column1: In February 2010, Ruto was suspended from his position as Agriculture Minister after his alleged involvement in the 2009 maize scandal that saw the country lose millions of shillings from fraudulent and irregular payments made for purchase of subsidized imported maize by business people and politicians. The then prime minister Raila Odinga termed Ruto's suspension necessary and which would allow for gathering of evidence to determine if any individuals should be prosecuted in these scandal, this was in line with a forensic audit  done by PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) on the maize scandal.<ref>{{Cite news
column2: title=The day Raila suspended and later fired Ruto

column1: Ruto has been publicly linked by several opposition figures, activists, and media reports to the May 2016 assassination of Jacob Juma, a businessman and outspoken government critic. In the months preceding his death, Juma used social media to [[allege]] that Ruto was plotting to kill him, claiming in December 2015 that his assassination had been discussed by senior figures. Following Juma's fatal shooting along [[Ngong Road]], former Lugari MP Cyrus Jirongo alleged during the memorial service that a personal rivalry existed between the two, claiming Juma had once physically assaulted Ruto. Jirongo further suggested that the same individuals involved in Juma's death were responsible for the murder of Meshack Yebei, a potential witness in Ruto's ICC trial.<ref>{{Cite web
column10: title=Jacob Juma made enemies online including Ruto

column1: President Ruto has consistently denied these allegations, characterizing them as politically motivated attacks intended to damage his reputation. He threatened to sue Jirongo and others for defamation, maintaining he never had physical contact with Juma.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=DP Ruto threatens legal action on Jirongo over Jacob Juma comment
column7: language=en-US}}</ref> While Ruto expressed his willingness to record a statement with the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI)<ref>{{Cite web
column9: title=I'm open to investigation over Jacob Juma's murder – DP Ruto
column13: language=en-KE}}</ref> if requested, the murder remains officially unsolved as of 2026, with no suspects charged in connection with the crime.<ref>{{Cite web
column15: title=Ruto tells off Cord over Juma death claims

column1: In June 2016, reports from the ''[[Financial Post]]'' detailed a dispute involving Pacific Wildcat, a Canadian mining company where Juma served as a director. Following the cancellation of the company's $2 billion niobium mining license in Kwale County by the Jubilee government, Juma [[Allegation
column2: alleged]] that then-Mining Minister [[Najib Balala]] had solicited a bribe to reinstate it. Company officials further alleged that Ruto and Balala had pressured the firm to transfer its license to a new entity in which the Kenyan government would hold a 50% stake for free.<ref name=""nation.africa"">{{Cite web
column4: title=Queries over whether Jacob Juma was a windbag or whistleblower
column8: language=en}}</ref> While Juma's opposition to the cancellation became a central theme of his social media activism and political correspondence, a [[High Court of Kenya]] ruling ultimately upheld the Minister's decision to revoke the license, finding that the cancellation was legally sound. Critics and media reports noted that the loss of these mining interests preceded Juma's transition into an outspoken critic of the administration's corruption, leading to various court filings and diplomatic petitions prior to his assassination.<ref name=""nation.africa""/>

column1: In October 2016, Ruto filed a defamation suit against activist and photojournalist [[Boniface Mwangi]] after the latter posted a social media message linking him to the assassination of Jacob Juma. Ruto's legal team argued that the claims were malicious and intended to damage his reputation as a public officer.The case drew further attention in December 2016 when Douglas Nyakundi, an individual claiming to be an employee at the Office of the Deputy President, approached Mwangi alleging he had a confession detailing the planning of Juma's murder by persons within Ruto's office. Nyakundi was subsequently arrested and charged with attempted extortion, with police alleging he had demanded money from Mwangi in exchange for the information.<ref>{{cite news
column4: title=Boniface Mwangi now wants state security
column10: work=Nairobi News}}</ref> During legal proceedings, the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) reported that Nyakundi had recanted his statement, claiming he had been coached to fabricate the allegations. The court subsequently ordered a mental evaluation for Nyakundi to determine his fitness to stand trial. As of 2026, the assassination of Jacob Juma remains officially unsolved.<ref name=""genesis"">{{cite news
column14: title=Revealed: The genesis of Ruto-Jacob Juma fall-out

column2: International Criminal Court investigation in Kenya}}

column1: In December 2010, the prosecutor of the [[International Criminal Court]] announced that he was seeking the summons of six people, including Ruto, over their involvement in the [[2007–2008 Kenyan crisis
column4: title=Kenya's post-election violence: ICC Prosecutor presents cases against six individuals for crimes against humanity
column11: url-status=live }}</ref> The ICC's Pre-Trial Chamber subsequently issued a summons for Ruto at the prosecutor's request.<ref>{{Citation
column13: title=Decision on the Prosecutor's Application for Summons to Appear for William Samoei Ruto, Henry Kiprono Kosgey and Joshua Arap Sang
column14: publisher=[[International Criminal Court]] Pre-Trial Chamber II
column18: url-status=live }}</ref> Ruto was accused of planning and organizing crimes against supporters of President Kibaki's Party of National Unity. He was charged with three counts of [[crimes against humanity]], one for murder, one for the forcible transfer of population, and one for persecution. On 23 January 2012, the ICC confirmed the charges against Ruto and [[Joshua Sang]], in a case that also involved [[Uhuru Kenyatta
column19: former president Uhuru Kenyatta]], [[Francis Muthaura]], [[Henry Kosgey]] and [[Major General Mohammed Hussein Ali]].<ref>{{Cite journal
column21: title=U.K. Court Orders Animal-Rights Activists to Stand Off
column30: url-access=subscription }}</ref> Ruto told the US government that the Kiambaa church fire on 1 January 2008 after the [[2007 Kenyan general election
column31: 2007 general election]] was accidental.<ref>[http://allafrica.com/stories/201103071351.html Ruto explains Kiambaa] {{Webarchive
column33: date=10 March 2011 }} ''Wikileaks''</ref> In 2009 the Waki Commission report stated that ""the incident which captured the attention of both Kenyans and the world was a deliberate burning of live people, mostly Kikuyu women, and children huddled together in a church"" in Kiambaa on 1 January 2008.<ref>{{Cite journal
column37: website=International Year Book and Statesmen's Who's Who
column39: url-access=subscription }}</ref> In April 2016, the International Criminal Court abandoned the prosecution of Ruto, stating that rampant witness intimidation and ""intolerable political interference"" had made it impossible for the case to proceed.<ref name=""theguardian1""/>  In the years leading up to the abandonment of the case, there were disappearances and murders of key witnesses in Ruto's ICC case, among them Meshack Yebei whose decomposing body was found at the Man Eater's Park in Tsavo, Voi in January 2015, and John Kituyi who was attacked and killed in cold blood by unknown assailants in April 2015.<ref>{{Cite web
column40: title=How individuals linked to 2007/08 ICC cases died mysteriously
column43: title=Meshack Yebei and the uneasy murder mystery for Hague court
column46: date=5 July 2020 }}</ref> The murders and disappearances remain unresolved to date.

column1: On 28 July 2017, Ruto's home was targeted by at least one attacker armed with a machete, and the police officer on duty guarding the residence was injured.<ref>{{cite web
column3: title=Kenya's deputy president William Ruto targeted by gunmen
column9: url-status=live}}</ref> During the time of the attack, he and his family were not at the compound as he had left hours earlier for a campaign rally in [[Kitale]]. There were reports of gunfire and several security sources said the attack was staged by multiple people. Police initially thought there were a few attackers because the attacker used different firearms.<ref>{{cite web
column11: title=Kenya Deputy President Ruto's home entered by knifeman
column19: title=More police sent to fight attacker at DP Ruto's home
column25: url-status=live}}</ref> Around 48 hours later, Kenya Police chief Joseph Boinnet announced that the attacker had been shot dead and the situation was under control.<ref>{{cite web
column27: title=Kenya police kill gunman at Deputy President Ruto's home

column1: === OCCRP Person of the Year Award ===
In 2024, Ruto received a record-breaking 40,000 public nominations for the [[Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project
column2: OCCRP]] Person of the Year award. The organization attributed the surge to intense domestic dissatisfaction following the 2024 Finance Bill protests and general economic frustration.<ref>{{Cite web
column4: title=Willliam Ruto withdraws Kenya finance bill after deadly protests
column8: language=en-GB}}</ref> However, OCCRP's final panel of investigative journalists did not award Ruto the title, clarifying that in many cases, public nominations lacked direct evidence of significant corruption or a longstanding pattern of abuses required for their selection.<ref>{{Cite web
column9: title=Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP)
column13: language=en-US}}</ref> The panel ultimately selected ousted Syrian President [[Bashar al-Assad]], citing his documented role in state-sponsored drug trafficking and human rights violations.<ref>{{Cite web
column16: title=Ruto's leadership under scrutiny as Kenya joins global human rights body
column21: title=Why was Kenya's president ranked 2nd most corrupt globally?
column25: language=en}}</ref> Separate from the OCCRP report, an August 2018 survey by [[Ipsos
column26: Ipsos Kenya]] released its Social, Political, Economic and Cultural (SPEC) Survey, which found that 33% of 2,016 respondents perceived Ruto, then Deputy President under [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], as the most corrupt political leader among those currently or previously in office. [[Anne Waiguru]], then Governor of Kirinyaga, was ranked second by 31% of respondents.<ref>{{Cite news
column27: title=Kenya: Ruto - IPSOS Graft Survey Simply Cooked, Stage-Managed Finding

column1: Ruto and his supporters strongly dismissed the poll, with his press secretary labeling it a ""libellous crusade"" by ""shadowy sponsors"" intended to influence the 2022 general election. Ruto further characterized the findings as ""fake news"" and ""propaganda"".<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Ipsos poll on corruption is ""fake news"" - DP Ruto
column6: language=en}}</ref> Similarly, Waiguru threatened legal action for defamation, noting she had never been charged or convicted of corruption in a court of law. Critics of the survey argued that perception-based polls measure public opinion rather than providing factual evidence of criminal activity.<ref>{{Cite news
column10: title=DP Ruto 'most corrupt' followed by Waiguru - Ipsos

column1: On the evening of 18 March, Ruto and First Lady Rachel Ruto hosted a state banquet at State House in Nairobi in honor of [[King Willem-Alexander]] and [[Queen Máxima of the Netherlands]]. After finishing his opening speech President Ruto, contrary to protocol, then introduced Patrick V. Verkooijen, the Dutch chancellor of the [[University of Nairobi]], as a surprise speaker rather than acknowledging his guest, the Dutch king, who was visibly surprised. Verkooijen then proceeded to give a 7.5 minute speech in which he extolled the accomplishments of Ruto, drawing criticism from the royal delegation.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title= President Kenia passeert koning tijdens staatsbanket: 'Zo hoort het niet'

column1: In July 2025, President Ruto announced that he would build a church on the grounds of [[State House, Nairobi]] using his own funds. The decision was widely criticised, with the [[Atheists In Kenya Society]] threatening to sue over what it called ""a promotion of Christian nationalism"", and Nairobi's Catholic archbishop [[Philip Anyolo]] urging a clarification on whether the proposal would favour certain denominations. The ''[[Daily Nation]]'' also published what is said were architectural designs for the structure, showing a large building with stained glass windows and capacity for 8,000 people, and said that it would be expected to cost $9 million, while raising concern over whether it would violate the secular principles enshrined within the [[Constitution of Kenya
column4: title=Kenyan leader to build huge church at presidential office

column1: In June 2024, a University student, Nelson Amenya, blew the whistle on a deal  that was underway between the government and [[Adani Group]] to lease Kenya's largest International Airport, [[JKIA]].<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=The student who blew whistle on Kenya airport controversy
column5: date=20 December 2024 }}</ref> Many Kenyans criticized this deal on the internet for not following the correct privatization procedure such as having public participation on the matter as required by law. The secret manner in which the deal was being conducted also made many Kenyans suspicious of the disregard of transparency. The president on numerous occasions refuted the claims that the airport was being sold, he added the deal was crucial for national development and for the modernization of JKIA.<ref>{{Cite web
column6: title=President Ruto defends Adani company, says its crucial for national development
column10: title=Ruto Defends Adani With Swipe at Kenyans Celebrating Deal's Collapse
column13: date=3 December 2024 }}</ref> Adani was also involved with the Energy sector in Kenya and had signed power transmission deals with the government aimed at increasing power transmission and rural electrification in the country. The deal was valued at $736 million.<ref>{{Cite web
column17: date=15 October 2024 }}</ref> Kenya's high court suspended the power deal. The court said the government could not move ahead with the 30-year agreement with Adani Energy Solutions until the court makes a determination on a case brought by Law Society of Kenya challenging the deal.<ref>{{Cite web
column18: title=Kenyan court suspends $736 million Adani power line deal
column20: work=Reuters}}</ref> In the same month Ruto reaffirmed that the country stands to gain significantly from the power transmission deal between Adani Group Holdings.<ref>{{Cite web
column21: title=President Ruto defends Kenya-Adani Group power-transmission deal

column1: On 21 November 2024 in a nation address, Ruto cancelled the Adani deals, which were valued at over $2.5 billion, after Adani was indicted by the US for corruption and bribery allegations.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Kenya cancels more than $2.5bn in deals with Adani after US indictment
column4: work=Aljazeera}}</ref> The news received positive reactions from lawmakers.

column1: In 2024 and 2025, the Ruto administration faced international and domestic scrutiny regarding its role in the [[Sudanese Civil War
column2: Sudanese civil war]]. Following a February 2024 meeting between Ruto and RSF leader [[Hemedti
column3: Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo]], reports from investigative outlets like [[NTV Kenya
column4: NTV]] and Bellingcat identified Kenyan-labeled military crates in Sudanese depots. Further allegations, highlighted by organizations such as SwissAid, suggested that Nairobi served as a transit hub for gold smuggled from RSF-controlled territories to [[Dubai]]. Sudanese officials and domestic critics alleged these ventures provided a financial and logistical backbone for the RSF, though the Kenyan government consistently denied direct involvement in the illicit trade.<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=Govt Responds to Claims of Ruto Supplying Weapons to Sudan

column1: Diplomatic tensions peaked in February 2025 after Kenya hosted the signing of a charter by the RSF and its allies to form a parallel government in Sudan. While the Sudanese military-led government condemned the move as ""diplomatic anarchy"" and an infringement on its sovereignty, President Ruto maintained that Kenya's involvement was strictly as a neutral mediator. Government spokesperson [[Mwaura Isaac Maigua
column2: Isaac Mwaura]] affirmed that Kenya remained committed to IGAD-led peace negotiations and [[humanitarian relief]], framing the hosting of various Sudanese factions as a necessary step toward ending the conflict and restoring civilian rule.<ref>{{Cite web
column4: title=Sudan RSF, allies, Sign charter in Nairobi to form parallel government

column1: On 9 October 2023, Ruto signed the Privatisation Bill 2023 into law, which gives the country's Ministry of National Treasury and Economic Planning powers to privatise public-owned enterprises without seeking approval from Parliament. Under the new law in place, privatisation of public entities will be done through initial public offering of shares, sale of shares by public tender, sale resulting from the exercise of pre-emptive rights or through any other method that will be defined by the Cabinet. This has been termed unconstitutional by civil societies and groups. The groups reiterated that the process is illegal and amounts to a material breach of procedure, having not gone through parliamentary ratification, stakeholder engagement and public participation contrary to sections 21,22 and 23 of the Privatisation Act, 2023, terming it null and void. There have also been fears for job losses should some entities get privatised. MPs have also raised their concern on how valuation has been carried out with some claiming entities have been undervalued, also questioning the transparency and legality of the entire process.  .<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Civil Society launches legal battle over privatisation of parastatals
column4: work=The Star }}</ref> He has since defended this move terming it necessary as it lessens fiscal burden from the state thus cutting government expenditure and that will also raise revenue in addition to fighting corruption. This was also defended by the then Treasury CS [[Njuguna Ndung'u]].<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=Ndungu:privatisation of parastatals meant to address corruption
column8: date=10 Feb 2023  }}</ref> Over 10 state parastatals have been up for privatisation, including [[Kenyatta International Convention Centre
column9: KICC]], [[JKIA]], Kenya Seed Company, [[National Oil Corporation of Kenya]], [[Kenya Literature Bureau]], with [[Kenya Pipeline Company]] being privatised later in 2025.<ref>{{Cite web
column10: title=Kenya Pipeline privatization kicks off as gov't seeks transaction advisors for IPO

column1: '''William Kipchirchir Samoei Arap Ruto''' <phonos file=""En-us-William Ruto.wav"">pronunciation</phonos> <span class=""nobold noexcerpt nowraplinks"" style=""font-size:;""><span style=""font-size: 85%;"">[[Order of the Golden Heart (Kenya)
column2: CGH]] (born 21 December 1966) is a Kenyan politician who is the fifth and current [[president of Kenya]] since 13 September 2022. Prior to becoming president, he served as the first elected [[Deputy President of Kenya
column3: deputy president of Kenya]] from 2013 to 2022.<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=Kenya's deputy president Ruto declared election winner
column14: title=The Office Of The Deputy President, Kenya
column36: work=iebc.or.ke}}</ref> He previously served in three [[Cabinet of Kenya
column38: portfolios]] as the [[Minister for Home Affairs]], the [[Ministry of Agriculture (Kenya)
column39: Minister of Agriculture]] and as [[Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (Kenya)

column2: Member of Parliament]] for [[Eldoret North Constituency
column3: Eldoret North]] constituency from 1997 to 2007 under the [[Kenya African National Union
column4: KANU]], and from 2007 to 2013 through the [[Orange Democratic Movement
column5: ODM]] party. He was the [[Minister for Home Affairs]] in the [[Daniel arap Moi]] administration from August to December 2002.

column1: Under the [[Mwai Kibaki]] administration, he was the [[Ministry of Agriculture (Kenya)
column2: Minister for Agriculture]] from 2008 to 2010 and [[Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (Kenya)
column3: Minister for Higher Education]] from April to October 2010. Ruto first contested for the presidency during the [[2007 Kenyan general election
column4: 2007 election]], but lost to [[Raila Odinga]] on the [[Orange Democratic Movement
column5: ODM]] party primaries; together with [[Musalia Mudavadi]], who finished second, he then supported the candidature of Odinga. He again ran for the presidency on the [[2013 Kenyan general election
column6: 2013 election]], but withdrew his candidature in favour of [[Uhuru Kenyatta]].

column1: He was later nominated to run for the deputy presidency in the [[2013 Kenyan general election
column3: United Republican Party]], becoming the [[running mate]] of [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] from [[The National Alliance]] (TNA). He was re-elected to the deputy presidency under the [[Jubilee Party]] in the [[2017 Kenyan general election]]. Following a political fallout, [[Uhuru Kenyatta
column4: Kenyatta]] endorsed [[Raila Odinga]] as his preferred successor.

column1: Ruto, now running under the [[United Democratic Alliance (Kenya)
column2: United Democratic Alliance]] (UDA), defeated Odinga for the [[President of Kenya
column3: presidency]] in the [[2022 Kenyan general election
column4: 2022 election]]. While the election was largely described as fair by the [[African Union]] and other international missions, it was contested by Odinga's allies, who alleged electoral fraud. However, the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]] upheld the results, ruling that the allegations lacked sufficient evidence to invalidate the outcome.<ref>{{Cite news
column5: title=Kenya Supreme Court upholds Ruto's presidential victory
column14: title=Four IEBC Commissioners distance themselves from final stage of presidential poll tallying

column2: geopolitical]] profile, positioning the country as a strategic partner for Western powers while championing pan-African interests. Under his leadership, Kenya became the first [[sub-Saharan Africa]]n nation to be designated as a [[Major non-NATO ally
column3: Major Non-NATO Ally]] by the [[United States]].<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=US names Kenya as major ally in face of growing Russian influence
column11: title=Designation of Kenya as a Major Non-NATO Ally
column15: language=en}}</ref> He is also an advocate for climate justice and global financial reform, chairing the inaugural Africa [[Climate Summit]] in 2023, which resulted in the Nairobi Declaration, a call for a global carbon tax and a more equitable international debt system.<ref>{{Cite web
column23: title=African Climate Summit issues unanimous call for world leaders to support global carbon tax on fossil fuels
column28: title=Nairobi Declaration makes strong push for accelerated climate action and financing mechanisms

column1: Regionally, Ruto has played a key role as a mediator in [[East Africa]]n conflicts, through the Nairobi Process<ref>{{Cite web
column5: website=www.eac.int}}</ref> aimed at ending the insurgency in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and his involvement in the Sudan peace talks. Domestically, his administration has built the [[Talanta Sports City]] stadium project and spearheaded the [[National Tree Growing Day
column6: National Tree Growing]] Restoration campaign, which aims to plant 15 billion trees by 2032 to combat climate change and restore Kenya's [[forest cover]].<ref>{{Cite web
column8: title=Kenya Invites CAF Inspection After Criticism Over Infrastructure Readiness for AFCON 2027 - Kenyans.co.ke
column12: language=en}}</ref> In June 2024, Ruto's proposed [[Kenya Finance Bill 2024
column13: finance bill]] was the subject of [[Kenya Finance Bill protests
column14: protests]] in which at least 22 people were killed, causing Ruto to back down and withdraw the bill.

column8: language=en}}</ref> William Ruto is of mixed [[Kipsigis people

Ruto began his political career when he became the treasurer of the [[Youth for Kanu '92

column2: 1997 general election]]. He surprisingly beat the incumbent, [[Reuben Chesire]], Moi's preferred candidate, as well as the [[Uasin Gishu]] KANU branch chairman and assistant minister.<ref>Courting the Kalenjin: The Failure of Dynasticism and the Strength of the ODM Wave in Kenya's Rift Valley Province, Gabrielle Lynch, African Affairs, Vol. 107, No. 429 (Oct. 2008), pp. 541–568</ref><ref>{{Cite web
column4: title=Mzee Moi was 'vicious', interesting fellow – DP Ruto
column9: url-status=live}}</ref> He later gained favour with Moi and was appointed [[Kenya African National Union
column10: KANU]] Director of Elections.<ref name=""auto"">{{Cite web
column12: title=How Ruto rose to be influential personality in Kenyan politics
column19: url-status=live}}</ref> His strong support in 2002 for Moi's preferred successor, [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], saw him get a place as assistant minister in the Home Affairs (Interior) ministry. Later in that [[2002 Kenyan general election
column20: election]], when some government ministers resigned to join the opposition, he was promoted to full [[Cabinet of Kenya
column21: Cabinet Minister]].<ref name=""auto4""/> KANU lost the election but he retained his parliamentary seat. Ruto was elected KANU Secretary General in 2005, with [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] elected as chairman.<ref name=""auto""/>

By this time, ODM had morphed into a political party.<ref name=""k24profile""/> Ruto sought the nomination of the [[Orange Democratic Movement]] (ODM) as its presidential candidate, but on 1 September 2007, he placed third with 368 votes. The winner was [[Raila Odinga]] with 2,656 votes and the runner-up was [[Musalia Mudavadi]] with 391.<ref>{{cite news

In April 2016, the Court dropped the charges against Ruto.<ref name=""theguardian1"">{{cite news

column1: On 21 April 2010, Ruto was transferred from the Agriculture Ministry and posted to the Higher Education Ministry, swapping posts with [[Sally Kosgei]].<ref>{{Cite web
column8: access-date=11 June 2023}}</ref> On 24 August 2011, Ruto was relieved of his ministerial duties but remained a member of parliament. He joined with Uhuru Kenyatta to form the Jubilee alliance for the 2013 presidential election.<ref>{{Cite news
column10: title=Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto confirm Kenyan alliance

column1: On 6 October 2014, Ruto was appointed acting president of Kenya by the then President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] following his summons to appear before the ICC. He served in the role between 6 and 9 October 2014 while President Kenyatta was away at The Hague. When he officially handed over power to Ruto at the Parliament on 6 October, Uhuru explained, ""To protect the sovereignty of the Republic of Kenya, I will sign a legal notice appointing Hon William Ruto as acting president while I attend the status conference.""<ref>{{Cite news
column2: title=The day William Ruto was president for 48 hours

column1: In the August [[2017 Kenyan general election
column2: 2017 General Elections]], Uhuru and Ruto were declared victors after garnering 54% of the total votes cast. However, the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]] nullified the election, and a fresh [[October 2017 Kenyan presidential election
column3: election]] was held in October 2017. The opposition boycotted the fresh election and Uhuru and Ruto were re-elected with 98% of the total votes cast. The [[Supreme Court of Kenya
column4: Supreme Court]] upheld the results of this second election.<ref>{{Cite web
column6: title=Kenya's Supreme Court upholds repeat presidential vote

column1: In December 2020 Ruto announced his alliance with the newly formed [[United Democratic Alliance (Kenya)
column4: title=Kenya: Has Deputy President Ruto joined the new UDA Party?

column21: url-status=live}}</ref> He was the only presidential candidate to attend the second part of the 2022 presidential debate.<ref>{{Cite web
column27: title=Moderators place DP William Ruto between a rock and a hard place during debate
column31: quote=United Democratic Alliance presidential candidate William Ruto was the only candidate who took part in the second tier of the debate, after his main rival, Raila Odinga, of the Azimio la Umoja-One Kenya coalition skipped.

column1: On 15 August 2022, six days after the [[2022 Kenyan general election
column2: general election held on 9 August]], the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission]] chair [[Wafula Chebukati]] announced that Ruto had won the presidential election, defeating candidate [[Raila Odinga]] of the [[Azimio La Umoja]] party. Ruto received 50.49% of the valid votes cast, while Odinga received 48.85%.<ref>{{cite news
column9: title= Kenya's top court confirms William Ruto's victory in presidential vote

column6: title= Kenya election: Raila Odinga challenges William Ruto win in Supreme Court
column8: url= https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-62631193 }}</ref> On 5 September, the Supreme Court judges unanimously found that evidence presented by Odinga's campaign inconclusive and upheld the election of Ruto as the winner of the election.<ref>{{cite news
column11: title= Kenya's Supreme Court upholds Ruto's narrow presidential win
column14: url= https://apnews.com/article/africa-elections-presidential-kenya-uhuru-kenyatta-c9f2ccef66f2267fe4aee0afdb8c9acc }}</ref> In response to the ruling, Odinga said he respected the Supreme Court's decision even though he strongly disagreed with it.<ref>{{cite news
column19: title= William Ruto's election victory upheld by Kenya's supreme court

column1: After taking office Ruto pledged to address climate change and end the use of fossil fuels in Kenya's electricity production by 2030.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Kenya's new president promises ambitious climate plan

column1: On 18 September 2022 President Ruto made his first foreign trip as head of state to the [[United Kingdom]], during which he attended the state funeral of the late [[Queen Elizabeth II]]<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Ruto among the 500 leaders attending Queen Elizabeth's State Funeral
column7: language=en}}</ref> on 19 September 2022 at [[Westminster Abbey]] in London.<ref>{{Cite web
column9: title=Ruto arrives in London for Queen Elizabeth's burial

column1: Two days later, on 21 September 2022, President Ruto made his debut address as head of state to the [[United Nations General Assembly]] ([[UNGA]]) in New York. He nodded to President [[Joe Biden
column3: Build Back Better]]''"" domestic plan, proposing a global effort toward ""building back better from the bottom upward."" The goal, he said, should be ""including the marginalized, working majority in the economic mainstream."" Other themes he addressed were the expansion of the representation of Africa on the [[U.N. Security Council]],<ref>{{Cite web
column5: title=Ruto Joins Biden In Rooting For An Expanded Security Council As Part Of UN Reforms
column9: language=en}}</ref> increased investment in the African continent, ""moving Africa from aid to investment"", tapping ""the ever-bustling"" human capital for economic prosperity and a concerted effort towards tackling climate change in the world.<ref>{{Cite web
column11: title=Kenya's president pitches for investment and warns about climate change.

column1: In September 2022, he said that the Horn of Africa was experiencing its worst [[drought]] in 40 years, adding that ""3.1 million people are facing severe drought"" in Kenya alone.<ref name=""france24""/>

Asked about the ongoing [[Tigray War]] in northern [[Ethiopia]] between government forces and Tigray rebels, Ruto said that ''""''whatever happens in Ethiopia gets to Kenya''""''.<ref name=""france24"">{{cite news

Somali Civil War]], he said that ''""''Kenyan troops will come back home as soon as we're done with the assignment that we have in Somalia''.""''<ref name=""france24""/>

column3: title=Kenya's Ruto launches 'hustler fund' small loan scheme

column1: On 29 September 2023, Ruto joined the Advisory Board of the [[Global Center on Adaptation]] following the Africa Climate Summit in Nairobi, Kenya.<ref>{{cite web
column2: title=William Ruto President Of Kenya Joins GCA Advisory Board

column1: On 25 June 2024 at least five people were killed when public order broke down over tax protests. Ruto proposed several tax rises because more than half of its annual tax revenues are spent to service debt. The increased taxes are proposed ""on everything from car ownership and financial transactions to sanitary pads.""<ref name=""bbc6"">{{cite news
column3: title=Kenya's president faces tough choices after day of bloodshed

column1: On 11 July Ruto sacked most of his cabinet save for the deputy president and prime cabinet secretary, and the next day the police chief Japhet Koome resigned after 40 people died over the past month in the [[Kenya Finance Bill protests]]. Koome was held responsible for police violence against protesters. It was noted that ""[a]bout 60% of Kenya's collected revenues goes to servicing debt.""<ref name=""bbc2"">{{cite news
column3: title=Japhet Koome: Kenya's police chief resigns amid deadly anti-tax protests }}</ref>

column1: In September 2024, Ruto and German Chancellor [[Olaf Scholz]] signed an agreement that opened the German labor market to up to 250,000 skilled and semi-skilled [[Gastarbeiter
column3: title=Germany opens its doors to Kenyan workers in controlled migration deal
column6: date=14 September 2024}}</ref> The agreement will also simplify the [[deportation]] of Kenyans from Germany. There are concerns about [[brain drain]] in Kenya, as professionals such as doctors and nurses could leave for better-paying jobs in Germany.<ref>{{Cite news
column8: title=Germany to welcome Kenyans in labour deal
column11: work=[[BBC]]}}</ref> The deal was made at a time when the [[Opposition to immigration
column13: AfD]] party is growing in popularity in Germany.<ref>{{cite news
column14: title=Germany to welcome Kenyans in labour deal

column1: Since 2015, the Weston Hotel, a business associated with Ruto, has been the subject of a legal dispute regarding the acquisition of its 0.773-acre site opposite Wilson Airport. The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) alleged that the land was public property and was illegally excised in 2002. In January 2019, the National Land Commission (NLC) determined the allotment was irregular but recommended that Ruto compensate the KCAA at market value. Ruto subsequently stated he was a bona fide purchaser who had no knowledge of the original illegality. The matter moved to the High Court after the KCAA rejected the compensation offer, demanding the hotel's demolition.<ref>{{Cite news
column2: title=Kenya: Weston Hotel Refuses to Vacate Lang'ata Land, Pay Kcaa
column9: title=How Weston Hotel land was grabbed from KCAA
