'''Virginia Edith Wambūi Otieno''' (1936–2011), born '''Virginia Edith Wambūi Waiyaki''', who became '''Wambūi Waiyaki Otieno Mbūgua''' after her second marriage, and generally known as Wambūi was born into a prominent [[Kikuyu people
column2: Kikuyu]] family and became a Kenyan activist, politician and writer.<ref name=""Adenekan 2011"">Adenekan (2011), ''Wambui Otieno Mbugua obituary''.</ref> Wambūi became prominent in 1987 because of a controversial legal fight between her and the clan of her [[Luo (Kenya)
column3: Luo]] husband [[Silvano Melea Otieno]] over the right to bury Otieno. The case involved the tension between [[customary law]] and [[civil law (common law)
column4: common law]] in modern-day [[Kenya]] in the case of an inter-tribal union.  The various legal hearings this case stretched over more than five months and the final verdict suggested that a Kenyan African was presumed to adhere to the customs of the [[tribe]] they were born into unless they clearly and unequivocally broke all contact with it. As Otieno retained some rather tenuous links with his clan, they were awarded the right to bury him, ignoring Wambui's wishes. However, Wambūi inherited most of her late husband's estate.<ref>{{cite book
column7: title=Burying Otieno: The politics of gender and ethnicity in Kenya

column1: Wambūi Otieno died on 30 August 2011 of heart failure.<ref name=""Wamai, 2011"">Wamai (2011), ''Tribute to Wambui, a maverick freedom heroine''.</ref>

Much of the commentary about Wambūi's ancestors and early life comes directly or indirectly from her autobiography, ''Mau Mau's Daughter: A Life History''. However, its account of her ancestor, Waiyaki wa Hinga, has been criticized for attempting to make him a proto-Nationalist and inflating his importance, and her role as a scout and urban guerrilla may have been overstated.<ref>Atieno Odhiambo (2003), ''Matunda ya Uhuru, Fruits of Independence'', p. 43.</ref><ref>Anderson (2002), ''Review of Mau Mau's Daughter'', pp. 352–3.</ref><ref>Cloete (2006), ''A Time of Living Dangerously'', pp. 114–15.</ref>
Wambūi was the great-granddaughter of Waiyaki wa Hinga, a [[Kikuyu people
column2: Kikuyu]] leader who was arrested in 1892 by officials of the [[Imperial British East Africa Company]] and who died in suspicious circumstances soon after the arrest. Wambūi claimed in her autobiography that he was murdered by being buried alive for opposing the violent seizure of Kikuyu land.<ref name=""Adenaken 2011"">Adenaken (2011), ''Wambui Otieno Mbugua obituary''.</ref><ref name=""Stamp 1991 p. 816"">Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', p. 816.</ref> However, Waiyaki wa Hinga had initially cooperated with [[Frederick Lugard, 1st Baron Lugard
column3: Frederick Lugard]] of that company in 1890, and his quarrel with Lugard's successor was over the latter's seizure of some of Waiyaki's cattle without payment rather than Waiyaki's opposition to colonial land expropriation.<ref>Atieno Odhiambo (2003), ''Matunda ya Uhuru, Fruits of Independence'', pp. 43–4.</ref>

column1: In Kikuyu oral tradition and folklore, [[Waiyaki Wa Hinga
column2: Waiyaki wa Hinga]], is represented as a major chief and fighter against the British invaders, but he had an ambiguous record of working with the Imperial British East Africa Company. His death was probably caused by injuries sustained during, and possibly after, his arrest and he was buried on his way to detention, whether already dead or assumed to be dying is unclear.<ref>Pugliese (2003). ''Complementary or Contending Nationhoods?''  pp. 100, 108, 112.</ref><ref>Presley (2011). ''Wambui Waiyaki Otieno Mbugua'', p. 212.</ref> Wambūi disputed the charge that Waiyaki collaborated with the British colonists, by preferring Kikuyu oral traditions to historians' versions that she labelled as [[Eurocentrism
column3: Eurocentric]], even where the historians are Kenyan, and claimed the family of Waiyaki wa Hinga were the natural leaders of Kenya because of his actions.<ref>Presley (2011). ''Wambui Waiyaki Otieno Mbugua'', pp. 212–13.</ref>

column1: Wambūi's grandfather, Mūnyua Waiyaki, donated some land he owned to the local [[Church of Scotland]] mission, as a result of which his son, Waiyaki Wantoni, often known as ""Tiras"" was educated at a Church of Scotland school and, in the 1940s, became Kenya's first African police inspector and later a chief inspector,<ref>Presley (2011). ''Wambui Waiyaki Otieno Mbugua'', p. 213.</ref> which Wambūi claimed was compensation for the death of Waiyaki wa Hinga.<ref>Adenaken (2011),""Wambui Otieno Mbugua obituary""</ref> Tiras Waiyaki became involved in nationalist politics in the 1950s and during the [[Kenyan Emergency]], he was detained in 1954. Wambūi claimed that this impoverished his family and interrupted his children's education, but his detention was only for four months followed by his reinstatement, after which he cooperated with the Kenyan colonial administration. Although Wambūi states he also covertly assisted Mau Mau, this was in minor ways which were outweighed by his pro-colonial actions.<ref>Presley (2011). ''Wambui Waiyaki Otieno Mbugua'', pp. 215–16.</ref><ref name=""Cloete 2006 pp. 123-5"">Cloete (2006), ''A Time of Living Dangerously'', pp. 123–5.</ref>

Wambūi was born in [[Kiambu District]] in southern Kikuyuland on 21 June 1936 to a well-off family of landowners. Her father, Tiras Waiyaki Wantoni, was a police inspector and she mentioned three elder brothers who had been educated in Britain. One of her brothers was Kenya's former [[foreign Minister]], Dr [[Munyua Waiyaki]]. She received a missionary education, including being a boarder at Mambere Girls School, a secondary school with the highest level of education then available for African girls.<ref name=""ReferenceA"">Adenaken (2011),''Wambui Otieno Mbugua obituary''</ref><ref>Cloete (2006), ''A Time of Living Dangerously.'' p. 123.</ref>

In 1952, when at secondary school, Wambūi swore an oath of allegiance to Mau Mau and in 1954 she left home to join the Mau Mau insurgency in Nairobi after the brief detention of her father. Wambūi spied on the British and mobilized women and domestic staff to obtain arms. She was also involved in the campaign to eradicate the ""colour bar"" in Nairobi, which designated separate areas in public spaces for Europeans, Asians and Africans. She was briefly arrested several times for these activities and issued with orders excluding her from Nairobi, which she flouted.<ref name=""Adenaken 2011""/><ref name=""Stamp 1991 p. 816""/> Although her activities in Nairobi can be linked to records of her arrests there, Wambūi's claims of a more active role in Mau Mau battles are not supported by official records.<ref>Cloete (2006), '' Time of Living Dangerously.''pp. 115, 129–31.</ref>

In the period up to 1960, Wambūi had three children with her fiancé, who she was unable to marry because of family opposition. After Mau Mau forces had been effectively defeated, she became involved in [[trade union]] activities and worked closely with [[Tom Mboya]] and other trade unionists. She states that her eventual arrest in July 1960 for mobilizing women for strikes and riots, and her subsequent detention, resulted from a betrayal by her fiancé.<ref>Otieno, ed. Presley (1998), ''Mau Mau's Daughter'', p. 85.</ref> She was detained in a camp in [[Lamu]] until January 1961, and records that she was raped and impregnated by a British prison officer while detained there.<ref>Otieno, ed. Presley (1998), ''Mau Mau's Daughter'', pp. 81, 83.</ref>

After her release from detention, Wambūi joined Tom Mboya's [[Nairobi People's Convention Party]] as leader of its [[Women's wing]]. This party later became part of the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU), and in 1963 Wambūi was elected head of the women's wing of KANU and was also involved in Kìama Kia Mūìngì, an organization that was a successor to Mau Mau.<ref name=""Adenekan 2011""/> She was one of the first women to run for political office in postcolonial Kenya as a KANU candidate in 1969 and stood again in 1974, although she was unsuccessful both times, and she served as an official in a number of Kenyan and international Women's organizations'.<ref name=""ReferenceA""/><ref name=""Wamai, 2011""/>

In 1985, Wambūi left KANU because of the party's manipulation of elections and lack of internal democracy and, in the last 30 years of her life, was involved with almost every Kenyan opposition party.<ref name=""Cloete 2006 pp. 123-5""/> In 1991, she joined the [[Forum for the Restoration of Democracy–Kenya
column2: Forum for Restoration of Democracy]] which aimed to promote multiparty politics in Kenya. This party experienced a split in 1997 and Wambūi joined the [[National Development Party (Kenya)
column3: National Development Party]] of Kenya, unsuccessfully standing for election in the same year. In 2007, she established a new political party the Kenya's People's Conventional Party and unsuccessfully contested a parliamentary seat as its candidate. Wambūi never realized her ambition to be elected to Kenya's parliament.<ref>Wamai (2011), ''Tribute to Wambui, a maverick freedom heroine''.</ref>

column1: Soon after her release from detention, Wambūi met Silviano Melea Otieno, a prominent lawyer of [[Luo (family of ethnic groups)
column2: Luo]] heritage based in Nairobi, and the couple married in 1963. Otieno accepted the four of Wambūi's children born before their marriage as his own, the couple had five children and also fostered the six orphaned children of a deceased friend of Otieno. All 15 children were well educated; their daughter, Gladwell Otieno, attended universities in the United States and Germany and one of her brothers and a foster brother attended United States universities.<ref name=""Wamai, 2011""/> Gladwell Otieno worked for [[Transparency International]] in Berlin and was Executive Director of Transparency International Kenya and is founder and Executive Director of ""AFRICOG"", the African Centre of open Governance.<ref>[http://globalinitiative.net/experts/gladwell-otieno/ The Global Initiative (2018). '' Gladwell Otieno profile''.]</ref>

column1: Wambūi's husband, Silviano Melea Otieno, died suddenly of a [[Myocardial infarction
column2: heart attack]] on 20 December 1986. He was a member of the Umira Kager [[clan]] of the Luo people, in contrast to Wambūi who was a Kikuyu.<ref>Cohen and Odhiambo (1992), ''Burying SM: The Politics of Knowledge and Sociology'', pp. 2–3, 26.</ref><ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', pp. 808–9, 816.</ref>  Otieno left no will or written wishes about his burial. According to Wambūi, this was because he felt his brother and clan would contest a will and possibly overturn it, whereas an [[intestacy]] might offer better protection for her and their children.<ref name=""Stamp 1991 p. 817"">Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', p. 817.</ref>

column1: Soon after Otieno's death, Wambūi announced that he would be buried on 3 January 1987 at a small farm the couple owned on the outskirts of [[Nairobi]], according to what she said was his wish. This was challenged by his brother, Joash Ochieng Ougo, who was his closest adult-male blood relation (as Otieno's sons were juveniles), and Omolo Siranga, the Nairobi representative of the Umira Kager clan.<ref>Cohen and Odhiambo (1992), ''Burying SM: The Politics of Knowledge and Sociology'', pp. 3–5.</ref><ref name=""Stamp 1991 p. 817""/>

The determinative legal issue was deciding on the relevant Kenyan law on burial, whether [[statute]], [[Common law]] or [[Customary law]], and who was the [[next of kin]] responsible for the funeral rites.<ref name=""Wanjala 1989 p. 110"">Wanjala (1989),''Conflicts of Law and Burial'', p. 110.</ref> Under Kenyan law at that time, a deceased person's will or the wishes of their spouse were not sufficient to determine a dispute between opposed parties,<ref>Cotran (1987), ''Casebook on Kenyan Customary Law'', p. 345.</ref> and several people gave uncorroborated versions of the verbal wishes Otieno was said to have given at various times about his funeral wishes that conflicted with Wambūi's version.<ref>Okech-Owiti (1989), ''Some Socio-Legal Issues'', p. 17.</ref>

The parties differed in terms of class, gender, ethnicity and their relationship to Otieno. Wambūi and Otieno exemplified an emerging Kenyan bourgeoisie, whereas his brother was a railway foreman<ref>Gordon (1995), ''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', pp. 891-3.</ref> The Otieno's had not married under customary law and were Christian. At home, they spoke English and Swahili, not Luo. All their children were Western educated and their friends were Nairobi professionals.<ref>Cohen and Odhiambo (1992), ''Burying SM: The Politics of Knowledge and Sociology'', p. 27.</ref><ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', pp. 815–6.</ref> Like other elite Kenyans, Otieno's loyalty was to his [[nuclear family]], and he generally disregarded possible obligations to his extended family and clan, although he remained a member of the clan association.<ref>Gordon (1995),''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', pp. 892, 898.</ref> He had little contact with his extended family and did not own a house or land in his home district, which he rarely visited except for family funerals. Wambūi had even less contact with his family or clan as, even before Otieno's death, his lineage refused to recognize their marriage as valid under Luo custom, considering it an affront to his family and clan.<ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', pp. 816–17.</ref>

Wambūi and the Umira Kager clan disputed the place and manner of Otieno's funeral.<ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', p. 809.</ref> Wambūi claimed his lifestyle made Luo custom inappropriate, and that she was Otieno's next of kin under common law, entitled to deal with his burial as she saw fit.<ref name=""Wanjala 1989 p. 110""/> She argued that, as she and Otieno were Christians, a [[Christian burial]] was appropriate. She did not believe in Luo ancestral spirits nor accept the custom of burial at Otieno's birthplace, and regarded the marginal role given to Luo widows as demeaning.<ref>Cohen and Odhiambo (1992), ''Burying S M: The Politics of Knowledge and Sociology'', pp. 4–5, 34–8.</ref>

Otieno's brother and clan's argument was that, despite his lifestyle, Otieno had not severed his relations with his clan, but respected and adhered to Luo custom and traditions, so Luo customary law was relevant to him. Under these customs, his brother was the adult blood relation charged with organising his burial, which takes the form a rite of passage for the dead person's spirit to join Luo ancestral spirits and which marginalizes widows.<ref>Ocholla-Ayayo (1989), ''Death and Burial – an Anthropological Perspective'' pp. 31-2.</ref> They also argued that Wambūi was not his blood relation and that, not only were his sons were underage, but their Western education and mixed parentage meant that they had not been born and bred in the Luo traditions, so that none of them could contest the brother's right to bury Otieno.<ref>Okoth-Okombo (1989), ''Semantic Issues'', p. 91.</ref>

The hearings in this in the Kenyan Courts in Nairobi began on 30 December 1986 and ended on 15 May 1987. The initial High Court action was Wambūi's successful request for a declaration that she was entitled to bury Otieno, and an [[injunction]] against clan members' attempts to prevent this.<ref>Mukaindo (2011), ''Revisiting the S M Otieno Case''.</ref> The two defendants appeal against this ruling was allowed by the Court of Appeal, which ordering a full hearing of the issues before another High Court judge.<ref name=""Kenya Law 1987"">Kenya Law (1987), ''Virginia Edith Wambui Otieno versus Joash Ochieng Ougo and Omolo Siranga''.</ref>

The High Court's judgement was that there was no specific Kenyan statute or common law on burial, and the Kenyan courts were obliged to consider customary law if at least one party to a case was subject to or affected by it. If Otieno was subject to Luo customary law, he should be buried according to Luo customs as outlined by the clan. There was evidence that he belonged to a clan association whose aims were to repatriate the bodies of clan members to their home district and organize their funerals there.<ref>Kenya Law (1987), ''Virginia Edith Wambui Otieno versus Joash Ochieng Ougo and Omolo Siranga''.</ref> The evidence that he had attended traditional funerals and participated in their rites and inherited land according to customary law also contradicted the assertion that he had severed all connection with his clan and tribe. However, the judgement noted that the case was not about the administration of Otieno's estate, which was governed by a statute on succession, not customary law.<ref name=""Kenya Law 1987""/> Wambūi inherited mist of her late husband's estate, either because she owned its assets jointly with her late husband or under the law on succession.<ref>Stamp (1991). ''Burying Otieno: The politics of gender and ethnicity in Kenya'', pp. 809, 820.</ref>

The case then returned to the Court of Appeal which gave its decision on 15 May 1987. Very little new arose, although Wambūi's lawyers argued that she would have the right to bury her husband under the English common law which applied from the time Kenya became a colony. The court found that there was no such common law and that, had she been appointed administrator of her husband's estate, she would have had the statutory right to bury him. As she had not been so appointed as there was no will, customary law would apply and he would be buried by his brother the late Joash Ochieng Ougo at his family home.<ref>van Doren (1988), ''Death African Style'', pp. 341–2.</ref>

Wambūi alleged that the real issue behind the court battle was Otieno's considerable estate, which his brother hoped to claim as his next of kin in Luo terms, and she argued that his clan had a history of seeking money relating to deceased members. However, Wambūi and Otieno had defeated such a claim by registering as many assets as possible in their joint names.<ref>A. Gordon (1995), ''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', p. 884.</ref><ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', p. 820.</ref> She also claimed in court that the Umira Kager clan wished her to enter into a [[levirate marriage]] with either Otieno's brother Joash Ochieng Ougo or some other clan member, as the clan would not allow Wambūi to ""walk away to her Kikuyu people with Otieno's property"".<ref>Stamp (1991), ''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', pp. 814, 822.</ref> However, she could not show that any compulsion had been involved.<ref name=""Kenya Law 1987""/>

In the 1980s, most Luo considered land as a permanent asset of the lineage, and burying its members on this land symbolizes the right of the lineage to retain it. They also considered that extended family members should share the wealth of richer members and, by combining these two concepts, the idea emerged among members of Umira Kager clan that burying Otieno on clan land entitled his [[Patrilineality
column2: patrilineage]] to share in his estate.<ref>Gordon (1995), ''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', pp. 896–7.</ref>

column1: Wambūi claimed that the Kenyan President, [[Daniel arap Moi]] supported the Luo and provided legal representation and funding to fight the case, as Wambūi was both a member of the formerly dominant Kikuyu group and a leader of the movement opposing Moi's autocratic regime.<ref>Gordon (1995),''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', p. 885.</ref> She also questioned the neutrality of the Appeal Court judges<ref>Stamp (1991), ''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', p. 822.</ref> However, van Doren, a professor of Law, reports that Wambūi counsel could not point to actual prejudice by these judges and considers that they and the High Court judge dealt as best they could with a situation where the relevant statute requires judges to have regard to African customary law.<ref>van Doren (1988), ''Death African Style'' pp 341, 345–7.</ref>

In the 30 years since the Otieno burial case, the Kenyan [[jurisprudence]] on burials has evolved to some degree. In 1996, the courts ruled that the circumstances of the deceased person's life had to be considered as well as customary laws, in 2004 held the wishes of the wife of the deceased and, in 2010 the wishes of the deceased, while not binding, should be taken into account.<ref>Mukaindo (2011), ''Revisiting the S M Otieno Case''.</ref>

Her 2003 marriage to Peter Mbūgua was the subject of a national controversy. Many of their relatives condemned the marriage. There have been allegations that the death of Mbūgua's mother, which happened only days after the marriage, was caused by the shock she got upon learning of the marriage.<ref name=""till"">Daily Nation, Saturday Magazine, October 3, 2010: [http://www.nation.co.ke/magazines/saturday/-/1216/476880/-/item/0/-/sh0xf3z/-/index.html Till death do us part... ]</ref>
As of 2008, they were living together with her stonemason husband in [[Karen, Kenya
column2: Karen]], [[Nairobi]].<ref name=""till"" />  In February 2011 they held a second wedding ceremony,  now at [[St. Andrew's Church, Nairobi
column3: St. Andrew's Church]] in Nairobi, while the first wedding had been a civil ceremony.<ref>''Daily Nation'', February 4, 2011: [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/Wambui%20and%20Mbugua%20cap%20their%20marriage%20with%20church%20wedding%20/-/1056/1101826/-/7jac19/-/index.html ""Wambui and Mbugua cap marriage with church wedding""].</ref>

column1: Wambūi had suffered heart failure previously and was relying on a [[pacemaker]], an electronic gadget implanted to function as the heart does. Wambūi Otieno died on August 30, 2011, in a Nairobi hospital.<ref>{{cite web
column3: title=Daily Nation: – Politics {{pipe}}Former freedom fighter Wambui dies in Nairobi

column1: Before her death, Wambūi distributed most of her assets including properties to her children and grandchildren and appointed her two daughters, Gladwell Otieno and Rosalyn Otieno, as her personal representatives in her will to administer what was left. In an echo of the events of 1987, Peter Mbūgua commenced legal proceedings in 2013 on the basis that Wambūi lacked the mental capacity to make a valid will.<ref>Kadida (2013), ''Wambui Otieno's widower says she was mad when she wrote will''.</ref>

Wambūi Waiyaki Otieno Mbūgua\n
column15: known_for          = [[Activism]]\n}}\n\'\'\'Virginia Edith Wambūi Otieno\'\'\' (1936–2011), born \'\'\'Virginia Edith Wambūi Waiyaki\'\'\', who became \'\'\'Wambūi Waiyaki Otieno Mbūgua\'\'\' after her second marriage, and generally known as Wambūi was born into a prominent [[Kikuyu people
column16: Kikuyu]] family and became a Kenyan activist, politician and writer.<ref name=""Adenekan 2011"">Adenekan (2011), \'\'Wambui Otieno Mbugua obituary\'\'.</ref> Wambūi became prominent in 1987 because of a controversial legal fight between her and the clan of her [[Luo (Kenya)
column17: Luo]] husband [[Silvano Melea Otieno]] over the right to bury Otieno. The case involved the tension between [[customary law]] and [[civil law (common law)
column18: common law]] in modern-day [[Kenya]] in the case of an inter-tribal union.  The various legal hearings this case stretched over more than five months and the final verdict suggested that a Kenyan African was presumed to adhere to the customs of the [[tribe]] they were born into unless they clearly and unequivocally broke all contact with it. As Otieno retained some rather tenuous links with his clan, they were awarded the right to bury him, ignoring Wambui\'s wishes. However, Wambūi inherited most of her late husband\'s estate.<ref>{{cite book
column21: title=Burying Otieno: The politics of gender and ethnicity in Kenya
column23:
page=809}}</ref>

Wambūi Otieno died on 30 August 2011 of heart failure.<ref name=""Wamai, 2011"">Wamai (2011), ''Tribute to Wambui, a maverick freedom heroine''.</ref>

', sections=[Section(title='==Ancestry and early life==', content='
Much of the commentary about Wambūi's ancestors and early life comes directly or indirectly from her autobiography, ''Mau Mau's Daughter: A Life History''. However, its account of her ancestor, Waiyaki wa Hinga, has been criticized for attempting to make him a proto-Nationalist and inflating his importance, and her role as a scout and urban guerrilla may have been overstated.<ref>Atieno Odhiambo (2003), ''Matunda ya Uhuru, Fruits of Independence'', p. 43.</ref><ref>Anderson (2002), ''Review of Mau Mau's Daughter'', pp. 352–3.</ref><ref>Cloete (2006), ''A Time of Living Dangerously'', pp. 114–15.</ref>

Wambūi was the great-granddaughter of Waiyaki wa Hinga, a [[Kikuyu people
column24: Kikuyu]] leader who was arrested in 1892 by officials of the [[Imperial British East Africa Company]] and who died in suspicious circumstances soon after the arrest. Wambūi claimed in her autobiography that he was murdered by being buried alive for opposing the violent seizure of Kikuyu land.<ref name=""Adenaken 2011"">Adenaken (2011), \'\'Wambui Otieno Mbugua obituary\'\'.</ref><ref name=""Stamp 1991 p. 816"">Stamp (1991),\'\'Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity\'\', p. 816.</ref> However, Waiyaki wa Hinga had initially cooperated with [[Frederick Lugard, 1st Baron Lugard
column25: Frederick Lugard]] of that company in 1890, and his quarrel with Lugard\'s successor was over the latter\'s seizure of some of Waiyaki\'s cattle without payment rather than Waiyaki\'s opposition to colonial land expropriation.<ref>Atieno Odhiambo (2003), \'\'Matunda ya Uhuru, Fruits of Independence\'\', pp. 43–4.</ref>\n\nIn Kikuyu oral tradition and folklore, [[Waiyaki Wa Hinga
column26: Waiyaki wa Hinga]], is represented as a major chief and fighter against the British invaders, but he had an ambiguous record of working with the Imperial British East Africa Company. His death was probably caused by injuries sustained during, and possibly after, his arrest and he was buried on his way to detention, whether already dead or assumed to be dying is unclear.<ref>Pugliese (2003). \'\'Complementary or Contending Nationhoods?\'\'  pp. 100, 108, 112.</ref><ref>Presley (2011). \'\'Wambui Waiyaki Otieno Mbugua\'\', p. 212.</ref> Wambūi disputed the charge that Waiyaki collaborated with the British colonists, by preferring Kikuyu oral traditions to historians\' versions that she labelled as [[Eurocentrism
column27:
Eurocentric]], even where the historians are Kenyan, and claimed the family of Waiyaki wa Hinga were the natural leaders of Kenya because of his actions.<ref>Presley (2011). ''Wambui Waiyaki Otieno Mbugua'', pp. 212–13.</ref>
 
Wambūi's grandfather, Mūnyua Waiyaki, donated some land he owned to the local [[Church of Scotland]] mission, as a result of which his son, Waiyaki Wantoni, often known as ""Tiras"" was educated at a Church of Scotland school and, in the 1940s, became Kenya's first African police inspector and later a chief inspector,<ref>Presley (2011). ''Wambui Waiyaki Otieno Mbugua'', p. 213.</ref> which Wambūi claimed was compensation for the death of Waiyaki wa Hinga.<ref>Adenaken (2011),""Wambui Otieno Mbugua obituary""</ref> Tiras Waiyaki became involved in nationalist politics in the 1950s and during the [[Kenyan Emergency]], he was detained in 1954. Wambūi claimed that this impoverished his family and interrupted his children's education, but his detention was only for four months followed by his reinstatement, after which he cooperated with the Kenyan colonial administration. Although Wambūi states he also covertly assisted Mau Mau, this was in minor ways which were outweighed by his pro-colonial actions.<ref>Presley (2011). ''Wambui Waiyaki Otieno Mbugua'', pp. 215–16.</ref><ref name=""Cloete 2006 pp. 123-5"">Cloete (2006), ''A Time of Living Dangerously'', pp. 123–5.</ref>

Wambūi was born in [[Kiambu District]] in southern Kikuyuland on 21 June 1936 to a well-off family of landowners. Her father, Tiras Waiyaki Wantoni, was a police inspector and she mentioned three elder brothers who had been educated in Britain. One of her brothers was Kenya's former [[foreign Minister]], Dr [[Munyua Waiyaki]]. She received a missionary education, including being a boarder at Mambere Girls School, a secondary school with the highest level of education then available for African girls.<ref name=""ReferenceA"">Adenaken (2011),''Wambui Otieno Mbugua obituary''</ref><ref>Cloete (2006), ''A Time of Living Dangerously.'' p. 123.</ref>

'), Section(title='== Mau Mau activities ==', content='
In 1952, when at secondary school, Wambūi swore an oath of allegiance to Mau Mau and in 1954 she left home to join the Mau Mau insurgency in Nairobi after the brief detention of her father. Wambūi spied on the British and mobilized women and domestic staff to obtain arms. She was also involved in the campaign to eradicate the ""colour bar"" in Nairobi, which designated separate areas in public spaces for Europeans, Asians and Africans. She was briefly arrested several times for these activities and issued with orders excluding her from Nairobi, which she flouted.<ref name=""Adenaken 2011""/><ref name=""Stamp 1991 p. 816""/> Although her activities in Nairobi can be linked to records of her arrests there, Wambūi's claims of a more active role in Mau Mau battles are not supported by official records.<ref>Cloete (2006), '' Time of Living Dangerously.''pp. 115, 129–31.</ref>

In the period up to 1960, Wambūi had three children with her fiancé, who she was unable to marry because of family opposition. After Mau Mau forces had been effectively defeated, she became involved in [[trade union]] activities and worked closely with [[Tom Mboya]] and other trade unionists. She states that her eventual arrest in July 1960 for mobilizing women for strikes and riots, and her subsequent detention, resulted from a betrayal by her fiancé.<ref>Otieno, ed. Presley (1998), ''Mau Mau's Daughter'', p. 85.</ref> She was detained in a camp in [[Lamu]] until January 1961, and records that she was raped and impregnated by a British prison officer while detained there.<ref>Otieno, ed. Presley (1998), ''Mau Mau's Daughter'', pp. 81, 83.</ref>

'), Section(title='==Political career==', content='
After her release from detention, Wambūi joined Tom Mboya's [[Nairobi People's Convention Party]] as leader of its [[Women's wing]]. This party later became part of the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU), and in 1963 Wambūi was elected head of the women's wing of KANU and was also involved in Kìama Kia Mūìngì, an organization that was a successor to Mau Mau.<ref name=""Adenekan 2011""/> She was one of the first women to run for political office in postcolonial Kenya as a KANU candidate in 1969 and stood again in 1974, although she was unsuccessful both times, and she served as an official in a number of Kenyan and international Women's organizations'.<ref name=""ReferenceA""/><ref name=""Wamai, 2011""/>

In 1985, Wambūi left KANU because of the party's manipulation of elections and lack of internal democracy and, in the last 30 years of her life, was involved with almost every Kenyan opposition party.<ref name=""Cloete 2006 pp. 123-5""/> In 1991, she joined the [[Forum for the Restoration of Democracy–Kenya
column28: Forum for Restoration of Democracy]] which aimed to promote multiparty politics in Kenya. This party experienced a split in 1997 and Wambūi joined the [[National Development Party (Kenya)
column29:
National Development Party]] of Kenya, unsuccessfully standing for election in the same year. In 2007, she established a new political party the Kenya's People's Conventional Party and unsuccessfully contested a parliamentary seat as its candidate. Wambūi never realized her ambition to be elected to Kenya's parliament.<ref>Wamai (2011), ''Tribute to Wambui, a maverick freedom heroine''.</ref>

'), Section(title='== Otieno burial case ==', content='
'), Section(title='===Background===', content='
Soon after her release from detention, Wambūi met Silviano Melea Otieno, a prominent lawyer of [[Luo (family of ethnic groups)
column30: Luo]] heritage based in Nairobi, and the couple married in 1963. Otieno accepted the four of Wambūi\'s children born before their marriage as his own, the couple had five children and also fostered the six orphaned children of a deceased friend of Otieno. All 15 children were well educated; their daughter, Gladwell Otieno, attended universities in the United States and Germany and one of her brothers and a foster brother attended United States universities.<ref name=""Wamai, 2011""/> Gladwell Otieno worked for [[Transparency International]] in Berlin and was Executive Director of Transparency International Kenya and is founder and Executive Director of ""AFRICOG"", the African Centre of open Governance.<ref>[http://globalinitiative.net/experts/gladwell-otieno/ The Global Initiative (2018). \'\' Gladwell Otieno profile\'\'.]</ref>\n\nWambūi\'s husband, Silviano Melea Otieno, died suddenly of a [[Myocardial infarction
column31:
heart attack]] on 20 December 1986. He was a member of the Umira Kager [[clan]] of the Luo people, in contrast to Wambūi who was a Kikuyu.<ref>Cohen and Odhiambo (1992), ''Burying SM: The Politics of Knowledge and Sociology'', pp. 2–3, 26.</ref><ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', pp. 808–9, 816.</ref>  Otieno left no will or written wishes about his burial. According to Wambūi, this was because he felt his brother and clan would contest a will and possibly overturn it, whereas an [[intestacy]] might offer better protection for her and their children.<ref name=""Stamp 1991 p. 817"">Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', p. 817.</ref>

Soon after Otieno's death, Wambūi announced that he would be buried on 3 January 1987 at a small farm the couple owned on the outskirts of [[Nairobi]], according to what she said was his wish. This was challenged by his brother, Joash Ochieng Ougo, who was his closest adult-male blood relation (as Otieno's sons were juveniles), and Omolo Siranga, the Nairobi representative of the Umira Kager clan.<ref>Cohen and Odhiambo (1992), ''Burying SM: The Politics of Knowledge and Sociology'', pp. 3–5.</ref><ref name=""Stamp 1991 p. 817""/>

'), Section(title='===Legal issues===', content='
The determinative legal issue was deciding on the relevant Kenyan law on burial, whether [[statute]], [[Common law]] or [[Customary law]], and who was the [[next of kin]] responsible for the funeral rites.<ref name=""Wanjala 1989 p. 110"">Wanjala (1989),''Conflicts of Law and Burial'', p. 110.</ref> Under Kenyan law at that time, a deceased person's will or the wishes of their spouse were not sufficient to determine a dispute between opposed parties,<ref>Cotran (1987), ''Casebook on Kenyan Customary Law'', p. 345.</ref> and several people gave uncorroborated versions of the verbal wishes Otieno was said to have given at various times about his funeral wishes that conflicted with Wambūi's version.<ref>Okech-Owiti (1989), ''Some Socio-Legal Issues'', p. 17.</ref>

The parties differed in terms of class, gender, ethnicity and their relationship to Otieno. Wambūi and Otieno exemplified an emerging Kenyan bourgeoisie, whereas his brother was a railway foreman<ref>Gordon (1995), ''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', pp. 891-3.</ref> The Otieno's had not married under customary law and were Christian. At home, they spoke English and Swahili, not Luo. All their children were Western educated and their friends were Nairobi professionals.<ref>Cohen and Odhiambo (1992), ''Burying SM: The Politics of Knowledge and Sociology'', p. 27.</ref><ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', pp. 815–6.</ref> Like other elite Kenyans, Otieno's loyalty was to his [[nuclear family]], and he generally disregarded possible obligations to his extended family and clan, although he remained a member of the clan association.<ref>Gordon (1995),''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', pp. 892, 898.</ref> He had little contact with his extended family and did not own a house or land in his home district, which he rarely visited except for family funerals. Wambūi had even less contact with his family or clan as, even before Otieno's death, his lineage refused to recognize their marriage as valid under Luo custom, considering it an affront to his family and clan.<ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', pp. 816–17.</ref>
 
Wambūi and the Umira Kager clan disputed the place and manner of Otieno's funeral.<ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', p. 809.</ref> Wambūi claimed his lifestyle made Luo custom inappropriate, and that she was Otieno's next of kin under common law, entitled to deal with his burial as she saw fit.<ref name=""Wanjala 1989 p. 110""/> She argued that, as she and Otieno were Christians, a [[Christian burial]] was appropriate. She did not believe in Luo ancestral spirits nor accept the custom of burial at Otieno's birthplace, and regarded the marginal role given to Luo widows as demeaning.<ref>Cohen and Odhiambo (1992), ''Burying S M: The Politics of Knowledge and Sociology'', pp. 4–5, 34–8.</ref>

Otieno's brother and clan's argument was that, despite his lifestyle, Otieno had not severed his relations with his clan, but respected and adhered to Luo custom and traditions, so Luo customary law was relevant to him. Under these customs, his brother was the adult blood relation charged with organising his burial, which takes the form a rite of passage for the dead person's spirit to join Luo ancestral spirits and which marginalizes widows.<ref>Ocholla-Ayayo (1989), ''Death and Burial – an Anthropological Perspective'' pp. 31-2.</ref> They also argued that Wambūi was not his blood relation and that, not only were his sons were underage, but their Western education and mixed parentage meant that they had not been born and bred in the Luo traditions, so that none of them could contest the brother's right to bury Otieno.<ref>Okoth-Okombo (1989), ''Semantic Issues'', p. 91.</ref>

'), Section(title='===Court hearings===', content='
The hearings in this in the Kenyan Courts in Nairobi began on 30 December 1986 and ended on 15 May 1987. The initial High Court action was Wambūi's successful request for a declaration that she was entitled to bury Otieno, and an [[injunction]] against clan members' attempts to prevent this.<ref>Mukaindo (2011), ''Revisiting the S M Otieno Case''.</ref> The two defendants appeal against this ruling was allowed by the Court of Appeal, which ordering a full hearing of the issues before another High Court judge.<ref name=""Kenya Law 1987"">Kenya Law (1987), ''Virginia Edith Wambui Otieno versus Joash Ochieng Ougo and Omolo Siranga''.</ref>
 
The High Court's judgement was that there was no specific Kenyan statute or common law on burial, and the Kenyan courts were obliged to consider customary law if at least one party to a case was subject to or affected by it. If Otieno was subject to Luo customary law, he should be buried according to Luo customs as outlined by the clan. There was evidence that he belonged to a clan association whose aims were to repatriate the bodies of clan members to their home district and organize their funerals there.<ref>Kenya Law (1987), ''Virginia Edith Wambui Otieno versus Joash Ochieng Ougo and Omolo Siranga''.</ref> The evidence that he had attended traditional funerals and participated in their rites and inherited land according to customary law also contradicted the assertion that he had severed all connection with his clan and tribe. However, the judgement noted that the case was not about the administration of Otieno's estate, which was governed by a statute on succession, not customary law.<ref name=""Kenya Law 1987""/> Wambūi inherited mist of her late husband's estate, either because she owned its assets jointly with her late husband or under the law on succession.<ref>Stamp (1991). ''Burying Otieno: The politics of gender and ethnicity in Kenya'', pp. 809, 820.</ref>

The case then returned to the Court of Appeal which gave its decision on 15 May 1987. Very little new arose, although Wambūi's lawyers argued that she would have the right to bury her husband under the English common law which applied from the time Kenya became a colony. The court found that there was no such common law and that, had she been appointed administrator of her husband's estate, she would have had the statutory right to bury him. As she had not been so appointed as there was no will, customary law would apply and he would be buried by his brother the late Joash Ochieng Ougo at his family home.<ref>van Doren (1988), ''Death African Style'', pp. 341–2.</ref>

'), Section(title='===Controversies===', content='
Wambūi alleged that the real issue behind the court battle was Otieno's considerable estate, which his brother hoped to claim as his next of kin in Luo terms, and she argued that his clan had a history of seeking money relating to deceased members. However, Wambūi and Otieno had defeated such a claim by registering as many assets as possible in their joint names.<ref>A. Gordon (1995), ''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', p. 884.</ref><ref>Stamp (1991),''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', p. 820.</ref> She also claimed in court that the Umira Kager clan wished her to enter into a [[levirate marriage]] with either Otieno's brother Joash Ochieng Ougo or some other clan member, as the clan would not allow Wambūi to ""walk away to her Kikuyu people with Otieno's property"".<ref>Stamp (1991), ''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', pp. 814, 822.</ref> However, she could not show that any compulsion had been involved.<ref name=""Kenya Law 1987""/>

In the 1980s, most Luo considered land as a permanent asset of the lineage, and burying its members on this land symbolizes the right of the lineage to retain it. They also considered that extended family members should share the wealth of richer members and, by combining these two concepts, the idea emerged among members of Umira Kager clan that burying Otieno on clan land entitled his [[Patrilineality
column32:
patrilineage]] to share in his estate.<ref>Gordon (1995), ''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', pp. 896–7.</ref>

Wambūi claimed that the Kenyan President, [[Daniel arap Moi]] supported the Luo and provided legal representation and funding to fight the case, as Wambūi was both a member of the formerly dominant Kikuyu group and a leader of the movement opposing Moi's autocratic regime.<ref>Gordon (1995),''Gender, Ethnicity and Class in Kenya'', p. 885.</ref> She also questioned the neutrality of the Appeal Court judges<ref>Stamp (1991), ''Burying Otieno: The Politics of Gender and Ethnicity'', p. 822.</ref> However, van Doren, a professor of Law, reports that Wambūi counsel could not point to actual prejudice by these judges and considers that they and the High Court judge dealt as best they could with a situation where the relevant statute requires judges to have regard to African customary law.<ref>van Doren (1988), ''Death African Style'' pp 341, 345–7.</ref>

In the 30 years since the Otieno burial case, the Kenyan [[jurisprudence]] on burials has evolved to some degree. In 1996, the courts ruled that the circumstances of the deceased person's life had to be considered as well as customary laws, in 2004 held the wishes of the wife of the deceased and, in 2010 the wishes of the deceased, while not binding, should be taken into account.<ref>Mukaindo (2011), ''Revisiting the S M Otieno Case''.</ref>

'), Section(title='== Later life ==', content='
Her 2003 marriage to Peter Mbūgua was the subject of a national controversy. Many of their relatives condemned the marriage. There have been allegations that the death of Mbūgua's mother, which happened only days after the marriage, was caused by the shock she got upon learning of the marriage.<ref name=""till"">Daily Nation, Saturday Magazine, October 3, 2010: [http://www.nation.co.ke/magazines/saturday/-/1216/476880/-/item/0/-/sh0xf3z/-/index.html Till death do us part... ]</ref>

As of 2008, they were living together with her stonemason husband in [[Karen, Kenya
column33: Karen]], [[Nairobi]].<ref name=""till"" />  In February 2011 they held a second wedding ceremony,  now at [[St. Andrew\'s Church, Nairobi
column34: St. Andrew\'s Church]] in Nairobi, while the first wedding had been a civil ceremony.<ref>\'\'Daily Nation\'\', February 4, 2011: [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/Wambui%20and%20Mbugua%20cap%20their%20marriage%20with%20church%20wedding%20/-/1056/1101826/-/7jac19/-/index.html ""Wambui and Mbugua cap marriage with church wedding""].</ref>\n\nWambūi had suffered heart failure previously and was relying on a [[pacemaker]], an electronic gadget implanted to function as the heart does. Wambūi Otieno died on August 30, 2011, in a Nairobi hospital.<ref>{{cite web
column36: title=Daily Nation: – Politics {{pipe}}Former freedom fighter Wambui dies in Nairobi
column39:
access-date=2011-08-30}}</ref>

Before her death, Wambūi distributed most of her assets including properties to her children and grandchildren and appointed her two daughters, Gladwell Otieno and Rosalyn Otieno, as her personal representatives in her will to administer what was left. In an echo of the events of 1987, Peter Mbūgua commenced legal proceedings in 2013 on the basis that Wambūi lacked the mental capacity to make a valid will.<ref>Kadida (2013), ''Wambui Otieno's widower says she was mad when she wrote will''.</ref>

column1: '''Veronica Mueni Nduva''', [[Order of the Chief of the Burning Spear
column2: CBS]] (born 1976) is a Kenyan public servant who served as the 7th [[Secretary General of the East African Community]] (EAC) from June 2024 to April 2026. She was the first woman to hold the position.<ref name=""citizen2024"">{{cite web
column3: title=Veronica Mueni Nduva sworn in as first female EAC Secretary General

column1: She succeeded [[Peter Mathuki]] and was sworn into office on 7 June 2024 during the 23rd Extra-Ordinary Meeting of the EAC Heads of State.<ref name=""eac_swearing"">{{cite web
column2: title=New EAC Secretary General sworn in at State House in Juba, South Sudan
column6: access-date=14 April 2026}}</ref> She was succeeded by Stephen Patrick Mbundi of Tanzania.

column1: Prior to her appointment, Nduva served in senior roles in the Government of Kenya, including Principal Secretary for Gender and Affirmative Action and Principal Secretary for Performance and Delivery Management.<ref name=""eac_profile"">{{cite web
Nduva was born in Kenya in 1976. She attended [[State House Girls' High School]] in Nairobi.
She graduated from the [[University of Nairobi]] with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and Public Administration in 2000.<ref name=""kenyatimes2024"">{{cite web
column2: title=Veronica Nduva: First Ever EAC Woman Secretary General
column6: access-date=14 April 2026}}</ref> She later obtained a Master of Arts in Communication from the University of Nairobi.<ref name=""eac_profile""/>

column1: Nduva worked in civil society organisations and governance-related roles in Kenya before joining the United States Embassy in Nairobi.<ref name=""eac_profile""/>
From 2014 to 2022, she served as a Senior Political Specialist and Special Adviser at the United States Embassy in Nairobi.<ref name=""hamburg"">{{cite web
column2: title=Speaker profile: CBS Veronica M. Nduva

column1: In November 2022, Nduva was appointed Principal Secretary for the State Department for Gender and Affirmative Action.<ref name=""eac_profile""/>
In October 2023, she was appointed Principal Secretary for the State Department for Performance and Delivery Management.<ref name=""ps_profile"">{{cite web
column2: title=Principal Secretary — State Department for Performance and Delivery Management

column1: ===Secretary General of the East African Community===
Nduva was appointed Secretary General of the East African Community in June 2024 following the recall of [[Peter Mathuki]].<ref name=""uturn"">{{cite web
column2: title=Kenya makes shock U-turn on its EAC Secretary General nomination

column1: As Secretary General, she served as the head of the EAC Secretariat and Secretary to the Summit of Heads of State.<ref name=""eac_profile""/>
Her tenure coincided with financial constraints within the EAC related to delayed contributions from partner states.<ref name=""kfp"">{{cite web
column2: title=Kenyan Mueni Nduva Sworn in as First Woman EAC Boss

column2: CBS]] (born 1976) is a Kenyan public servant who served as the 7th [[Secretary General of the East African Community]] (EAC) from June 2024 to April 2026. She was the first woman to hold the position.<ref name=""citizen2024"">{{cite web

column6: access-date=14 April 2026}}</ref> She was succeeded by Stephen Patrick Mbundi of Tanzania.

column2: title=Veronica Nduva: First Ever EAC Woman Secretary General
column6: access-date=14 April 2026}}</ref> She later obtained a Master of Arts in Communication from the University of Nairobi.<ref name=""eac_profile""/>

column15: aʊ}}; born 22 September 1957) is a Kenyan politician. She is a former long-standing member of parliament for [[Gichugu Constituency]] and an Advocate of the [[High Court (Kenya)
column16: High Court of Kenya]]. She was [[Minister of Justice (Kenya)
column17: Minister for Justice]] until resigning from that position in April 2009. She has consistently fought for the protection of [[women's rights]] and improvements to the democratic process.<ref name=aljazeera/>

column1: Karua ran for presidency in 2013 under the [[Narc-Kenya]] ticket making her the third woman to run for the highest office, after [[Charity Ngilu]] and [[Wangari Maathai]] in the [[1997 Kenyan general election
column2: 1997 elections]]. She emerged sixth in the race. She was picked to run for deputy president after being nominated as the running mate of presidential candidate [[Raila Odinga]] in the [[2022 Kenyan general election]].<ref>{{Cite news
column4: title=Kenya elections 2022: Raila Odinga picks Martha Karua as running mate
column8: access-date=2022-05-16}}</ref> Karua later rebranded NARC Kenya to the People's Liberation Party (PLP) in February 2025.

column1: The daughter of Jackson Karua and his wife Josephine Wanjiru, Martha Karua was born on 22 September 1957 in the then larger [[Embu District]] (later [[Kirinyaga District]]) in the [[Central Province (Kenya)
column2: Central Province]] of Kenya. Brought up in the village of Kimunye in [[Gichugu Constituency]],<ref>Gichugu Constituency</ref> she is the second child in a family of eight, four girls and four boys.<ref name=""sk"">{{cite web
column3: title=Martha Karua Biography, Family, Husband and Children

column1: She attended Mugumo primary school, Kabare Girls Boarding School, St Michael's boarding school [[Kerugoya
column2: Keroguya]]. She later attended Kiburia Girls Secondary School, Ngiriambu Girl's secondary school, and Karoti Girl's secondary schools where she passed her East African School Certificate at Karoti Girls High School in [[Kirinyaga County]]. She then attended Nairobi Girl's secondary school for A levels.<ref>{{cite news
column8: accessdate=15 February 2017 }}</ref> She studied law at the [[University of Nairobi]] from 1977 to 1980. Between 1980 and 1981 she was enrolled at the [[Kenya School of Law]] for the statutory postgraduate law course that is a prerequisite to admission to the Kenyan roll of advocates and licensing to practice law in Kenya.<ref name=foundry/>

column1: After graduating, from 1981 to 1987 Karua worked as a [[magistrate]] in various courts including those at [[Makadara Constituency
column2: Makadara]], [[Nakuru]] and [[Kibera]], receiving credit for careful discernment.<ref name=sk/> In 1987, she left to start her own law firm, '''Martha Karua & Co. Advocates''', which she ran until 2002. Cases included the treason trial of [[Koigi Wamwere]] and that of the Kenyan member of parliament Mirugi Kariuki.<ref name=foundry/><ref>{{cite web
column4: title=Interview conducted and recorded by Robert M. Press
column8: accessdate=16 February 2017 }}</ref> At the risk of being blacklisted by the [[Daniel arap Moi
column9: Moi government]], she defended several [[human rights]] activists.<ref name=sk/> Her work contributed to [[family law]], especially in regard to matrimonial property.<ref name=sk/>

column1: Karua has also represented opposition figures in other African countries, including [[Kizza Besigye]] in Uganda, and [[Tundu Lissu]] in Tanzania. On 18 May 2025, Karua was arrested and deported upon arrival at [[Julius Nyerere International Airport]] in [[Dar es Salaam]] to represent Tundu Lissu in court.<ref>{{cite news
column3: title=Kenyan presidential candidate and lawyer deported from Tanzania

column1: Karua was a member of the opposition political movements that successfully agitated for the re-introduction of multi-party democracy in [[Kenya]] in the early 1990s. Kenya was at the time under the authoritarian rule of the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU), the only legally recognised political party in Kenya and which was led by the late president [[Daniel arap Moi]].<ref>{{cite web

Karua joined [[Kenneth Matiba]]'s Ford-Asili party. In September 1992, she walked out of the party nomination elections which she regarded as compromised leaving her sole opponent Geoffrey Karekia Kariithi to be declared winner. She joined the [[Democratic Party (Kenya)
column2: Democratic Party]] (DP) where she won the party ticket in November 1992, proceeded to win the election as [[Gichugu Constituency]] member of Parliament in December 1992 against the incumbent Kareithi, freeing Gichugu constituents from the Kareithi–Nahashon Njuno rivalry. Karua became the MP for Gichugu constituency and the first woman lawyer to be popularly elected to Parliament. She was elected as the Democratic party's legal affairs secretary in 1993.<ref>

1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20220702140747/http://www.eastandard.net/archives/politics/InsidePage.php?id=1144007235&cid=289& It’s not for love of Ruto that Kiraitu cornered Karua]}}, ''The East African Standard'', 22 February 2009

column1: In 1998, Karua declined the position of Shadow Minister for Culture and Social Services which conflicted with her position of National Secretary for Constitutional Affairs (an elected office) that made her the official spokesperson on legal matters of the party. She opted to resign her position as the National Secretary for legal and constitutional Affairs.<ref name=""professional"">[http://www.marthakarua.net/professional.htm www.marthakarua.net] {{webarchive

In 2001, when the Constitutional Review Bill was laid before the House, the entire Opposition with the exception of Karua walked out of Parliament. The Bill had been rejected by the Opposition as well as Civil Society but Karua was of the view that as elected representatives, instead of walking out, it would be more prudent to remain in Parliament and put the objections on record. She therefore chose to remain in the Parliament and her objections to the Bill were duly recorded in the Hansard.<ref name=""professional""/>
Later she was among those who formed the political coalition [[National Rainbow Coalition
column2: NARC]] that won the [[2002 Kenyan general election
column3: 2002 general election in Kenya]] ending KANU's nearly four decades of leadership in Kenya's politics, having actively participated in agitation for expanded democratic space and respect for human rights as a member and later a leader in the [[Law Society of Kenya]].<ref name=aljazeera>{{cite web

column1: Until 6 April 2009 she was the Minister of Justice, National Cohesion & Constitutional Affairs. She also previously served as the Minister of Water Resources Management & Development, and was behind the implementation of the Water Act 2002, which has since then accelerated the pace of water reforms and service provision in Kenya.<ref name=aljazeera/><ref name=sk/>
Karua remained Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister in the Cabinet appointed by Kibaki on 8 January 2008, following the controversial [[2007 Kenyan presidential election
column3: 1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20220819052042/http://www.eastandard.net/archives/InsidePage.php?id=1143980114&cid=4& ""Kibaki Names Cabinet""]}}, ''The Standard'', 8 January 2008.</ref> In an interview with BBC's ''[[HARDtalk]]'' in January 2008, Karua said, regarding the [[Kenyan crisis, 2007-2008
column4: violent crisis]] that had developed over the election results, that while the government had anticipated that the opposition [[Orange Democratic Movement]] (ODM) of [[Raila Odinga]] might be ""planning mayhem if they lost"", it was surprised by ""the magnitude"" of it, calling the violence ""ethnic cleansing"". Asked to clarify, Karua said that she was stating ""categorically"" that the ODM planned ethnic cleansing. Odinga subsequently called Karua's accusation ""outrageous"".<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/7192958.stm ""Odinga denies 'ethnic cleansing'""], BBC News, 16 January 2008.</ref> Karua headed the government's team in negotiations with the opposition regarding the political dispute that resulted from the election.<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/7242451.stm ""Kenya government anger with Annan""], BBC News, 13 February 2008.</ref> The political crisis eventually led to the signing of a power-sharing agreement between Kibaki and Odinga. In the grand coalition Cabinet that was announced on 13 April 2008, Karua remained in her post as Minister of Justice, National Cohesion and Constitutional Affairs.<ref>Anthony Kariuki, [http://politics.nationmedia.com/inner.asp?pcat=NEWS&cat=TOP&sid=1787 ""Kibaki names Raila PM in new Cabinet""]{{dead link

column1: She was endorsed as the national chairperson of the [[NARC-Kenya]] political party on 15 November 2008. There was virtually no competitive election during the party's national delegates' convention at the [[Bomas of Kenya]] in Nairobi as all the officials including Ms Karua were being endorsed. After her endorsement she immediately declared she would be gunning for the highest political seat that being [[President (government title)
column2: President]] in the Kenya's 2012 elections.<ref>MUCHEMI WACHIRA, [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/politics/-/1064/491434/-/yvok78z/-/index.html ""Karua endorsed as Narc Kenya boss ""], Daily Nation, 15 November 2008.</ref>

column1: Karua resigned as Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs on 6 April 2009, citing frustrations in discharging her duties. column2: /wænˈɡɑːri kəˈraʊ/]]; born 22 September 1957) is a Kenyan politician. She is a former long-standing member of parliament for [[Gichugu Constituency]] and an Advocate of the [[High Court (Kenya)
column3: High Court of Kenya]]. She was [[Minister of Justice (Kenya)
column4: Minister for Justice]] until resigning from that position in April 2009. She has consistently fought for the protection of [[women's rights]] and improvements to the democratic process.<ref name=aljazeera/>

column2: 1997 elections]]. She emerged sixth in the race. She was picked to run for deputy president after being nominated as the running mate of presidential candidate [[Raila Odinga]] in the [[2022 Kenyan general election]].<ref>{{Cite news
column4: title=Kenya elections 2022: Raila Odinga picks Martha Karua as running mate
column8: access-date=2022-05-16}}</ref> Karua later rebranded NARC Kenya to the People's Liberation Party (PLP) in February 2025.

column1: The daughter of Jackson Karua and his wife Josephine Wanjiru, Martha Karua was born on 22 September 1957 in the then larger [[Embu District]] (later [[Kirinyaga District]]) in the [[Central Province (Kenya)
column2: Central Province]] of Kenya. Brought up in the village of Kimunye in [[Gichugu Constituency]],<ref>Gichugu Constituency</ref> she is the second child in a family of eight, four girls and four boys.<ref name=""sk"">{{cite web
column3: title=Martha Karua Biography, Family, Husband and Children

column1: She attended Mugumo primary school, Kabare Girls Boarding School, St Michael's boarding school [[Kerugoya
column2: Keroguya]]. She later attended Kiburia Girls Secondary School, Ngiriambu Girl's secondary school, and Karoti Girl's secondary schools where she passed her East African School Certificate at Karoti Girls High School in [[Kirinyaga County]]. She then attended Nairobi Girl's secondary school for A levels.<ref>{{cite news
column8: accessdate=15 February 2017 }}</ref> She studied law at the [[University of Nairobi]] from 1977 to 1980. Between 1980 and 1981 she was enrolled at the [[Kenya School of Law]] for the statutory postgraduate law course that is a prerequisite to admission to the Kenyan roll of advocates and licensing to practice law in Kenya.<ref name=foundry/>

column1: After graduating, from 1981 to 1987 Karua worked as a [[magistrate]] in various courts including those at [[Makadara Constituency
column2: Makadara]], [[Nakuru]] and [[Kibera]], receiving credit for careful discernment.<ref name=sk/> In 1987, she left to start her own law firm, '''Martha Karua & Co. Advocates''', which she ran until 2002. Cases included the treason trial of [[Koigi Wamwere]] and that of the Kenyan member of parliament Mirugi Kariuki.<ref name=foundry/><ref>{{cite web
column4: title=Interview conducted and recorded by Robert M. Press
column8: accessdate=16 February 2017 }}</ref> At the risk of being blacklisted by the [[Daniel arap Moi

column1: Karua has also represented opposition figures in other African countries, including [[Kizza Besigye]] in Uganda, and [[Tundu Lissu]] in Tanzania. On 18 May 2025, Karua was arrested and deported upon arrival at [[Julius Nyerere International Airport]] in [[Dar es Salaam]] to represent Tundu Lissu in court.<ref>{{cite news
column3: title=Kenyan presidential candidate and lawyer deported from Tanzania

column1: Karua was a member of the opposition political movements that successfully agitated for the re-introduction of multi-party democracy in [[Kenya]] in the early 1990s. Kenya was at the time under the authoritarian rule of the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU), the only legally recognised political party in Kenya and which was led by the late president [[Daniel arap Moi]].<ref>{{cite web

Karua joined [[Kenneth Matiba]]'s Ford-Asili party. In September 1992, she walked out of the party nomination elections which she regarded as compromised leaving her sole opponent Geoffrey Karekia Kariithi to be declared winner. She joined the [[Democratic Party (Kenya)
column2: Democratic Party]] (DP) where she won the party ticket in November 1992, proceeded to win the election as [[Gichugu Constituency]] member of Parliament in December 1992 against the incumbent Kareithi, freeing Gichugu constituents from the Kareithi–Nahashon Njuno rivalry. Karua became the MP for Gichugu constituency and the first woman lawyer to be popularly elected to Parliament. She was elected as the Democratic party's legal affairs secretary in 1993.<ref>

column1: In 1998, Karua declined the position of Shadow Minister for Culture and Social Services which conflicted with her position of National Secretary for Constitutional Affairs (an elected office) that made her the official spokesperson on legal matters of the party. She opted to resign her position as the National Secretary for legal and constitutional Affairs.<ref name=""professional"">[http://www.marthakarua.net/professional.htm www.marthakarua.net] {{webarchive

In 2001, when the Constitutional Review Bill was laid before the House, the entire Opposition with the exception of Karua walked out of Parliament. The Bill had been rejected by the Opposition as well as Civil Society but Karua was of the view that as elected representatives, instead of walking out, it would be more prudent to remain in Parliament and put the objections on record. She therefore chose to remain in the Parliament and her objections to the Bill were duly recorded in the Hansard.<ref name=""professional""/>
Later she was among those who formed the political coalition [[National Rainbow Coalition
column2: NARC]] that won the [[2002 Kenyan general election
column3: 2002 general election in Kenya]] ending KANU's nearly four decades of leadership in Kenya's politics, having actively participated in agitation for expanded democratic space and respect for human rights as a member and later a leader in the [[Law Society of Kenya]].<ref name=aljazeera>{{cite web

column1: Until 6 April 2009 she was the Minister of Justice, National Cohesion & Constitutional Affairs. She also previously served as the Minister of Water Resources Management & Development, and was behind the implementation of the Water Act 2002, which has since then accelerated the pace of water reforms and service provision in Kenya.<ref name=aljazeera/><ref name=sk/>
Karua remained Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister in the Cabinet appointed by Kibaki on 8 January 2008, following the controversial [[2007 Kenyan presidential election
column3: 1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20220819052042/http://www.eastandard.net/archives/InsidePage.php?id=1143980114&cid=4& ""Kibaki Names Cabinet""]}}, ''The Standard'', 8 January 2008.</ref> In an interview with BBC's ''[[HARDtalk]]'' in January 2008, Karua said, regarding the [[Kenyan crisis, 2007-2008
column4: violent crisis]] that had developed over the election results, that while the government had anticipated that the opposition [[Orange Democratic Movement]] (ODM) of [[Raila Odinga]] might be ""planning mayhem if they lost"", it was surprised by ""the magnitude"" of it, calling the violence ""ethnic cleansing"". Asked to clarify, Karua said that she was stating ""categorically"" that the ODM planned ethnic cleansing. Odinga subsequently called Karua's accusation ""outrageous"".<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/7192958.stm ""Odinga denies 'ethnic cleansing'""], BBC News, 16 January 2008.</ref> Karua headed the government's team in negotiations with the opposition regarding the political dispute that resulted from the election.<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/7242451.stm ""Kenya government anger with Annan""], BBC News, 13 February 2008.</ref> The political crisis eventually led to the signing of a power-sharing agreement between Kibaki and Odinga. In the grand coalition Cabinet that was announced on 13 April 2008, Karua remained in her post as Minister of Justice, National Cohesion and Constitutional Affairs.<ref>Anthony Kariuki, [http://politics.nationmedia.com/inner.asp?pcat=NEWS&cat=TOP&sid=1787 ""Kibaki names Raila PM in new Cabinet""]{{dead link

column131: Moi government]], she defended several [[human rights]] activists.<ref name=sk/> Her work contributed to [[family law]], especially in regard to matrimonial property.<ref name=sk/>\n\nKarua has also represented opposition figures in other African countries, including [[Kizza Besigye]] in Uganda, and [[Tundu Lissu]] in Tanzania. On 18 May 2025, Karua was arrested and deported upon arrival at [[Julius Nyerere International Airport]] in [[Dar es Salaam]] to represent Tundu Lissu in court.<ref>{{cite news
column133: title=Kenyan presidential candidate and lawyer deported from Tanzania
column136:
