'), Section(title='=== 1990–2002 ===', content='
Karua was a member of the opposition political movements that successfully agitated for the re-introduction of multi-party democracy in [[Kenya]] in the early 1990s. Kenya was at the time under the authoritarian rule of the [[Kenya African National Union]] (KANU), the only legally recognised political party in Kenya and which was led by the late president [[Daniel arap Moi]].<ref>{{cite web
column142: accessdate=19 February 2017 }}</ref>\n\nKarua joined [[Kenneth Matiba]]\'s Ford-Asili party. In September 1992, she walked out of the party nomination elections which she regarded as compromised leaving her sole opponent Geoffrey Karekia Kariithi to be declared winner. She joined the [[Democratic Party (Kenya)
column143: Democratic Party]] (DP) where she won the party ticket in November 1992, proceeded to win the election as [[Gichugu Constituency]] member of Parliament in December 1992 against the incumbent Kareithi, freeing Gichugu constituents from the Kareithi–Nahashon Njuno rivalry. Karua became the MP for Gichugu constituency and the first woman lawyer to be popularly elected to Parliament. She was elected as the Democratic party\'s legal affairs secretary in 1993.<ref>\nGakuu Mathenge {{usurped
column144:
1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20220702140747/http://www.eastandard.net/archives/politics/InsidePage.php?id=1144007235&cid=289& It’s not for love of Ruto that Kiraitu cornered Karua]}}, ''The East African Standard'', 22 February 2009 
</ref>

In 1998, Karua declined the position of Shadow Minister for Culture and Social Services which conflicted with her position of National Secretary for Constitutional Affairs (an elected office) that made her the official spokesperson on legal matters of the party. She opted to resign her position as the National Secretary for legal and constitutional Affairs.<ref name=""professional"">[http://www.marthakarua.net/professional.htm www.marthakarua.net] {{webarchive
column146:
date=23 July 2011 }}</ref>

In 2001, when the Constitutional Review Bill was laid before the House, the entire Opposition with the exception of Karua walked out of Parliament. The Bill had been rejected by the Opposition as well as Civil Society but Karua was of the view that as elected representatives, instead of walking out, it would be more prudent to remain in Parliament and put the objections on record. She therefore chose to remain in the Parliament and her objections to the Bill were duly recorded in the Hansard.<ref name=""professional""/>

Later she was among those who formed the political coalition [[National Rainbow Coalition
column147: NARC]] that won the [[2002 Kenyan general election
column148: 2002 general election in Kenya]] ending KANU\'s nearly four decades of leadership in Kenya\'s politics, having actively participated in agitation for expanded democratic space and respect for human rights as a member and later a leader in the [[Law Society of Kenya]].<ref name=aljazeera>{{cite web
column153:
accessdate=19 February 2017 }}</ref>

'), Section(title='=== 2003–2009 ===', content='
Until 6 April 2009 she was the Minister of Justice, National Cohesion & Constitutional Affairs. She also previously served as the Minister of Water Resources Management & Development, and was behind the implementation of the Water Act 2002, which has since then accelerated the pace of water reforms and service provision in Kenya.<ref name=aljazeera/><ref name=sk/>

Karua remained Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister in the Cabinet appointed by Kibaki on 8 January 2008, following the controversial [[2007 Kenyan presidential election
column155: 1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20220819052042/http://www.eastandard.net/archives/InsidePage.php?id=1143980114&cid=4& ""Kibaki Names Cabinet""]}}, \'\'The Standard\'\', 8 January 2008.</ref> In an interview with BBC\'s \'\'[[HARDtalk]]\'\' in January 2008, Karua said, regarding the [[Kenyan crisis, 2007-2008
column156: violent crisis]] that had developed over the election results, that while the government had anticipated that the opposition [[Orange Democratic Movement]] (ODM) of [[Raila Odinga]] might be ""planning mayhem if they lost"", it was surprised by ""the magnitude"" of it, calling the violence ""ethnic cleansing"". Asked to clarify, Karua said that she was stating ""categorically"" that the ODM planned ethnic cleansing. Odinga subsequently called Karua\'s accusation ""outrageous"".<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/7192958.stm ""Odinga denies \'ethnic cleansing\'""], BBC News, 16 January 2008.</ref> Karua headed the government\'s team in negotiations with the opposition regarding the political dispute that resulted from the election.<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/7242451.stm ""Kenya government anger with Annan""], BBC News, 13 February 2008.</ref> The political crisis eventually led to the signing of a power-sharing agreement between Kibaki and Odinga. In the grand coalition Cabinet that was announced on 13 April 2008, Karua remained in her post as Minister of Justice, National Cohesion and Constitutional Affairs.<ref>Anthony Kariuki, [http://politics.nationmedia.com/inner.asp?pcat=NEWS&cat=TOP&sid=1787 ""Kibaki names Raila PM in new Cabinet""]{{dead link
column159: fix-attempted=yes }}, nationmedia.com, 13 April 2008.</ref>\n\nShe was endorsed as the national chairperson of the [[NARC-Kenya]] political party on 15 November 2008. There was virtually no competitive election during the party\'s national delegates\' convention at the [[Bomas of Kenya]] in Nairobi as all the officials including Ms Karua were being endorsed. After her endorsement she immediately declared she would be gunning for the highest political seat that being [[President (government title)
column160:
President]] in the Kenya's 2012 elections.<ref>MUCHEMI WACHIRA, [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/politics/-/1064/491434/-/yvok78z/-/index.html ""Karua endorsed as Narc Kenya boss ""], Daily Nation, 15 November 2008.</ref>

Karua resigned as Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs on 6 April 2009, citing frustrations in discharging her duties. A clear example of her frustrations was when President [[Mwai Kibaki]] appointed Judges without her knowledge a few days before her resignation.<ref>ANTHONY KARIUKI, [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/politics/-/1064/557608/-/yexrmcz/-/index.html Kenya Justice minister Karua resigns], ''Daily Nation'', 6 April 2009.</ref> She was the first Minister to resign voluntarily since 2003.

'), Section(title='=== 2013–present ===', content=""
Karua contested the [[2013 Kenyan presidential election]], under the [[National Rainbow Coalition – Kenya
column161: NARC Kenya]] party ticket. New Kenyan law barred presidential contenders from simultaneously seeking a parliamentary seat, so she had to give up her interest in her somewhat safe Gichugu seat, with potential risk of being cast out of politics altogether (if she lost her presidential bid). She came in sixth with 43,881 votes in a contested election outcome.<ref>{{cite news
column163: title=Karua concedes defeat, ready to work with Uhuru
column167: accessdate=19 February 2017 }}</ref>\n\nMartha Karua would make a come-back in Kenya's political scene in the [[2017 Kenyan general election
column168: 2017 general election]] seeking for a gubernatorial seat in [[Kirinyaga County]]. She lost to [[Anne Waiguru]] in a heavily contested election after garnering 122,091 votes against Waiguru's 161,373 votes. Karua contested the election citing election irregularities and filed a petition at the High Court seeking to have Waiguru's election nullified, losing the petition at the High court through Court of Appeal and ultimately at the Supreme Court. Karua proceeded to file a petition in the [[East African Court of Justice]], suing Kenyan government for failure of its Judicial arm to dispense justice in the petition.<ref>{{cite news
column170: title=Karua loses Supreme Court petition against Waiguru's election
column176: title=To Murgor and Aukot: Save face, leave before it's too late
column183: url-status=dead}}</ref> She was among the opposition leaders who US President [[Barack Obama]] met when he was hosted by [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] in 2015 in Obama's only presidential visit to Kenya.<ref>{{cite news
column185: title=This is what Obama told Martha Karua - She has had sleepless nights for two weeks
column191: url-status=dead}}</ref> Politically, she seems to have inclined toward [[Coalition for Reforms and Democracy
column192: CORD]], the main opposition political outfit led by [[Raila Odinga]].<ref>{{cite web
column194: title=Martha Karua Speaks about her Relationship with Raila Odinga
column200: url-status=dead}}</ref> Karua later abandoned her political relationship with Raila and supported [[Jubilee Party]] ahead of the [[2017 Kenyan general election]].<ref>{{cite news
column202: title=Martha Karua meets Raila Odinga after ditching him
column206:
accessdate=19 February 2017 }}</ref>

In December 2015 Karua admitted to receiving a Ksh 2 million donation to her presidential campaign costs from [[British American Tobacco]]. Karua said that she thought that the contribution by Paul Hopkins, a BAT employee, was a personal donation. The money was paid via [[Mary M'Mukindia]] who was running Karua's campaign. Karua has the reputation of being untainted by corruption save for this report of donation of alleged tainted money. No culpability has been proven and the British investigations concluded without any charges against Paul Hopkins. Karua has maintained that she cannot be corrupted and invited Kenyan authorities to investigate any alleged wrongdoing.

On 20 September 2021, Karua was unanimously elected as the Interim Mount Kenya Unity Forum Spokesperson by a section of leaders from Central Kenya. {{blockquote
column207: We have chosen Martha Karua to be our official convener and our spokesperson
column211: Azimio la Umoja–One Kenya Coalition Party]] in August 2022 would have made her the first Kenyan woman Deputy President, and the highest ranking Kenyan woman in history.<ref>{{Cite news
column212: title=Kenya elections 2022: Raila Odinga names Martha Karua as running mate
column215:
access-date=2022-05-25}}</ref>

""), Section(title='=== Reputation ===', content=""
At one time in her [[Kirinyaga District]] when [[Kenya African National Union
column216: KANU]] was still in power, Karua walked out on [[Daniel arap Moi
column217: President Moi]] who was then addressing a crowd at the district's stadium. This was an unusual display of open defiance against Moi, who was then feared and ruled the country as an [[authoritarian]].<ref>{{cite news
column219: title=Kenya: Karua: Why I Walked Out on Moi
column225: title=The other side of Martha Karua
column229: accessdate=19 February 2017 }}</ref>\n\nShe has been an activist for the widening of democratic space and gender issues in Kenya. She has been involved in championing women's rights through public interest litigation, lobbying and advocacy for laws that enhance and protect women's rights. This was through her work with various women's organizations, particularly the International Federation of Women Lawyers (FIDA-Kenya) and the League of Kenya Women Voters.<ref name=aljazeera/><ref>{{cite web
column231: title=Impacts of Women in Political Leadership in Kenya: Struggle for Participation in Governance through Affirmative Action
column234: accessdate=19 February 2017 }}</ref><ref>Bernard Namunane and David Mugonyi, [http://www.nation.co.ke/News/-/1056/531732/-/u2fqgu/-/index.html Chaos in cabinet as Karua and Ruto clash], ''Daily Nation'', 17 February 2009.</ref>\n\nKarua is part of the legal team for the Ugandan opposition politician [[Kizza Besigye]]. On 22 June 2026, she was arbitrarily detained at [[Entebbe International Airport]] before being forcibly deported from [[Uganda]].<ref>{{Cite news
column236: title=Uganda: Authorities must investigate unlawful detention and deportation of Kenyan human rights lawyer
column243:
language=en}}</ref>

column1: Lucy Mūthon'''i''' was born in 1936. Her parents were Rev. John Kagai, a pastor of the [[Presbyterian Church of East Africa]] and Rose Nyachomba, in [[Mukurwe-ini]], [[Nyeri County]], (formerly Nyeri District in [[Central Province (Kenya)
column8: last=Obwocha}}</ref> She was educated at [[Alliance Girls High School]],<ref>{{cite web
column10: title=Alliance Girls High School: Historical Perspectives
column16: url-status=usurped }}</ref> then trained as a teacher, working first at Kamwenja Teachers College and later at Kambui College in [[Kiambu]], where she rose to the post of principal.<ref name=""NationObit""/>

column1: She met [[Emilio Mwai Kibaki]] in 1959. After a two-year romance, they married in 1961, with Lucy quitting her teaching career in 1963.<ref name=""NationObit""/> They had four children.
Lucy died on 26 April 2016 at [[Bupa Cromwell Hospital]] in London, after a brief hospitalization at the Nairobi Hospital for chest pains.<ref name=""NationObit""/> She was 80.

column1: '''Nerima Wako-Ojiwa''' (née '''Nerima Wako'''), is a Kenyan [[political analyst]], who serves as the [[executive director]] of '''Siasa Place''', an organization, led by young people that engages young Kenyans,<ref name=""1R"">{{cite web
column5: title=Nerima Wako: The political analyst with beauty and brains
column8: location=Nairobi}}</ref> educating them about the constitution, governance and electoral processes, through community engagements and [[social media]].<ref name=""2R"">{{cite web
column10: title=Youth should be an advantage, not a limitation

column1: Nerima was born in [[Nairobi]], Kenya's capital, circa 1989, the third-born in a family of four children. She attended St. Nicholas Primary School, before finishing her high school at Aga Khan Academy, both in Nairobi.<ref name=""1R""/>
After high school, she secured a scholarship to study at [[Jacksonville State University]], in [[Jacksonville, Alabama
column2: Jacksonville]], [[Alabama]] in the United States. She graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[Journalism]] and [[Sociology]]. Later, she was awarded a [[Master of Public Administration]] degree, also by Jacksonville State University.<ref name=""1R""/>

column1: While at university, Nerima participated in [[campus politics]] and was elected president of the International Student's Organization. This allowed her to receive a solid grounding in her political attributes and weaknesses.<ref name=""1R""/><ref name=""2R""/>
In 2015, she together with other young people started a youth-led organization called Siasa Place.<ref name=""3R"">{{cite web

date=10 September 2017}}</ref> For the first year, they funded the organization's operations out of their own pockets, before they received any outside funding. Nerima serves as the executive director.<ref name=""1R""/><ref name=""2R""/>
In 2024, she publicly condemned the creation of [[Artificial intelligence
column2: AI]]-based jobs by [[American companies]] in [[Kenya]],<ref>{{Cite web
column12: title=Kenyan workers with AI jobs thought they had tickets to the future until the grim reality set in
column16: language=en-US}}</ref> which she labeled as ""modern-like [[slavery]]"".<ref>{{Cite web
column20: title=Kenyans who trained OpenAI models decry poor pay, working conditions

column4: title=Celebrating Women: Nerima Wako-Ojiwa: Political Analyst
column12: url-status=dead }}</ref> She is a niece to Senator [[Amos Wako]] who represents  [[Busia County]] in the [[Senate of Kenya

column1: '''Dennitah Ghati''' is a [[Kenyan]] politician who is a nominated member of the [[Kenya National Assembly]], representing people with disabilities. She is a member of the  [[Orange Democratic Movement]].<ref name=Kenya-parliament>{{cite web

Dennitah Ghati was born in 1980 in a rural village in [[Migori]] and attended Kenya Institute of Mass Communication in Nairobi and [[Kenyatta University]] before working as a journalist at The East African Standard Newspaper.<ref name=ksm>{{cite web
column3: title=I was on top of the world then disability struck: MP Dennitah Ghatis's story

column1: Ghati obtained a scholarship to [[Columbia University]] in the USA where she obtained a Master's degree and worked in New York for the American Jewish World Service. She subsequently worked for the League of Kenyan Women Voters and as a program manager for UNICEF Somalia.<ref name=Kenya-parliament/>
Ghati was elected to the National Assembly at the [[2013 Kenyan general election
column2: 2013 general election]] as the [[County woman representative (Kenya)
column3: woman representative]] for [[Migori]] county with a majority of 51%, representing the [[Orange Democratic Movement]].<ref>{{cite book
column6: publisher= Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission
column7: page= <!-- or pages= --> }}</ref> Following the election the Peoples' Democratic Party candidate Fatuma Zainabu Mohammed challenged the election result in court, alleging intimidation, vote buying and bribery. The case was dismissed confirming Ghati's election.<ref>{{cite web

column1: In 2014 she was involved in a road traffic accident in which she suffered a broken spine, leaving her permanently disabled. She now uses a wheelchair.<ref>{{cite web
column3: title=If I could walk again: Former Migori County Women Representative Dennitah Ghati speaks out on the accident that left her crippled

column1: In 2017 Ghati was nominated by the ODM to serve in one of the appointed seats in the national assembly as one of 12 members nominated by the political parties.<ref name=members>{{cite web
column5: access-date=7 August 2020}}</ref> These 12 un-elected seats were introduced by the [[Constitution of Kenya]] in 2010 to represent the special interests of youth, persons with disabilities and workers.<ref>{{cite web
column7: title= FACTSHEET: Kenya's new parliament by numbers
column12: access-date=10 September 2020}}</ref> Ghati is a representative of people with disabilities.<ref name=ksm/>

column2: woman representative]] for [[Uasin Gishu]] County<ref name=Kenya-parliament>{{cite web
column8: bot=InternetArchiveBot }}.</ref> She is a member of the [[United Democratic Alliance (Kenya)

column1: Gladys obtained a Bachelor of Laws degree from the [[University of Nairobi]], a Diploma in Law from Kenya School of Law, a master's degree from the [[University of Cape Town]], and an MBA from [[Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology]].<ref name=Kenya-parliament/>

column8: title=I was sacked unfairly, Gladys tells court in plaint

column13: title=Gladys was lawfully sacked, court says
column16: date=19 September 2014}}</ref> In 2017 she was acquitted of criminal charges of corruption and abuse of office.<ref>{{cite web
column18: title=State withdraws abuse of office charges against Gladys Shollei

column1: She was elected to the National Assembly as woman representative for Uasin Gishu in the [[2017 Kenyan general election
column2: 2017 general election]], representing the Jubilee Party. She is chairperson of the Committee on Delegated Legislation.<ref name=Kenya-parliament/>

column3: title=Gladys Boss seeks to scrap post of Woman Rep

column1: She sponsored the Kenya Reparations Bill 2019 that seeks to provide compensation for victims of historic human rights abuses.<ref>{{cite web

column1: Joyce Laboso was elected to the [[Parliament of Kenya]] to represent the [[Sotik Constituency]] in a [[by-election]] held on 25 September 2008. She succeeded her sister, [[Lorna Laboso]], who died in a plane crash. A nominee of the [[Jubilee Party]], she beat 11 other contestants after she garnered 23,880 with  a vote margin of 10,000 over her closest challenger, retired '''Brigadier Alexander Sitienei''' (a former aide to [[Daniel arap Moi]]) who received 13,843 votes.
She was the [[African, Caribbean and Pacific Group of States
column2: ACP]] Co-president of the [[ACP–EU Joint Parliamentary Assembly]].<ref>[http://www.europarl.europa.eu/intcoop/acp/10_01/default_en.htm ""ACP-EU""]. ''www.europarl.europa.eu''.</ref>

column1: She worked as a lecturer in the Department of Language and Linguistics at [[Egerton University]] and served as a Commissioner of the National Commission on [[Gender and Development]].<ref>Makiche, Edwin (23 April 2013). [http://www.standardmedia.co.ke/?articleID=2000082161&story_title=the-rise-and-rise-of-joyce-laboso ""The rise and rise of Joyce Laboso""]. standardmedia.co.ke</ref>
Laboso was one of three first female governors in Kenya, along with Kitui County Governor [[Charity Ngilu]]<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Charity Ngilu wins round 2 : The Standard
column5: accessdate=30 July 2019}}</ref> and Kirinyaga County Governor [[Anne Waiguru]].<ref>{{Cite web
column7: title=Waiguru win upheld, Karua moves to top court : The Standard
column9: accessdate=30 July 2019}}</ref> Laboso beat Isaac Rutto, the incumbent who had joined NASA Coalition. Rutto later conceded defeat in public.<ref>{{Cite web
column11: title=Ruto asked to concede defeat after losing tragically in Bomet

column1: Laboso attended Kaplong and Molo Primary Schools, before proceeding to Kaplong Girls Secondary School to pursue her [[GCE Ordinary Level
column2: O-Level]]. She later joined [[Kenya High School
column3: The Kenya High School]] where she sat for her [[A level]].

column1: Laboso was first diagnosed with cancer in 1991. According to her husband, Edwin, Laboso managed to survive cancer for 28 years. The disease struck her again severely in March 2019. The family sought medical attention both in the UK and India, unfortunately, the doctors informed them that nothing much could be done to save the governor's life. She later succumbed to cancer on 29 July 2019 at Nairobi Hospital. A requiem service for her was conducted on 2 August 2019 and her burial was held at her home in Fort Ternan, Kisumu County on 3 August 2019.<ref>{{Cite web

She served as the Cabinet Secretary for Foreign Affairs of Kenya from May 2013 to February 2018, when President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], after re-election, moved her to the Education docket.<ref name=""Amsiafas"">{{cite news

column1: Mohamed was born on 5 October 1961 in [[Kakamega County
column3: ethnic Somali]] family. She is the eighth of nine siblings.<ref name=""Ftstubb"">{{cite news
column6: title=From tiny schoolgirl to Unep big boss
column10: date=14 August 2011}}</ref> Her family belongs to the [[Dhulbahante]] clan,<ref name=""Wadekogs"">{{cite news
column15: date=23 April 2013}}</ref> and hails from the [[Sool]] region in [[Somalia]].<ref name=""Tskatupso"">{{cite news
column16: title=Somali-Kenyan appointed to UN post (SSC origin)
column23: archive-date=27 September 2013 }}</ref> Mohamed spent her childhood in a modest household in Amalemba, [[Kakamega]], where she passed much of her time reading [[Sherlock Holmes]] stories and other detective fiction. She later developed a taste for international affairs.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/>

column1: For her elementary studies, Mohamed attended the Township Primary School in Kakamega and later [[Butere Girls]] and Highlands Academy. Her mother believed strongly in the importance of education, and would frequently drop by her classes to monitor her performance. Upon graduation, Mohamed moved to [[Ukraine]] on a scholarship to study at the [[Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv
column2: University of Kyiv]].<ref name=""Ftstubb""/> She completed the institution's courses, earning a [[Master of Laws]] (LLM) in [[international law]]. Mohamed later obtained a [[postgraduate diploma
column3: Postgraduate Diploma]] (PGDip) in [[international relations]] from the [[University of Oxford]]. Through a Fellowship at the [[United Nations Institute for Training and Research]] (UNITAR), she also followed several training courses on international law.<ref name=""Wtoam"">{{cite web
column4: title=AMBASSADOR AMINA C. MOHAMED, CBS, CAV

column1: In 2002, Amina Mohamed married her late husband Khalid Ahmed Hossain, a Bengali businessman to whom she credited a lot of her success. Ms Mohamed has a son from her marriage to Mr Hossain, two step-children from Hossain's previous marriage, and also cares for four orphans.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/>
Mohamed is multilingual, speaking her native [[Somali language
column5: Swahili]], with a working knowledge of [[French language
column7: title=Meet Amina Mohamed, Kenya's Best Cabinet Minister

column1: Mohamed began her career in 1985 as a legal officer at the Kenyan Ministry of Local Government. Her duties included assessing [[World Bank]] projects and tabling municipal by-laws.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/> Between 1986 and 1990, Mohamed served as a Legal Advisor in Kenya's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, where she drafted and negotiated various bilateral and international treaties.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/><ref name=""faffairske"">{{cite web
column5: publisher=Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kenya
column9: url-status=dead}}</ref> Among these were Bilateral Air Services Agreements with the [[United Arab Emirates]], [[Oman]], [[Iran]] and the [[United Kingdom]], as well as the African Convention on the Rights of the Child. Although a number of job opportunities overseas were available, Mohamed chose to remain with her parents as her father was ailing.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/>

column1: From 1990 to 1993, Mohamed served as a Legal Advisor to Kenya's mission at the UN head office in [[Geneva]], [[Switzerland]].<ref name=""Ftstubb""/><ref name=""faffairske""/> There, she worked alongside officials from the [[International Labour Organization]], [[World Health Organization]] and [[General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade]]/[[World Trade Organization]].<ref name=""Ftstubb""/> She took a brief sabbatical to pursue higher studies in the UK, before returning to diplomatic service in Geneva. In 1997, Mohamed began serving as Legal Advisor to the Kenyan delegation at the [[UN Security Council]].<ref name=""faffairske""/>
===Roles in Kenya and with the UN===

Between 2000 and 2006, Mohamed worked as the Ambassador and Permanent Representative for the Kenya diplomatic mission in Geneva. column62: Somali]] descent. She is the immediate former Cabinet Secretary for Sports, Heritage and Culture in Kenya.<ref>{{Cite web
column66: title=Echesa sacked in new Cabinet reshuffle as Amina moved from Education » Capital News
column70: language=en-US}}</ref> She previously served as chairwoman of the [[International Organization for Migration]] and the [[World Trade Organization]]\'s General Council, as well as Assistant Secretary-General and Deputy Executive Director of the [[United Nations Environment Programme]].  She served as the Cabinet Secretary for Foreign Affairs of Kenya from May 2013 to February 2018, when President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]], after re-election, moved her to the Education docket.<ref name=""Amsiafas"">{{cite news
column71: title=Amina Mohammed sworn-in as Foreign Affairs Secretary
column80: title=Amina Mohamed to carry on with education reforms
column81: date=3 July 2020}}</ref> In March 2019, she was moved to the Sports Ministry replacing Rashid Echesa.<ref>{{Cite web
column82: title=CS Amina Mohammed\'s troubled cabinet career
column87:
language=en-US}}</ref> The KNEC Director, [[George Magoha]], replaced her in the [[Education]] docket.

', sections=[Section(title='==Early life and education==', content='
Mohamed was born on 5 October 1961 in [[Kakamega County
column89: ethnic Somali]] family. She is the eighth of nine siblings.<ref name=""Ftstubb"">{{cite news
column92: title=From tiny schoolgirl to Unep big boss
column96: date=14 August 2011}}</ref> Her family belongs to the [[Dhulbahante]] clan,<ref name=""Wadekogs"">{{cite news
column101: date=23 April 2013}}</ref> and hails from the [[Sool]] region in [[Somalia]].<ref name=""Tskatupso"">{{cite news
column102: title=Somali-Kenyan appointed to UN post (SSC origin)
column109: archive-date=27 September 2013 }}</ref> Mohamed spent her childhood in a modest household in Amalemba, [[Kakamega]], where she passed much of her time reading [[Sherlock Holmes]] stories and other detective fiction. She later developed a taste for international affairs.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/>\n\nFor her elementary studies, Mohamed attended the Township Primary School in Kakamega and later [[Butere Girls]] and Highlands Academy. Her mother believed strongly in the importance of education, and would frequently drop by her classes to monitor her performance. Upon graduation, Mohamed moved to [[Ukraine]] on a scholarship to study at the [[Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv
column110: University of Kyiv]].<ref name=""Ftstubb""/> She completed the institution\'s courses, earning a [[Master of Laws]] (LLM) in [[international law]]. Mohamed later obtained a [[postgraduate diploma
column111: Postgraduate Diploma]] (PGDip) in [[international relations]] from the [[University of Oxford]]. Through a Fellowship at the [[United Nations Institute for Training and Research]] (UNITAR), she also followed several training courses on international law.<ref name=""Wtoam"">{{cite web
column112: title=AMBASSADOR AMINA C. MOHAMED, CBS, CAV
column115:
access-date=7 April 2015}}</ref>

In 2002, Amina Mohamed married her late husband Khalid Ahmed Hossain, a Bengali businessman to whom she credited a lot of her success. Ms Mohamed has a son from her marriage to Mr Hossain, two step-children from Hossain's previous marriage, and also cares for four orphans.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/>

Mohamed is multilingual, speaking her native [[Somali language
column119: Swahili]], with a working knowledge of [[French language
column121: title=Meet Amina Mohamed, Kenya\'s Best Cabinet Minister
column125:
access-date=6 January 2017}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===Legal advisor roles===', content='
Mohamed began her career in 1985 as a legal officer at the Kenyan Ministry of Local Government. Her duties included assessing [[World Bank]] projects and tabling municipal by-laws.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/> Between 1986 and 1990, Mohamed served as a Legal Advisor in Kenya's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, where she drafted and negotiated various bilateral and international treaties.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/><ref name=""faffairske"">{{cite web
column129: publisher=Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kenya
column133:
url-status=dead}}</ref> Among these were Bilateral Air Services Agreements with the [[United Arab Emirates]], [[Oman]], [[Iran]] and the [[United Kingdom]], as well as the African Convention on the Rights of the Child. Although a number of job opportunities overseas were available, Mohamed chose to remain with her parents as her father was ailing.<ref name=""Ftstubb""/>

From 1990 to 1993, Mohamed served as a Legal Advisor to Kenya's mission at the UN head office in [[Geneva]], [[Switzerland]].<ref name=""Ftstubb""/><ref name=""faffairske""/> There, she worked alongside officials from the [[International Labour Organization]], [[World Health Organization]] and [[General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade]]/[[World Trade Organization]].<ref name=""Ftstubb""/> She took a brief sabbatical to pursue higher studies in the UK, before returning to diplomatic service in Geneva. In 1997, Mohamed began serving as Legal Advisor to the Kenyan delegation at the [[UN Security Council]].<ref name=""faffairske""/>

'), Section(title='===Roles in Kenya and with the UN===', content='
Between 2000 and 2006, Mohamed worked as the Ambassador and Permanent Representative for the Kenya diplomatic mission in Geneva. She was also the chairperson, coordinator and spokesperson for the African Group in the [[WTO]]'s [[Human Rights Commission]]. In 2002, Mohamed served as president of the [[Conference on Disarmament]] and was appointed the first female chairperson of the [[International Organization for Migration]].<ref name=""Ftstubb""/><ref name=""faffairske""/> At the time, Kenya was the only African country included in the organization. When approached for the chairmanship, Mohamed agreed to accept the candidacy only if the organization opened up to more African countries.<ref name=""CNBCAfrica_2017""/>

She chaired the Trade Policy Review Body in 2003, and served as the chairman of the [[Dispute Settlement Body]] in 2004.<ref name=""faffairske""/> In 2005, Mohamed became the first woman to chair the [[World Trade Organization General Council
column134: WTO\'s General Council]].<ref name=""Ftstubb""/><ref name=""Amokaadedotuep"">{{cite web
column135: title=Amina Mohamed of Kenya appointed as Deputy Executive Director of the UN Environment Programme
column141:
url-status=dead}}</ref> She was also a Member of the Executive Boards and Committees of the WIPO, ILO, WHO, [[UNCTAD]], [[UNHCR]] and [[UNAIDS]] from 2001 to 2005. Between 2006 and 2007, Mohamed served as Director for both Europe and Commonwealth Countries as well as Diaspora matters for Kenya. She also chaired the Department of Foreign Trade and Economic Affairs' Committee on Strengthening and Restructuring.<ref name=""faffairske""/>

'), Section(title='===Secretary of the Ministry of Justice and the UN===', content='
She was the Permanent Secretary in the [[Ministry of Justice, National Cohesion and Constitutional Affairs (Kenya)
column142:
Ministry of Justice, National Cohesion and Constitutional Affairs of Kenya]] from 2008 to 2011. In that role, in 2010 she supervised the redrafting of the [[Constitution of Kenya]]. During the 2010–2011 calendar year, Mohamed served as the president of the United Nations Conference on Transnational Crime in [[Vienna]].<ref name=""faffairske""/> In July 2011,<ref name=""CNBCAfrica_2017""/> Mohamed was named Assistant Secretary-General and Deputy Executive Director of the [[United Nations Environment Programme]] (UNEP).<ref name=""Amokaadedotuep""/>

'), Section(title='===Cabinet Secretary for Foreign Affairs===', content='
On 23 April 2013, Mohamed was appointed Kenya's Cabinet [[Minister for Foreign Affairs (Kenya)
column143: Secretary for Foreign Affairs]], one of 18 Cabinet Secretary nominees to the new [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] administration.<ref name=""Cupfff"">{{cite news
column146: title=Cabinet: Uhuru picks four fresh faces
column150: date=23 April 2013}}</ref> She was later sworn into office on 20 May 2013 at Sagana State Lodge.<ref name=""Amsiafas""/>\n\nAccording to the \'\'[[Business Daily Africa]]\'\' publication, ""Kenya\'s vigorous lobbying and aggressive [[Pan-Africanism]] agenda gained momentum with the collapse of International and Criminal Court (ICC) cases against Mr [[Uhuru Kenyatta
column152: Ruto]] partly because attributed to Ms Mohamed\'s skillful diplomatic maneuvers.""<ref name=""BusinessDaily_2017""/> The same publication reported that Mohamed by late 2016 had ""come under heavy criticism for remaining tight-lipped over the suffering of Kenyan detainees in [[Ethiopia]]."" Also, in December 2016 she stated that Kenya supported ""[[Saharawi Arab Democratic Republic]]\'s quest for self-rule and its membership of the [[African Union]],"" which proved controversial with [[Morocco]] and other Arab states.<ref name=""BusinessDaily_2017"">{{Citation\n
column153: title =Kenya\'s Amina beaten to top AU post by Chadian rival\n
column157:
access-date =19 May 2017}}</ref> She is currently the chairwoman of the World Trade Organization (WTO) Ministerial Conference.<ref name=""CNBCAfrica_2017""/>

'), Section(title='===African Union Commission Chair Campaign===', content='
In 2017, Mohamed was nominated by President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] to serve as chair of the [[African Union Commission]] (AUC).<ref>{{Cite news
column159: title=Kenya fronts CS Amina Mohamed for AU chair post
column162: access-date=2017-02-01}}</ref> Despite lobbying for the role from the Kenyan government, Mohamed lost the position to [[Moussa Faki]], the foreign affairs minister of [[Chad]].<ref name=""BusinessDaily_2017""/> Uganda afterwards denied reports in February that it had failed to support Mohamed in her bid for AUC chair, stating that ""Uganda wishes to state categorically that our support to the candidature of Amina before and during elections was unequivocal... Uganda wishes to reassure the government and the people of Kenya, and Amina in particular, that we remain a reliable ally and partner given our warm and close relations and our commitment to the EAC integration"". The \'\'[[Daily Nation]]\'\' stated that Burundi and Djibouti were also suspected of withdrawing support, with Tanzania denying it had done so.<ref name=""DailyNation_2017"">{{Citation \n
column167:
access-date =20 May 2017 }}</ref>

'), Section(title='===Other activities===', content='
In late April 2017, she had a series of meetings with US officials such as Senator [[Bob Corker]], [[Thomas A. Shannon Jr.
column168: Tom Shannon]], and Constance Hamilton, where she urged the US to continue to interact with Kenya for the benefit of both nations.<ref>{{Citation\n
column171: title =Kenya: Do Not Sever Ties With Kenya – CS Pleads With US\n
column175: access-date =20 May 2017 }}</ref> On 9 May 2017, she was honored by the [[Japanese government]] at the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace
column176: Imperial Palace]] for ""promoting economic relations between Nairobi and Tokyo"".<ref name=""DailyNation_Sun_2017"">{{Citation\n
column179: title =Foreign Affairs boss Mohamed to receive award\n
column183: access-date =20 May 2017 }}</ref> She was the only African personally invested at the event with the award, the [[Grand Cordon of the Order of the Rising Sun]]. At the time, [[CNBC]] wrote that Mohamed was ""known as an excellent strategist with proven negotiation and managerial skills"".<ref name=""CNBCAfrica_2017"">{{Citation\n
column184: title =Kenya\'s AMB Amina Mohamed conferred one of Japan\'s highest honours\n
column191: url-status =dead\n }}</ref> On 20 May 2017, it was reported that Mohamed had met with Russian foreign minister [[Sergei Lavrov]] in [[Beijing]], afterwards stating that she felt the meetings signaled possible renewed engagements between Kenya and [[Russia]].<ref>{{Citation\n
column194: title =Kenya: Why Uhuru Reached Out to Russian Counterpart Vladimir Putin\n
column198:
access-date = 20 May 2017}}</ref>

'), Section(title='===Cabinet Secretary for Education===', content='
On 26 January 2018, President [[Uhuru Kenyatta
column199: Kenyatta]] appointed Amina Mohammed to be the Education Cabinet Secretary for his second term.<ref name=""Ayega"">{{Cite web
column203: title=Amina named Education CS as Monica Juma takes over at Foreign Affairs » Capital News
column207: language=en-US}}</ref> She pledged to continue with the reforms initiated by her predecessor [[Fred Matiang\'i
column210: title = Amina Mohamed to carry on with education reforms
column213: Ambassador Monica Juma]] was promoted to head the Foreign Affairs docket.\n\nAt the Education Ministry, Amina Mohammed was lauded for the administration of the 2018 national examinations.<ref>{{Cite web
column215: title=What Amina Achieved During Her Tenure As Education Minister
column218:
language=en-US}}</ref> She also achieved a 93% transition of pupils finishing primary school to join high school – the highest in Kenyan history at the time. She also devised and implemented a Special Needs Education policy and restructured the [[Higher Education Loans Board]], which provides student loans in Kenya. Her reforms in the Vocational Training Centres increased enrollment in vocational training by 100%.<ref name=""Ayega""/> She also completed and piloted the Competency-Based Curriculum. However, her decision to delay the implementation of the Curriculum in 2019 proved controversial and she reversed herself on it after a dress-down from President Uhuru Kenyatta. Her decision to lower the entry grade to teacher training colleges to a D was also overturned by the Kenyan High Court. These decisions are thought to have contributed to her being moved to the Sports, Heritage and Culture Ministry in March 2019.

column236: title=Kenya nominates Amina Mohamed to be WTO Director-General
column241: access-date=7 July 2020}}</ref> She proceeded to the second round of the selection process, and was long seen as a frontrunner in diplomatic circles.<ref>{{cite news
column242: title=Factbox: Who's bidding to be next World Trade Organization chief?
column249:

She sits on the Advisory Council of the Africa Prosperity Network, an organisation dedicated to mobilising Africa's private sector to own and drive with greater urgency the continent's economic integration agenda and in collaboration with political and institutional leadership.

column1: '''Susan Wakarura Kihika''' is a Kenyan lawyer, [[politician]], and the first female [[governor]] of [[Nakuru County]]. She was also among the seven female Governors that were elected in the 9 August [[2022 Kenyan general election]] against a total 40 male governors, marking significant progress from the three female governors that had been elected in the 2017 elections.<ref>{{Cite web
column4: title=History as Kenyans elect seven women governors

column1: She was elected as a [[Senate of Kenya
column5: title=History as Kenya set to have first elected women senators

column4: location=Nairobi}}</ref> on the [[Jubilee Party]] as a [[Whip (politics)
column5: whip]]. Susan held the position until the May 2020 when she was replaced by Senator [[Irungu Kang'ata]].<ref>{{Cite web
column12: language=en}}</ref> Prior to that, she served as the first female speaker of the [[Nakuru County]] Assembly<ref name=""1R"" /> and held the position of the Vice Chair of the County Assemblies Forum (CAF)[https://www.devex.com/organizations/county-assemblies-forum-caf-kenya-150821].<ref>{{Cite web
column14: title=Susan Kihika - Biography and Life Story » Famous Nakuru

column1: Kihika has been involved in community projects and charity work including supporting women groups across the county. She is a strong advocate for the rights and welfare of children, especially those living with disabilities. Kihika assumed office on 25 August 2022.
Alice, her mother, was her father's second wife.<ref name=""2R"">{{cite web
column4: title=I am much more than my father's daughter, says Nakuru County Assembly Speaker Susan Kihika
column10: location=Nairobi}}</ref> Susan attended Busara Forest View Academy in [[Nyahururu]] and [[Bishop Gatimu Ngandu Girls High School
column11: Bishop Gatimu Ngandu Girls’ High School]] in [[Nyeri]]. She then migrated to the [[United States]] around 1992, for further education.<ref name=""2R"" />

column1: She was admitted to the [[University of North Texas]], graduating with a Bachelor of Arts in [[Political Science]]. In 2006, she graduated with a [[Juris Doctor]] degree from the Law School of [[Southern Methodist University]], in [[Dallas]], Texas. Subsequently, she was admitted to the Texas Bar, after passing the requisite examinations.<ref name=""3R"">{{cite web
column11: title=Susan Kihika Biography, Education and Politics}}</ref>

column1: Following her graduation from law school, she worked in the public service.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Majority Whip {{!}} The Kenyan Parliament Website
column5: website=www.parliament.go.ke}}</ref> Later she left public service and established ''The Kihika Law Firm'' in [[Dallas]], Texas which specialized mostly in representing [https://famousnakuru.co.ke/susan-kihika-biography-life-story/ immigrants]. In 2012, after 20 years in the United States, Kihika  travelled back to [[Kenya]].<ref name=""1R""/><ref name=""2R""/><ref name=""3R""/>

column1: In 2013, she contested the [[Bahati Constituency]] parliamentary seat but lost to Kimani [https://famousnakuru.co.ke/susan-kihika-biography-life-story/ Ngunjiri]. She vied for the Nakuru County Speaker’s seat where she defeated 7 [https://susankihika.com/about-susan-kihika/ opponents] to emerge as the first Assembly Speaker of Nakuru County.<ref name=""2R""/><ref name=""3R""/>

In 2017, she contested the [[Nakuru County]] senatorial seat and won on a [[Jubilee Party]] ticket as the first female Senator of Nakuru County. Kihika’s vision is to see peaceful coexistence within Nakuru [https://womenaspirants-kenya.org/candidates/susan-kihika/ County] She has also been involved in supporting social issues, economic empowerment initiatives and addressing [https://womenaspirants-kenya.org/candidates/susan-kihika/ insecurity]
In  2018, Senator Susan Kihika was elected as the first Vice President of the Bureau of the Forum of Women Parliamentarians.<ref>{{Cite web
column11: language=en}}</ref> In October of the same year, Kihika took over first as the acting President and later as President replacing her predecessor Hon. [[Ulrika Karlsson (politician)

column1: On 9 August 2022, she stood to be the [[Nakuru County]] Governor and won on a [[United Democratic Alliance (Kenya)
column2: UDA]] ticket. Susan defeated [[Lee Kinyanjui]] who was on a [[Jubilee Party]] ticket and became the first woman Governor for Nakuru County. She is commonly referred to by her county people as the ""Woman of Firsts"".

column1: In July 2024, she faced sharp criticism for having to deliver from abroad. This was after her absence from county duties became public, after which it was confirmed she was on maternity leave. This was termed contrasting her philosophy of women empowerment and making healthcare for all women accessible and of high standard . She later claimed that it would have been inappropriate for her juniors to see her naked.<ref>{{Cite web

'''Susan Wakarura Kihika''' is a Kenyan lawyer, [[politician]], and the first female [[governor]] of [[Nakuru County]]. She was also among the seven female Governors that were elected in the 9 August [[2022 Kenyan general election]] against a total 40 male governors, marking significant progress from the three female governors that had been elected in the 2017 elections.<ref>{{Cite web
column4: title=History as Kenyans elect seven women governors

column1: She was elected as a [[Senate of Kenya
column5: title=History as Kenya set to have first elected women senators

column4: location=Nairobi}}</ref> on the [[Jubilee Party]] as a [[Whip (politics)
column5: whip]]. Susan held the position until the May 2020 when she was replaced by Senator [[Irungu Kang'ata]].<ref>{{Cite web
column12: language=en}}</ref> Prior to that, she served as the first female speaker of the [[Nakuru County]] Assembly<ref name=""1R"" /> and held the position of the Vice Chair of the County Assemblies Forum (CAF)[https://www.devex.com/organizations/county-assemblies-forum-caf-kenya-150821].<ref>{{Cite web
column14: title=Susan Kihika - Biography and Life Story » Famous Nakuru

column1: Kihika has been involved in community projects and charity work including supporting women groups across the county. She is a strong advocate for the rights and welfare of children, especially those living with disabilities. Kihika assumed office on 25 August 2022.
Alice, her mother, was her father's second wife.<ref name=""2R"">{{cite web
column4: title=I am much more than my father's daughter, says Nakuru County Assembly Speaker Susan Kihika
column10: location=Nairobi}}</ref> Susan attended Busara Forest View Academy in [[Nyahururu]] and [[Bishop Gatimu Ngandu Girls High School
column11: Bishop Gatimu Ngandu Girls’ High School]] in [[Nyeri]]. She then migrated to the [[United States]] around 1992, for further education.<ref name=""2R"" />

column1: She was admitted to the [[University of North Texas]], graduating with a Bachelor of Arts in [[Political Science]]. In 2006, she graduated with a [[Juris Doctor]] degree from the Law School of [[Southern Methodist University]], in [[Dallas]], Texas. Subsequently, she was admitted to the Texas Bar, after passing the requisite examinations.<ref name=""3R"">{{cite web
column11: title=Susan Kihika Biography, Education and Politics}}</ref>

column1: Following her graduation from law school, she worked in the public service.<ref>{{Cite web
column2: title=Majority Whip {{!}} The Kenyan Parliament Website
column5: website=www.parliament.go.ke}}</ref> Later she left public service and established ''The Kihika Law Firm'' in [[Dallas]], Texas which specialized mostly in representing [https://famousnakuru.co.ke/susan-kihika-biography-life-story/ immigrants]. In 2012, after 20 years in the United States, Kihika  travelled back to [[Kenya]].<ref name=""1R""/><ref name=""2R""/><ref name=""3R""/>

column1: In 2013, she contested the [[Bahati Constituency]] parliamentary seat but lost to Kimani [https://famousnakuru.co.ke/susan-kihika-biography-life-story/ Ngunjiri]. She vied for the Nakuru County Speaker’s seat where she defeated 7 [https://susankihika.com/about-susan-kihika/ opponents] to emerge as the first Assembly Speaker of Nakuru County.<ref name=""2R""/><ref name=""3R""/>

In 2017, she contested the [[Nakuru County]] senatorial seat and won on a [[Jubilee Party]] ticket as the first female Senator of Nakuru County. Kihika’s vision is to see peaceful coexistence within Nakuru [https://womenaspirants-kenya.org/candidates/susan-kihika/ County] She has also been involved in supporting social issues, economic empowerment initiatives and addressing [https://womenaspirants-kenya.org/candidates/susan-kihika/ insecurity]
In  2018, Senator Susan Kihika was elected as the first Vice President of the Bureau of the Forum of Women Parliamentarians.<ref>{{Cite web
column11: language=en}}</ref> In October of the same year, Kihika took over first as the acting President and later as President replacing her predecessor Hon. [[Ulrika Karlsson (politician)

column1: On 9 August 2022, she stood to be the [[Nakuru County]] Governor and won on a [[United Democratic Alliance (Kenya)
column2: UDA]] ticket. Susan defeated [[Lee Kinyanjui]] who was on a [[Jubilee Party]] ticket and became the first woman Governor for Nakuru County. She is commonly referred to by her county people as the ""Woman of Firsts"".

column1: In July 2024, she faced sharp criticism for having to deliver from abroad. This was after her absence from county duties became public, after which it was confirmed she was on maternity leave. This was termed contrasting her philosophy of women empowerment and making healthcare for all women accessible and of high standard . She later claimed that it would have been inappropriate for her juniors to see her naked.<ref>{{Cite web

column6: accessdate=29 October 2019}}</ref> She would later study in the [[United States]], [[Sweden]] and [[Italy]].<ref name=""parl""/>

column1: Ngungi started her education at Kamatungu Primary School from 1981 to 1989, where she obtained her [[Kenya Certificate of Primary Education
column2: KCPE]]. She joined Ikuu Girls Secondary School between 1990 and 1993, where she got a B-minus grade from her KCSE. <ref name="":0"" /><ref name="":1"" />

column1: She has a Diploma in [[Occupational therapy
column2: Occupational Therapy]] got from the [[Kenya Medical Training College]] between 1998 and 2001,  and a Diploma in Project Management from the Kenya Institute of Management (2008-2009). In 2009, she earned a Bachelor of Arts in Psychology and Sociology from [[Kenyatta University]] and a master's degree in Sociology from [[Egerton University]] in 2015.<ref name="":0"" /><ref name="":1"" /><ref name="":2"" />

column1: Ngungi is the Women Representative for [[Tharaka-Nithi County]] in [[Kenya]]. She was a Project Director at MCK Thiti Child Development Centre in 2009 - 2010 and then briefly as a Children Officer with the Committee of Experts on [[Constitutional review
column2: Constitutional Review]] in 2010. <ref name="":0"" /><ref name="":2"" /><ref name="":3"" />

column1: She served as the Children Officer under the Ministry of Gender, Children & Social Services from 2010 to 2014. She later joined the County Assembly of [[Tharaka-Nithi County
column2: Tharaka-Nithi]] as Deputy Sub-County Administrator until 2017. From 2017 to 2022, she was the [[Speaker (politics)

column1: '''Sicily Kanini Kariūki''' is a Kenyan politician who has been the Cabinet Secretary for [[Water supply and sanitation in Kenya
column2: Water, Sanitation and Irrigation]], since 20 January 2020.<ref>{{Cite web
column4: title = Kiunjuri fired as Uhuru reshuffles cabinet}}</ref> She was previously the Cabinet Secretary for Health.<ref name=""One"">{{cite web
column6: title=Six women make it to Cabinet list
column12: location=Kampala}}</ref> She was also previously the Cabinet Secretary for Public Service, Youth and Gender Affairs, from December 2015 until January 2018.<ref name=""Two"">{{cite web
column17: title=Cabinet Secretary for Public Service, Youth and Gender Affairs
column18: author=Kenya Ministry of Public Service, Youth and Gender Affairs

column1: Kariūki was born in Kiambu County, Kenya.<ref name=""Back"">{{cite web
column6: title=I'll not join politics, says Gender minister Sicily Kariuki

column1: Kariūki has a [[bachelor's degree]], from the [[University of Nairobi]]. Her [[Master of Business Administration]] (MBA) degree, was awarded by the [[Eastern and Southern African Management Institute]] (ESAMI) in conjunction with [[Maastricht School of Management]] in the [[Netherlands]]. She also has a [[Law
column2: Postgraduate Diploma in Law and Regulation]], from [[Michigan State University]] in the United States.<ref name=""Three"">{{cite web

column1: Kariūki enjoyed a wide-ranging career in the business world, including as an officer of the Kenya Investment Authority, and as [[chief executive officer]] of ''Fresh Produce Exporters Association of Kenya''.<ref name=""Three""/>

Kariūki then served as the [[Managing Director]] and [[CEO]] of ""Tea Board of Kenya"". In 2012, while at the helm of the tea board, the tea industry rose to become the top earner of foreign exchange in the country, accounting for KSh130 billion (approx. US$1.3 billion), in 2012. She also served as the Principal Secretary, in the Department of [[Agriculture]], in the Kenyan [[Ministry of Agriculture (Kenya)
column2: Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries]].<ref name=""Three""/>

column1: In December 2015, Kariūki was appointed as the Cabinet Secretary for Public Service, Youth and Gender Affairs.<ref>{{cite web
column3: title=Cabinet nominee on the spot for working before vetting
column8: location=Nairobi}}</ref> She served in that capacity until January 2018, when she was appointed Cabinet Secretary for Health.<ref name=""One""/>

column1: In her capacity as minister, Kariūki was appointed by WHO Director-General [[Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus]] to serve on the Independent High-level Commission on Non-Communicable Diseases from 2018 until 2019.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20180206011119/http://www.who.int/ncds/governance/high-level-commission/mission/commissioners/en/ WHO Independent High-level Commission on NCDs] [[World Health Organization]] (WHO).</ref>

column1: '''Alice Wambūi Ng'ang'a''' or '''Alice Wambūi''' is a [[Kenyan]] politician who was elected to be the Member of Parliament for the [[Thika Town Constituency]] in Kiambu County.

Wambūi started at St. Annes Lioki in 1989 and in 1992 she left, starting [[Africa Nazarene University]] in 2003. She graduated in 2006 with a degree in banking and finance.<ref name=parlilife>{{Cite web
column2: title=HON. NGANGA ALICE WAMBUI {{!}} The Kenyan Parliament Website

column1: She stood at the 2010 by-election as a [[Kenya National Congress]] candidate. The winner took 42,000 votes and she followed with nearly 25,000.<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=Has Kabogo met his match in MP Ng'ang'a?

column28: page=56}}</ref> This became her reference as the ""mother of the nation"",<ref name=""Kiluva-Ndunda2001"" /> becoming Mama Ngìna Kenyatta, independent Kenya's glamorous [[First Lady]] when Kenyatta became president in 1964. column2: title                     = Undersecretary at the [[United Nations]] Headquarters in [[New York City]] & Former Commissioner of the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission]] of Kenya

column1: '''Roselyn Kwamboka Akombe''' (born 1976) is a Kenyan former commissioner of the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission]] (IEBC) of Kenya.<ref name=""1R"">{{cite web

She became famous within the Kenyan media after appearing before the board that was interviewing potential appointees for the commission and said that she was ready to take her new position as a commissioner, although this would mean taking a pay cut of 70 percent from her previous job as an Under-Secretary at the [[United Nations]]. She argued that this was a sacrifice she was ready to make for her country. She became famous internationally after controversially resigning from her post as a commissioner on 18 October 2017 amidst a political crisis in Kenya.<ref name=""1R""/><ref name=""2R"">{{cite web
Shortly after her resignation, she flew out of the country citing fears for her life within the prevailing political climate.<ref name=""2R""/><ref name=""3R"">{{cite web
column4: title=Ex-IEBC official Roselyn Akombe returns to work at UN

column1: She was born in 1976, in present-day [[Nyamira County]], in what was then [[Nyanza Province]], [[Kenya]]. She grew up and attended local primary and secondary schools. She obtained her first degree, a [[Bachelor of Education]], from the [[University of Nairobi]]. Later, she obtained a [[Master of Science]] degree in [[International Affairs
column2: Global Affairs]], from [[Rutgers University]], in the [[United States]], followed by a [[Doctor of Philosophy]], in the same subject, also from Rutgers University.<ref name=""4R"">{{cite web
column7: work=Age, Family, Education, Net-worth, Personal Life

column1: Akombe was employed as a senior adviser to the Under-Secretary General for political affairs at the [[United Nations]] [[Secretariat (administrative office)

In January 2017, she was appointed as a commissioner at the IEBC, which intrigued the public when it became public knowledge that she would be taking a pay cut of 70 percent from her former job by working for the commission. She explained that this was a matter of patriotism to her country and that she had the desire to help the country run a free and fair election and wished to play a role in it.<ref name=""5R"">{{cite web
column9: location=Nairobi}}</ref> The media also reported that “She has been granted special leave without pay to serve in the Kenyan Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission,” and that  “she'll provide technical electoral support to the commission in preparation for the 2017 elections and support efforts to prevent post-electoral violence in Kenya.” By working with IEBC Akombe would not receive any salary as an employee of the UN. Akombe's basic salary as a commissioner of IEBC is estimated at KES 800,000 (about US$8000) per month.<ref name=""6R"">{{cite web

column1: Following her employment at IEBC, Roselyn instantly became the face of the commission, and was present in many press briefings given to the public. In fact, she was responsible for discharging many of these press conferences, in which she was noted as an eloquent and smooth talker.<ref name=""5R""/> This made many people think that she was the deputy chair-person of the commission, although she was just a commissioner. According to the Kenya [[Daily Nation]], Akombe is a ""a youthful, straight-talking and dreadlocked commissioner with high cheekbones who explained things with a ready smile."" Her roles in the commission included training field officers, addressing press conferences, reporting to the chairman and CEO of the commission and taking other roles to ensure the credibility and fairness in Kenyan elections.<ref name=""1R""/>
On 18 October 2017, Akombe resigned from her position as a commissioner of the IEBC during a time when the country was in a crisis following the [[Supreme Court of Kenya
column2: Supreme Court]] nullification of the 2017 Kenyan Election Her decision almost plunged the largest East African Economy to constitutional crisis. On 1 September 2017, the Supreme Court of Kenya passed judgement that declared the 8 August 2017 Presidential Elections results null and void. The court ruled that the IEBC had failed to meet the requirements set within the constitution for a free and fair elections and ordered a repeat of the elections within 60 days.<ref name=""7R"">{{cite web
column4: title=Kenya Supreme Court nullifies presidential election
column6: newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] Quting [[The New York Times]]

column1: As a consequence, IEBC set to conduct fresh elections and announced a new election date as 17 October 2017, and later pushed it to 26 October 2017. However, the opposition party [[National Super Alliance]] (NASA), under the leadership of [[Raila Amolo Odinga]] piled pressure on the commission, saying that it could not possibly conduct an election as currently constituted. This view was supported by all politicians affiliated with the NASA candidate, Raila Amolo Odinga, including his running-mate Kalonzo Musyoka. In fact, it led to the boycott by all members of parliament and senate from house sittings with the argument that they did not recognize President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] as a legally elected president. However, that view was strongly opposed by Uhuru Kenyatta and all politicians affiliated with his [[Jubilee Party]], arguing that Raila had not right to guide IEBC on its operations. The difference between these two protagonists led to what some have termed as a political crisis in Kenya.<ref name=""8R"">{{cite web
column4: title=Kenya poll body's credibility in question

column1: Attempting to maintain a neutral ground, IEBC tried to hold meetings between the opposition and the government to no avail.<ref name=""9R"">{{cite web
column2: title=IEBC Meeting With NASA, Jubilee Failed

column1: In the days following the court ruling, Raila and his NASA party consistently issued ultimatums, which it termed as its irreducible minimums without which a free, fair and credible elections could not take place in Kenya. As IEBC came out to say that it could not meet these minimums, Raila Odinga stunned the country and the international community by saying that he had withdrawn from the repeat presidential race because the commission was incapable of giving Kenyan's a free, fair and credible election. This led to a political crisis in Kenya as Raila and his party agitated for a cancellation of the repeat elections on 26 October 2017, while Uhuru and his party pushed for the repeat election. In the wake of all this political turmoil, it became apparent that the commission was infiltrated by moles and operators from Jubilee party and NASA party and that it had been compromised. Among the suspected mole scheming with politicians was Roselyn Akombe<ref name=""8R""/>
On 18 October 2017, Akombe confirmed these rumors when she resigned in her resignation letter that was published online.<ref name=""9R2"">{{cite web
column2: title=IEBC Commissioner Roselyn Akombe's full statement on why she resigned

column1: ====Impacts on the repeat of Kenyan 2017 presidential elections====

The Commissioner's resignation caused a media sensation. The fresh elections proceeded despite the fact that Raila Odinga, one of the key candidates, had withdrawn from the polls and had urged his supporters not to participate in voting. Uhuru Kenyatta was declared President and sworn in.<ref name=""10R"">{{cite web
column3: title=Uhuru Kenyatta wins repeat election with 7.4 million votes

In January 2017, she was appointed as a commissioner at the IEBC, which intrigued the public when it became public knowledge that she would be taking a pay cut of 70 percent from her former job by working for the commission. She explained that this was a matter of patriotism to her country and that she had the desire to help the country run a free and fair election and wished to play a role in it.<ref name=""5R"">{{cite web
column63: location=Nairobi}}</ref> The media also reported that “She has been granted special leave without pay to serve in the Kenyan Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission,” and that  “she\'ll provide technical electoral support to the commission in preparation for the 2017 elections and support efforts to prevent post-electoral violence in Kenya.” By working with IEBC Akombe would not receive any salary as an employee of the UN. Akombe\'s basic salary as a commissioner of IEBC is estimated at KES 800,000 (about US$8000) per month.<ref name=""6R"">{{cite web
column70:
location=Nairobi}}</ref>

Following her employment at IEBC, Roselyn instantly became the face of the commission, and was present in many press briefings given to the public. In fact, she was responsible for discharging many of these press conferences, in which she was noted as an eloquent and smooth talker.<ref name=""5R""/> This made many people think that she was the deputy chair-person of the commission, although she was just a commissioner. According to the Kenya [[Daily Nation]], Akombe is a ""a youthful, straight-talking and dreadlocked commissioner with high cheekbones who explained things with a ready smile."" Her roles in the commission included training field officers, addressing press conferences, reporting to the chairman and CEO of the commission and taking other roles to ensure the credibility and fairness in Kenyan elections.<ref name=""1R""/>

'), Section(title='====Resignation controversy ====', content='
On 18 October 2017, Akombe resigned from her position as a commissioner of the IEBC during a time when the country was in a crisis following the [[Supreme Court of Kenya
column71: Supreme Court]] nullification of the 2017 Kenyan Election Her decision almost plunged the largest East African Economy to constitutional crisis. On 1 September 2017, the Supreme Court of Kenya passed judgement that declared the 8 August 2017 Presidential Elections results null and void. The court ruled that the IEBC had failed to meet the requirements set within the constitution for a free and fair elections and ordered a repeat of the elections within 60 days.<ref name=""7R"">{{cite web
column73: title=Kenya Supreme Court nullifies presidential election
column75: newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] Quting [[The New York Times]]
column77: author=Kimiko de Freytas-Tamura}}</ref>\n \nAs a consequence, IEBC set to conduct fresh elections and announced a new election date as 17 October 2017, and later pushed it to 26 October 2017. However, the opposition party [[National Super Alliance]] (NASA), under the leadership of [[Raila Amolo Odinga]] piled pressure on the commission, saying that it could not possibly conduct an election as currently constituted. This view was supported by all politicians affiliated with the NASA candidate, Raila Amolo Odinga, including his running-mate Kalonzo Musyoka. In fact, it led to the boycott by all members of parliament and senate from house sittings with the argument that they did not recognize President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] as a legally elected president. However, that view was strongly opposed by Uhuru Kenyatta and all politicians affiliated with his [[Jubilee Party]], arguing that Raila had not right to guide IEBC on its operations. The difference between these two protagonists led to what some have termed as a political crisis in Kenya.<ref name=""8R"">{{cite web
column80: title=Kenya poll body\'s credibility in question
column85: location=Nairobi}}</ref>\n\nAttempting to maintain a neutral ground, IEBC tried to hold meetings between the opposition and the government to no avail.<ref name=""9R"">{{cite web
column86: title=IEBC Meeting With NASA, Jubilee Failed
column93:
location=Nairobi}}</ref> 
In the days following the court ruling, Raila and his NASA party consistently issued ultimatums, which it termed as its irreducible minimums without which a free, fair and credible elections could not take place in Kenya. As IEBC came out to say that it could not meet these minimums, Raila Odinga stunned the country and the international community by saying that he had withdrawn from the repeat presidential race because the commission was incapable of giving Kenyan's a free, fair and credible election. This led to a political crisis in Kenya as Raila and his party agitated for a cancellation of the repeat elections on 26 October 2017, while Uhuru and his party pushed for the repeat election. In the wake of all this political turmoil, it became apparent that the commission was infiltrated by moles and operators from Jubilee party and NASA party and that it had been compromised. Among the suspected mole scheming with politicians was Roselyn Akombe<ref name=""8R""/>

On 18 October 2017, Akombe confirmed these rumors when she resigned in her resignation letter that was published online.<ref name=""9R2"">{{cite web
column94: title=IEBC Commissioner Roselyn Akombe\'s full statement on why she resigned
column100:
location=Nairobi}}</ref>

'), Section(title='====Impacts on the repeat of Kenyan 2017 presidential elections====', content='
The Commissioner's resignation caused a media sensation. The fresh elections proceeded despite the fact that Raila Odinga, one of the key candidates, had withdrawn from the polls and had urged his supporters not to participate in voting. Uhuru Kenyatta was declared President and sworn in.<ref name=""10R"">{{cite web
column102: title=Uhuru Kenyatta wins repeat election with 7.4 million votes
column107:

column1: '''Lorna Chepkemoi Laboso''' (8 November 1961 – 10 June 2008) was a Kenyan Politician born in Kericho District. She was briefly a [[Member of Parliament]] and an Assistant Minister in the Ministry of Home Affairs in the Vice President's Office in 2008.<ref name=Nation>Dominic Wabala and Fred Mukinda, [http://www.nationmedia.com/dailynation/nmgcontententry.asp?category_id=1&newsid=125082 ""Kones killed in crash""] {{webarchive

Laboso received an Undergraduate Bachelor of Arts Degree In Mass Communication from [[Daystar University]] in 2007. She was elected to the [[National Assembly of Kenya]] for the first time in the [[2007 Kenyan parliamentary election
column2: December 2007 parliamentary election]]<ref>[http://kenyalondonnews.co.uk/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=1829&Itemid=1 ""Kenya Mourns its legislators: Kipkalya Kones and Lorna Laboso die in a Plane Crash.""], ''Kenya London News''.</ref> as the MP of [[Sotik Constituency]]. In the grand coalition Cabinet formed in April 2008, she was appointed as Assistant Minister in the Office of the Vice President.<ref name=Nation/>

column1: She was killed along with Minister of Roads [[Kipkalya Kones]] in a plane crash on June 10, 2008.<ref name=Two>[http://www.int.iol.co.za/index.php?set_id=1&click_id=68&art_id=nw20080610182455856C880094 ""Two Kenyan government ministers die""], Sapa-AFP (''IOL''), June 10, 2008.</ref><ref name=BBC>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/7446832.stm ""Ministers killed in Kenya crash""], [[BBC News]], 10 June 2008.</ref> The plane crashed into a building in Kajong'a market near Nairagie Enkare in [[Enoosupukia]], [[Narok District]],<ref name=Nation/> near [[Narok]]<ref name=Two/><ref name=BBC/> and the [[Masai Mara
column2: Masai Mara game reserve]].<ref name=BBC/> The plane carrying Laboso and Kones, a [[Cessna]] light aircraft, had taken off from [[Wilson Airport (Kenya)
column3: Wilson Airport]] in [[Nairobi]];<ref name=Nation/><ref name=Two/><ref name=BBC/> they had been flying to [[Kericho]] in the Rift Valley to help with the organization of logistics for ODM candidate [[Benjamin Langat]] in the by-election that was scheduled to be held in [[Ainamoi Constituency]] on June 11.<ref name=Nation/> In addition to Kones and Laboso, the pilot and a security guard were killed.<ref name=Nation/><ref name=BBC/>

column1: President [[Mwai Kibaki]] sent his condolences and ordered flags to fly at half mast, saying that Kenya had ""lost leaders of immense potential at their prime age and with a promising future."" Prime Minister [[Raila Odinga]], the ODM leader, said that it was a ""sad moment""; believing that it was too late to delay the planned by-elections, he urged ODM supporters to use the by-elections as a tribute to Laboso and Kones by turning out to vote for the ODM's candidates.<ref name=Nation/>

The ""List of alleged perpetrators"" of the 2007/2008 post-electoral violence of the Kenya National Human Rights Commission however lists her among the suspects on place 1 (page 177) and charges her with ""planning and incitement to violence"".<ref>{{Cite web
column3: title=On the Brink of the Precipice: A Human Rights Account of Kenya's Post 2007 Election Violence – FINAL REPORT
column7: publisher=Kenya National Commission on Human Rights

column1: Following the death of Laboso, a by-election was held in the Sotik Constituency on 25 September 2008. The seat was won by Laboso's sister, [[Joyce Cherono Laboso
column2: Joyce Cherono]] for the ODM.<ref>The Standard, September 26, 2008: {{usurped
column3: 1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20091210000128/http://www.eastandard.net/InsidePage.php?id=1143995671&cid=4& ODM wins in Bomet and Sotik]}}</ref>

column1: '''Farida Karoney''' is a Kenyan who was nominated by President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] as Cabinet Secretary for Lands, on 26 January 2018.<ref name=""One"">{{cite web
column4: title=New Cabinet: President Kenyatta's statement in full

column1: author=Presidential Strategic Communications (PSCU)}}</ref> Immediately prior to her present position, she served as the [[chief operating officer]] (COO) of the ''Royal Media Services'' (RMS), a media conglomerate that includes radio and television stations. Before that, she served as the Group Editorial Director at RMS.<ref name=""Two"">{{cite web
column4: title=Uhuru picks Citizen TV's boss for cabinet position

column1: Farida Karoney attended [[Kenyatta University]], from 1989 until 1992, graduating with a [[Bachelor of Education
column2: Bachelor of Science Education]] degree in [[Botany]] and [[Zoology]]. She then went on to the [[University of Nairobi]] (UoN), where she obtained a [[Mass communication
column3: Postgraduate Diploma in Mass Communication]], in 1996, after one year of study.<ref name=""Bio"">{{cite web
column7: title=Farida Karoney: Chief Operating Officer at Royal Media Services

column3: first=Farida}}</ref> She enrolled in the MBA degree course at UoN in 2005, graduating in 2008 with a [[Master of Business Administration]], specializing in [[Strategy]]. Later, she obtained a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree, also from UoN, specializing in [[strategic management]].<ref name=""Bio""/>

column1: For a period of less than one year, in 1993, Farida taught biology at ''Khamis High School'' in [[Mombasa]]. In June 1994, she joined [[Kenya Television Network]] (KTN), first as a freelance correspondent, then as a reporter, rising to the position of Features Editor, at the time she left KTN in December 2000.<ref name=""Bio""/>

In January 2001, she joined the [[Nation Media Group]] (NMG), as an editor and rose to the rank of Associate Editor by July 2004, when she left NMG. She then worked as the Managing Editor at [[The Standard (Kenya)
column2: The Standard Group]], for a period of two years, from September 2004 until August 2006.<ref name=""Bio""/>

column1: From there, Farida worked as a freelance contributor to
[[Radio France Internationale]], working in that capacity for about one year, between 2006 and 2007. For the last six months of that period, she also freelanced for the [[Al Jazeera English
column2: Al Jazeera]] [[English language]] network, as a producer.<ref name=""Bio""/>

column1: In 2007  she went back to Standard Media Group and worked as the Head of Editorial at their flagship TV station, KTN, for about one year. During that period, she concurrently served as the assistant director for broadcasting at Standard Group Limited, until December 2008. For five consecutive years, beginning in February 2009, Farida Karoney served as the Group Editorial Director at Royal Media Services, until 2014. In August 2014, she was promoted to the position of chief operating officer, at RMS, a position she occupied at the time of her nomination to become the Cabinet Secretary for Lands.<ref name=""Bio""/><ref>{{cite web
column3: title=Six women make it to Cabinet list
